NexTech Solutions buys BOOMSLANG in latest counter-UAS expansion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
07:30:33 UTC
16:30:33 KST

- NexTech Solutions acquired BOOMSLANG Aerospace on August 7, adding the MONGOOSE counter-UAS system to its product lineup.
- The deal is NexTech's fifth acquisition since a 2023 strategic investment from private equity firm Clairvest.
NexTech Solutions has acquired BOOMSLANG Aerospace, a developer of unmanned aerial systems and counter-drone technology, the Huntsville, Alabama-based defense contractor announced August 24. The deal closed August 7.
The acquisition is the fifth NexTech Solutions has completed since 2023, when the company took a strategic investment from Clairvest, a Toronto-based private equity firm, to serve as a platform for growth in the defense technology sector.
BOOMSLANG brings a counter-UAS system called MONGOOSE, along with its broader family of unmanned aerial systems, into NexTech’s product lineup. The company’s engineering team has worked on UAS design and counter-UAS systems, according to NexTech.
NexTech said BOOMSLANG’s technology will be folded into its existing counter-UAS architecture, which already includes products such as MANTLE, VidTerra COMPASS and JEFF-K. The company described the combination as extending its coverage across detection, defeat and airborne mission sets, though it did not specify contract values, customer names or delivery timelines tied to the acquisition.
“BOOMSLANG Aerospace has built exactly the kind of technology our customers are asking for: cutting-edge, mission-ready, and purpose-built for the current threat environment at the edge,” said Joseph Paull, CEO of NexTech Solutions. “We are excited to integrate the MONGOOSE C-UAS system and BOOMSLANG UAS family of systems into our networked ecosystem of products.”
“Together, we can move faster from concept to fielded capability for the customers who need it most,” said Alan Cornett, president and co-founder of BOOMSLANG Aerospace.
“BOOMSLANG’s approach to unmanned aerial systems and their C-UAS technology aligns perfectly with the modular, requirements-driven C-UAS strategy we are building at NTS,” said David Pollman, director of counter-UAS operations at NexTech. Pollman previously served as deputy division chief of operations at the Department of War’s Joint Counter-UAS Office, where he worked on evaluating the department’s counter-UAS strategy before joining NexTech in 2024.
NexTech has operated for more than 13 years, providing systems engineering, testing and evaluation, and operational support to the Department of War and other U.S. government customers. The company has offices in Huntsville, Tampa and Northern Virginia.
Counter-UAS systems are designed to detect and, in some cases, disable or destroy small drones. Demand for such systems among U.S. military and government buyers has grown as adversaries and non-state actors have made increasing use of low-cost drones for surveillance and attacks.
NexTech has pursued a series of acquisitions and partnerships since the Clairvest investment. The company announced a counter-UAS partnership with Xtend and a separate collaboration with Monkton on secure mobility technology, and it has continued developing its MANTLE platform, including a mobile version for Android devices.

Nevada sues Trump administration over reduction in Colorado River water use
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
07:28:17 UTC
16:28:17 KST

Berk Kutay Gokmen
25 August 2026•Update: 25 August 2026
The US state of Nevada has sued the administration of President Donald Trump over a federal plan requiring the state and two others to reduce Colorado River water use, marking the first legal challenge to Washington’s effort to prevent the river from reaching a critical point.
In its federal court filing on Monday, Nevada said the Interior Department’s drought management plan could cause “devastating environmental, socioeconomic, and health and human safety impacts to southern Nevada and its citizens.”
The plan was created after the seven Colorado River states failed to agree on how to respond to worsening shortages, according to The Washington Post.
The dispute centers on a river that supplies about 40 million people in the southwestern United States and Mexico. Nevada officials said the proposed reductions could cut as much as 71% of the state’s annual allocation. The river provides roughly 90% of the water used by Las Vegas and surrounding communities.
“This isn’t about political posturing,” Nevada Governor Joe Lombardo said. “This is a matter of survival for a community that represents about two-thirds of our state’s citizens and the lion’s share of its economy.”
Years of overuse and a severe drought worsened by climate change have pushed the river into crisis. Federal data show this year’s flow is about 37% of average, while Lakes Powell and Mead have reached record-low levels.
The federal plan requires the US states of Arizona, California, and Nevada to reduce use by about 20% over the next two years. It also allows for deeper cuts later if shortages persist, while imposing no mandatory reductions on the Upper Basin states.
Nevada’s lawsuit argues the plan violates rules governing the river and fails to adequately account for the economic consequences of reducing urban water supplies.

MANILA, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- The Philippine Department of Health (DOH) on Monday reported a 29-percent spike in leptospirosis cases from July 26 to Aug. 8, with 495 cases recorded across the nation during that period.
Total cases from January to Aug. 22 reached 4,285 nationwide, down 37 percent year-on-year, but health officials warned of further increases due to the disease's incubation period of 5 to 15 days.
The National Capital Region, Cagayan Valley, and Central Luzon registered the highest number of cases. The government urged those exposed to floodwater to seek medical consultation within 24 to 48 hours, even without symptoms, according to the DOH. ■

Japan civic group holds exhibition on Japanese army's wartime poison gas use
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
15:26:20 CST
16:26:20 KST

TOKYO, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- An exhibition on the Japanese military's production and use of poison gas during World War II (WWII) is being held from Aug. 23 to 28 in Yokohama City, Kanagawa Prefecture, Japan.
Organized by a Japanese civic group, the "Japanese Military Poison Gas Exhibition" aims to expose the atrocities committed by the Japanese military, specifically the wartime production of poison gas and the waging of gas warfare during its war of aggression against China, and to reveal the crimes against humanity perpetrated by Japanese militarism.
According to materials presented at the exhibition, Japan produced poison gas on Okunoshima Island in Hiroshima Prefecture, manufactured poison-gas shells in Kitakyushu City in Fukuoka Prefecture, and trained personnel for chemical warfare in Narashino City in Chiba Prefecture, among other locations during WWII. The Japanese military also conducted chemical warfare operations in various parts of China.
After Japan's defeat, some chemical weapons were left behind in China, continuing to cause harm to local people. The Japanese government, however, has neither issued a formal apology nor provided compensation.
The exhibition uses photographs and written materials to document the history, while Japanese civilian researchers, photojournalists and others involved in researching the subject have been invited to speak at the venue.
Japanese photojournalist Kenji Higuchi has investigated issues related to poison gas warfare on Okunoshima Island since 1970, documenting victims of poison gas as well as the remains of facilities where chemical weapons were produced through his lens.
Speaking at the event, Higuchi recounted his experiences reporting on the subject and called on the Japanese government to face history squarely.
"Conducting chemical warfare was an atrocity committed by the Japanese military in its war of aggression against China, yet the Japanese government seeks to erase this part of history," Higuchi told Xinhua. "They committed such evil acts, and it is a disgrace for the country. That is why they want to erase it from history."
Masao, a visitor from Yokosuka, said Higuchi's account at the exhibition made him realize that this part of history had remained largely unknown for a long time.
"I never learned about this history at school. They don't teach this at school. It was really shocking to see these materials for the first time," another Japanese visitor told Xinhua.
Higuchi stressed the importance of preserving and conveying the historical record. "This history must be made clear. What was wrong was wrong, and what was right was right. We must become people capable of distinguishing right from wrong," he said. ■

Nevada launches first legal challenge to new U.S. Colorado River plan
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
15:26:09 CST
16:26:09 KST

LOS ANGELES, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- The U.S. state of Nevada filed a federal lawsuit on Monday challenging the federal government's newly adopted Colorado River management plan, marking the first legal challenge to rules issued three days earlier for sharing reduced water supplies among western U.S. states.
The lawsuit was filed by the state, the Colorado River Commission of Nevada and the Southern Nevada Water Authority. It asks the District Court for the District of Nevada to set aside the Interior Department's decision and block its implementation until alleged legal and technical problems are addressed, according to the Nevada governor's office.
The Interior Department said the rules would reduce combined annual water deliveries to the three Lower Basin states -- Arizona, California and Nevada -- by about 1.54 billion cubic meters in each of 2027 and 2028. Under the federal framework, the four Upper Basin states -- Colorado, New Mexico, Utah and Wyoming -- would face voluntary rather than mandatory conservation measures.
The two-year operating rules are scheduled to take effect on Oct. 1, while the accompanying record of decision establishes a framework through 2036, according to federal decision documents.
Nevada's objections center on that longer-term framework, which authorizes larger reductions in dry years, according to the complaint. Nevada Governor Joe Lombardo said the plan could reduce southern Nevada's Colorado River allocation by more than 70 percent.
"This isn't about political posturing; this is a matter of survival for a community that represents about two-thirds of our state's citizens and the lion's share of its economy," Lombardo said in a statement on Monday.
The complaint places the deepest reductions from 2029 under severe-shortage conditions. Nevada would give up about 62 million cubic meters annually in 2027 and 2028 under a sharing arrangement proposed by the Lower Basin states, according to the Interior Department.
That reduction would amount to roughly 17 percent of Nevada's annual allocation of about 370 million cubic meters.
The lawsuit alleges that the federal decision violates the Administrative Procedure Act, the National Environmental Policy Act and the system of compacts, federal statutes, court decisions and regulations governing the river, known as the "Law of the River."
It also alleges that federal officials failed to adequately assess potential effects of deeper cuts on southern Nevada's economy, public health and water infrastructure, and did not sufficiently consider an alternative proposed by the Lower Basin states.
The complaint names Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and Bureau of Reclamation Commissioner Aubrey Bettencourt, along with their agencies, as defendants.
The Interior Department said the rules are intended to keep reservoir operations reliable and protect federal infrastructure while allowing for adjustments as drought conditions evolve and negotiations among the seven basin states continue.
The seven basin states have yet to reach an agreement on longer-term rules for sharing reduced supplies, according to the department's decision documents.
The latest available Bureau of Reclamation data showed that Lake Mead and Lake Powell, the Colorado River's two largest reservoirs, remained at record-low levels. ■

Feature: A menu simmered for a 26-year reunion feast on Chinese sand
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
15:26:04 CST
16:26:04 KST

HOHHOT, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- Twenty-six years had passed before Yin Yuzhen, a national-honored sand-control villager in China's Inner Mongolia, finally sat down to have a reunion feast with her American friend Ronald Sakolsky.
More than half a month before the reunion, she had already begun preparing a feast for Sakolsky, a retired teacher, making sure he could savor the homely, authentic flavors.
The night before their reunion, Yin still gathered around the table with her family, going over who would steam the cakes and how every dish should look and taste.
"Everything must be done properly. Each dish should look beautiful and taste delicious," she told them. "No chicken essence. Just the real flavor."
At noon on Monday, laughter filled Yin's home. Around the table sat Yin, her family and Sakolsky, sharing a long-awaited reunion meal after 26 years apart.
For each dish, Yin had chosen an auspicious meaning: boiled mutton, a symbol of desert generosity; braised fish for abundance year after year; stir-fried green beans for smooth sailing. One by one, she introduced them to her old friend.
The menu had been revised again and again prior to the reunion meal.
While waiting for her friend's visit, she slipped out to her vegetable garden whenever she had a spare moment, imagining stir-frying a plate of long beans for Sakolsky, or thinking how good steamed pumpkin would taste to her old friend.
When the desert roses had bloomed, Yin turned them into the filling of mooncakes. Her family made more than 5 kg of mooncakes to welcome Sakolsky as the Mid-Autumn Festival is approaching.
"I put roses in the filling so he can taste the sweetness of the desert," she said. "Mooncakes mean reunion. I want him to try a traditional Chinese food and take some back to his family in the United States."
By the time the menu list reached more than a dozen, she still felt it was not enough. "I wanted to bring out the very best of the desert to welcome him," she said.
For Yin, the menu was more than a list of dishes. It carried the taste of home, the warmth of an old friendship, and the landscape's quiet transformation. The once-barren desert has become a place of green and abundance.
The story behind the feast began in 1999, when Sakolsky taught English at a school in central China's Henan Province under a teachers' exchange program between the two countries.
By then, Yin had spent more than a decade battling desertification that had severely threatened her livelihood, even half burying her house during sandstorms. "I'd rather wear myself out planting trees than let sand defeat me," she vowed.
After watching a television news report about Yin's tireless work planting trees in the Maowusu Sandy Land, the fourth-largest sandy area in China, Sakolsky was deeply moved and raised 5,000 U.S. dollars to help Yin and her husband with their afforestation efforts.
At the time, the donation was a staggering amount that was enough for Yin to build a house, cover her children's upbringing costs, and even completely change the trajectory of her family's life.
The saplings bought and planted with that donation have since grown into a forest of more than 50,000 towering trees.
When they first met in 2000, Yin's family had little to offer. All she could prepare was a bowl of plain noodles. In those years, the sandy land yielded so little that a bowl of noodles was among the finest meals a family could offer. The sand storms were so strong that one could find a layer of sand settle at the bottom of the bowl by the time the noodles were finished.
Learning that Sakolsky remembered the taste all these years, Yin ground fresh-harvested wheat into flour and made him another bowl of noodles for the reunion feast. This time, she displayed some special culinary skills.
"I stretched a single strand of dough to fill an entire bowl. This is our 'long-lasting noodle,'" Yin said. In Chinese tradition, extra-long noodles symbolize enduring friendship.
"The noodles are the best," said Sakolsky. "This is all from the desert. She helped Mother Earth, and Mother Earth said thank you. That's very simple, and that's something else China taught me."
Indeed, over more than four decades, Yin and her family transformed some 70,000 mu (around 4,667 hectares) of barren sand into green land, turning desert into fields, vegetable plots, and orchards.
Before the reunion meal, Yin led Sakolsky through her yard, where colorful corn, red-skinned potatoes and plump pumpkins were laid out like a small harvest exhibition.
"Look at all these vegetables and fruits," she said. "This land once could not even grow a blade of grass."
Yin's story is part of a much larger picture. Over the decades, China has set up special funds, offered preferential tax policies, and mobilized farmers and locals in afforestation campaigns.
Today, beyond dedicated local farmers like Yin, China's afforestation campaign also attracts large numbers of environment-conscious volunteers, especially young urban dwellers and international students.
Official figures show that China has contributed about one-quarter of the world's increase in green vegetation and rehabilitated 152 million mu of desertified land between 2021 and 2025.
"Our results in sand control are not only visible but can be tasted," Yin said. "If you protect the earth, the earth will reward you." ■

Justice minister says Taiwan follows UN anti-corruption pact despite nonmembership
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
07:23:12 UTC
16:23:12 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan follows the UN’s anti-corruption convention and uses international reviews to improve its policies, Justice Minister Cheng Ming-chien (鄭銘謙) said Tuesday.
Speaking at a review meeting for the Republic of China’s third national report under the convention, Cheng said the UN Convention against Corruption is a major international framework for preventing and fighting corruption. It covers preventive measures, criminalization and law enforcement, international cooperation, and asset recovery, CNA reported.
Taiwan voluntarily follows the convention and underwent international reviews in 2018 and 2022, Cheng said. He said the reviews help the government assess whether its policies are effective, identify weaknesses, and set priorities for reform.
For the first time, Taiwan’s third national report uses the same self-assessment checklist used by countries that have joined the convention. Government agencies reviewed how Taiwan has implemented each part of the convention.
Cheng said anti-corruption systems must keep pace with technological change. He said international reviews can help Taiwan respond to emerging risks and improve its laws and policies.
Minister without Portfolio Lin Ming-hsin (林明昕) said geopolitical risks, rapid advances in AI and digital technology, cross-border crime, and illegal financial flows are making anti-corruption work more complex. He said clean government, transparency, and the rule of law are important for public trust and national competitiveness, per UDN.
The government released its third national report in April. The report reviews Taiwan’s recent implementation of the convention and its response to recommendations from the second international review.
It highlights progress in 10 areas, including transparency, risk management, government procurement, whistleblower protection, corporate governance, money laundering prevention, and international cooperation. It also covers open data, law enforcement, and cooperation between the public and private sectors.
Lin said Taiwan scored 68 points in Transparency International’s 2025 Corruption Perceptions Index, ranking 24th among 182 countries and territories. He said international scrutiny can help demonstrate Taiwan’s anti-corruption progress abroad.
Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) said corruption is no longer only a domestic issue because money and criminal activity increasingly cross national borders. He said transparency, accountability, and clean government are important foundations of democracy and good governance.
Taiwan began implementing the UN Convention against Corruption domestically in 2015. Its third national report covers anti-corruption laws, preventive measures, asset recovery, criminalization and law enforcement, and international cooperation.
The international review will last four days and includes discussions among international experts, government agencies, and nongovernmental organizations. The review committee is scheduled to present its final recommendations Friday.

New details but no answers a year after an Israeli strike on a Gaza hospital killed journalists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
07:23:01 UTC
16:23:01 KST

New details but no answers a year after an Israeli strike on a Gaza hospital killed journalists
TEL AVIV, Israel (AP) — It’s been a year since Israeli soldiers killed 22 Palestinians, including journalists and rescue workers, in a double strike on a hospital in Gaza. No one has been held accountable.
Israeli officials said the target was a suspected Hamas camera on the roof of Nasser Hospital. Among those killed were Reuters cameraman Hussam al-Masri and Mariam Dagga, a visual journalist who worked for The Associated Press and other news organizations.
Despite repeated requests by AP, the army has not provided details about the investigation or a timeline for when it could be completed. Rights groups say Israel rarely holds troops accountable for killing Palestinians, pointing to long investigations that rarely lead to prosecution.
As global outrage over the Aug. 25, 2025, strike grew, the Israeli military said that in addition to taking out the camera, six of those killed were linked to Hamas, without providing evidence.
But an Israeli soldier, speaking on condition of anonymity for fear of retribution, now says the military could find no evidence linking the camera, which belonged to al-Masri, to Hamas. The soldier, who was privy to discussions surrounding the military’s response, said none of the six was the intended target of the strike.
AP sent detailed questions to the military about the allegations, as well as other questions about the strikes. The military didn’t address the questions but said via text that the incident is being examined and findings will be transferred to the Military Advocate General’s Corps to reach a verdict on whether to open a criminal investigation. It didn’t provide a timeline.
AP reported at the time that one of the six Israel said was linked to Hamas was not on the hospital’s list of casualties and two others were medical or emergency personnel. That, along with the soldier’s account, raises serious questions about Israel’s rationale for the strike.
Why did troops fail to identify the cameraman as al-Masri, even though journalists were known to film at the hospital? Why did they strike a second time, causing most of the deaths and raising accusations of a “double tap” attack on first responders, which would be a war crime?
“A year later, we remain devastated by their deaths and are still searching for answers from the Israeli authorities about what happened that day,” AP Executive Editor Julie Pace said.
“The information we have received to date has fallen short of the clear answers and accountability that an incident of this gravity requires.”
Nasser Hospital was a vital location for journalists
News agencies like Reuters and AP supplied live video footage to newsrooms around the world from the hospital, one of the few functioning in Gaza at the time. AP repeatedly informed the army that its journalists were stationed there.
The first strike killed al-Masri and another person. As other journalists, including Dagga, and rescue workers rushed up an external staircase to help the wounded and document what happened, the military struck again, killing 20 people. Based on footage and multiple eyewitnesses, none was armed. In all, Israel struck the hospital four times using high-explosive tank shells.
Israeli officials afterward said Hamas was using the camera to observe nearby troops. They alleged “suspicious behavior” around the camera, but the only example they gave was that a towel draped over the camera and the person filming appeared to be an effort at concealment.
The Reuters journalist, al-Masri, routinely covered equipment with a white cloth to protect it from the sun and dust, a common practice among videojournalists in Gaza and other hot climates.
Last week, the army announced criminal investigations into two other high-profile attacks by its troops in Gaza — the 2024 killing of 5-year-old Hind Rajab and her family, and the 2025 killing of 15 paramedics. It cleared troops in three other attacks that killed workers from international aid groups.
Soldier details an attempt at damage control
The soldier was connected to AP through Breaking the Silence, a group founded over two decades ago by Israeli veterans that collects testimony from soldiers and is critical of Israel’s actions in the Palestinian territories.
The soldier said that after high-profile strikes that kill civilians without clear military purpose, army officials retroactively search for militant links among those killed.
Breaking the Silence said its testimonies show there is a “retroactive incrimination process” in which Palestinians who are killed are automatically counted as militants, even when unarmed.
Retroactive incrimination is used as a “near automatic justification for every bullet, shell or missile fired, and as a tool used to avoid carrying out real investigations,” Nadav Weiman, the group’s executive director, said.
AP independently confirmed some details of the soldier’s account, which is consistent with the military’s public response. Breaking the Silence said it had corroborated the account with its own sources.
The Israeli military has raided or laid siege to hospitals throughout the war, accusing Hamas of using them as command centers and to hide fighters, though it’s provided evidence for only some of its claims.
Hamas security men have been seen in hospitals during the war, controlling access to certain areas. Earlier this year, Doctors Without Borders suspended some operations at Nasser Hospital for several months after patients and staff reported seeing armed, masked men roaming parts of the building.
Tank shells were fired after a drone failed
The soldier, and a former military official with knowledge of the situation, said a high-ranking army official initially approved use of a precision weapon to take down the camera but an attempt by drone failed for unknown reasons. The former official spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorized to talk to the media.
The division commander then approved an alternative method, said the soldier, without saying what the method was. It’s unclear who made the decision to fire tank rounds, which can cause more extensive damage than drone strikes.
Oded Ailam, former head of the counterterrorism division in Israel’s Mossad spy service, said that while commanders on the ground have a degree of freedom, they don’t have a “blank check.”
“If the change is significant, particularly where it may affect the risk to civilians, it must remain within the authority, rules and intent of the original order, or require renewed approval,” he said.
Israeli troops have killed over 200 journalists in the war
Israeli troops have killed 207 Palestinian reporters in Gaza since Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023, attack ignited the war, according to the New York-based Committee to Protect Journalists. Israel has barred foreign journalists from entering Gaza, giving Palestinian journalists a critical role in covering the conflict.
Sara Qudah, CPJ’s Middle East and North Africa regional director, said Israel has a responsibility to conduct a prompt and transparent investigation. “When journalists can be killed without credible accountability, it becomes harder and more dangerous for the press to document conflicts and for the public to know what is happening,” she said.
The lack of answers has been agonizing for the families.
Ezz al-Din al-Masri said he doesn’t understand why his brother, Hussam, was killed. “Unfortunately, we found that the blood of journalists in Gaza is cheap … as if the rules protecting journalists do not apply to them,” he said.
Dagga, 33, had just taken her last photos before rushing up the stairs. Whenever her father, Riyad Abu Dagga, visits her grave, he carries her phone and camera with him — she always had them with her. He visits her apartment near Nasser Hospital and cries.
“Had any of the daughters of the soldiers been killed unjustly, they would not have stayed silent,” he said of the Israelis. “They would want to know why.”

AP reporter Wafaa Shurafa in Deir al-Balah, Gaza Strip, contributed to this report.

The extension is already behind schedule because the city did not settle on a route in 2025. The proposal could be put to a city council vote as early as November, followed by a review that may take up to two years before construction begins.
Until the extension is complete, workers will rely on buses 78 and 80. ESMC employees traveling from the city typically take the S-Bahn or a tram before transferring to a bus.
ESMC is a joint venture between Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., Bosch, Infineon, and NXP.

Army defends training center over waste dumping scandal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
07:22:48 UTC
16:22:48 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Army on Monday defended its Northern Combined Training Center against allegations of possible collusion in a waste dumping scandal, saying the military facility was a victim of the scheme.
The controversy began after the Taoyuan City Department of Environmental Protection discovered during an inspection in February that a local company had transported waste stored at its facility to the Northern Combined Training Center for use as road backfill, per Liberty Times. The training center had contracted Hung Ping Construction to improve roads at the facility by replacing red earth with Class B5 recycled aggregate made from bricks or concrete chunks.
Prosecutors said Hung Ping Construction owner Chen Hsin-hung (陳信宏) signed false contracts with multiple companies to make it appear that recycled aggregate was being used for the roadwork instead of waste. During an excavation at the site in April, investigators found that the material used as backfill contained concrete chunks, polystyrene, wires, iron, plastics, rubber tubing, and other waste, per PTS.
Prosecutors ordered the training center, Hung Ping Construction, and five other companies involved in the case to submit plans to remove the waste buried at the training ground. Chen and eight other suspects, along with six companies, were indicted in connection with the case.
KMT Legislator Ma Wen-chun (馬文君) questioned how roughly 100,000 cubic meters of waste, equivalent to about 39 Olympic-size swimming pools, could have been buried at the facility without being detected, per UDN. She said the operation was unlikely to have gone unnoticed, given the perimeter checks, construction supervision, and inspections of the materials used.
Ma also challenged the military’s assertion that the contaminated backfill does not affect training safety, urging the Army to release the results of load-bearing and other tests conducted on the roads. She called on prosecutors to investigate the flow of more than NT$1.3 billion (US$40.8 million) in alleged illicit gains attributed to Chen and his associates and determine whether any military personnel were involved.
The Army said the training center remained a victim of the scheme and that an investigation found no evidence it had conspired with the contractors, per CNA. However, the Army acknowledged shortcomings in the center’s oversight and said it had established an internal team to investigate administrative failures.

Magnitude 5.8 earthquake strikes off southeast Taiwan

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Green procurement reported by private companies and organizations in Taiwan topped NT$100 billion (US$3.1 billion) last year for the first time, CTEE reported.
The Ministry of Environment said Tuesday that the total reached NT$100.6 billion, up about 35% from 2024. The initiative encourages businesses and organizations to purchase and report environmentally friendly products and services, with the goal of expanding green business opportunities and promoting sustainable consumption, according to Phoenix Tours.
Among different industries, large traditional manufacturing companies remained major contributors. Large non-manufacturing companies, meanwhile, recorded the strongest growth, with their purchases rising from NT$9.85 billion in 2024 to NT$19 billion last year, an increase of 92.94%.
Smaller businesses are also playing a growing role in greener supply chains. Green procurement reported by small and medium-sized non-manufacturing companies more than doubled last year, rising 113% from the previous year.
Participation is expanding beyond businesses to educational and medical institutions. Green purchases reported in the category covering these and other organizations increased 68% last year.
The initiative recognizes organizations with strong records. Among last year’s award recipients, 74 companies received awards for the third consecutive year, while 83 won for the first time.
Taiwan has set a target of NT$160 billion in combined green procurement by the public and private sectors by 2030. The ministry said the practice has evolved beyond purchasing decisions, giving businesses a way to encourage lower-carbon changes across their supply chains while supporting Taiwan’s goal of reaching net-zero emissions by 2050.
The ministry said it will expand the types of purchases eligible for reporting, including products with environmental certifications, resource-circulation products, and other environmentally friendly products. It also plans to include newer models such as leasing instead of purchasing.

What to know about Trump's tariffs on Canada and the escalating trade war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
07:21:46 UTC
16:21:46 KST

What to know about Trump's tariffs on Canada and the escalating trade war
Canada plans to respond to US President Donald Trump's new tariffs on Tuesday, as the once close neighbouring allies spiral into a trade war. Ottawa and Washington failed to reach a deal on Friday to avert new 50 percent US tariffs on select Canadian goods after weeks of talks.
Canada will announce retaliatory tariffs against the United States on Tuesday after US President Donald Trump told Canadian leaders on Monday to “fall in line” or face consequences “far worse” than existing tariffs and Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney accused Washington of trying to subordinate Canada.
After trade negotiations crumbled at the eleventh hour, Trump's 50 percent tariffs on scores of Canadian imports kicked in over the weekend.
The new levies, which took effect Saturday, are set to impact about 5 percent of Canada's annual exports to the US – or $20 billion in goods ranging from hockey sticks to agricultural products. Carney quickly promised that his government would roll out retaliatory measures “dollar for dollar” starting September 8.
Additional threats have piled up in the meantime. Ontario Premier Doug Ford told The Associated Press on Monday that “everything is on the table," noting his province would be ready to cut off electricity and critical minerals to the US if the trade war worsens. Meanwhile, Trump suggested his administration could also increase taxes on Canadian automobiles next year.
The US and Canada once held one of the world's most durable trade alliances, but the latest escalation plunges the North American neighbours deeper into a rupture that has kept both sides of the border on edge throughout Trump's second term in office. Steeper tariffs raise costs for businesses – and almost always trickle down to households in the form of higher prices.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Here's what we know.
The 50 percent tariffs from the US are set to affect $20 billion of Canadian goods.
Canada sends the vast majority of its goods exports to the US (72 percent last year), and the Trump administration says the new taxes will be levied on products ranging from hockey sticks to wine and cement. The list is long. According to documents published by the White House, other goods subject to the tax include honey, seeds and agricultural products – as well as select makeup, perfumes, clothing, jewellery, furniture, cameras, fabric and more.
The 50 percent levy also applies to some products that were previously protected under the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA), a trade pact from Trump's first term. This marks a shift from past levies – and further underlines questions around the future of the USMCA overall.
Trump reinstated a long-dormant Great Depression-era law: Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930.
When the US and world economies were in collapse nearly a century ago, Congress passed the 1930 law as part of broader Smoot-Hawley legislation (named after its congressional sponsors). But Section 338 – which authorises the president to slap import taxes of up to 50 percent on imports from countries that have discriminated against US businesses – has never been used specifically to raise tariffs until now.
No investigation is required to justify the levies. Nor is there any limit on how long they can stay in place. Since there's no precedent however, the latest tariffs may also see legal challenge.
Trump has claimed that Canada unfairly discriminates against US exports of automobiles, alcohol and dairy products. The president expressed anger over Canada's retaliation against his own tariffs in 2025 – noting how Canadian imports of American alcohol and cars started to fall last spring.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
On Saturday, Carney quickly promised to match the new levies “dollar for dollar” – later announcing that those countermeasures would begin September 8. He noted Canada would target US steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper and electronics.
In the meantime, provincial leaders like Ford have reiterated Canadians' willingness to endure economic pain rather than give in to US pressure.
Trump "underestimates Canada. We’re all in,” Ford said Monday. Beyond potentially cutting off electricity and critical minerals from Ontario, he also called for Canada to consider using oil and potash as leverage.
Meanwhile, Trump made new threats on social media. He threatened to increase tariffs on Canadian cars, trucks, automotive parts and steel to 50 percent starting January 1, 2027. Like other countries, Canada currently faces a broader 25 percent tariff on autos. A 50 percent sectoral tariff on most steel imports is already in effect.
“WE DON’T NEED CANADA, THEY NEED US!” Trump wrote Monday.
Read more‘We don’t need Canada’: Trump threatens to double auto tariffs after trade talks collapse
Carney on Monday said Washington’s auto-sector proposals would “gradually dismantle” Canadian production. He also questioned what Trump’s latest move would mean for workers in US states who depend on Canadian demand.
The prime minister added that Canada remained willing to negotiate, but only if the US approached the talks as a partnership between sovereign countries. He said “an attitude at the negotiation table that Canada is a subsidiary of the United States” is “not something we’re going to accept.”
Tariffs are taxes paid by importers or businesses that buy goods from abroad. Their impact typically trickles down to consumers through higher prices – and, as seen over the last year, they can also create uncertainty for workers across affected sectors.
“Nearly all industries and professions are likely to see downstream effects from this spiraling trade dispute,” Augustine Lo, of law firm Dorsey & Whitney, which advises clients on international trade, said Saturday.
The 50 percent tariffs come on top of previously imposed levies, including a 10 percent rate that Trump slapped on Canada just last month – ostensibly for failing to do enough to prevent imports produced by forced labour and separate sectoral levies globally.
The growing trade war underscores Trump’s willingness to risk breaking established alliances. And Canada’s reluctance to accept a deal may reflect recent experience.
Read moreTrump says Canada wants 'benefits of being a State, without being one' as trade war deepens
Trump has threatened tariffs in response to everything from a TV ad criticising his trade policies (later pulled by Ontario's government) to Canadian wildfires that blackened skies across North America.
Steeper tariffs have already contributed to higher inflation, but have appeared to level off in recent months, according to researchers at the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis – most notably after the Supreme Court struck down some of Trump's most sweeping levies in February.
Still, the weekend's escalation with Canada marks the latest instance of Trump turning to other laws to impose tariffs. And Washington’s ongoing war with Iran has driven prices even higher. With the cost of living at the center of many voters' minds in a midterm election year, political ramifications could mount for the Republican president in the coming months.
(FRANCE 24 with AP)

Foreign tourists boost Greek tourism in June – domestic demand is in decline
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
07:15:45 UTC
16:15:45 KST

According to provisional data from the Hellenic Statistical Authority, 5.58 million arrivals and 24.06 million overnight stays were recorded in tourist lodgings in June 2026.
Tourism activity at accommodation establishments in Greece increased in June 2026, with foreign visitors acting as the main driver of both arrivals and overnight stays, while domestic demand recorded a slight decline.
According to preliminary data from the Hellenic Statistical Authority (ELSTAT), a total of 5.58 million arrivals and 24.06 million overnight stays were recorded in tourist accommodation in June 2026. Compared with June 2025, arrivals increased by 1.3%, while overnight stays rose by 1.4%.
The data cover hotel-type accommodation, campsites and collective short-stay establishments, such as rooms to let.
International tourism demand was largely what supported the increase. Arrivals of foreign visitors reached 4.58 million, up 1.7% from 4.50 million a year earlier. Overnight stays by foreign visitors also increased by 1.7%, reaching 21.54 million, from 21.17 million in June 2025.
The picture in the domestic market was quite different. Arrivals of residents fell by 0.4%, to just over 1 million, from 1.006 million in the same month of 2025, while their overnight stays decreased by 0.9%, to around 2.53 million.
The gap between domestic and foreign tourism becomes even more evident when their share of the total market is examined. Foreign visitors accounted for 82% of total arrivals in June and an even higher 89.5% of overnight stays. Residents covered the remaining 18% of arrivals and 10.5% of overnight stays.
Faster growth in short-stay accommodation
The strongest increase was recorded by collective short-stay accommodation, which includes rooms to let.
Arrivals in this category increased by 4.2% year-on-year, reaching 1.23 million from 1.18 million in June 2025. At the same time, overnight stays rose by 2.8%, to 5.59 million from 5.43 million.
Demand from abroad was particularly strong. Arrivals of foreign visitors at short-stay accommodation increased by 4.5%, approaching 1.03 million, while their overnight stays rose by 3.3%, reaching 4.91 million.
Arrivals of residents at these establishments also increased, by 2.7%, to 197,599. However, overnight stays by Greek visitors edged down slightly by 0.3%, to 677,681.
Growth was more limited in hotel-type accommodation and campsites. Together they welcomed 4.35 million arrivals, up 0.6%, while overnight stays increased by 1%, to 18.47 million.
In the same category, arrivals of foreign visitors rose by 0.9%, to 3.55 million, and their overnight stays by 1.3%, to 16.62 million. By contrast, domestic traffic fell, as both arrivals and overnight stays by residents declined by 1.1%, to 804,565 arrivals and 1.85 million overnight stays respectively.
The breakdown by type of accommodation confirms the heavy reliance on foreign visitors. Non-residents accounted for 81.7% of arrivals at hotel-type establishments, 83.9% at short-stay accommodation and 70.9% at campsites.
The corresponding shares in overnight stays were even higher, with foreign visitors responsible for 90.5% of nights spent in hotel-type accommodation, 87.9% in short-stay establishments and 64.6% in campsites.
Average length of stay at 4.3 nights
The average length of stay across all accommodation types remained unchanged from a year earlier, at 4.3 overnight stays.
Foreign visitors stayed noticeably longer, with an average of 4.7 overnight stays, compared with 2.5 overnight stays for residents.
In hotel-type accommodation and campsites, the average stay stood at 4.2 overnight stays, unchanged from June 2025, while in short-stay establishments it was 4.6 overnight stays.
Non-residents stayed an average of 4.7 overnight stays in hotel-type accommodation and campsites and 4.8 overnight stays in short-stay establishments. Residents stayed an average of 2.3 overnight stays in hotel-type accommodation and campsites, while in short-stay establishments their average stay fell to 3.4 overnight stays from 3.5 a year earlier.
Rise compared with the pandemic years continues
ELSTAT's long-term chart also shows the substantial increase in June tourism flows compared with 2021.
Arrivals rose from 1.92 million in June 2021 to 4.47 million in 2022, 5.13 million in 2023, 5.33 million in 2024 and 5.51 million in 2025, reaching 5.58 million in June 2026.
Overnight stays followed a similar trajectory, rising from 7.27 million in June 2021 to 19.74 million in 2022, 22.55 million in 2023, 23.24 million in 2024, 23.72 million in 2025 and 24.06 million this June.
The June figures therefore show that the Greek market for tourist accommodation continues to move upwards, albeit at relatively moderate rates. At the same time, the sector's strong dependence on international demand is once again highlighted, as foreign visitors account for more than four in five arrivals and almost nine in ten overnight stays.
ELSTAT notes that the data for June 2026 are provisional. The survey covers accommodation across the country and records arrivals and overnight stays by residents and non-residents, while final annual figures are published six months after the end of the reference year.

- Senate Democrats are calling for an Armed Services Committee hearing on extended U.S. Navy deployments tied to operations against Iran.
- The USS Abraham Lincoln has been at sea more than 250 days, and the USS Gerald R. Ford suffered a fire and plumbing failures during its own extended deployment.
A group of Senate Armed Services Committee Democrats is asking Chairman Roger Wicker to hold a public hearing on extended deployments tied to U.S. military operations against Iran, according to a letter released August 24 by Senators Gary Peters (D-Mich.), Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) and Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.).
The letter cites conditions aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, which left San Diego on November 21 and has remained at sea for more than 250 days without a scheduled return date. The carrier’s roughly 5,000 sailors and Marines went more than 200 consecutive days without a port call, according to Sen. Richard Blumenthal, a modern-day record for a U.S. Navy carrier.
Military Times reported August 11 that multiple sailors aboard the Lincoln had attempted to go overboard during the deployment, based on accounts from family members. CNN separately confirmed with U.S. officials that a sailor went overboard on August 3 and was recovered within an hour by a search-and-rescue helicopter, treated aboard ship and transferred for further care. A second overboard incident involving the same strike group occurred last spring, according to a sailor aboard the Lincoln and two U.S. officials who spoke to CNN.
Family members confronted Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao at a town hall in San Diego, with one spouse describing a message from her husband saying he hoped he would not wake up the next morning, according to Military Times and Stars and Stripes reporting cited in the letter.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has disputed the Military Times account, calling it “completely misrepresented.” The Navy has said no service members aboard the Lincoln have died and that the August 3 sailor was quickly and safely recovered.
The senators’ letter also points to the USS Gerald R. Ford, which suffered a laundry-room fire on March 12 that took more than 30 hours to extinguish, injured two sailors and damaged roughly 100 sleeping berths. The Navy initially described the fire as contained and said the ship remained fully operational. Later footage obtained by CNN showed more extensive damage, including burned bunks and exposed wiring in crew living spaces.
The Ford left frontline operations and sailed to Souda Bay, Crete, for repairs, then stopped in Split, Croatia, before returning to sea on April 2. The ship had also experienced recurring failures in its roughly 650-toilet vacuum waste system throughout the deployment. The carrier ultimately spent about 11 months at sea, exceeding the Navy’s typical seven-month deployment target, before returning to Norfolk in May for scheduled maintenance.
Both carriers were redirected from other missions to support Iran operations. The Lincoln had been headed for a routine Indo-Pacific patrol before its diversion to the Middle East in January. The Ford was pulled from a planned deployment to Europe, sent briefly to the Caribbean in connection with operations against Venezuela, and then routed to the Middle East.
“The toll this unauthorized, disastrous war is taking on our troops is unconscionable,” the senators wrote, characterizing the military campaign against Iran as illegal and citing what they described as a pattern of inadequate planning for extended deployments.
The senators asked the Armed Services Committee to examine morale conditions, financial strain on military families, and the Department of War’s plan for ending the extended deployments. They also requested that the department detail how it plans to sustain troops in the region if the campaign continues.
The USS George Washington has since been ordered to relieve the Lincoln, according to a U.S. official cited by CNN. As of the senators’ letter, no public timeline had been given for the Lincoln’s return to San Diego, and Chairman Wicker had not publicly responded to the hearing request.

Chinese factory workers accidentally caught on camera glasses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
07:10:39 UTC
16:10:39 KST

Camera glasses contain footage that appears to have been accidentally filmed inside Chinese factory
Factory workers who helped make a Chinese-brand of camera glasses appear to have been unknowingly filmed by the devices in accidental videos.
7.30 bought a pair of budget glasses made by Shenzhen-based company Oho Sunshine online and found footage already on the device, which appears to be from inside the factory.
The collection of four short videos, dated last year, shows a number of workers sitting at their desks inspecting the glasses, while listening to jaunty electronic music.
One video clearly identifies a worker lifting a pair and shaking them vigorously.
Another three videos, up to 10 minutes long and dated this year, show only black with atmospheric audio, suggesting the glasses were activated while inside a case or box.
The shoot button on the side of the frames is sensitive and easily switched on.
7.30 approached Oho Sunshine, with questions about the apparent privacy breach but received no response.
Oho Sunshine was founded in 2009 in the Chinese city of Shenzhen in Guandong province, north of Hong Kong, as a smart wearable technologies manufacturer, according to the company's website.
The accidental leak perhaps proves not even the workers who make camera glasses are safe from being filmed and provides a rare insight into the globalised production chain.
Rise of camera glasses
Camera glasses are enjoying a surge in popularity as cheap brands flood the market. Oho is just one of numerous companies manufacturing similar devices.
They look like ordinary glasses and allow you to record video and audio, largely without people knowing.
While some models have a built-in light to indicate filming, there are now services that remove the indicator cheaply.
The glasses can play music and make calls, with more high-tech versions allowing users to live-stream or swipe through messages on a display in the lenses.
Meta's fashionable Ray-Ban smart glasses can cost up to $700 a pair, but basic versions can be bought online for as little as $40.
Kmart Australia's $89 Anko brand of camera glasses recently sold out, prompting an online petition to stop their sale amid concerns about privacy and their use by male content creators recording women without their knowledge and uploading the videos to potentially millions of followers.
While filming in public places is generally legal, the devices have raised new concerns around privacy.
Filmed without consent on 'rizz cam'
Beth Knight, 18, found herself the subject of lurid commentary from online users after a man filmed her with camera glasses and uploaded it to social media without her knowledge.
At the time of the incident late last year, she was 17 and by herself at London's busy Waterloo station.
"I'd missed my train, so I had 40 minutes to wait in the station," Ms Knight told 7.30.
"Then pretty much immediately a man approached me and opened with, 'I've seen you, I found you attractive,' and I immediately shut him down, and I said I had a boyfriend."
She discovered that their conversation had been turned into content after she heard about other cases.
"I started looking up buzzwords. I was looking up, "picking up girls", "Meta Glasses", "Waterloo", all of those into the TikTok search bar, and that's when I found his page."
She saw a video of her interaction titled, "POV: You approach her instead of walking by".
"It was framed as a successful pick-up, like a win, when I know in the moment I was incredibly uncomfortable … because it was a strange man refusing to accept my soft hint of a no," she said.
"He had very much framed it as, 'Look, I've picked her up, I got her Instagram, I've won here,' and over the top of the video he was instructing men watching that when girls say they have a boyfriend they're lying."
Ms Knight was not lying and thought the man would get the message and leave.
The man is a content creator who touts himself as a pick-up artist and advertises male coaching on his social media account.
Digital extremism researcher Milica Stilinovic, from Sydney University, said such content was known as "rizz cam" — rizz being slang for charisma — where women are sometimes filmed without their consent.
"I would find it horrendous to be treated that way and then subjected to a global audience," she told 7.30.
Ms Stilinovic led a study that reviewed more than 350 Instagram videos filmed with camera glasses.
"Pick-up artists are adjacent to the manosphere, or part of the manosphere, and they have a dual purpose to exist," she said.
"One is to build the self-confidence of men, supposedly through the subjugation of women, and the second part is to sell male coaching, which is basically like a multi-level marketing scheme.
"Some of the worst examples included underage girls. Some of [the filmers] approached women who were inebriated. Some of them approached women who were semi-nude at beaches."
Ms Knight said her experience left her feeling angry.
"It's weird to watch it back," she said.
"But the anger definitely came from the fact that it was spun so heavily to look good on his part.
"I went home and sobbed to my parents."
She said she asked the content creator to take the video down, but he blocked her.
7.30 has contacted the creator for comment, but he did not respond.
Is it legal?
According to Australia's Privacy Commissioner, Carly Kind, the use of camera glasses in public is largely legal, with laws varying across states.
"Wearing smart glasses in public to capture images of things that happen in public is generally not illegal under Australian law," Ms Kind told 7.30.
"[But] when you are in a private premises or a private space, and that might include a private home, a vehicle, or potentially a semi-private space like a gym or a workplace, for example, then you're likely going to run up against laws that do prohibit the use of surveillance devices."
In Victoria, where filming inside a private business is generally allowed, one content creator known as "The Latte Bloke" uses camera glasses to review coffee around Melbourne.
He is not a pick-up artist, but his videos feature staff and customers.
One 19-year-old cafe worker said she did not consent to being filmed while serving him.
Her aunt, Tara Venn, told 7.30 her niece was upset after seeing herself in a video online.
She was new in the job.
"It was a bit affronting [for her]," Ms Venn said.
She said content creators should consider the ethics of filming someone.
"Common sense says you are polite and you ask if you are going to invade a person's privacy by filming them without them knowing,"
"I just want people to think and to actually use good manners and decency."
The content creator declined to be interviewed but told 7.30:
"Latte Bloke is all about filming the latte experience and having a bit of fun reviewing the coffee. The focus has never been on the staff or customers, and I'd never intentionally want to make anyone feel uncomfortable."
Potential real-world consequences
Attorney-General Michelle Rowland has asked Australia's Privacy Commissioner to make recommendations about camera glasses in Australia.
Ms Kind says she was already worried about them.
"If you think about their use in workplaces, there's a high likelihood that corporate espionage could be permitted through these kinds of glasses without proper control,"
"I think the theft of personal information through the use of the glasses is also a potential offence that we could see spiralling out here, and [there are] obviously real risks around vulnerable groups, women and children."
In New South Wales it is illegal to create or share sexually explicit videos or audio of someone without their consent.
Last year, new federal privacy laws made serious invasions of privacy an offence; however, the commissioner told 7.30 there was a high bar to prove it was intentional and caused harm.
In the UK, some pubs and restaurants have reportedly banned the devices, while in Germany, rights advocacy group HateAid has lodged a complaint to German prosecutors against Meta and other companies, claiming such devices breach the country's covert recording laws.
Ms Stilinovic wants camera glasses temporarily banned in Australia.
"I would suggest that we stop the rollout of smart glasses until regulation and policymakers have caught up to keep societies safe,"

‘Children were in pieces’: memories still raw 6 months after Iran school strike
Families grieve at least 155 killed in US-linked Tomahawk missile attack on Minab school during opening hours of war
For months, Masoumeh Zakeri has endlessly replayed the last night she spent with her nine-year-old daughter before she was killed in a strike on her school during the opening hours of the US-Israel war with Iran.
Motahreh excitedly talked about coming holidays, planned weddings and the clothes she wanted to buy. She had a Ramadan pre-fast meal shortly before dawn and then Zakeri tucked her into bed.

Greek air traffic controllers pushed to limit by tourism boom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
07:08:05 UTC
16:08:05 KST

A surge in flights, staff shortages and ageing infrastructure are increasing pressure on controllers as Greece races to modernise its aviation network.
On the screens at the Control Centre in Athens, the symbols representing aircraft form an ever denser network. At the height of the summer season, air traffic controllers are called on to manage thousands of flights in Greek skies that seem to be reaching the limits of their capacity.
Olga Toki, vice-president of the Hellenic Air Traffic Controllers Association, paints a picture of intense strain: Traffic is so heavy, she says, that at certain times it is hard to find any additional space for new aircraft.
The figures illustrate the scale of the burden. According to the Hellenic Civil Aviation Authority, in low-demand months, Greek airports usually handle around 1,000 to 1,500 flights a day. In the first week of July, however, the daily average soared to 2,700 flights.
The picture is similar across the wider region. Eurocontrol estimates that air traffic in south-eastern Europe, which includes Greek airspace, is about 40% higher than in 2019.
The increase goes hand in hand with the spectacular rebound of Greek tourism. Visitor arrivals reached 38 million last year, surpassing the previous record of 2019 by 23%, in a country of around 10 million inhabitants.
The malfunction that exposed the system's weaknesses
The pressure on the system had become evident long before the peak of the summer season. On 4 January, a serious malfunction in the communications system between controllers and aircraft exposed the weaknesses of the existing infrastructure.
Controllers could still see the flights on their radar screens, but they could not communicate by voice with the pilots. The authorities were forced to close Greek airspace for several hours, resulting in flight cancellations and aircraft being diverted to neighbouring countries.
The incident accelerated the announcement of a major modernisation programme with a budget of around €300 million. Among other things, it provides for the installation of new digital communications systems and the replacement of ageing radar equipment.
Installation of the new systems began in mid-August, and the overall plan foresees the completion of the upgrades by 2028.
At the same time, Greece is under pressure at the European level as well. The European Commission took the country to the Court of Justice of the European Union last year, arguing that it had failed to adapt its air navigation procedures in time to the international Performance-Based Navigation (PBN) standard.
Heavy traffic, limited staff
Inside the control room, Greek airspace is divided into ten sectors. Each sector is overseen by one controller, assisted by a colleague. In summer, though, the surge in traffic runs up against another long-standing problem: staff shortages.
Shift supervisor Giorgos Stamoulakatos estimates that the current 154 controllers fall well short of the service's real needs, which he puts at around 250.
Recruitment has been stepped up, with 92 new controllers due in 2025 and another 77 in 2026. However, this reinforcement cannot deliver results immediately, as it takes about five years of training before a new controller acquires the necessary operational experience.
Twice as many aircraft in the space of an hour
Areti Anastopoulou has worked in air traffic control for more than three decades. One of her tasks is to organise the sequence of aircraft coming in to land, ensuring the necessary distances between them.
Under normal conditions, she explains, a controller can handle around 20 aircraft in an hour. In peak periods, however, that number can reach 40, inevitably causing delays and adding to the pressure.
In one illustrative case, 33 aircraft landed in just one hour, even though the planned upper limit is 28. She says she has repeatedly had to ask crews to reduce speed or change course in order to maintain the required safety distances.
As she points out, controllers are making an extremely demanding effort to keep operations safe in an environment where margins are becoming ever tighter.
Additional pressure from the Middle East
Geopolitical instability in the Middle East has added to the already strained situation. According to Eurocontrol, about 300 extra flights now pass through Greek airspace every day, a number that accounts for almost 6% of total daily traffic.
Greece's geographical position creates further demands. As Olga Toki points out, beyond commercial flights the competent services also monitor the activities of Turkish aircraft and unmanned systems, further increasing the workload.
Delays increasingly felt by passengers
Inevitably, the consequences are felt all the way to the arrivals halls.
Jose Lopez, who recently arrived in Athens from Barcelona with a delay of about half an hour, did not find the experience particularly surprising. For mid-August, he said, such a delay is not unusual, and in the past he has faced much longer waits.
Christos, who works at a large hotel in Athens, is less forgiving. According to him, delays are more frequent than last year, and he has sometimes had to wait as long as seven hours for guests arriving from the United States.
For controllers, the issue is not the growth of tourism as such, but whether the infrastructure can keep pace with it. As Anastopoulou sums up, tourism is a crucial asset for the Greek economy, but the constant increase in flights cannot be sustained without corresponding investment in human resources, technology and infrastructure.

Spanish workers spend equivalent of 231 days paying taxes, study says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
07:05:43 UTC
16:05:43 KST

Tax Freedom Day fell on 20 August, according to Fundación Civismo. The think tank says the average worker’s tax burden has increased by 54 days since 2018, partly because of higher social contributions and income tax thresholds failing to keep pace with inflation.
Spaniards had to wait until 20 August this year to reach the so-called Tax Freedom Day — the point at which, according to one think tank’s calculations, the average worker has earned enough income to cover their taxes and social security contributions.
According to a study by Fundación Civismo, a Spanish liberal think tank, the estimated burden was equivalent to 231 days in 2026, two more than last year. The foundation said the increase was not necessarily the result of explicit tax rises alone.
When Pedro Sánchez became prime minister in 2018, the foundation put the figure at 177 days, with Tax Freedom Day falling on 27 June. Since then, its estimated date has moved back by 54 days.
The foundation attributes the increase to income tax bands failing to keep pace with inflation, rising social security contributions, the return of some higher value-added tax (VAT) rates and new local levies. As a result, the foundation says workers are paying more of their income in taxes and contributions.
To calculate the tax burden, the foundation uses the total cost of employing an average worker, including contributions paid by both the employee and the employer. In its reference case, an employee earning a gross annual salary of €32,446 costs their employer €42,390.70 once employer contributions are included.
The worker receives an estimated €24,724.91 in net pay, while €17,665.79 — or 41.7% of the total employment cost — goes towards income tax and employer and employee social security contributions. This means that for every €100 spent on employing the worker, €58.30 reaches them as take-home pay.
This means that, for every €100 of labour cost, workers take home only €58.30.
The report also points out that workers can end up paying more income tax even though their wages have barely increased. This happens because the tax brackets have not been adjusted fully for inflation at the same pace as wages. This can push workers into higher tax bands even if their purchasing power has barely improved.
VAT and other regional and municipal taxes add to the estimated burden. Civismo calculates that the average worker pays around €2,213 in VAT each year, equivalent to almost 33 days of net income.
The study also includes regional and municipal levies such as the local property tax (IBI), vehicle tax and inheritance and gift taxes. According to Fundación Civismo, these and other charges that it groups together as “silent taxation” amount to approximately €4,110 a year, equivalent to more than two months of the model worker’s net income.
The estimated date of the Tax Freedom Day varies between Spain’s 17 autonomous communities because regional income tax rates, deductions and locally imposed taxes differ. According to the study, the Basque Country had the earliest date, on 14 August, followed by Madrid on 15 August. Catalonia and Extremadura recorded the latest dates, on 26 August.
However, Tax Freedom Day is not an official government measure and its methodology is disputed. Spanish newspaper El País quoted experts critical of the indicator, who also argued that the measure counts taxes as a cost without reflecting the healthcare, education, pensions and other public services they finance.
Spain’s official tax-to-GDP ratio provides a different comparison. It stood at around 38% in 2025, according to Eurostat data cited by the newspaper, up from 35.2% in 2019 but still below the levels recorded in several other large European economies.

Majority of South Koreans view US 'unfavorably,' 1st time in over 20 years: Survey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
07:04:30 UTC
16:04:30 KST

Aamir Latif
25 August 2026•Update: 25 August 2026
For the first time in over two decades, a majority of South Koreans have an unfavorable opinion of the US, a survey showed.
Some 55% of the participants expressed an unfavorable opinion of the US, up from 39% last year, according to the survey conducted by the Washington-based Pew Research Center.
The survey, released Monday, revealed that 18% of respondents had a "very unfavorable view," up from 9% in 2025.
Fewer than half of South Koreans, 45%, have a favorable view of the US, marking a 16-point drop from 61% last year, and a 35-point drop from 2018, the second year of US President Donald Trump’s first term, when it stood at 80%.
The US has some 39,000 soldiers deployed in South Korea under a defense treaty with Seoul, according to Trump, who recently ordered the Pentagon to scale back annual joint military exercises with South Korea.
In response, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung reiterated his push for military independence from Washington.
Around six in 10 South Korean adults, 57%, consider the US a reliable partner. That’s down from 83% in 2022, during the Joe Biden administration.
There has also been a decrease in the share of South Koreans who think the US takes into account the interests of countries like their own when making international policy decisions. This year, 21% of South Koreans think the US does this a great deal or a fair amount. That’s down from 38% in 2023.
The share of South Koreans who say that Washington contributes a great deal or a fair amount to peace and stability around the world has also fallen, from 74% in 2023 to 47% this year.
Only 14% approve of Trump's handling of tariffs. Earlier this year, Trump threatened to raise tariffs on South Korean goods to 25% if the country’s legislature did not approve a proposed trade deal.
The South Korean parliament later approved the deal.
Around three-quarters of South Koreans disapprove of the way Trump is dealing with Iran. That includes nearly half, 47%, who strongly disapprove.
Despite viewing Washington less favorably this year, South Koreans still overwhelmingly name the US as their country’s most important ally. This share has decreased slightly since last year, 84% compared to 89%.
