Uganda's Gaza 'stabilisation force' plan sparks debate in Africa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
07:04:24 UTC
16:04:24 KST

Breadcrumb
Uganda's participation in Gaza 'stabilisation force' sparks debate in Africa
Uganda's parliament approved the deployment of army troops to the" International Stabilisation Force" in the Gaza Strip at the beginning of August as part of US President Donald Trump's plan. The move marks the first official declaration by an African country of its readiness to participate in Gaza.
The approval came on 6 August after Ugandan Defence Minister Kiria Kiwanuka told lawmakers that Trump had asked President Yoweri Museveni in July for Uganda to contribute to the proposed international force in Gaza.
After the Ugandan parliament's approval, a Ugandan soldier in military uniform posted a video on social media in which he appeared alongside the words, "Gaza, we are coming", indicating that the idea of a military deployment had begun circulating within Uganda's military and media circles.
The Ugandan government has not yet specified the number of troops it may deploy to the territory or when they would be sent.
Israel's public broadcaster reported last Monday, 17 August, that senior officers from Uganda and Burundi had arrived at the US command headquarters in Kiryat Gat in the occupied Palestinian territories as part of advanced talks with the two countries to send hundreds of soldiers to the territory as part of the multinational stabilisation force.
The broadcaster also said last Thursday, 20 August, that Morocco had been chosen to train members of the force.
Ugandan forces in the Gaza stabilisation force has sparked debate inside the Ugandan parliament, with opposition lawmakers calling for more information about the nature of the mission, the number of troops, its funding, and the guarantees provided to soldiers and their families.
The opposition also warned of the security and political risks associated with sending troops to a devastated territory and under highly complex field conditions.
Uganda has extensive experience in peacekeeping operations, particularly in Africa, where its forces participate in missions in Somalia, South Sudan and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
The defence minister cited this experience to justify the Ugandan army's ability to participate in a new international mission.
Without African backing
The decision has also raised questions about Kampala's approval of it and whether it has broad African backing or bypasses African consensus by being taken without Uganda consulting its partners in the African Union.
The African Union has consistently supported the Palestinian cause in principle and calls for the implementation of a two-state solution.
However, Israel has built relations with several African countries over decades, viewing the continent as an arena of Arab-Israeli competition.
In 2021, the union accepted Israel as an "observer member", a move that prompted Palestinian and Arab protests and was later revoked.
Uganda's relations with Israel, meanwhile, have continued to grow.
The Ugandan judge Julia Sebutinde, vice-president of the International Court of Justice, has attracted attention after she was described as believing that "God relies on her to stand with Israel". Sebutinde opposed the six rulings imposed by the court in 2024 to protect Palestinians and stop the genocide in Gaza.
Ugandan military leadership also recently said that any attempts to "destroy" Israel, amid the US-Israeli war on Iran, could prompt Uganda to intervene in support of the occupying state.
Uganda is also one of the largest importers of military technology and spyware from the occupying state.
In this context, Sudanese writer and researcher Abbas Saleh, who is based in the Ethiopian capital Addis Ababa, told The New Arab that Uganda's potential participation in the proposed international force for the Gaza Strip reflects a renewed predicament facing the African Union.
Decisions and positions adopted by the continental organisation often appear non-binding on member states, which may adopt unilateral policies that conflict with the union's collective positions.
"Despite the clear positions adopted by the African Union on the Palestinian cause, its rejection of Israeli violations and its repeated calls for an end to the war and the protection of civilians, the involvement of some member states in international security arrangements linked to Gaza could weaken the unity of the African position and expose the organisation's limited ability to turn its political positions into practical commitments by its members," he pointed out.
According to Saleh, Uganda is among the countries whose name has for years been associated with a broad security and military role in Africa, as well as close relations with Western powers, particularly in the Great Lakes region and the Horn of Africa.
He explained that this role "has given it a prominent position in several regional security issues but has at times made its foreign policy a subject of debate over the extent to which its decisions are independent of the calculations of international powers".
"The Ugandan move is significant beyond the participation of a single country, as it could set a precedent encouraging other countries that had been hesitant or reluctant to join the proposed international force, particularly if they are provided with appropriate political and security guarantees or international incentives," Saleh opined.
He stressed that participation in a military mission inside Gaza carries significant risks, given the complexities of the security and political situation, continuing disagreements over the future of the territory and governance and security arrangements, and the sensitivity surrounding the presence of foreign forces in the Palestinian territories.
"Uganda's move places the African Union before a difficult test: how can the organisation maintain a unified African position on the Palestinian cause while each member state has broad scope to make its foreign and security decisions independently?" he added. "The union's ability to deal with these contradictions could be an important indicator of the effectiveness of its political positions, not only towards Palestine, but also towards international crises affecting the continent and the interests of its countries."
Contradictions, differences
Meanwhile, researcher on Sahel and Sahara affairs Mohamed Torshin told The New Arab that the participation of Ugandan forces in the peace process in Gaza clearly reflects the scale of contradictions within the African Union and its limited ability to impose or implement decisions taken collectively, whether at the level of the AU Commission, the Peace and Security Council or the General Assembly.
Although African Union decisions and collective positions are supposed to form a common political framework for member states, the Ugandan position, along with other previous cases, reveals clear differences in the positions of African countries towards several sensitive regional and international issues.
In many cases, these differences push some countries or regional blocs to adopt policies and approaches that conflict with the union's collective position.
According to Torshin, the repercussions are not limited to a particular issue but extend to the effectiveness of African decision-making in general.
When a member state, in his view, adopts a position that clearly contradicts the union's collective position, this weakens the organisation's ability to present itself as a unified political actor and limits its ability to exercise diplomatic influence on issues requiring a coherent continental position.
In this context, Torshin noted that the repetition of such cases could widen the gap between decisions issued by African Union institutions and the policies pursued by some member states at the national level.
"This would gradually weaken the ability of the AU Commission and its political bodies to turn collective positions and decisions into effective and binding policies, making African decision-making more vulnerable to fragmentation and differences between countries and regional blocs," he added.
Torshin pointed out that the lack of protocol and political coordination between different African countries, ministries and institutions, and the absence of unified positions and decisions on common issues, could create space for international parties with interests and programmes in Africa to deal with countries individually and implement their policies and projects according to their own interests, away from the collective frameworks and decisions of the African Union.
He argued that "as this divergence and the multiplicity of positions within the continental organisation continue, international powers may find themselves with greater room to manoeuvre and negotiate with African countries bilaterally, gradually weakening the union's ability to formulate and defend a unified African agenda".
"In the long term, the continuation of this fragmentation could affect the future of African integration, making the implementation of continental policies and projects more closely tied to the interests of countries and external partners, and less subject to the collective vision that the union is supposed to represent," Torshin warned.

During Burnham’s first trip to Kyiv as prime minister, on Monday, he reiterated the UK’s “unwavering” support for Ukraine. Ukraine in turn handed over what officials have called a “goldmine” of battlefield data to help bolster British security.
In a meeting with the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Burnham reiterated there would be “no change in the UK’s steadfast support” for Kyiv. He also urged Ukraine’s allies to send more interceptor missiles to Kyiv as it struggles under continued Russian bombardment, and co-chaired his first coalition of the willing meeting, where he said the group was doing “everything we can” to “dig into our own stocks and help others dig into their stocks”.
Zelenskyy has repeatedly pleaded for more US-made Patriot interceptor missiles in recent months as Kyiv’s stocks have diminished. During the interview with Bloomberg, Burnham said he felt “really confident” the problem was “fixable”, but added: “There are other players who could help in the mix who we have influence with. It’s probably going to be a solution that involves a lot of layers and a lot of negotiation.”

A No 10 spokesperson said: “It had been an honest and productive conversation during the coalition of the willing, the leaders agreed, and it was clear the international community needed to step up and ensure Ukraine got the support it needed to defend itself from Russia’s barbaric attacks going into the winter.
“The prime minister emphasised the strength of unity among coalition members and reiterated that there would be no change in the UK’s steadfast support.
“That was further symbolised by the announcement that the UK had agreed that defence firm MBDA could release classified information on UK components for the long-range missile, Scalp, the prime minister said.”
Burnham and Zelenskyy had also signed an agreement to give the Ministry of Defence, working with selected British companies, access to Ukraine’s “Avengers” AI database, Downing Street said.
The deal is expected to help the UK learn from Ukraine’s experience on the battlefield and develop AI-powered solutions to national security challenges in both countries.
A Kremlin adviser has suggested UK factories producing drones for Ukraine could come under attack from “unknown sources”, after Britain’s agreement to share long-range missile blueprints with Kyiv.
Andrei Fedorov, a Russian former deputy foreign minister, told BBC Newsnight he could not “100% exclude” the prospect of “semi-military” action against Britain.
Fedorov said: “Sooner or later, there might be not only verbal, but maybe some visible reaction from Russia towards the UK.”
Asked to elaborate, he said: “There are different discussions how it should look like – it might be so-called technical reaction, maybe some hackers attack from unknown source, not from official level of course. There might be different political steps and I cannot exclude 100% that there might be some semi-military, for example.”
Pressed to define “semi-military” he said: “For example, something might happen with enterprises, with the factories which are producing drones for Ukraine, etc etc.” Asked whether this meant British factories being attacked militarily by Russia, he said: “They could be attacked, not by Russia, but by … from unknown sources.”

Poland receives first K2 tanks from new $6.5B deal

2026-08-25

- Poland received 28 K2 tanks, the first delivery from an August 2025 contract with Hyundai Rotem, assigning them to the 16th Mechanized Division.
- Future batches under the contract will include the K2PL variant, with 61 of 64 units to be assembled in Poland using domestic components.
Poland has received its first batch of tanks from a second, $6.5 billion contract with South Korea’s Hyundai Rotem, Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said Tuesday.
Twenty-eight K2 tanks arrived in Poland and will go to the 16th Mechanized Division, he said.
The contract was signed August 1, 2025, and covers 180 additional tanks. It follows an earlier deal for 180 K2GF tanks that Poland completed receiving in November 2025.
Kosiniak-Kamysz said the tanks delivered in this batch are standard K2 models, and that future shipments under the same contract will include the K2PL variant, a Polish-modified version built in part from domestically produced components. The second contract calls for 116 K2GF tanks between 2026 and 2027, followed by 64 K2PL tanks between 2028 and 2030. Of those K2PL tanks, 61 are set to be assembled in Poland at the Bumar-Łabędy plant in Gliwice, which belongs to the state-owned defense group PGZ.
The K2 Black Panther is a South Korean third-generation main battle tank armed with a 120 mm smoothbore gun and an autoloader. It also carries a 7.62 mm machine gun and a 12.7 mm heavy machine gun.
Kosiniak-Kamysz described the delivery as a step that expands Poland’s domestic production capacity and strengthens the country’s defense posture, tying the arrival of the K2PL variant to the broader technology-transfer terms of the contract.
The 16th Pomeranian Mechanized Division, based in northeastern Poland, has been the primary recipient of K2 tanks under the earlier contract, which equipped the 20th Bartoszyce Mechanized Brigade, the 9th Braniewo Armored Cavalry Brigade and the 15th Giżycko Mechanized Brigade. Six additional tanks from that contract went to the Land Forces Training Center in Poznań.
The second contract, worth roughly $6.5 billion, also includes 81 support vehicles based on the K2 chassis: 25 combat engineering vehicles, 25 armored bridge layers and 31 armored recovery vehicles, along with ammunition, a logistics and training package, and technology transfer. Brigadier General Artur Kuptel, head of Poland’s Armament Agency, signed the agreement on the Polish side at the Bumar-Łabędy facility, with Hyundai Rotem CEO Lee Yong-Bae signing for the South Korean company.
Poland’s tank purchases from South Korea are part of a broader rearmament effort that has included M1A2 SEPv3 Abrams tanks from the United States and continued operation of Leopard 2 tanks acquired from Germany. Poland had roughly 117 M1A2 SEPv3 tanks delivered as of early 2026. Officials have said Poland aims to field around 900 tanks across the three platforms by 2030, which would make it one of the largest tank fleets in Europe.

Speeding for online glory: the internet subculture where young men drive dangerously for likes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
07:00:51 UTC
16:00:51 KST

The hashtags tell the story of the potentially lethal social media subculture where young men film themselves hurtling at illegal speeds down busy roads: #speedhunters, #needforspeed, #racing.
The fast-driving internet trend on TikTok, Instagram and YouTube is fed by footage shot from a driver’s perspective of cars going “#fullsend” – the jargon for roaring down dual carriageways – and “#gapping” or “#swimming”, as in weaving dangerously through packed traffic. The posts attract thousands, sometimes millions of views and have been described by Andy Burnham on Monday as “truly reprehensible”.
The prime minister spoke out after seven deaths on Saturday, including two police officers and five young men aged 17 to 23, when the young men drove the wrong way down the A66 in Teesside after a police chase. It has been reported one of the young men killed in the car previously posted fast-driving clips. Cleveland police said there was currently “no evidence that filming of the activities on Friday night and Saturday morning was for the purposes of TikTok”.
Last week a similar incident shocked Ireland when five teenagers – some of whom had previously posted videos of reckless driving – were killed when their car travelling in the wrong direction on the M9 crashed into another vehicle. The Irish police said: “In some cases it is being done for social media likes.”
Several factors are behind this trend, experts say. Young men have long been sensation seekers with a tendency to push whatever limits adults impose, according to Sonia Livingstone, professor of social psychology at the London School of Economics and an expert in social media harms.
Social media now extends the momentary thrill of speed with the promise of clout and glory as the drivers’ exploits spread through the internet. It is a case, Livingstone said, of “putting their foot down in the offline world knowing it wins them points in the online world”. If views rise high enough, there is also the prospect of cash rewards from some of the social media companies.
“There is a lot of research on how the online world of fame and visibility is increasingly significant for boys and young men in a context in which they don’t have a lot of other ways of affirmation,” said Livingstone, who called the incidents absolutely horrifying.
“We might ask how else boys and young men get a moment of affirmation,” she said. “Many young people are feeling depressed and hopeless about the future. It doesn’t offer them opportunities to shine and a path where they can see their future.”
The reach of the most popular accounts can be huge. Joseph Ondrak, director at Peryton Intelligence, a company that monitors harmful online subcultures, identified a user called Squeeze Benz with more than a million followers on TikTok and Instagram and another called wheres981 with 457,000 YouTube followers. Their clips “show some incredibly dangerous driving” and have been “key in popularising the squeezing/swimming/gapping trend”, said Ondrak. He said infamy and subcultural influence appeared to be greater driving forces than monetisation.
“Both of these accounts and others like them also have an army of ‘clippers’ taking key moments from streams and longer videos and editing them for short-form and compilation consumption for higher engagement and reach,” Ondrak said.
The government reaction has been to demand the big tech platforms remove posts of dangerous driving. A spokesperson said Lisa Nandy, the culture secretary, is seeking assurances from the tech companies and from the online communications regulator Ofcom “that this content is being proactively sought and removed in line with their legal obligations and that accounts that post this type of activity are shut down immediately”.
Ofcom last month launched a separate investigation into TikTok amid concerns about children being exposed to harmful content. Dangerous driving is not mentioned among the categories of illegal content listed in the 2023 Online Safety Act which focuses on issues such as child sexual abuse, terrorism, suicide and self-harm. However, it could be considered harmful to children under the category of content promoting dangerous challenges. If so, the law requires platforms to protect children – but not anyone 18 or over – from seeing it.
TikTok said it removes videos and accounts that break its rules including content that glorifies violence, or promotes crimes that could harm people, that depicts activities likely to be imitated and that could cause significant physical harm, including risky driving. Yet clips of dangerous driving were not hard to find on Monday.
One TikTok user, CrazyGappers, showed a driver hurtling down the M25 towards Dartford in a clip titled “Serious driving #driving #gapped #racing”. Another shows a driver accelerating to high speeds along unlit lanes with the caption “nothing can top full sending your car on your favourite b roads” #fullsends #backroads”. On Instagram Ukdriverz has a clip titled “200mph on UK roads” with the caption “entertainment purposes only” while on YouTube, 2.5 million people have watched a clip of a Honda being driven at breakneck speed through a council estate and then down a narrow country road.
Instagram’s owner, Meta, said it prohibits people from promoting, advocating for or encouraging participation in high-risk viral challenges, including the trend of dangerous driving against incoming traffic. After the Guardian highlighted it, Google, which runs YouTube, removed the channel showing the speeding Honda.
“We don’t allow content featuring harmful or dangerous activities that risk serious physical harm on YouTube,” a spokesperson said. “As such, we quickly removed the flagged videos, and terminated the associated channel.”

The war on ‘loudcasting’ phones can be won, but it will take some very British nudging | Dan Hancox
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
07:00:51 UTC
16:00:51 KST

‘Interesting cities can’t be quiet”, runs one of grime DJ and music industry thinker Elijah’s epigrams – and in its essential spirit, he is right. Silent, tidy, prim cities should be treated with suspicion. Any such atmosphere denotes that something has gone wrong at a macro level: either you’ve wound up in an authoritarian regime or, worse, Switzerland.
But not all urban sounds are created equal, and some are more unwelcome than others. Take the tide of (Instagram, TikTok, YouTube) reels crashing on the shores of our collective attention on public transport, thanks to the astonishing number of grown adults who think it’s OK to surf the slopwave without headphones.
These rotters are accompanied by people taking their phone or video calls out loud on speakerphone. In the early days of mobile phones it was a widely agreed social truism that the white-collar worker unselfconsciously bellowing “I’m on the train!” into their BlackBerry was a grade-A public nuisance, plausibly worthy of throwing in the stocks. Well, at least then we were only being subjected to one end of the conversation.
The spread of 5G across the country is making such unsolicited noise more possible and more common: “loudcasting”, the BBC called it in a recent in-depth look at the phenomenon. A public backlash is suddenly mounting. Never one to miss an opportunity for free press coverage, last week Wetherspoons boss Tim Martin banned it from his pubs.
It’s funny how social pressure points like this fade in and out of public view, as the technology that touches our lives evolves: 19 years ago, the same practice was christened “sodcasting” by Pascal Wyse in this newspaper – at that point there were no reels, no AI drivel, no streaming video calls, no such thing as an Instagram influencer, nor Instagram either. The moral panic back then was about tinny MP3s being played aloud from much more basic mobile phones – and the purported juvenile delinquency that had surely led to such a crisis.
I probably annoyed a lot of Guardian readers that year, writing more than 2,000 words in defence of sodcasting: more precisely, in defence of teenagers playing music on their phones on the bus, the train or otherwise in public. There was something qualitatively different about that iteration, I would argue. It was a necessary claiming of public space by people who are often bullied out of it: adults-in-training, still working out how to exist in the outside world as independent beings, still learning to navigate their own social lives, and (an underrated asset, this) learning to enjoy music together, as a group activity. For the rest of us, this form of sodcasting amounted to an occasional, brief and usually joyful burst of alfresco music – and we could all do with hearing Crazy Cousinz and Giggs more often anyway.
The 2010 furore about sodcasting followed a decade of punching down by Britain’s power-wielding adults against its most marginalised young people – the “chavs” and “hoodies” against whom New Labour and the tabloids collectively went to war, driven by the reactionary moralism of what was risibly called “the respect agenda”. A time of asbos, public spaces protection orders and curfews for young people.
Interestingly – and admittedly anecdotally; this stuff isn’t easy to measure – sodcasting 1.0 seemed to disappear as a phenomenon after a year or two. New social behaviours that emerge in response to new popular technologies tend to do so: things settle down as a new consensus on how we should all use them is slowly reached, and reached collectively.
Let’s hope that happens again, because what we are all hearing on buses and trains thanks to sodcasting 2.0 is measurably more antisocial and individualistic: for one thing, 2010’s groups of teen sodcasters weren’t changing songs every 10 seconds. For another – warning, more anecdotal analysis incoming – these days it always seems to be full-grown adults rather than teenagers taking calls on speakerphone or watching reels with no headphones. It is maddening behaviour to anyone who has experienced it: like being on a bus or a train with someone who is flicking TV channels, constantly.
So, as Lenin once asked of matters of similarly grave importance: what is to be done? Last year, the Lib Dems proposed a £1,000 fine for sodcasting – an amusingly illiberal policy to make one of their centrepieces. For what it’s worth, I don’t think a fine is very useful, realistic or enforceable – though, God bless the ironclad French state, for it managed to find a way to do exactly that, fining a man €200 (£170) for taking a call on loudspeaker on a station platform.
The truth is that we have more sane and effective options for shaping public behaviour in the form of nudge messaging. Transport for London has a strong history of this, via adverts on its trains, tubes and buses. In 2008, its Considerate Travel campaign seemed to help quieten down the mobile phone DJs and its current Act Like a Friend and Travel Kind campaigns aim to address hate crime, misogynistic creeps and encourage others to help passengers who may be unwell. Sodcasting 2.0 pisses me off no end, too, but I think people can change with a little nudging.
Stefan Stern made an excellent case in these pages recently that we should all remove our headphones – and turn off the content altogether – to hear and more fully participate in the noisy, messy city around us. Hopefully we can achieve this via social consensus, gentle persuasion, and without the soundtrack of someone broadcasting AI monkey videos. And if all else fails, well, sod it: let’s nudge the culprits into the stocks.
- 
  Dan Hancox is a writer and editor covering music, politics and cities. His latest book is Multitudes: How Crowds Made the Modern World

Going with the grain: how restoring biodiversity led one farmer back to heritage wheat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
07:00:50 UTC
16:00:50 KST

It is the earliest harvest Henry Astor can remember. But walking through the scorched wheatfields of his Cotswolds farm, signs of life are everywhere – swarms of insects, kaleidoscopic wildflower meadows, bushy hedgerows several metres wide. A yellowhammer perches on a nearby tree.
There are 18 other red-listed birds on the farm, says Astor, who this year ringed 23 barn owls, three kestrels, two little owls as well as goshawk chicks. “Last winter we had clouds of goldfinch, chaffinch and greenfinch,” he says. Britain has lost 73 million birds since 1970; but at Bruern Farms, a small but welcome reversal is taking shape.
Between 30,000 and 40,000 trees have been planted over the past decade, many as part of a flood-mitigation scheme, some in a 17-hectare (42-acre) agroforestry section interspersing wheat with heritage fruits such as Cox’s pippin and Blenheim orange apples. Wildflower meadows are rebuilding soil fertility.
As part of his obligations as a member of the North East Cotswold Farmer Cluster, which Astor co-founded, a plot is left for bird feeding, to boost populations. According to the cluster co-chair, Tim Field, this has resulted in flocks of linnets, goldfinch and chaffinch across 40 farms involved in the feeding project, while one farm has seen more than 400 teal feeding among watercress in a wetland area.
Catastrophic biodiversity loss since the postwar “green revolution” has been well documented. Wheat played its part, as heritage grains and mixed populations gave way to vast monocultures of dwarf wheat. Several initiatives are attempting to reverse course with nature-friendly farming, the farms in Astor’s farmer cluster among them.
In all, Astor and neighbouring farmers have 800 hectares of floodplain meadow under restoration, while 3,000 hectares have been set aside for flood mitigation along the River Evenlode, including Bruern Farms’ land.
Despite this progress, Field is one of those unconvinced by the government’s recently announced “30 by 30” nature restoration plans.
“Farmer groups aren’t getting the recognition they deserve, yet we are proof that when farms are aggregated by purpose, we can be more powerful for landscape restoration at scale than has ever been achieved by public or [environmental NGO]-driven schemes.”
Astor grew up on the 490-hectare farm his grandfather bought in 1936, but left for a career as a documentary maker and in advertising. In 2017 he returned, with his wife and three young sons, to run the farm. “My father said let the farm manager farm it, do not get involved,” Astor recalls.
That might initially have been the plan, but the farm Astor returned to was not the one he remembered. When the Milk Marketing Board was abolished in 1994, causing prices to plummet, Bruern ditched dairy. It went from being a mixed farm to wholly arable, farmed by contractors who, Astor says, “don’t really care about trees or hedgerows or nature; it’s a business, they just want maximum yield”.
Yet profits were minimal. Astor says wheat farmers grow a commodity that decreases in value each year, while the costs of machinery and chemicals rise – most recently, fuel and fertiliser increased sharply during the Iran war.
Bruern Farms’ transition from conventional to heritage wheat, grown with the environment in mind, happened in stages. First came an “awakening” at a supermarket. “A bag of crappy flour was £1.20, or £1,200 a tonne. I’m selling wheat at 15p a kilo. Who is taking that money?” Astor thought.
In 2020, he was approached by Fielden whisky to grow heritage grains, including red lammas, orange devon and kent old hoary, on 140 hectares. It led him down a “rabbit hole”, sourcing the likes of miller’s choice, a “population wheat” from the South East Grain Alliance. Before modern wheat was introduced there was variety, he says. “They’d have ‘population wheat’ – 30-40 varieties [grown together], which I do today. It builds disease resistance, weather resistance; you have diversity in the field, and much longer roots, so you’re reaching the minerals.”
Proponents say heritage wheat is also more nutrient-dense, has a protein structure that results in more digestible bread and, when stoneground, retains more of its nutrients than conventional wheat.
In 2021, Helen Evans, a baker at the now-closed Flor in London, inquired about Astor’s conventional wheat, which he still grows on some of his land but hopes to phase out. “I didn’t know anything about baking,” says Astor.
At this point, he was still sending his grain to a nearby mill for processing. Commercial mills reject approximately 60% of the conventional grain sent to them for being too low in protein, and Astor began to wonder why he was accepting this when his flour was clearly in demand.
Astor began personally delivering 300kg of flour a week to Flor. He did not make a profit, but the idea of bypassing wholesalers took shape. He contacted local bakeries and bought a mill. “There was something fundamentally exciting about the idea of growing something, milling it, then having that relationship with a baker,” says Astor.
Astor says his goal is to mill 500 tonnes a year, which will allow him to reduce his cropping by half, promote biodiversity on the remaining land, reduce carbon emissions and run a viable business.
Now supplying more than 40 bakeries, Astor operates the mill as a separate business, paying his farm more than it would receive on the commodity market: £800 instead of £600 a tonne for heritage grain. Last year, the bakery chain Gail’s introduced its Bruern Farms sourdough, which is being launched on Ocado in September, followed by Waitrose in November.
But simply changing the crop will not solve everything. When Astor sent soil samples to an expert last year, they said it was low in minerals, due in part to the area’s heavy clay, which makes drainage an issue and microbial activity sluggish.
He hopes to boost the soil through natural means, such as volcanic ash and microbial teas. He applies minimal fertiliser, and the farm has not used pesticides in 15 years, preferring “intensive intercropping”, with wildflowers to attract predators that feed on aphids.
Carlos Guerra, a soil expert at the University of Coimbra in Portugal, supports this approach. He says modern wheat monocultures have “simplified soils as much as they have simplified landscapes – reducing plant and root diversity, weakening microbial communities, and increasing vulnerability to erosion, compaction and organic-matter loss”.
Replacing these systems with a diversity of cultures, as well as eliminating pesticides, planting wildflower meadows, reducing soil disturbance and using organic or microbial preparations, “can help rebuild soil structure, biodiversity and nutrient cycling”.
Astor hopes his system can be replicated throughout the country, which he believes would make farms profitable and boost food security.
His vision is nostalgic. The farm of his childhood was a “self-sufficient community”: a mixed farm supporting several families. “I’m not interested in farming the way my father farmed – 100% arable with subsidies and chemicals. I’m interested in farming the way my grandfather farmed.
“There was a connection to the village,” he says. “The community were eating the food we were growing on the farm.”
For Astor, this is not just talk. The shop and cafe employ 15 people and the farm supports rural enterprise. A 1.2-hectare market garden is run by a nearby restaurant. One local couple has 150 sheep on the land; another young woman is building a separate flock of Herdwicks. The sheep are integrated into the rotation, helping fertilise the fields.
This year, Astor harvested 190 tonnes of heritage wheat, up from 48 last year. He expects to reach the golden 500 figure by 2028.
“I have three missions,” he says. “Growing nutritional food, feeding the community, and increasing biodiversity.”

Finnish satellite firm ICEYE launches India subsidiary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
06:57:36 UTC
15:57:36 KST

- ICEYE formally established ICEYE India in New Delhi on August 24 to serve the country's defense and intelligence customers.
- The company plans to build satellite manufacturing capability in India using local suppliers and engineering talent, though no timeline has been disclosed.
ICEYE, the Finnish satellite operator, has formally established a corporate entity in New Delhi called ICEYE India, the company announced August 24. The move gives ICEYE a direct legal and operational presence in a market it has been supplying for several years without a local subsidiary.
ICEYE operates the world’s largest constellation of synthetic aperture radar (SAR) satellites, a form of imaging that uses radar rather than visible light to capture ground data. SAR imagery works through cloud cover and at night, which sets it apart from optical satellite systems.
The company said ICEYE India’s immediate focus is giving Indian defense and intelligence customers access to its satellite imagery and related intelligence products. ICEYE also said it plans to engage more broadly with India’s space and defense sector through supply-chain participation, technology validation and local capability building.
The New Delhi entity will also serve as the base for ICEYE’s manufacturing plans in India. The company said it intends to build production capability in-country, drawing on local suppliers and engineering talent, to serve Indian defense, surveillance and environmental monitoring customers. ICEYE did not disclose a timeline, investment figure or planned facility location for that manufacturing effort.
“ICEYE India means real engineering and manufacturing capability on the ground. We’re excited to build this together with the government and local partners and to support India as it strengthens its own sovereign intelligence capability,” said Rafal Modrzewski, CEO and co-founder of ICEYE.
The company said it is exploring collaboration with Indian launch providers, electronics and component manufacturers, and other technology partners, without naming specific firms or agreements.
India has been building out its own space-based surveillance capacity, and the government has pushed a policy of domestic defense manufacturing under its Aatmanirbhar Bharat, or self-reliant India, initiative. ICEYE said its approach of building local industrial capability in each country it enters aligns with those goals.
The Indian subsidiary follows a similar move by ICEYE in Germany last month, where the company also set up a national entity. National subsidiaries have become a common structure among Western satellite and defense firms seeking to bid on government contracts that require some form of sovereign or in-country control.
ICEYE has built its business around small, relatively low-cost SAR satellites that can be deployed in larger numbers than traditional radar satellites, allowing more frequent revisits of a given location. The company’s satellites currently offer imagery resolution as fine as 16 cm.
ICEYE has supplied SAR satellites to Brazil’s Air Force since 2020 and provided tactical satellite imagery to Ukraine following Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. In 2025, the company signed a deal worth roughly $200 million with Poland covering radar satellites and ground infrastructure.

More porters, fewer passengers: What really caused Ben-Gurion Airport’s staff strike? - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
06:57:19 UTC
15:57:19 KST

Since the recent wildcat strike at Ben Gurion Airport, staffing at the Israel Airports Authority (IAA) has become the main flashpoint between management and the workers' union.
The union points to a critical deficit of roughly 500 employees across all departments, arguing that an unreasonable workload ultimately triggered the system's collapse. Union Chairman Pinchas Idan claimed there are simply not enough porters to handle luggage loading and unloading, forcing staff into grueling, consecutive 12-hour shifts in unbearable heat under inhumane conditions. He added that the severe shortage is exacerbated by employees serving on active military reserve duty.
The numbers tell a different story
Anyone spending ten minutes outside at midday can sympathize with the grueling physical strain of hauling heavy baggage between aircraft and luggage carts in the summer heat. However, data obtained by Walla reveals a contrasting picture: The number of porters at Ben Gurion Airport has actually grown over the past six years, even as overall passenger traffic declined.
The baseline for comparison is 2019, widely regarded as a peak year for passenger volume at Ben Gurion. In August 2019, 2.807 million passengers passed through the airport, serviced by a workforce of 386 porters. By comparison, August 2026 is projected to see approximately 2.675 million passengers, whereas the porter workforce has expanded to 402. This reflects a net addition of 16 porters alongside a decrease of roughly 130,000 passengers.
Furthermore, a source familiar with the matter told Walla that the union never formally submitted a written request to management regarding a worker shortage.
"A union always wants more workers, and that's fine," says a source familiar with the matter. "But in this case, there is no shortage of porters because there are actually more of them. Besides, operational needs on the ground are no justification for shutting down a country."
The workers' union firmly rejects these assertions, insisting that continuous appeals were submitted to management over two months ago.
Tenured vs. temporary staffing friction
However, another source suggests the core issue stems not from total headcount, but from an imbalance between tenured and temporary staff: "In 2019, there were more temporary porters at Ben Gurion Airport. Over the years, the proportion of tenured staff increased while temporary staff declined. Temporary workers experience less burnout, are more flexible, and show higher motivation, whereas tenured staff are less willing to work. The operational model needs an overhaul - something that must be executed in cooperation with the workers' union."
Despite that structural challenge, the likelihood of Idan permitting a shift from tenured positions toward temporary hiring appears virtually non-existent - particularly amid reports that management intends to push for his removal as union chief.
Chairman of the Israel Airports Authority Yiftah Ron-Tal declined to confirm any efforts to oust Idan from leadership. "I am currently focused on managing the crisis and am not dealing with that," he says. "I have established an inquiry team to investigate the incident and draw conclusions."

Ben-Gurion Airport management had known for months about the employee shortage, which led to the recent severe disruptions earlier this month, Attorney Naomi Landau, who represents the Israel Airports Authority (IAA) employees’ union, said on the 103FM program Where’s the Money on Monday.
At the beginning of the discussion, Yael Ayalon, editor of Where’s the Money, addressed how the disruptions began and the Histadrut labor federation’s involvement.
According to her, "this time, these labor disruptions were initiated by or coordinated between the workers’ union and employees on the ground. The Histadrut discovered the dispute and the chaos only after it had already started. Although it gave formal support to the move, even in the official statement by the Histadrut chairman that same day, during the first hours of the chaos, it was stated that no such instruction or directive had been issued by the Histadrut for a strike or labor dispute."
Ayalon also addressed the lack of an official labor dispute declaration, saying that, "The Histadrut chairman was abroad; the Histadrut was on recess. The chairman of the transportation workers’ union was also abroad. That does not prevent them from intervening, but the most significant point is that despite the Histadrut speaking out about the manpower shortage, it did not declare the issue a labor dispute. Essentially, the workers’ union had limited abilities from the outset, and it could not legally launch a strike, which is what happened in practice."
Later, Attorney Landau joined the conversation and sought to demonstrate that the manpower shortage at Ben-Gurion Airport had been known for months. She quoted remarks made by Pinchas Idan last May, when he said, "I don’t know how we will get through August; we need another 400 workers. I say with full responsibility, there will probably be lines in the coming period. Management is doing everything to recruit. But right now, many more workers are still missing."
Management faced difficulties recruiting for Ben-Gurion, despite known shortages
Landau argued that additional officials within the Airports Authority had also warned about the shortage in advance, emphasizing how difficult it was the recruit workers for the required positions. "The heads of departments warned about this, absolutely," she added.
"I am already saying that management tried to recruit, and it is very difficult to recruit workers for these positions during this period. These are challenging jobs, because being a baggage handler or a firefighter at Ben-Gurion Airport during this period is very difficult. In addition, even if workers are recruited, they must undergo training, complete additional requirements, and receive security clearance to work there."
Landau then pointed the finger at the Israel Airports Authority management, claiming that the decision that led to the closure of the counters was made by management.
"Management panicked," she said, further explaining that "once those 18 workers collapsed and left after nine hours of work in the heat, instead of moving other workers from other areas of the airport who could provide support, management decided to close the counters, and only management has the authority to do that. Pinchas himself was shocked by the matter."
Airport workers' union preferred negotiation over dispute
Landau also addressed why the workers’ union did not declare a labor dispute, claiming that Idan initially preferred to negotiate with management. According to her, "We considered it, and Pinchas decided to negotiate with management. He received promises. You do not enter a labor dispute so easily, because once you enter one, there is only one path that leads to a strike, and then the workers say, 'What did you do to me?' Pinchas Idan did not want to close the airport. What exactly would closing it in August give him? What would it give the workers’ union? It gives them absolutely nothing."
At the end of the interview, Landau addressed efforts to recruit additional workers and the dispute over responsibility for the events. "Management announced that it is recruiting nearly 100 workers who are currently on unpaid leave and will fill the ranks," she added.
"And still, even when there is a fully staffed shift, there is still a manpower shortage under these conditions. There was no strike, and the ones who closed the counters were management. There was no dispute between management and the workers, except that management claimed there was no shortage of workers."

North Macedonia has made ties with Israel ‘foreign-policy priority’, FM tells 'Post' - exclusive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
06:56:51 UTC
15:56:51 KST

North Macedonia has made strengthening relations with Israel a priority of its foreign policy and is seeking to expand cooperation in areas ranging from defense and investment to tourism and water management, Foreign Minister Timčo Mucunski told The Jerusalem Post during his first official visit to Israel.
Mucunski spoke to the Post in Jerusalem on Monday following talks with Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar, during a short visit focused heavily on expanding bilateral ties.
“We have had a very strong relationship with Israel, but also myself with Gideon, over the last few years,” Mucunski said. “I think that this visit is an opportunity to move the bilateral relationship to the next step, to move from a place where we’re at right now, which is excellent bilateral relations, to having that relationship develop into various different areas of mutual importance.”
During their meeting, Sa’ar and Mucunski signed two cooperation agreements and discussed expanding ties in agriculture, water management, security, innovation, tourism, health, and education.
Expanding, investing in defense ties
Mucunski told the Post that the two sides also discussed cooperation between their defense industries, increasing investment and restoring direct air links between Israel and Macedonia.
“One of the first things that we talked about is if we can work together to establish a direct flight between Tel Aviv and Skopje, or Tel Aviv and Ohrid, which is our main tourist center and a city that I believe that every Israeli would love to visit at some point,” he said.
The two ministers also signed agreements focusing on education, culture, and sports, while tasking their teams with looking at further opportunities in water management, agriculture, investment, and defense.
Mucunski described a direct flight as an important first step toward increasing the movement of people and businesses between the countries.
“We would love to have more and more tourists from Israel visiting Skopje, visiting Ohrid, but as well as the entirety of our country,” he said.
The visit comes amid a noticeable increase in high-level contacts between Israel and North Macedonia - Skopje Mayor Orce Gjiogjievski visited for the MUNI EXPO in June, and MP Rashela Mizarahi led a parliamentary delegation from the Balkan nation in January. Mucunski said the trend reflects a deliberate policy adopted by the government of Prime Minister Hristijan Mickoski.
Mickoski believes in stronger collaboration with Israel
“Prime Minister Mickoski himself believes that stronger collaboration with Israel is a necessity for our country to also be successful,” he said. “There are many things that we can learn from you. There are many common values that we share, both domestically and internationally.
“Since the formation of our government, we have made the bilateral relationship with Israel one of the priorities of our foreign policy,” he added.
Mucunski said he and Sa’ar communicate “on a fairly regular basis” and have remained in frequent contact despite Monday marking his first visit to the country.
Sa’ar, meanwhile, thanked North Macedonia for standing alongside Israel in international forums, particularly since the October 7 massacre.
“North Macedonia has demonstrated its friendship by standing up to these attempts in the international arena,” Sa’ar said. “We appreciate its voting record and its support for Israel. Israel values its friends who stand by it in difficult times.”
For Mucunski, one example of the relationship came following the deadly nightclub fire in Kočani in March 2025, which left 63 people dead, when Israel dispatched a medical delegation to Macedonia to help treat victims.
“Gideon Sa’ar was one of the first foreign ministers to call me,” Mucunski recalled. “I might not remember the content of the call, but I remember what happened very quickly after.”
A team of Israeli doctors arrived shortly afterward and began working alongside Macedonian medical teams, he said.
“They were performing surgery in our hospitals and helping our doctors with their experience and their in-depth knowledge, and helping to save the lives of many young individuals,” Mucunski said. “This situation was proof that Israel stands by my country.”
A European gateway for Israelis
Mucunski said North Macedonia now hopes to position itself as a destination not only for Israeli tourists but also for Israeli companies seeking access to European markets.
“We want to be a gateway for Israelis who want to visit Europe,” he said. “But we want to be a gateway not just for tourists, but also for Israeli businesses.”
He pointed to Macedonia’s position along two major European transport corridors, investment in energy connectivity, and its efforts to attract foreign investment.
“We can also be a gateway for Israelis who want to invest in a European market that hasn’t been fully utilized by the Israeli business community,” Mucunski said.
Monday’s visit lasted only around 24 hours, but Mucunski said he expected it to be the first of more visits to Israel.
“This is my first visit,” he said, “but I am absolutely sure that it will not be my last.”
The Jerusalem Post will publish a longer, in-depth interview with Foreign Minister Timčo Mucunski later this week.

Death of a titan of French radio and TV: Emmanuel Macron pays tribute to Philippe Bouvard
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
06:55:44 UTC
15:55:44 KST

After an illustrious career spanning more than six decades – for which he holds a world record – beloved French cultural figure Philippe Bouvard has died aged 95. President Emmanuel Macron has paid tribute to “a free spirit”.
French journalist, TV presenter, radio host and cultural titan Philippe Bouvard has died aged 96.
Known as the creator of RTL’s daily comedy radio programme Les Grosses Têtes, which he hosted from 1977 to 2014, Bouvard was a great discoverer of comic talent and one of France’s foremost columnists.
He hosted the television program Le Petit Théâtre de Bouvard from 1982 to 1986 and helmed the radio programme Allô Bouvard from 2014 until his retirement in 2025 at age 95, after a career of more than 60 years in radio.
Bouvard holds the world record as the presenter with the most time and seasons at a single radio station.
Since the news of his death on Monday, tributes have poured in from the worlds of television and comedy, as well as politics.
French President Emmanuel Macron said that “France has lost a free spirit”.
He wrote the following tribute on X: “Philippe Bouvard will have accompanied generations of French people with his voice, his wit, his freedom of tone, and his humor -this quintessentially French taste for the witty remark. France loses a free spirit, a Grosse Tête. Thoughts to his family, his loved ones, and all those who listened to him and loved him.”
Born on 6 December 1929 in Coulommiers (Seine-et-Marne), Philippe Bouvard was renowned for his curiosity, wit, mischievous sense of humour and infectious laughter.
He started his career as a journalist and published more than 30,000 articles and over 50 books. Throughout his time on RTL, he launched the careers of numerous comedians and actors, such as Muriel Robin, Mimie Mathy, Michèle Bernier, Pascal Légitimus, the duo Chevallier and Laspalès, and countless others.
When announcing his retirement last year, Régis Ravanas, Managing Director of RTL Radio in France, said that Bouvard had “revolutionised radio”, while Gauthier Hourcade, Director of Programming, praised him as “a cultured pioneer of humour on the airwaves” with a “lively, independent and impertinent spirit”.
Reacting to his death, fellow French journalist and TV host Michel Drucker remembered a man who was “exceptionally talented”.
He told RTL that Bouvard was “a man of many talents: an author, a writer, a tireless worker, someone who knew this profession inside out”, a man who will “leave an indelible mark”.
RIP Philippe Bouvard 1929 - 2026

General Staff: Russia has lost 1,479,300 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
06:55:33 UTC
15:55:33 KST

Russia has lost around 1,479,300 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Aug. 25.
The figure includes 1,230 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report, Russia has also lost 12,293 tanks, 25,220 armored combat vehicles, 139,221 vehicles and fuel tanks, 48,567 artillery systems, 2,058 multiple launch rocket systems, 1,587 air defense systems, 440 aircraft, 354 helicopters, 479,882 unmanned aerial vehicles, 2,378 unmanned ground systems, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 to 140,000 are thought to be killed in action (KIA).
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to a lot more missing in action (MIAs).
The intensity of Russian drones and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

President says Syria ‘shakes off dark stain’ with removal from US terror list

The Aug 24 move gave Syria’s “a path to prosperity”, according to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

Australia’s music industry bans AI-generated tracks from official charts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
06:53:03 UTC
15:53:03 KST

Australia’s music industry bans AI-generated tracks from official charts
MELBOURNE, Australia (AP) — Australia’s recorded music industry will bar tracks wholly generated by artificial intelligence from official charts as burgeoning generative technologies threaten artists’ livelihoods, a representative said on Tuesday.
The crackdown comes as a variation of Madonna’s pop hit “Like a Prayer” created by an Australian producer using AI-generated vocals and drums has spent 16 weeks in the Australian top 20, stoking debate about generative AI’s place in music. It peaked at number two on the Australian Record Industry Association’s top 20 Australian singles chart in May and remained in fourth place on Tuesday.
Wholly AI-generated tracks will be banned from the ARIA charts from Monday next week, but some AI-assisted music will remain eligible, an ARIA statement said.
Tracks can be eligible only if “humans wrote the song and performed the lead vocal and the primary instruments,” among other requirements, the statement said.
AI-generated music would also be ineligible for the Australian industry’s prestigious ARIA awards.
ARIA chief executive Annabelle Herd said: “These changes reflect our intent to remain dynamic and promote the human nature of artistry in what is — to say the least — a rapidly developing space.”
“The ARIA Charts will always remain a transparent measurement of the music Australia consumes, but a chart that rewards unlicensed AI output would undercut the very basis of the recorded music we exist to represent,” Herd added.
Eligible music must also be produced using legal AI services. Music was appearing on streaming services that had apparently been developed with AI tools trained on artists’ music without authorization.
The Australian rules are in step with new principles released in July by the London-based International Federation of the Phonographic Industry. The federation represents the recording industry worldwide.
The international guidelines state that to qualify for official music charts, a track must be “substantially human made.”
Sydney Conservatorium of Music composer and lecturer Alexis Weaver told Australian Broadcasting Corp. the debate around AI in music was “exceptionally fraught and very emotional for a lot of musicians and so everyone will have a different opinion.”
Weaver applauded ARIA’s move as a “wonderful step forward” that sent a message ARIA wanted to “prioritize and value human creativity.”
“It can be quite hard to avoid AI tools in the current landscape,” Weaver said. “There is a way to use it while you’re still steering the ship and making the main creative choices.”

====================================================================================================

Sean wanted to raise his son here. Then came the 'massive black box'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
06:52:44 UTC
15:52:44 KST

In Brief
- New federal government rules will ban future data centres from being built near homes and schools.
- But residents living alongside them say they've been left out and feel powerless.
When Sean Brown moved to West Footscray two years ago, days after his son was born, he thought he'd found a good spot to raise a family — green space, a train station nearby, and a community with room to grow.
Instead, his home is now 300 metres from one of the largest data centres in the country.
"It's a massive black box in the middle of a residential area. There's this visual heaviness to it that you can't really escape," Brown tells SBS News.
NextDC's M3 facility in the Melbourne suburb brings a constant humming noise audible even 100m away, he says, while ongoing construction means near-constant light, noise and disruption.
Parking is scarce with facility workers competing for street spots, and Brown says whole streets have lost power for full days at a time during infrastructure works, with little warning and no compensation. He's also worried about health risks, and the future of his entire suburb.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Branded by its chief executive, Craig Scroggie, as "Australia's largest hyperscale AI factory", the M3 site is set to double in size by 2027 — covering 10 hectares in size, and drawing 225MW of power, 24 hours a day.
A separate facility, the Perri Melbourne Data Centre (PMDC), has been approved and planned just a few blocks over.
There are currently 162 operational data centres across Australia, with a further 90 proposed, according to the Climate Council — and it's unclear whether planned rules to data centres in residential areas will apply to any of them.
Government crackdown on new data centres
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese will use a speech to the Business Council of Australia's annual dinner on Tuesday night to announce new national rules that would block future data centres from being built near homes, schools, or prime agricultural land.
Developers will also be required to add more renewable energy to the grid than their data centres consume, minimise water use, and ensure new sites are appropriate for their size — avoiding land that could otherwise be used for housing.
"Australia is in a strong position to attract investment in data centres, but maintaining social licence will be essential," Albanese will say.
"That means ensuring energy bills do not rise, water security is maintained and locations are appropriate."
Asked about communities already living with data centres, Albanese did not directly answer when pressed on ABC Perth on Tuesday, instead pointing to the same social licence framework.
Asked by SBS News whether any measures would target existing sites or address community concern that the new rules don't cover people already affected, the prime minister's office declined to comment.
A big gap
While Brown welcomes the changes in principle, he says they don't reach the people already living with the consequences.
"If it doesn't fix the problems that have been caused in West Footscray, what's the point of it?" Brown said. "This community's just been completely sold down the river if we're not looked after. Why do our children continue to bear this risk?"
He's sceptical that the sites would have been approved under the new government frameworks and says it needs to expand to existing data centres, not just the new ones.
"If areas where they've already been inappropriately built are just left to fend for themselves, how is that fair at all?"
Associate Professor Dr Ehsan Noroozinejad, a researcher at the Urban Transformations Research Centre at Western Sydney University, welcomed the government's changes but said a clear gap remained.
"The proposed rules mainly shape future development, so they do not automatically resolve concerns around existing facilities," he told SBS News.
"Communities already living near data centres need clear standards for noise, water use, backup generators, traffic and energy impacts, backed by transparent monitoring."
Noroozinejad said Australia still needs data centres, but problems arise when they aren't put in the right places with the right infrastructure.
"It's important not to assume every data centre creates the same problems," he said. "The real issue is performance, location, and whether costs are shifted onto the surrounding community."
Dr Michael Vardon, from the Fenner School of Environment and Society at Australian National University, says the deeper problem is procedural: communities have almost no input before a facility is approved.
"This is about where new facilities go, and setback rules do not apply retrospectively," Vardon tells SBS News.
"The approval comes first, the community finds out afterwards, and by then the only remaining policy lever is the operating conditions."
Olivia Shen, director of the strategic technologies program with the United States Studies Centre at the University of Sydney, says a key provision of the changes will be whether they apply to both expansion of existing data centres as well as new projects.
"Many data centres have operated in Australia for decades, often without the surrounding community even realising they are there," Shen tells SBS News. "However, if existing data centres are allowed to expand to a point where they encroach on homes, schools and agricultural land, then this becomes a bit of a policy loophole."
'We feel really powerless'
Another West Footscray resident, Kendal Coombs, bought a house four years ago about 200 metres from the M3 site, when the block was still vacant.
She said she was initially told by council that the site was going to be a "business park", but realised a few months after moving in that it was a data centre — which was initially not a concern until its rapid expansion.
"We're all angry and concerned but it's hard to know what to do, we feel really powerless," she says.
"These projects destroy communities. If they're making these determinations [that future data centres can't be built near homes or schools] because it is too unsafe or too much of a risk to our health to live near them, then they need to pay reparations to the residents affected."
Brown says the centres have made it harder to sell up and leave.
"There's a lot of people here who are really angry about what impact this is going to have on their house prices — because I sure as hell wouldn't live near a data centre," he says. "I wouldn't buy this house."
He's pushing for compensation: voluntary housing buybacks at competitive market rates for those who no longer want to live there, relocation costs covered for owners and renters alike, and payment for disruption already endured.
NextDC has not responded to these proposals, Brown says, adding government intervention is needed.
Both Noroozinejad and Vardon say more transparency and reporting is needed for existing data centres in neighbourhoods — particularly information around water and energy use, noise, independent monitoring, and a complaints register.
Practical measures such as acoustic upgrades, landscaping, traffic management and limits on backup-generator testing can also help, Noroozinejad says.
But for Brown, it might be too late.
"They've just killed this area now," he says. "We're witnessing the death of a suburb."
NextDC declined to comment.

Beyond Empowerment: Helping women to stay in work
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
06:51:14 UTC
15:51:14 KST

Women cannot participate fully in the economy if they carry a disproportionate share of unpaid care work.
For years, CSR programmes aimed at women have focused on familiar themes such as scholarships, skill training, self-help groups and entrepreneurship. But a more fundamental barrier is increasingly coming into focus: women cannot participate fully in the economy if they carry a disproportionate share of unpaid care work.India’s 2024 Time Use Survey found that 81.5% of women aged six and above participated in unpaid domestic services on a given day, compared with 27.1% of men. Women who participated spent an average of 289 minutes a day on such work, against 88 minutes for men. The gap is also visible in unpaid caregiving, where 34% of women participated compared with 17.9% of men.
The economic consequences are clear. India’s female labour force participation rate was 40% in 2025, compared with 79.1% for men. Among women outside the labour force, 44.4% cited childcare or commitments in homemaking as their main reason.This is changing how the private sector can think about inclusion. Instead of asking only how to train or employ more women, CSR programmes can address issues that prevent them from entering and staying in paid work.
Women continue to shoulder a far greater share of unpaid domestic and caregiving work than men, a gap that affects labour-force participation and is increasingly being addressed through childcare, livelihood and inclusion-focused CSR initiatives.
Childcare is an obvious starting point. The govt’s Palna scheme provides day-care facilities for children aged six months to six years, including early stimulation, pre-school education, nutrition and health services.
By March 2025, 11,395 Anganwadi-cumcreches were approved across states and UTs, although only 1,761 were operational.This gap creates space for corporate and civil society partnerships. Vedanta’s Nand Ghar initiative is one example. Mobile Creches offers another model, combining childcare with support for children from marginalised communities.The significance of such programmes is that childcare need not be viewed simply as a welfare service. It can be economic infrastructure. If reliable childcare frees up women’s time, the next question is whether that time translates into income, assets and greater economic agency.This is where CSR-backed livelihood programmes can connect with care interventions. Mann Deshi Foundation, for example, reports having supported more than 1 million women, with 9 lakh reached through its women’s business schools since 2012.Its 2024-25 data shows that 94% of trained women reported an increase in monthly average income, with the average rise at 56%, while 76% gained ownership of assets. Its Rural Chamber of Commerce for Women reports reaching 1.3 lakh women for financial linkages, with average monthly income rising from Rs 4,300 to Rs 15,296 afterwards.The lesson for CSR is important. Training women without looking at constraints on their time, access to finance and ability to reach markets can produce limited gains. A more complete intervention connects childcare and care services with skilling, credit, entrepreneurship, market access and asset ownership.The same principle applies to disability inclusion. CSR-led organisations are increasingly helping move disability programmes from charity towards employment and economic participation. Other CSR and civil society partnerships address livelihood barriers among vulnerable groups.
What emerges is a broader understanding of inclusion. Women cannot be empowered simply by giving them a training certificate. A person with a disability cannot be included simply by providing an assistive device. A migrant worker cannot be protected merely by registration on a government portal. Effective social investment must address the barriers between a person and economic participation: care, mobility, documentation, accessibility, skills, credit and employment. For CSR, that represents a shift from funding individual interventions to building pathways. The opportunity is significant.

Trees ‘giving up’: Climate change hammers historic English gardens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
06:50:00 UTC
15:50:00 KST

Trees ‘giving up’: Climate change hammers historic English gardens
- Historic English gardens, like Hampton Court, face severe damage from climate change, with mature trees dying due to heatwaves and droughts.
- Gardeners struggle to maintain traditional plants and trees, considering new drought-resistant species for future sustainability.
- Experts warn rapid climate shifts threaten garden heritage, urging difficult changes to preserve these cultural landscapes for coming decades.
AI generated
LONDON – At Hampton Court Palace in Britain, head gardener Graham Dillamore strode across the burnt beige grass in the spectacular formal gardens south-west of London, laid out in the 17th century.
“If we have a summer like this next year, by God, it’s going to be a struggle,” said Dillamore, who has spent more than 20 years tending the gardens of the Baroque and Tudor red-brick palace where King Henry VIII once caroused.
Created by master designers such as Lancelot “Capability” Brown and William Kent, the gardens of stately homes such as Hampton Court, Blenheim Palace, and Chatsworth House are among England’s top visitor attractions.
But their historic style of planting and ancient trees are being hammered by climate change – including record heatwaves and drought in the summer of 2026.
Gardeners told AFP they were not embarrassed by straw-like lawns – feeling visitors, also facing water restrictions, are understanding – but the concern is for the long-term consequences and keeping the spirit of their gardens alive.
Mature trees that take decades to establish are drooping, and some have leaves turning brown in August in a stress reaction to excessive heat.
“Some of these trees have actually given up. They’re not going to come back, they’re finished,” said Dillamore, who also oversees gardens at Kensington Palace, the official London residence of Prince William and his wife, Catherine.
“We’re losing mature tree stock and that’s tragic in a historic garden.”
“We’ve already lost trees,” said Rosie Fyles, head of gardens at Chiswick House in west London, whose Kent-designed shady lawns dotted with statues and cedars of Lebanon date back to the 18th century.
Suffering most are trees “we really associate with an English garden or an English landscape”, she said: Oaks, sycamores, birch, limes.
“I think there’s only so much stress they can withstand,” said the gardener, who tends 1,800 trees.
It is not practicable to water mature trees, gardeners explained.
At Chiswick, staff were watering drooping camellias and lilacs, shrubs that normally thrive in sun.
The garden has boosted its capacity to harvest rainwater, but its stocks ran out several months ago.
“There’s only so much we can intervene and control,” said Fyles, admitting this was hard to accept as a professional gardener.
“It’s sobering. It means that we’re having to think about what we plant going forward, what trees will be sustainable going forward in the future climate.”
“I get the feeling we’re in uncharted territory,” said Dillamore.
“I’ve never felt so uncertain about the future in historic gardens and landscapes as I do now.”
‘On the front line’
Staff at historic gardens surveyed by the National Lottery Heritage Fund earlier in 2026 all said climate change was having an impact – not just drought, but also heavy storms and excessive rain in winter that spawns fungus and bugs.
Historic gardens are “really on the front line of climate change”, said Drew Bennellick, the Heritage Fund’s head of lands, seas and nature policy, and “the changes are happening actually quite quickly now”.
“We’ve seen sites that lost 80 per cent of their tree cover,” he told AFP.
Climate modelling by researchers at the Royal Botanic Gardens at Kew, a UNESCO World Heritage site, predicted that by 2090, 50 per cent of their trees will be at risk of death.
Historic gardens “must be protected and preserved”, said Dillamore.
“But they’ve also got to change over the next few years – otherwise we’re going to lose them.”
And this calls for “some very, very difficult decisions”, he admitted.
Some are shifting to Mediterranean plants, Bennellick said, “more grasses, more herbaceous perennials that can survive the drought conditions”.
At Hampton Court, Dillamore pointed to vibrant pink flowers with bright-green foliage.
Garden designer Ann-Marie Powell created test beds of long-lived plants happy in high temperatures, including Siskiyou Pink plants, native to the southern United States.
Planted in April, they look vigorous despite no automatic irrigation, as do other flowers such as daisy-like echinaceas from US prairies.
Dillamore said he was happy with the result.
Hampton Court and Chiswick have also stopped digging over flowerbeds and relaxed about weeds.
The Royal Horticultural Society gardening charity announced in August it is considering moving some of its heat-stressed hydrangea collection from Surrey, south-west of London, to other regions of England.
“The gardens tell the story of Hampton Court just as much as the palace, so I can’t pack this garden up and move it,” said Dillamore.
“We’ve got to retain that feel, the spirit of the place.” AFP

Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC) Prime Minister Unal Ustel on Monday condemned attempts by a far-right Greek Cypriot party to block a youth football training camp planned by Spanish club Barcelona in the country.

Ustel said the obstruction efforts reflected what he described as the unchanged attitude of Greek Cypriot politics toward the Turkish Cypriot people.
“We did not submit to this mentality yesterday, and we will not submit to it today,” he said.
“Turkish Cypriot youth will meet young people from all over the world, take part in sports, and share their art and culture. Our state will continue to pave the way for our people’s determination in this direction.”
Ustel recalled that the Nexus Festival, which was expected to be held in the TRNC, was canceled following pressure from the Greek Cypriot side.
Serbian music organization EXIT, which had previously announced its participation in the September festival near Kyrenia Castle, was forced to withdraw, according to Turkish Cypriot officials.
The withdrawal was reportedly influenced by diplomatic initiatives undertaken by the Greek Cypriot administration with the Serbian government following pressure from ELAM.
The far-right party has also called for diplomatic pressure on the countries of artists expected to participate in the Zamna Music Festival in an effort to prevent international attendance.
