German investigators find third drone and suspected explosives at Leipzig/Halle Airport, local media says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
06:49:10 UTC
15:49:10 KST

Leipzig/Halle airport in eastern Germany plays a key role in the transport of military goods, including by the German military and NATO allies, and also serves as a base for Ukraine's Antonov Airlines.
Investigators in Germany have found a third drone and what they suspect are explosives believed to be linked to an attempted attack on Leipzig/Halle airport earlier this month, public broadcasters NDR and WDR and the Süddeutsche Zeitung daily reported on Tuesday.
The drone was discovered west of the airport on 14 August, 10 days after the initial attack attempt.
Investigators reportedly also discovered around 50 grams of what they suspect is the military explosive hexogen, according to local media.
Other leads took investigators to Kursdorf, north of the airport. There, officers found a device which may have been used to control a drone. According to current findings, an antenna and electronic components had been taped to a tree.
In the immediate vicinity, emergency services also found scorched earth and metal fragments. Investigators are examining whether this could be a possible blast site.
The attempted attack
German police deployed a bomb disposal robot at the overnight into the 5 August after a drone was found on the tarmac near a Ukrainian cargo plane, sparking alarm and forcing the diversion of numerous flights.
One aircraft that had to abort its scheduled landing at Leipzig-Halle airport then collided mid-air with an unknown object nearby but later landed safely elsewhere, the government said.
It was later confirmed that a drone equipped with explosives and a detonator had been found near an aircraft belonging to the Ukrainian cargo carrier Antonov Airlines, a NATO spokesperson said on Wednesday,
According to the Kyiv Independent news site, the suspicious object was destroyed in a controlled explosion.
Police spokesperson Olaf Hoppe told Euronews that, at the same time as the sighting, an object was found in the area of the southern runway which the federal police examined. He declined to confirm that a drone had been sighted.
X-ray analysis revealed it to be a drone.
The airport in eastern Germany plays a key role in the transport of military goods, including by the German military and NATO allies, and also serves as a base for Ukraine's Antonov Airlines.
Video footage from a local news agency showed the bomb disposal robot near an Antonov plane painted with the Ukrainian colours yellow and blue and with the words "Be Brave Like Kherson" written on the side, a reference to a Ukrainian region battered by Russian strikes.
The Bild daily reported that the plane that collided with an unknown object mid-air was a DHL cargo aircraft that was hit about six kilometres away, sustaining minor damage on the nose that was discovered when it later landed safely at Hanover airport.
German police first reported on Wednesday morning that a "security-related incident" had temporarily halted flights to the airport.
"Shortly before midnight, an unidentified flying object was sighted near Leipzig-Halle Airport, prompting the diversion of several aircraft, including a passenger plane, to other airports", they said.
A passenger plane from Mallorca as well as several cargo planes heading there had to be sent to other locations.
Series of drone sightings
Germany and other European countries have repeatedly observed drones flying over sensitive sites such as airports, military bases and industrial plants.
Authorities in Germany, one of Ukraine's biggest military supporters, have said they suspect Russia of orchestrating many of the incidents as part of a campaign of sabotage, espionage and disinformation.
In July 2024 a parcel burst into flames on the ground at Leipzig airport before it could be loaded onto a DHL cargo plane, part of what security services treated as a suspected Moscow-linked arson sabotage plot.
Russia has denied being behind any such incidents.
Last year a Chinese national was convicted for passing on information about flight schedules and cargo movements at Leipzig-Halle airport to a man spying for Beijing.
In October last year, local media reported that a laser installation had been deployed near Munich airport to protect the facility from drone sightings. That came after the airport was closed for two consecutive days over suspicious drone sightings.
In November, flight operations at Berlin's Brandenburg Airport were interrupted for around two hours due to a drone sighting in its airspace.
Incidents of unidentified drones flying in Germany's airspace are on the rise with the country's air navigation service DFS saying 144 drone overflights were logged last year, with 35 incidents clustered around Frankfurt Airport.

Stone collection turns into an international business

2026-08-25
06:42:04 UTC
15:42:04 KST

Sedat Çam examines each stone he finds, shares them on social media and began selling his collection online in 2020 as interest grew.
What started as a literal trip over a stone turned into a lifelong obsession for one biologist, whose collection has since expanded to nearly 15,000 specimens across 250 distinct varieties, some of which are now exported internationally.
Sedat Çam, 42, who lives in Hatay’s Antakya district and works as a finance officer at a private company, began collecting stones in 2016 after tripping over one during a walk. His curiosity about stones grew as he began researching them and collecting different varieties during nature hikes whenever he had free time.
Çam carefully examines each stone he finds and shares them with fellow enthusiasts on social media. Growing interest in his collection led him to enter e-commerce in 2020.
In 2023, he converted the roof of his home in Kuruyer neighborhood into a workshop to better display his collection.
The workshop now houses nearly 15,000 natural stones from 250 varieties, including citrine, amethyst, fluorite, coral, obsidian, aquamarine and garden quartz. Çam sells the stones both in Türkiye and abroad.
Çam told state-run Anadolu Agency that he spends his free time either searching for stones in nature or working on his collection at his workshop.
He said searching for stones in nature helps him escape stress and find peace, adding that every stone he discovers gives him a different sense of enjoyment.
Çam brings the stones he collects to his workshop for detailed examination and carefully cleans each one.
“We only use pressurized hot water to clean the stones. We never use chemicals and we are against using them. We have never used chemicals for cleaning and do not intend to do so. We have special equipment for this. We also use paintbrush-style brushes and specially purchased toothbrushes to remove particles between the stones. We clean our stones thoroughly with toothpicks and long needles and try to send them to collectors who are passionate about stones,” he said.
Çam said that in addition to stones he collects himself in nature, he also sources stones from different parts of Türkiye, as well as countries including India, Pakistan, China and Japan.
He said stone enthusiasts contact him through social media.
“We have demand from abroad. We have sent stones to Argentina, Belgium, France, England and Romania. Last week, five boxes of stones were also sent to Greece. Our prices start at 200 Turkish Liras, while our most expensive product is priced at up to 45,000 liras,” he said.

====================================================================================================

The Iran war is bringing cyberwarfare into critical infrastructure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
06:37:32 UTC
15:37:32 KST

The Iran war is bringing cyberwarfare into critical infrastructure
Recent attacks in the UK and the US demonstrate critical vulnerabilities that governments need to urgently address.
Media reports about a cyberattack that forced a British power plant offline for four days should be taken seriously far beyond the United Kingdom. It gives us a glimpse of how the Iran conflict could develop and signals to governments and businesses around the world that they need to be ready for a new battlefield.
The facility reportedly targeted by Iran-linked hackers was relatively small, and the British government has stressed that there was no risk to the wider energy system. That is important context, but it would be a mistake to judge the significance of this attack purely by how much electricity was lost. The question for every country operating critical infrastructure is what happens when the target is bigger.
We have already seen reasons to be concerned elsewhere as well. Water and wastewater systems across at least 12 states in the United States have recently reported cyberattacks. More than 30 community water systems were affected in Minnesota alone. In Georgia, one incident caused a drop in water pressure and led to a boil-water advisory.
The US government has not publicly accused Iran of the attacks, but reports point to a hacker group linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). These incidents mark an important shift in cybersecurity.
For years, much of the public conversation around cyberthreats focused on data. People understood that hackers could steal passwords, empty bank accounts, leak personal information or lock a company out of its computer system. Critical infrastructure creates a very different risk because the systems being attacked control parts of the physical world.
For societies to function, electricity has to be generated and distributed, water has to be pumped and treated, transport networks have to operate and telecommunications have to stay online. Increasingly, technology sits underneath all of these systems.
That technology creates enormous efficiencies, but it also creates opportunities for attackers. In the US, authorities have specifically warned about Iranian-affiliated actors targeting internet-connected programmable logic controllers, the industrial technology used to control physical equipment and processes. US agencies have identified activity across water, energy and government services, including attempts that have resulted in operational disruption.
This is the part of the Iran conflict that countries well beyond the Middle East need to consider. Geography offers far less protection in cyberwarfare.
An organisation does not need to be sitting in Tehran or Tel Aviv to find itself caught up in the conflict. Infrastructure thousands of miles away can become a target because of the country it operates in, the technology it uses, its suppliers or simply because an attacker sees an opportunity to cause disruption.
We should also be careful about assuming that the objective of every attack is catastrophic damage. An attacker may want intelligence, disruption, publicity or leverage. They may simply want to demonstrate that they can get in.
That makes smaller incidents important. If an attacker compromises a relatively minor facility, the immediate consequences may be limited, but the access itself can tell us something about capability and intent.
There is another problem which governments cannot afford to ignore: critical infrastructure does not operate in neat isolation.
Energy supports communications, transport, healthcare, finance and industry. Communications underpin payments and emergency services. Water systems need power and digital controls. A successful attack does not necessarily need to bring down an entire national system to create serious consequences if disruption begins to spread through organisations that depend on one another.
This is why resilience now matters just as much as defence.
There is a dangerous temptation in cybersecurity to build strategies around preventing attackers from getting inside. Prevention remains essential, but no government or company can sensibly work on the assumption that every attack will be stopped.
Operators need to know what happens after somebody gets through. Can essential services continue? Can systems be isolated? Are manual controls available where appropriate? How quickly can operations be restored? Do organisations understand which suppliers and connected systems they depend upon?
The FBI has already been advising affected US water utilities to practise how they would revert to manual controls if automated systems were compromised. That is a revealing piece of advice because it acknowledges the reality facing critical infrastructure operators: resilience to cyberattacks ultimately has to include the ability to keep the physical world working when technology fails.
Governments and operators should be reviewing their exposure now, particularly where operational technology is accessible from the internet, checking the security of suppliers and preparing for the possibility that an attacker succeeds despite their defences.
The uncomfortable lesson from the past few weeks is that cybersecurity is becoming about far more than protecting information. When cyberattacks can interfere with electricity and water, cybersecurity becomes part of protecting vital systems that ensure societies continue to function.
We should be preparing on that basis now, because discovering the weaknesses in critical infrastructure during a serious attack would be far too late.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

====================================================================================================

'She didn't care what anybody thought': Margaret Olley in five paintings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
06:36:42 UTC
15:36:42 KST

Five artworks to see at Margaret Olley: Australian Intimiste at the National Art School
In 1945, Margaret Olley — one of Australia's most celebrated painters — graduated from the National Art School, then known as East Sydney Technical College, with first-class honours.
Within two years the Lismore-born artist would win the first-ever Mosman Art Prize and join Sydney's post-war art scene, alongside artists like William Dobell, Sidney Nolan and Donald Friend.
During her life she would hold more than 90 solo exhibitions; influence artists like Cressida Campbell and Ben Quilty; establish a trust to buy paintings for public galleries; and be painted for an Archibald Prize-winning portrait not once, but twice.
Now, she's being celebrated with a retrospective at her alma mater, titled Australia Intimiste. The intimism of the title refers to the late 19th-century art movement where artists like Pierre Bonnard and Édouard Vuillard painted intimate, domestic scenes from which Olley gathered much inspiration.
"She loved this place," curator Katrina Cashman says of the National Art School, where Olley began her career.
"She spent her whole life working towards the pursuit of beauty.
"She worked very diligently and worked very hard to maintain [her success]. She had her ups and downs. She had various health struggles over the years. She suffered from depression at times.
"But she was relentless in that pursuit of her primary passion: beauty."
Portrait in the mirror
Olley painted Portrait in the mirror in 1948 when she was just 25, living on Sydney's Lower North Shore with her friend and fellow artist Margaret Cilento.
Cashman describes it as a turning point in Olley's career: "She's really establishing herself. She's recognising that she needs a space away from the National Art School to create her own work."
While she had graduated three years earlier, Olley was still a regular on campus, attending evening classes until the year she painted Portrait in the mirror.
That same year, Olley held her first solo exhibition, in Sydney, where both the Art Gallery of New South Wales and the National Gallery of Victoria purchased works.
"This painting is so special because it shows us who she is and who she's going to become," Cashman says.
Portrait in the mirror is one of many self-portraits of Olley.
"Her own image was something she could find solace in, and it expressed her interior world," Cashman says.
The dressing room table in the painting is adorned with flowers, fruit and postcards of famous works of art.
"[Portrait in the mirror is] the very beginning of her focusing on objects, on cherished items, and the classic still life study … but putting her own spin on [it]" Cashman says.
"She loved flowers as much as she loved people — they were a visual language in themselves … [And] she's surrounded her image with these beautiful pieces of art that she loves."
Spare bedroom
In 1970, Olley painted Spare bedroom in her family home of Farndon in Brisbane's West End.
"I love this work because it's actually a very rich interior," Cashman says.
The room depicted — in a "rusty sienna brown" — was a kind of side room, leading to a sunroom out the back.
"It's a painting of absence, but you get that feeling of presence," Cashman says.
"Even the way the chairs are positioned — you get that feeling somebody's just walked out of the room.
"You've got this beautiful, filtered light coming through from a window, presumably in the next room. You've got this feeling of spaciousness and air, like the space is well-ventilated, with a breeze flowing through it."
Cashman admires the simplicity of Spare bedroom, compared to some of Olley's more densely populated paintings.
"It has a lot to say about the idea of the intimate interior," Cashman says.
It's a style of painting unlike the abstract art or large-scale paintings that were fashionable at the time.
"Still life paintings were not de rigueur," Cashman explains.
"So, I think [Olley] was out of step in some ways with a certain part of the art sector who would not have considered this to be contemporary art with a capital C.
"But she persisted regardless. She didn't care what anybody thought of her work."
Kitchen still life
Olley would often paint in the evening with fellow artist David Strachan, who she met in the 40s.
"[Strachan] believed that the night-time was kind of pregnant with creative possibilities," Cashman explains. "There's something happening in the energy of the night."
After he died in 1970 in a car accident, she got permission from his sister to continue using his Sydney home as a studio, where, in 1976, she painted Kitchen still life.
"It's a simple image," Cashman says. "We see the pots on the stove, the garlic, the onions, the kale, the salt and pepper, the accoutrements. We've got this beautiful dark blue panel at the back, which is the window to the evening sky outside."
Cashman likes the "strange feel" of the painting. "It's slightly menacing with the knife. They're about to cut up the onions or they're about to do the cooking, but there's something about the way that knife is placed."
The ingredients and utensils also seem to indicate there's a "person in that space" — a presence within an absence as in Spare bedroom.
"I just love the energy of this painting, knowing it's painted at night, the stillness, the quiet, that moody blue sky," Cashman says.
Homage to Manet
Often, Olley would replicate the paintings of famous artists in her work, including 1987's Homage to Manet.
She painted a bowl of cherries and a jug of blue flowers in her kitchen, where she pinned a postcard of French artist Édouard Manet's 1868-9 painting The Balcony and a poster-size version of the work's seated figure: Berthe Morisot, a painter who married Manet's brother Eugene.
The Balcony itself was inspired by Spanish artist Francisco Goya's Majas on the Balcony.
"It's a self-consciously devotional act to include these works [in her art]," Cashman says.
"It's not a postmodern appropriation with any sense of irony. She's not poking fun. It very genuinely is an homage to these great painters that she knows and loves."
Cashman also admires the painting's "extraordinary" use of colour, "the richness of the patina, the focus on the female protagonist, and the focus on the delicacy of the flowers".
Incorporating famous artworks into her paintings was in some ways a means for Olley to work on her craft.
"Transcription is a part of art teaching," Cashman explains. "It's a deliberate thing to be able to transcribe another person's work and learn from it."
It was also simply a reflection of life. Olley's home was "completely strewn with images by other artists", Cashman says.
"Margaret was continually being replenished and refreshed by [other artists' work]."
The yellow room triptych
Olley continued to paint until the end of her life. She was preparing for an exhibition when she died in 2011, at the age of 88.
In her final years, she painted The yellow room triptych, a living room scene spanning 2.7 metres.
"She's choosing yellow as the colour to represent sunlight and the colour itself emits this sense of light," Cashman says.
It's that light the curator finds so compelling.
"The sunlight coming through the window is bouncing off that wall on the right-hand side and glimmering across the gold in the Chinese screen, and diffuse light is coming off those lemons.
"The energy and the mastery of colour is what makes [Olley] so special."
The yellow room triptych draws together much of Olley's practice, like the paintings by fellow artists, including Dance by French artist Henri Matisse; and the precious objects meticulously arranged beneath the window.
"We've still got that passage to the garden, just beyond, and that vibrancy of that green and the freshness of the light that's coming through and spilling onto the arrangement," Cashman says. "Then in the background she's got these very muted pinks and browns."
Like so many of Olley's still life paintings, the space also feels lived in — like someone has only just left the room.
"For me, that ripple in the fabric [of the curtains] suggests someone whose hand has just touched that," Cashman says.
Margaret Olley: Australian Intimiste is at the National Art School, Sydney, until October 24.

"Our Southeast Asian region is not immune from these risks. Indeed, it is no longer a mere climate change but an acute climate crisis our global community needs to address together," he said at the opening ceremony of a parliamentary multi-stakeholder dialogue on responsible investment for food and climate security in ASEAN.

Farmers across Southeast Asia face severe vulnerabilities from volatile weather patterns, including intensified droughts and devastating floods. To mitigate these threats, Yeap called for a strategic shift in regional funding.
"It is necessary to invest more in developing climate-resilient agriculture, climate adaptation, water resource management, and smart early warning systems," he said.
Yeap highlighted that the ASEAN Guidelines on Promoting Responsible Investment in Food, Agriculture, and Forestry (ASEAN RAI), adopted in 2018, serve as a visionary framework.
The guidelines outline core principles to safely direct investments flowing into the region's food, agriculture, and forestry sectors, he added.
"Crucially, the ASEAN RAI identifies food security, as well as climate change mitigation and adaptation, as central pillars of responsible investment," he said.
Yeap emphasized that passing laws is only the beginning. He urged members of parliament across the region to actively monitor executive branches and relevant agencies to ensure that national agricultural strategies and investment promotion policies actually deliver on food and climate security. ■

BEIJING, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- A draft revision to the Agriculture Law was submitted Tuesday to a standing committee session of China's top legislature for a second review.
The latest draft seeks to improve measures supporting agricultural and rural economic development.
The Agriculture Law, a fundamental piece of legislation governing the agricultural and rural economy, was first enacted in 1993, and comprehensively revised in 2002. The law was amended in 2009 and 2012 through individual provisions, respectively.
The draft revision was first submitted to a session of the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress for deliberation in April this year and was later released to solicit public opinion.
Based on broad consultation, the second draft adds provisions to coordinate efforts to promote agricultural technology, green production, quality improvement and brand building.
It also proposes safeguarding seed security and modernizing the seed industry, improving the coverage and service quality of agricultural insurance, and encouraging the integration of new technologies into agricultural production, operations and management.
To strengthen rural development and governance, the revised draft includes provisions to boost rural governance and continuously enhance farmers' sense of fulfillment, happiness and security.
The draft requires governments at all levels to establish long-term mechanisms to eliminate unnecessary formalities and ease burdens at the primary level. It also calls for support for international exchanges and cooperation in agriculture, as well as active participation in global governance on sustainable agricultural development and food security.
The legislative session runs from Tuesday to Friday. ■

Economic Watch: U.S. consumers crave affordable Chinese EVs amid soaring car prices
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
14:36:00 CST
15:36:00 KST

by Julia Pierrepont III
LOS ANGELES, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- As American automakers increasingly focus on higher-priced, more profitable vehicles, a growing number of ordinary Americans are calling for highly cost-effective imports from China to fill the void.
"I'm an auto mechanic," Juan Vega, a local Angeleno, told Xinhua in a recent interview. "And Chinese cars give great value for the price compared to American cars. In America, we say it's all about market competition, so why can't I buy an affordable Chinese car if I want one?"
That sentiment is becoming increasingly common because cars made in China by companies such as BYD and Geely can cost as little as the equivalent of 10,000 to 20,000 U.S. dollars but are effectively shut out of the U.S. passenger-car market by tariffs and other restrictions. Meanwhile, average new-vehicle transaction prices in the country have risen to around 49,000 dollars to 50,000 dollars in recent years. Typical monthly payments have remained high, as elevated interest rates, insurance premiums and repair costs have added to the burden.
Despite facing steep tariffs, Waymo, which operates public commercial robotaxi services in several U.S. metropolitan areas, has imported over 3,200 Chinese-built Zeekr electric minivans into the United States since 2024. But for millions of ordinary Americans, the new-car market is becoming less a marketplace than a gated community.
Detroit's product strategy has shifted decisively toward trucks, SUVs and premium models because those vehicles offer higher profit margins. Ford has largely abandoned traditional sedans in the U.S. market, while General Motors and Stellantis have leaned heavily on pickups, large SUVs and higher-priced configurations, leaving many U.S. consumers with fewer affordable options.
Sam Fiorani, vice president of Global Vehicle Forecasting at AutoForecast Solutions, has argued that Chinese automakers have succeeded in producing reasonably priced small and midsize cars that appeal to consumers.
"The ride, the handling, the comfort and the luxury tech were off the charts," said car enthusiast Ken Wheeler, 39, who had test-driven a Chinese vehicle at a Consumer Electronics Show (CES) event. "And the price -- I'm sold!"
With U.S. car costs so high, Edmunds, a car-shopping research firm, said in a recent survey that 73 percent of U.S. consumers had delayed buying a vehicle because of high prices. "Affordability concerns among American car shoppers aren't going away anytime soon," it concluded.
"U.S. car prices are killing us," said R. Clark, 39, a Californian native and restaurant worker with modest wages and a family of three. "I gotta put off buying a new one again this year, even though my current one is in for repairs half the time."
For workers who need reliable transportation to get to jobs, schools, medical care and childcare, the loss of affordable cars can have consequences far beyond household budgets.
But affordable cars from China remain effectively off-limits to American consumers, largely because of steep tariffs and other trade and security restrictions.
The result, consumer advocates and some industry analysts say, is a policy collision: Washington says it is protecting American jobs and national security, while many households are left struggling with higher car bills and fewer affordable transportation options.
Chinese automakers have built small electric cars that sell overseas at prices well below many U.S. options and have received praise for their efficiency, technology and value. Even so, the tariff barrier makes direct competition in the U.S. market impossible, forestalling market testing. The problem has deepened since the United States imposed steep tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles.
Chinese automakers have increasingly turned to international celebrities to promote their brands. Leonardo DiCaprio became a brand ambassador for BYD's new-energy vehicles in China in 2016, while Daniel Craig has more recently appeared in advertising for BYD's premium brand, Denza.
Views from the automotive community shed light on the issue.
Clint Simone, senior features editor at Edmunds, told Reuters that he had driven several Chinese vehicles at CES earlier this year and was struck by their value proposition. "The technology they offer for those lower price tags was astounding," Simone said.
Ben Nelmes, chief executive of New Automotive, told CBS News earlier this year, "China is miles ahead of the rest of the world."
"If China is willing to make a good car I can actually afford and Detroit won't, then bring it on," a family man who called himself Clark told Xinhua. "The government should either help guys like us by pressuring American carmakers to step up with rides in our price range -- or get out of the way and let China do it."
But despite stepping away from the low-priced sedan market, Detroit automakers and their allies warn that a wave of low-cost Chinese vehicles could damage U.S. factories, suppliers and dealerships.
"They used that tired old argument against Japanese cars in the 1970s, and Detroit didn't go under then, did it?" Vega told Xinhua.
Critics said those older arguments may protect shareholders, executives and lobbyists at the expense of ordinary American consumers. They argued the policy has created a protective wall around companies that increasingly prefer to sell fewer, more expensive vehicles rather than competing aggressively for budget-conscious buyers.
Policy discussions in Washington frequently focus on industrial strategy, geopolitical rivalry and the profits of major manufacturers. Policymakers can overlook how deeply transportation affordability affects ordinary Americans. A rule that looks prudent from a national security briefing can be punitive to a worker who cannot afford the vehicles left on the lot. ■

Pacific nations could save hundreds of millions of dollars from renewable shift: report

14:35:45 CST
15:35:45 KST

SYDNEY, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- Pacific island countries could save hundreds of millions of dollars annually by replacing imported fossil fuels with renewable energy, according to a report released on Tuesday.
The report by Australia's University of New South Wales Institute for Climate Risk & Response found Pacific nations spend between 10 and 25 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) on fossil fuel imports.
As around 80 percent of the Pacific's energy supply comes from imported oil products, this year's Middle East conflict has driven Pacific diesel prices up by about 35 percent, intensifying pressure on economies heavily dependent on imported fuels, the report said.
The region spends about 1 billion U.S. dollars annually importing diesel for electricity generation, and replacing diesel power with solar energy, batteries and upgraded electricity grids could save around 700 million U.S. dollars a year, it said.
The report estimated that the Pacific needs about 2.2 gigawatts of new renewable generation and 8,800 megawatt-hours of battery storage to replace diesel power.
However, it said around 650 million U.S. dollars in international finance is needed annually to meet the region's renewable-energy targets, compared with about 216 million U.S. dollars received in 2024. ■

====================================================================================================

Economic Watch: Japan's rice market swings from shortage fears to oversupply woes
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
14:35:43 CST
15:35:43 KST

TOKYO, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- Sushi, rice balls, curry rice and eel rice - rice is an indispensable part of Japanese people's daily diet. Yet over the past year or so, rice prices in Japan have gone on a roller-coaster ride: prices surged from the summer of 2024, at one point triggering a nationwide "rice shortage," only to fall rapidly since the beginning of this year as inventories grew and newly harvested rice entered the market. Farmers in some producing areas are now even facing the prospect of selling rice at a loss.
Analysts believe that the dramatic shift from consumers being unable to afford rice to producers struggling to sell it reflects an imbalance between supply and demand in Japan's rice market. If prices continue to decline, farmers' willingness to grow rice could be undermined, further weakening the country's agricultural production base.
VOLATILE RICE PRICES
Rice prices in Japan began rising sharply in the summer of 2024, with supermarkets in many areas imposing purchase limits or running out of supplies. The Japanese government released several rounds of reserve rice in an effort to stabilize prices, but the measures had limited effect.
In 2025, prices of rice-related products rose 67.5 percent, the largest increase since comparable records began in 1971. The average retail price for a 5-kilogram bag of rice in Japan reached a record peak of 4,416 yen (about 27.7 U.S. dollars) at the end of last year.
Prices have gradually declined this year. According to the latest data from Japan's Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries, the average retail price for a 5-kilogram bag of rice stood at 3,191 yen during the week of Aug. 10-16.
The arrival of newly harvested rice is putting further downward pressure on prices. Advance payments made by the National Federation of Agricultural Cooperative Associations (ZEN-NOH) to farmers are regarded as an important benchmark for new rice prices. Recent figures from major producing regions indicate substantial reductions in advance payments, suggesting that prices for the new crop could fall further.
According to Japanese media reports, Niigata Prefecture, Japan's largest rice-producing region, has set the advance payment for ordinary Koshihikari rice produced in 2026 at 18,500 yen per 60 kilograms, down 38 percent from the previous year. Hokkaido Prefecture has set the advance payment for its main rice varieties at 17,000 yen per 60 kilograms, a decline of 41 percent.
Some supermarkets have already begun selling rice harvested in 2026, but an unusual phenomenon has emerged: newly harvested rice is in some cases cheaper than older rice. Naoya Matsudaira, assistant professor at the School of Agriculture, Utsunomiya University, said this price inversion between new and old rice could persist.
PERSISTENT IMBALANCE
Whether rice prices are soaring or plunging, the fundamental problem is an imbalance between supply and demand.
In reviewing the "rice shortage" in its 2025 agricultural white paper, the agriculture ministry acknowledged that the government had underestimated rice demand and consequently failed to arrange sufficient planting acreage. High temperatures and other factors also reduced yields and quality, tightening supply. Earthquake warnings and other developments prompted consumers to stockpile rice, further widening the supply gap. Delays in the government's assessment of market conditions and in releasing reserve rice also prolonged the shortage.
Japan's rice market is now facing the opposite imbalance: supply has expanded significantly while demand has weakened.
"Supply and demand are currently out of balance to the worst extent," said Sadao Yamamoto, president of major rice wholesaler ZEN-NOH Pearl Rice.
On the supply side, rice inventories have surged. According to agriculture ministry statistics, private-sector rice inventories stood at 2.43 million tons at the end of June, up 57 percent year on year and the highest level on record. The figure is well above the 1.8 million to 2 million tons generally considered an appropriate level.
The rapid increase in inventories reflects several factors, including expanded planting after the government raised its expectations for rice demand, as well as the release of reserve rice and increased rice imports.
On the demand side, the previous surge in prices appears to have changed consumer behavior.
Masaaki Yamaguchi, a senior analyst at Nomura Securities, said that as rice prices soared, rice consumption in Japan declined again last year. Statistics from an organization supporting stable rice supplies show that Japan's per-capita monthly rice consumption was 4.435 kilograms in fiscal 2025, a 6.1 percent year-on-year decrease and the lowest level in seven years.
Some analysts believe that as rice became more expensive, an increasing number of Japanese households switched to noodles and bread, which are cheaper alternatives.
An editorial in the Tokyo Shimbun noted that although rice prices have fallen, they remain substantially higher than before the "rice shortage," meaning many consumers may still consider rice expensive.
FOOD SECURITY CONCERNS
Falling rice prices have eased the burden on consumers, but they have created new pressure on producers and distributors. Japanese media and experts warn that prolonged low prices could drive some farmers out of agriculture, potentially affecting the country's food security.
Japanese farmers have little reason to celebrate this year's good rice harvest. Production costs have continued to rise, with prices of agricultural chemicals, fertilizers and other inputs pushed higher amid geopolitical tensions in the Middle East.
Ryoji Ito, an assistant professor at Niigata University, said that in Niigata, farmers could face a situation in which "the more they produce, the more they lose" unless they can sell 60 kilograms of rice for between 20,000 and 24,000 yen.
Yoichi Takahashi, a rice farmer in Niigata, said he had calculated his business costs when purchasing agricultural machinery on the assumption that rice would sell for about 24,000 yen per 60 kilograms. With prices now falling, his income could decline by around 10 million yen.
Rice wholesalers are also under pressure. A rice warehouse in Chiba Prefecture is almost full, with about 300 tons of rice from last year still in storage even as the new crop is about to enter the market. To make room for new supplies, low-price competition and clearance sales have already emerged.
Japan's agricultural sector has long faced challenges including high production costs, low efficiency and a shrinking workforce. The large number of small-scale farms and fragmented farmland makes it difficult for farmers to reduce costs and improve efficiency.
The number of agricultural operators in Japan has also continued to decline. In 2025, there were only 836,000, down 60 percent from 2005. Kimio Inagaki, a research fellow at Mitsubishi Research Institute, estimates that the figure could fall to just 200,000 by 2050.
"If rice prices fall to a level that no longer allows farmers to continue growing rice, Japan's rice production could gradually decline," said Yoshito Shinno, president of the Central Union of Agricultural Cooperatives. ■

Wei said the results could support the development of standardized propulsion systems.
FARCX-1 used a domestically developed liquid-propellant system that operated for three seconds and carried the rocket to an altitude of 532 meters. Wei said the test yielded valuable data for later improvements.

It is now clear that around 300 people have fallen ill as a result of a salmonella outbreak linked to the eggs, reports daily Gazet van Antwerpen. The FASFC confirmed the news to the VRT.
“These are people who have consulted a doctor with symptoms that could indicate food poisoning,” says spokesperson Hélène Bonte. “Symptoms include fever, stomachache, vomiting and diarrhea.”
“A doctor who suspects that the symptoms are caused by contaminated food can take a stool sample for analysis. If salmonella is found, its DNA is compared with the DNA we have from the company in question. That is how the link is established.”
It is possible that many more people have fallen ill. “The figures are always an underestimate. Not everyone becomes seriously ill from salmonella. People in good health will, at most, experience some flu-like symptoms; they do not always go to the doctor for this and tend to recover quickly. Young children, the elderly and pregnant women can become more seriously ill.”
4 codes to look out for
The eggs were withdrawn from sale on 10 August, but people may still have some at home. “Eggs have a shelf life of 4 weeks after they are laid. The eggs currently on sale in shops are safe. If you bought eggs before 10 August, it’s best to check the codes on them again. There are four codes involved. They can be found on our website. It’s best not to eat those eggs anymore.”
Which are the codes of the affected eggs?
2-BE-1073-01
2-BE-1073-02
2-BE-1073-03
2-BE-1073-04
You can return eggs with these codes to the shop where you bought them.

Researchers say formation near Ağrı may be Noah’s Ark
Unknown

The new study used the BakhtarRadar subsurface radar system to identify layers and anomalies deep beneath the Durupınar Formation.
An international team studying the Durupınar Formation near Mount Ağrı claim that the ship-shaped structure may not simply be a rock but could be the remains of Noah’s Ark.
Located 29 kilometers south of Mount Ağrı, Türkiye’s highest mountain at 5,137 meters, the ship-shaped Durupınar Formation has long divided opinion. Andrew Jones, founder of the U.S.-based Noah’s Ark Scans research group, claims that the formation could be Noah’s Ark based on analyses of 88 soil samples collected from the site in 2024.
Many scientists, however, argue that the Durupınar Formation is a geological structure created by natural processes. The debate has now drawn the attention of Iranian-born scientist Dr. Khosrow Bakhtar, an expert in geomechanics, electromagnetism and subsurface radar technologies.
According to the Daily Mail, a team led by Bakhtar has said that the Durupınar Formation could contain remains of Noah’s Ark.
The study reportedly used a specialized imaging system known as BakhtarRadar, developed through research associated with the U.S. Air Force, to examine areas deeper underground than previous surveys.
The team said it detected strong subsurface anomalies and distinct layers within the 157-meter-long formation, challenging the view that it is a single homogeneous rock mass.
“My team and I are evaluating the subsurface data. With the capabilities of BakhtarRadar, we will distinguish petrified, man-made timber from natural bedrock formations,” Bakhtar said.
The new study led by Bakhtar reportedly used the BakhtarRadar subsurface radar system to identify layers and anomalies deep beneath the Durupınar Formation.
The electromagnetic technology can produce three-dimensional images of underground structures without physically excavating the site, and the team said it had obtained significant digital data from the Durupınar area.
Jones, who has been working for years to prove that the Durupınar Formation is Noah’s Ark, said the “ultimate goal is to enter the ship,” adding that permission from Türkiye would be required to do so.
According to the biblical account, Noah, his family and animals of every kind survived a great flood aboard the ark around 4,300 years ago.

Researchers will conduct environmental DNA testing at an 86,000-year-old cave in the northwestern province of Çanakkale this September, aiming to solve the mystery of why no organic remains have been found despite the discovery of 40,000 stone tools.
The İnkaya Cave, nestled in the Bahadırlı village of the local Çan district, yielded zero organic materials during previous excavations. Ankara University Professor İsmail Özer from the Faculty of Language, History and Geography’s Anthropology Department and Paleoanthropology Section called the situation an anomaly.
“We are doing e-DNA, environmental DNA analysis in the field for the first time this year to identify the bacteria consuming the organic material,” he said. Experts from the university’s genetic evolution laboratory will collect soil samples to determine the region’s paleoecological structure.
The analysis could reveal surrounding vegetation, animal remains and the exact human species utilizing the cave. This data promises to shed light on Paleolithic period migrations between Anatolia and the Balkans.
Özer discovered the site during the 2016 Muğla and Çanakkale Provinces Surface Survey. An international team subsequently carried out periodic excavations from 2017 to 2020 under the Troy Museum Directorate. The site gained presidential decree status in 2021.
A coalition of state and private entities supports the ongoing 2026 works. These include the Culture and Tourism Ministry, the Cultural Heritage and Museums General Directorate, the Ankara University Rectorate, the Çanakkale Governorate, Truva Bakır Maden İşletmeleri A.Ş. and T-Design Mühendislik Şirketi.
Environmental DNA analysis allows scientists to detect genetic material left behind by organisms in soil without physical fossils. This technique helps archaeologists identify microscopic biological footprints in ancient sediments.

The 'extraordinarily expensive' project reshaping a state — and drawing political battlelines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
06:33:35 UTC
15:33:35 KST

In brief
- Victorian Premier Ben Carroll says changes to the Suburban Rail Loop will mean it is "built under budget".
- There has been division over the infrastructure project's costs, with the state Opposition vowing to review it if elected.
Victorian Premier Ben Carroll has announced $2 billion in cuts to the state's largest infrastructure project, the Suburban Rail Loop (SRL), saying: "I respect your money."
His comments underline the controversy over the 90km underground rapid transit project, which will link Melbourne's middle suburbs and allow passengers to travel across the city without passing through the CBD.
The state government says the mega-project will reshape Melbourne into a multi-nodal city, bringing services and jobs closer to where people live, building more homes, and creating more jobs.
But its enormous cost, disputed economic benefits and lengthy construction timeline have also made it one of Australia's most controversial infrastructure projects.
Liam Davies, a lecturer in sustainability and urban planning at RMIT University, said the SRL was a step towards transforming Melbourne's city-centric public transport system into an interconnected network.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"Melbourne's greatest challenge is that it has become an extraordinarily large city, physically," he told SBS News.
"We can't just adopt the transport strategy for a denser, more compact city like London. We need to do something of our own, and the SRL is an attempt to do that in a Melburnian context."
With Labor and the Coalition deeply divided on the SRL, the project's future could be decided when Victorians head to the polls in November.
Why is the project so controversial?
The SRL will connect Melbourne's middle suburbs from Cheltenham in the south-east to Werribee in the west via Melbourne Airport through a 90km underground rail line.
The project is split into three stages. The first section — SRL East — is under construction, running from Cheltenham to Box Hill via six new underground stations. The first trains are expected by 2035.
Critics argue the mega-project's business case doesn't stack up, and the multi-billion-dollar price tag is a financial liability for Victoria, which has the second-highest debt per capita of any state or territory, behind the Northern Territory.
More than $33 billion has already been invested in SRL East, according to the premier.
A Parliamentary Budget Office analysis puts the price tag for building the East and North sections at $96.4 billion, though there is currently no fully costed estimate for the entire project, which includes the final stage, SRL West.
An evaluation last year by Infrastructure Australia — an advisory body to the federal government — found the SRL's business case was insufficiently detailed and relied on future stages to justify its benefits.
It also urged the Victorian government to develop "exit strategies" should the project be unable to be completed.
Allegations of corruption and unlawful conduct in state-funded projects, which recently led to a royal commission into the construction industry being called, have also heightened public concerns about the SRL.
Davies said there are questions about which other infrastructure projects will miss out on investment because of the SRL.
"This is still an extraordinarily expensive project," he said.
"Is this the only project that we build over the next 35 to 50 years, or do we build other projects at the same time?
"If it's the only project that we build, I don't think it's the best allocation of resources."
Are there alternatives?
Carroll, who replaced Jacinta Allan as premier last month, has clearly recognised that many Victorians are unhappy with the eye-watering cost.
On Tuesday, he announced $2 billion in savings, with underground station interchanges at Box Hill and Glen Waverley no longer to be built, instead replaced by surface transfers.
Among other changes, a second station entrance will not be built at Clayton, and pedestrian bridges in Burwood and Cheltenham have also been axed.
"I respect your money," Carroll said in a statement.
"The SRL will be built on time. Today's changes mean it will be built under budget."
Davies said construction of SRL East was well advanced, with tunnel boring machines in place to begin excavating twin 26km tunnels.
"The reality is that that project is so far along; it will continue," he said.
But it's the project's latter stages which have scope for change.
Davies said better rail services and upgrades to the northern and western suburb lines, including electrification of the entire track, would fulfil many of the policy ambitions of SRL West at a fraction of the time and cost.
"We have an exploding population in our northern and western suburbs, and the infrastructure is not keeping up at all," he said.
He said there could also be alternatives to the SRL North, such as elevated rail, light rail, or a rapid bus transit system with dedicated bus lanes.
"There are challenges to each of those options; each of them has trade-offs," he said.
"All of them would be cheaper options than what we currently have, which is tens of billions of dollars in tunnelling."
Where do the parties stand?
The project's future could hinge on the outcome of the state's November election.
Labor has committed to seeing the SRL through, arguing it's essential infrastructure for a growing Melbourne.
The state Opposition has previously called for the project to be scrapped, arguing that it's too costly and the funds should be redirected to other, higher-priority transport projects, such as a long-sought-after airport line.
In 2024, Liberal MLC Evan Mulholland described the SRL as a "vanity project" that was "robbing the next generation of getting the infrastructure that they deserve".
But the Coalition's position has evolved over time, with Opposition leader Jess Wilson now promising to pause and review the project if elected.
Whatever the outcome, the project will remain a defining political issue for years to come.
"Transport projects are big and expensive, and they almost always have controversy," Davies said.
"It's almost impossible to build something that everyone is going to be absolutely happy with. Maybe this is just another example of that."

Cross-country skiing requires year-round endurance training. Athletes lacking snow access often use roller skis on paved roads to simulate the glide of winter skiing.

Millions of Teslas recalled in China over door handle safety
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
06:30:27 UTC
15:30:27 KST

People work on the Tesla Model Y production line at the Tesla Gigafactory assembly plant during a media organized tour, in Shanghai, China (AP Photo)
Tesla is recalling nearly three million cars in China with interior door handles that could hamper a person's ability to exit their vehicle in an emergency, Beijing's national market watchdog said.
Eight Chinese carmakers also filed recalls over similar safety risks, China's State Administration for Market Regulation (SAMR) announced on Aug. 21.
Some recalls were effective immediately, while others began over the weekend and on Aug. 24.
Tesla's recall involves 2.9 million domestically-made units of its Model 3 and Model Y electric cars and begins on September 25.
The U.S. carmaker — which operates a huge factory in Shanghai — is also recalling around 46,000 imported units of its Model 3, Model X and Model S cars, the SAMR announcement said.
The recalled cars have inner emergency mechanical handles "similar in color to the interior, making them difficult to identify and operate" in emergencies, the watchdog said.
In Tesla's Model 3, for example, passengers must reach into a compartment inside the door pocket and find a release cable to manually open the rear door, according to the company's website.
"In extreme situations such as severe collisions causing the vehicle's low-voltage system to fail, (the handles) may affect passengers' ability to quickly open car doors for escape and rescue operations outside the vehicle," SAMR said.
SAMR said Tesla was separately recalling 2.7 million domestically-made Model 3 and Model Y EVs over issues with monitoring systems while a driver is using steering assist functions.
It was not clear whether some Teslas were counted in both recalls.
Chinese EV makers including Xiaomi, XPeng, Geely, Chery and Leapmotor are also recalling cars with handles that blend in with their interior.
Xiaomi began recalling around 390,000 units of its 2024 SU7 series on Aug. 21, and XPeng started recalling nearly 265,000 cars on Aug. 22.
Beijing-based BAIC BluePark, a subsidiary of state-owned automaker BAIC, on Aug. 22 began recalling around 46,000 Arcfox Kaola EVs over a "lack of dedicated text prompts" near the emergency mechanism on its right rear sliding door.
Beginning on Aug. 24, Geely is recalling around 92,000 cars from its luxury brand Zeekr.
Companies offered to attach warning labels near the handles for free, and some said they would remotely upgrade software involving lowering windows after a crash.
Safety concerns have risen in China recently over sleek car designs that are prone to losing operability in the event of a crash.
The mass recalls are in line with China's plan to ban hidden door handles on cars from January 1, 2027, local media reports said.
Those rules, announced in February by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, will require door handles to have both interior and exterior mechanical releases.
Electronic door handles were introduced with Tesla's 2012 launch of the Model S, later becoming popular with Chinese EV brands prioritising high-tech features.
Folding into the body of the car, such door handles provide a slight boost to efficiency by reducing drag while the vehicle is in motion.

Paris announces three theme parks near the city, funded by Saudi Arabia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
06:26:28 UTC
15:26:28 KST

These three theme parks, one of them based on "Dragon Ball Z," will create 22,000 jobs, Emmanuel Macron has announced. Saudi Arabia will invest €6 billion.
It is an "unprecedented" project, Emmanuel Macron said. On Monday 24 August, France and Saudi Arabia signed a letter regarding a six-billion-euro investment to create three theme parks near Cergy-Pontoise, around 30 kilometres north-west of Paris, the French president's office announced.
The announcement about this "colossal" project was made during a two-day visit to France by Saudi Arabia's de facto ruler, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Macron's office said.
"22,000 jobs created. Unseen since Disneyland Paris. A new global destination", the president of the Republic wrote on X, thanking Saudi Arabia and Qiddiya, one of the many subsidiaries of the country's Public Investment Fund, "for their confidence in our country, in our talents and in our future".
This project "was born out of a discussion between the president of the Republic and the crown prince in December 2024" in Riyadh, where they discovered their "shared passion" for manga, "and more specifically Dragon Ball Z", an adviser to Emmanuel Macron told the press.
The first of the three parks is expected to be dedicated to this iconic Japanese franchise, although this has not been officially confirmed. The themes of the other two parks have not yet been revealed.
Two mega-projects in Saudi Arabia
The parks will be built and opened in stages. Construction is expected to take several years, the president's office said, without specifying an opening date.
Asked about entrusting such a project to Riyadh despite criticism of its human rights record, the president's office sidestepped the issue. "At no point, when we attract a project, do we seek to lecture others", it replied.
The presidency said that two other contracts had been signed with French companies during the Saudi prince's visit. One with shipping company CMA CGM, to help develop the port of Jeddah on the Red Sea, worth 434 million dollars. The other with rail transport group Alstom, to supply metro trains for Riyadh's metro, worth 580 million dollars.
A heavily criticised visit
The trip is one of the crown prince's rare visits abroad; Paris notes that he seldom leaves his country, except for international summits. It was his first such trip in almost a year.
On Sunday, Emmanuel Macron hosted the Saudi crown prince at the Esports World Cup, while Monday's talks were also due to cover strategic issues, including the situation in the Middle East.
But the visit by the Saudi leader has sparked strong criticism in France. Three journalists' unions protested against Paris's decision to host him, recalling the existence of a French investigation opened into allegations of torture and enforced disappearance, following a complaint filed in 2021 over the murder of journalist Jamal Khashoggi.
Jamal Khashoggi, a Saudi national living in the United States and a critic of the Saudi ruling family, was assassinated in 2018 in the Saudi consulate in Istanbul. His dismembered body has never been found.
US intelligence concluded that Mohammed bin Salman was directly involved in the killing, and a United Nations investigation described the journalist's death as an "extrajudicial killing for which Saudi Arabia is responsible".
In December 2021, Emmanuel Macron became one of the first Western leaders to meet the prince after Khashoggi's assassination. The Saudi crown prince has since made several visits to France.
'Choose France'
In his message posted on X, Emmanuel Macron highlighted the "Choose France" programme, which he said had made the signing of this project possible. "That is the whole point of Choose France: to go after the most ambitious projects and make France the country where they become reality. Create jobs. Make France shine", he said.
Since the first "Choose France" call for projects in 2018, a year after Emmanuel Macron came to power, more than 230 projects have been announced, representing some 87 billion euros and several thousand jobs, according to the Élysée.
France has attracted the most foreign investment in Europe for seven consecutive years, according to consultancy EY, but Emmanuel Macron said this "doesn't come out of nowhere".
EY said that France attracted 852 projects last year, out of 5,026 recorded in 47 European countries, a 17% drop in a challenging international environment.
France has attracted a remarkable number of AI-related projects, more than anywhere else in Europe, but industry has suffered, notably the automotive, chemicals and metals sectors.

Putin adviser raises attacks on British drone factories
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
07:25:18 BST
15:25:18 KST

An adviser to President Putin has said British factories producing drones for Ukraine could be attacked by what he called unknown sources, as part of a possible Russian response to UK military support for Kyiv, in an interview with BBC Newsnight.
Andrei Fedorov, a former Russian deputy foreign minister who advises the Kremlin, was speaking to Adam Fleming on the programme on Monday. Asked what a semi-military response might involve, he said: “For example, something might happen with enterprises, with factories which are producing drones for Ukraine, etc, etc.”
Pressed on whether he meant British factories in Britain being attacked militarily by Russia, he said: “They could be attacked not by Russia, but by from unknown sources.”
Fedorov said pressure was building on Putin to act against the United Kingdom, telling the programme: “There’s a very serious political and public pressure on President Putin today, to undertake certain measures against UK, because he is considering UK as part of the war in Ukraine, and assistance from the UK is considered as a direct involvement of UK in this war.”
Asked where that pressure came from, he said: “It’s coming from the public opinion polls, it’s coming from journalists, from mass media, it is coming from military. And UK, of course, as considered in the context of Ukraine, is evil Number 1.”
He said Putin had described current developments as the opening of Pandora’s box, and that there had been a very negative reaction in the Kremlin.
On what form a response might take, Fedorov told the programme: “In the coming future we will face a new stage of escalation, in the Ukrainian conflict, and sooner or later, there might be not only verbal but maybe some visible reaction from Russia towards the UK.”
He said the options under discussion included a technical reaction, possibly a hacker attack from an unofficial source, along with political steps, and that he could not entirely exclude something semi-military.
Asked whether he personally would be content with such an attack, he said he would not, adding: “The problem is that we are now facing, in front of the danger, that Ukrainian conflict will be beyond Ukrainian borders. And remembering that UK is a member of NATO, and UK is a nuclear state, the risk is, of course, much higher than it was before, even a couple of months ago.”
Challenged on how such an attack could be justified under international law, he said: “Frankly speaking, who cares today about international law?” He said many in Russian society believed the president had waited too long to answer the UK.
On cyber targets, he said a hacker attack would be directed at a specific enterprise or system rather than broadly, and confirmed when asked that this would mean something governmental, security or military related, “especially to production of the drones or some components for Storm Shadow missiles.”
Fedorov linked the Kremlin’s assessment directly to the transfer of missile blueprints, saying the step meant that from Moscow’s point of view Britain was much more involved, and that a system capable of producing missiles, whether Storm Shadow or a Ukrainian modification, would be considerably more effective than what came before.
He described Moscow as considering the actions of the British Prime Minister as direct military involvement in the conflict.
On the domestic picture, Fedorov acknowledged that fuel queues and Ukrainian strikes on warehouses, including those belonging to the online retailers Wildberries and Ozon, were having an effect, but said he could not say public opinion had changed seriously. He noted that parliamentary elections are due on the 18th or 20th of September and that the war is regarded as a consolidating factor for them.
Put to him that anti-war parties had been blocked from standing, he confirmed that Yabloko had been kicked out of the race.
Fedorov holds no current government office, and his remarks carry no official standing. Figures of his kind are used periodically to place a position in the public domain without the Kremlin owning it, and the construction he uses, attacks carried out not by Russia but by unknown sources, is the same formula applied to the sabotage of undersea cables, arson at warehouses across Europe and parcel bombs placed on cargo aircraft.
British defence manufacturing sites have been treated as a protective security concern for some time. MI5 has warned repeatedly about Russian sabotage plots on British soil, and several prosecutions have followed attacks on premises linked to Ukraine, including an arson at a warehouse in Leyton in east London in 2024 for which men were convicted under the National Security Act.
The interview was broadcast on BBC Newsnight on 24 August.

On the ninth anniversary of the mass exodus of Rohingya to Bangladesh, 16 diplomatic missions, including those of the UK, Australia, Canada, and the EU, in Dhaka on Tuesday recalled the Rohingya's right to return to their home country, Myanmar.
Bangladesh has been sheltering about 1.2 million persecuted Rohingya on the southeastern Cox’s Bazar coast after they fled a brutal Myanmar military crackdown and started crossing the border on Aug. 25, 2017.
However, nine years after the mass exodus, conflict is escalating across Rakhine and humanitarian needs are rising, according to the foreign missions’ joint statement.
“Deepening insecurity, airstrikes on civilian infrastructure and the Myanmar authorities’ blockades on aid and trade are worsening the humanitarian crisis,” the statement said, marking Rohingya Genocide Remembrance Day, observed on Aug. 25.
This instability is driving further displacement into Bangladesh, and across the region, leading to tragic loss of life through dangerous sea crossings, it said, adding that these conditions do not currently allow for voluntary, safe, dignified, and sustainable repatriation.
They said conditions for Rohingya return will require a strategic, coordinated, and long-term approach to address the root causes of displacement, build trust between communities, and support greater peace and stability in Myanmar.
They also said they will continue to work with Bangladesh to find pathways toward building the conditions for repatriation.
“As this crisis enters its tenth year, we must ensure that the Rohingya people are not forgotten. We will continue to amplify the voices of Rohingya communities, pursue justice and accountability, and work with Bangladesh and international partners to sustain global support,” the statement added.

Burnham said he left feeling “really optimistic” that Ukraine’s current difficulties in defending itself against Russian ballistic missile strikes due to low stocks of interceptor missiles are “fixable.”
According to Burnham, European leaders are considering holding another meeting of the Coalition of the Willing on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly to discuss obtaining U.S.-made interceptor missiles from other countries.
“Not confirmed yet, but that seemed like where most people’s minds were going,” the UK Prime Minister said.
He noted that the UK does not use the Patriot missiles Ukraine needs, while other European countries should “step up” on this issue.
“There are other players who could help in the mix who we have influence with. It’s probably going to be a solution that involves a lot of layers and a lot of negotiation,” Burnham said.
As reported, Ukraine’s Permanent Representative to the UN Andrii Melnyk called the Security Council’s inability to counter Russia’s genocidal actions shameful and urged partners to transfer all available Patriot missiles to Kyiv.

EU sea defence: the new race to protect cables, pipelines and trade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
06:15:10 UTC
15:15:10 KST

Is the deep blue sea the next frontier for defence? Global economies are increasingly dependent on vulnerable subsea data and energy pipelines. So, the EU and its members are shifting budgets towards maritime defence tools.
In just the last decade, the EU has spent almost €118 billion in maritime defence, with a sharp 23.6 percent increase in 2022 after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
Data from the EU Blue Economy Observatory show a sharp rise in domestic maritime defence spending, reaching a record high of €11.6 billion. Submarines alone account for 27 percent of the EU's total production value; the rest includes surface ships, aircraft, and other types of warfare.
The bloc decided to transition from a purely commercial ‘blue’ economy approach to a securitised maritime strategy. In 2023, it updated its European Union Maritime Security Strategy (EUMSS) to protect critical seabed infrastructure.
Then it locked in its strategic defence priorities by launching dedicated European Defence Projects of Common Interest and implementing a Submarine Cable Security Toolbox to counter grey-zone threats and protect underwater networks.
Protecting international trade
The global economy relies almost completely on secure, open seas. More than 95 percent of international digital traffic moves through them. Financial transfers happen through over 1.4 million kilometres of submarine fibre-optic cables, which carry an estimated €9.2 trillion in financial transactions every single day. Approximately two-thirds of the world’s oil and gas is either extracted at sea or transported by water.
80 percent of global trade volume is transported by ocean shipping. For the EU, maritime transport accounts for 75.6 percent of all imports and 73 percent of all exports. It totals around €1.126 trillion in goods annually. A disruption at key maritime chokepoints risks triggering inflation and global manufacturing shortages.
An attack on these sea lanes and underwater assets would paralyse Europe, so it needs more than traditional naval patrols. “Underwater Domain Awareness is a critical activity to know what is happening below the surface, particularly around cables, pipelines and offshore energy infrastructure, prioritising those identified as critical for the security of the Union”, said Jürgen Scraback, Head of the Maritime Domain Unit at the European Defence Agency.
As threats increasingly come from low-cost drones, uncrewed underwater vehicles and mine warfare, governments are investing in autonomous technologies and surveillance systems. Between 2016 and 2025, the EU's annual production value of crewless vehicles, including aerial and submarine drones, increased by 132 percent to €847 million. Fixed-wing unmanned systems accounted for one third of that output, worth €277 million, while production of traditional unmanned submarine platforms fell by 23 percent over the same period.
Fleet modernisation continues to focus on both conventional naval assets and autonomous platforms. Manned surface ships now account for 65 percent of EU maritime defence vehicle production value and serve as the primary platforms for command, logistics and force projection.
Submarines represent another 27 percent of production, supported by new procurement programmes and investment in next-generation underwater weapons. At the same time, autonomous surface vessels and unmanned underwater vehicles are becoming increasingly important for surveillance, reconnaissance and infrastructure monitoring missions.
Investments also extend to digital tech for maritime surveillance, with European operators deploying AI-enabled unmanned systems to monitor ports, offshore energy infrastructure, and submarine cables, detecting threats across large areas
For Scraback, “autonomous and unmanned systems combined with AI-enabled data fusion are among the technologies likely to have the greatest impact. They can provide persistent surveillance over large areas without requiring expensive crewed platforms to remain almost permanently deployed”.
How is the EU boosting maritime defence?
The 2014 Maritime Security Strategy guides Europe's maritime strategy, protecting citizens, the economy, infrastructure, and borders, while redefining Europe’s approach to maritime defence.
“The new strategy calls for a greater emphasis on the hard power aspects of maritime defence and security, where the EU had previously faced challenges in establishing a role and identity”, said Chris Kremidas-Courtney, senior advisor at the European Policy Centre and associate fellow at the Geneva Centre for Security Policy. It identifies “the protection of critical infrastructure in the maritime domain as a key priority”, she added.
The Industrial Maritime Strategy, adopted in March 2026, backs this shift. It boosts Europe's naval production through a new EU Industrial Maritime Value Chain Alliance and reinforces naval, underwater, and dual-use capabilities, including a dual-use ferry construction programme.
By July, Europe allocated €325 million to five European Defence Projects of Common Interest, including one maritime and seabed defence project to strengthen its industrial base. Since February, a new Counter-Drone Action Plan has shifted production towards unmanned naval drones and counter-drone systems for aerial, surface, and underwater threats.
The EU funds its naval ramp-up through defence tools, such as the European Defence Industrial Strategy and the €1.5 billion European Defence Industry Programme. The Readiness 2030 roadmap totals over €800 billion, including naval capabilities and sea lines of communication protection.
The bloc also invests in detection and surveillance technologies to fight threats and sabotage to seabed cables. As cables cover large areas, are privately owned and can be easily damaged, “the best approach is a layered resilience system designed to make interference detectable, limit the disruption caused by a successful attack and restore service quickly”, Kremidas-Courtney explained.
This thinking now drives EU policy. The Action Plan on Cable Security (2025) strengthens Europe’s ability to prevent, detect, respond to, and recover from cable incidents that disrupt critical functions like communication and energy supply. The €92 million OceanEye expands maritime awareness using AI, autonomous sensors, and digital twins.
Under Horizon Europe, the UnderSect and Smart Maritime and Underwater Guardian projects invest nearly €6 million each in underwater threat-detection systems for ports and maritime infrastructure. European Defence Fund (EDF) projects, such as SHIELD and SOUND2, develop AI systems to detect threats using underwater acoustic signals.
Ramping up maritime defence goes beyond detecting and repairing cable breaks. For Kremidas-Courtney, authorities should identify behavioural patterns such as unexplained slowing, shipping lane deviations, and manipulation of identification signals.
“The most effective solution to me is an integrated information-and-action network that fuses undersea sensors, AIS data, coastal radar, satellite imagery, intelligence and port records into a continuously staffed existing regional maritime operations centre”, she explained.
Who invests the most?
Between 2016 and 2025, cumulative EU production of maritime defence vehicles and equipment reached €117.8 billion. According to the EU Commission’s Blue Economy Observatory, production remained concentrated in four countries. France, Germany, Italy and Spain together account for 87 percent of the bloc's maritime defence industrial output. The Netherlands, Sweden and Poland contribute a further 8 percent, largely through surveillance technologies and maritime security systems.
In 2025, France generated 37 percent of the EU’s total production of maritime defence vehicles. Germany and Italy each contributed 19 percent, and Spain followed with 8 percent. These four countries accounted for 82 percent of the EU’s total output value and 60 percent of the EU's total defence expenditure. This shows that defence spending remains higher in member states with a long tradition of armaments.
“A few large navies can provide scarce high-end capabilities, but they can’t secure every coastline, patrol the sea lanes, and protect every piece of undersea infrastructure. Europe doesn’t need everyone to build a fleet to match Italy's or France's, but it does need credible, distributed forces connected by interoperable systems and a shared maritime picture. The only way to make that work is a whole-of-Europe approach which includes the UK and Norway”, Kremidas-Courtney warned.
At company level, the France-based Naval Group led with 24 percent of the EU’s total output, producing advanced surface combatants (frigates and corvettes), nuclear-powered submarines, and unmanned surface and underwater systems. Italy’s Fincantieri (15 percent) specialises in warships and underwater defence systems, including torpedoes and sonars.
The German Thyssenkrupp Marine Systems accounted for 8 percent of the EU’s overall market for maritime defence vehicles, focusing on surface vessels and submarine construction. Spain’s Navantia (7 percent) builds multi-mission frigates, AIP-equipped submarines, aircraft carriers and patrol vessels.
The EDF supports European companies in developing joint defence technologies and equipment. It invests €2.7 billion in collaborative defence research and €5.3 billion in collaborative capability development for the period 2021-2027. The 2025 EDF totals €1.07 billion and funds 57 projects, including E-DOMINION, which develops a digital architecture and combat cloud for European navies.
According to Scraback, “we need to continue shifting from fragmented national solutions towards interoperable, scalable and jointly developed capabilities”. He explained that the European Defence Project of Common Interest on Integrated Maritime and Seabed Defence “can be a key vehicle for this, bringing Member States, existing European programmes and investments together under one coherent framework”.
