Netanyahu got his Iran war, but maybe not his desired result
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
03:03:00 UTC
12:03:00 KST

Netanyahu got his Iran war, but maybe not his desired result
- Israel launched a war against Iran aiming to weaken it, but Iran survived and may become more determined to pursue nuclear weapons.
- US President Trump’s shifting stance complicated the conflict, leading to a ceasefire and uncertain future negotiations.
- The war damaged Israel’s public image, strained US-Israel relations, and may create lasting hostility between Israel, the US, and the Iranian people.
AI generated
JERUSALEM – After decades of urging the US to attack Iran, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu finally got his wish.
But after six months of inconclusive hostilities, Israel may ultimately find itself in a worse position than it was before the war.
The Islamic republic, which Netanyahu has long cast as an existential threat, has not only survived but also appears emboldened.
Underlying Netanyahu’s dilemma has been the wild swings in the approach of US President Donald Trump, who joined Israel in launching the conflict in late February, but by April abruptly called a ceasefire and sought a negotiated settlement in the face of souring public opinion and soaring oil prices.
“It’s a colossal failure of Israeli strategy regarding Iran,” said Danny Citrinowicz, a former top Israeli intelligence analyst on Iran who is now at the Tel Aviv-based Institute for National Security Studies.
“Yes, we had operational achievements, but strategically we’ve failed.”
Israel, on the very first day, killed Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, the supreme leader who ruthlessly suppressed dissent in Iran, including mass protests earlier in 2026, and backed anti-Israeli groups such as Hamas, which led the Oct 7, 2023, attacks.
But Khamenei was also seen as holding back on full-blown pursuit of nuclear weapons, a reluctance that could now end if the Islamic republic feels it has lost its conventional deterrents.
While Trump has recently declared economic warfare on Iran and periodically ordered new strikes, he has voiced support for a deal that would see sanctions relief.
Netanyahu had adamantly rejected a 2015 nuclear deal negotiated by then US President Barack Obama.
Citrinowicz said Israel now had a choice between accepting a new nuclear deal that would strengthen Iran, or trying to weaken it further and increasing the risk that it will seek a nuclear weapon.
“Israel is trying to do both, but it’s not going to work,” he said.
Degrading v toppling
An extraordinary 92 per cent of Israelis believe Iran won or gained more from the conflict, according to a June survey by the Hebrew University of Jerusalem in collaboration with the Agam Institute – a warning sign for Netanyahu ahead of the Oct 27 elections.
The Israeli leader had said he was hoping to “create conditions for regime change” but did not explicitly make toppling the Islamic republic his goal.
Instead, some see Netanyahu following an Israeli playbook witnessed in Gaza, Lebanon and Syria – inflict overwhelming damage that will allow Israel to return and attack later as it sees fit, a strategy the country euphemistically calls “mowing the grass”.
“Netanyahu doesn’t see this as a loss. He has the United States directly at war with Iran, with Israel for now on the sidelines,” one foreign diplomat based in Israel told AFP on condition of anonymity.
Iranian counter-strikes killed 25 people in Israel and four in the occupied West Bank, but Iran has focused its fire more recently on Gulf Arab states that provide bases for US troops.
Alex Grinberg, a senior fellow focused on Iran at the Turan Research Centre, said the war set back Iran significantly by eliminating infrastructure and people in the nuclear programme and imposing massive economic damage.
“I think Israel did achieve its strategic goals, meaning denying the Iranian regime the strategic capacity to threaten Israel,” he said, while casting doubt on the prospects for a favourable US-Iran deal.
Risking public opinion
The war has already complicated Israel’s relationship with its most crucial ally and may preclude any possibility of a future reconciliation with the Iranian people.
The increasingly unpopular conflict triggered a surge of criticism of Israel in the US, where its war against Hamas in Gaza had already dealt a heavy blow to its standing in the public eye.
Public perceptions of Israel inside Iran are difficult to gauge, as polling is difficult, but the two countries were allies before the Islamic Revolution, and protests before the war indicated noticeable public opposition to the clerical government.
While Netanyahu and Trump have both publicly professed to support the Iranian people, the US and Israel have issued apocalyptic threats over the course of the war that appeared to make little distinction between the Islamic republic and its citizens, and their strikes have destroyed infrastructure, including top universities.
There is “a real possibility of lasting hostility towards Israel and the United States, particularly if the war is remembered through civilian casualties and damage to the country rather than solely through the removal of senior regime figures”, said Liora Hendelman-Baavur, a senior research fellow at the Alliance Centre for Iranian Studies at Tel Aviv University.
“That hostility would not necessarily restore the Islamic republic’s legitimacy, but it could complicate future relations long after the present leadership has changed.” AFP

Dzeko then helped Schalke regain control, delivering a cross for Moussa Sylla to make it 3-2 in the 98th minute. The Bosnian was also involved in Schalke's fourth, with Sylla crossing for substitute Junior Adamu to head home in stoppage time at the end of the first period of extra time.
Dzeko completed the scoring from Gosens' pass in the 117th minute.
"We are happy that we are through. We were dominant for 90 minutes but lacked power in the final third and were vulnerable from set pieces," Gosens said. "We conceded goals at unfortunate moments, but we are through and that is the main thing."
Schalke will kick off its Bundesliga campaign away to Augsburg on Sunday.
Elsewhere in the first round, Bundesliga sides Hamburg and Cologne advanced with victories over third-tier opponents. Hamburg beat SC Verl 3-0, while Cologne came from behind to edge Wurzburger Kickers 2-1. ■

Concerns AFP drugs team may implicate Australia in US boat strikes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
03:00:01 UTC
12:00:01 KST

In short:
The Australian Federal Police has declined to reveal its budget or operational expectations for an international taskforce in Colombia aimed at stemming drug flows across the Pacific.
AFP commissioner Krissy Barrett said the team's officers would work with Colombian, US, Mexican, New Zealand and Pacific law authorities, and also INTERPOL.
Greens senator David Shoebridge and an ex-AFP executive have raised concerns the initiative could contribute to the Trump administration's strikes on alleged trafficking vessels.
Unanswered questions about the Australian Federal Police's (AFP's) new anti-drugs taskforce in Colombia have sparked concerns the initiative could contribute to the Trump administration's air strikes against alleged trafficking vessels.
In May, commissioner Krissy Barrett announced the AFP and New Zealand Police would fund an international joint investigations team (IJIT) "to gather evidence about illicit drug shipments to help stop it coming to our region".
"The magnitude and endless maritime trafficking of illicit drugs to, and through the Pacific, has become a serious national security threat for the Pacific and Australia," Commissioner Barrett said in a statement.
"Our AFP members in Bogota, with Colombian law enforcement, have deployed to remote parts of the Colombian jungle to deliberately destroy cocaine production laboratories."
The commissioner said, despite the seizure of more than 20 tonnes of cocaine in Colombia in recent years and the AFP's presence there since 2000, the IJIT was needed because "it is time for us to be bolder and do more".
IJIT officers would work with Colombia's attorney-general's office, national police and navy, as well as "US law enforcement", INTERPOL, Mexican, New Zealand and Pacific authorities, she said.
Since September last year, the Trump administration has declared the US is in an armed conflict with Latin American drug gangs and launched lethal strikes against alleged "narco-trafficking" vessels in the Pacific Ocean and Caribbean Sea.
The strikes have killed at least 221 people and not reduced the flow of cocaine into the US, The Washington Post reported.
Some academics and legal experts call the strikes "extrajudicial executions" that violate US and international law.
Loading...
Greens senator David Shoebridge called for more transparency about the IJIT's work and said any Australian complicity in aiding the strikes would raise "warning signs".
"Australia should have no part in providing information to the US, and its military and policing authorities, for extrajudicial murder," he told the ABC.
Phil Kowalick, president of the Australian Institute of Professional Intelligence Officers and a former AFP senior executive, said "tactical and technical intelligence" sharing in joint taskforces was common.
He said it "would be a concern" if Australian IJIT intelligence aided a lethal US strike, but acknowledged it would be impossible to control how partner countries used information shared with them by Australian authorities.
Questions about IJIT's budget and expectations shut down
The ABC questioned the AFP in June about the IJIT's allocated budget, operational commitments and measure of how it would be deemed successful, as part of a Freedom of Information request.
In its response, the AFP said it had 60 documents that would answer those questions.
The documents included budget summaries, executive briefs, internal emails, statements of intent written in English and Spanish, and a memorandum of agreement.
The AFP declined to release the detail of the documents to the ABC, citing national security and international relations concerns.
It said the information's publication would be harmful to relations between Australia and Colombia or divulge confidential detail regarding how AFP officers operate.
"The International Joint Investigations Team (IJIT) operates as a multinational investigation team that is still in the negotiation phase between countries," the AFP's response said.
"Releasing the operational roles, resource commitments and strategic priorities of the IJIT would significantly adversely affect trust with our international law enforcement partners, intelligence sharing arrangements and ongoing joint operations."
The AFP did not respond to further questions from the ABC about whether Australian intelligence would be shared with the US as part of the IJIT.
Senator Shoebridge said while some sensitive policing information should be kept private to avoid tipping off criminals, he described the AFP's refusal to answer as "overarching secrecy".
"It's hard to believe … every single element of every single document needs to be kept secret and, if any of it is released, it will somehow empower Colombian drug lords and imperil our bilateral relationship with Colombia," he said.
"If the public is paying for police operations in a third country, there should be a well-articulated goal available to the public to work out whether it's value for money or it's a program that Australia should be a party to."
Shadow Home Affairs Minister Jonno Duniam supported the AFP's efforts to crack down on illicit drugs being moved towards Australia, but echoed Senator Shoebridge's concerns.
"Australians are entitled to know whether taxpayer-funded initiatives are actually delivering results," he told the ABC.
"Operational sensitivities should not prevent appropriate transparency and disclosure around expenditure, objectives and outcomes."
Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke did not respond to the ABC's request for comment.
In this year's federal budget, more than $1.16 million was allocated to the AFP for "ordinary annual services" in policing assistance efforts abroad and on Australian external territories in 2026-27.
That figure is expected to rise to $1.4m next year, before dropping to $1.01m and $1.03m in the following two years, but the budget did not detail how much was set aside specifically for the IJIT.
Commissioner Barrett says 17 tonnes of illicit drugs, mostly cocaine, has been seized by "local and international" police since January this year and stopped from reaching Australia through the Pacific.
The ABC understands, to July this year, most of the offshore seizures were made in French Polynesia, AFP officers were not physically involved in any interceptions and none were in Australian territorial waters.
The Australian Border Force also told the ABC it detected almost 13 tonnes of "major" illicit drugs at the country's ports of entry by May 31.
The AFP takes part in intelligence sharing and police development training programs in Pacific countries.
Mr Kowalick said while he had not seen the detail of the AFP's IJIT postings, he expected them to include a small team of officers liaising with Colombian police and said the cost to Australian taxpayers could be "quite significant".
AFP officers would also likely not be among Colombian police teams sent to the front lines of anti-drug raids in the jungle, Mr Kowalick said.
He told the ABC he expected immersive cultural and language training prior to being deployed in order to forge worthwhile relationships with Colombian authorities.
Those measures have been tested in the past.
A hack of the Colombian attorney-general's department in 2022, reported by The Sydney Morning Herald, revealed the efforts of two AFP officers stationed there were hampered by persistent IT problems and an inability to communicate and assess evidence in Spanish without local translators, who were often overworked or unavailable.
Colombia's National Police, on behalf of the Ministry of National Defence, rejected the ABC's request for further comment about the IJIT.
Australians consuming 'more drugs than ever'
Australians' annual drug use continues to increase, the Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission's (ACIC's) latest wastewater data from 14.5 million people shows.
ACIC chief executive Heather Cook said in April a record 26.8 tonnes of methylamphetamine, cocaine, heroin and MDMA was consumed between August 2024 and 2025, marking a 21 per cent annual increase and street value of $14.3 billion.
The 2026 UN World Drug Report showed most globally trafficked cocaine flowing into Australia originated in the Americas and Europe, while methamphetamine mostly comes from South-East Asia.
Between 2007 and 2023, 10.60 to 12.20 per cent of Australians used drugs, while 4.2 per cent of people in Australia and New Zealand aged 15 to 64 used cocaine in 2024, the UN says.
The magnitude of the drugs challenge in Colombia is immense.
Colombia accounted for 966 tonnes of cocaine made in 2024, representing 40 per cent of the world's total supply, from coca bushes spanning at least 261,000 hectares of land, or more than the entire area of the Australian Capital Territory.
Colombian authorities also detected gangs using unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) as early as 2017 to fly as much as 130 kilograms of cocaine up to 100 kilometres.
Between 1993 and 2023, at least 228 drug-laden semi-submersible vessels were seized by Colombian authorities, the UN says.
Abelardo de la Espriella was this month sworn in as Colombia's president after an election campaign that promised a harsh crackdown on crime and drug trafficking, with the vocal backing of US President Donald Trump.
UNSW Latin America expert Anthea McCarthy-Jones said the threat posed to Australia by cocaine from Colombia was "a long-standing issue" that has grown "exponentially".
"We have quite an affluent population who pays some of the highest prices in the world for illicit drugs," she told the ABC.
"That's a problem that can't easily be fixed … it's also a problem we can't arrest our way out of."
Dr McCarthy-Jones said the magnitude of the threat justified the AFP seeking to do more, but making a difference could be difficult because of the sophistication of Latin American narco-gangs.
"There's so much brokerage between different networks that make this complex mosaic as difficult to disrupt as it currently is,"
"The fact that there seems to be an increased interest and activity around developing [and] strengthening existing relationships with key stakeholders in this whole issue is a really good step," she said.
"It's something that will set Australia up to be in a better position to confront these types of challenges."

Brazil: Amnesty International experiment exposes Meta’s failure to catch election-related disinformation ads on Facebook
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
03:00:00 UTC
12:00:00 KST

- Ahead of Brazil’s presidential election, Amnesty International submits Facebook advertisements to test robustness of Meta’s moderation system
- More than half of the ads spreading election-related disinformation are accepted
- The others are flagged but not rejected outright for containing election-related disinformation
Amnesty International has today warned that Meta may be failing to effectively address election-related disinformation spread through its Facebook Advertisements platform ahead of Brazil’s presidential election on 4 October.
Social media has been used to spread disinformation in Brazil for years. To investigate how Facebook handled election-related disinformation in advertising, Amnesty International conducted an experiment by submitting ‘mock’ ads containing election-related disinformation to Facebook. The content ranged from ads alleging election fraud to ads that used disinformation to advocate for a military takeover. The experiment found that eight of the submitted ads were accepted, while the remaining seven were flagged for identity verification as they appeared to be related to a social issue, election or politics, rather than being rejected specifically because they contained election-related disinformation. Amnesty ensured that these test ads did not go live, despite Facebook’s failure to stop them.
“The fact that Meta’s moderation system failed to catch more than half of Amnesty International’s election-related disinformation ads is deeply alarming. It shows that Meta is not doing enough to prevent its platform from being a vector of disinformation, while continuing to profit from the content and advertising systems that enable its spread,”
Jurema Werneck, Executive Director of Amnesty International Brazil
The Experiment
Amnesty International submitted 15 Brazilian Portuguese-language ads to Facebook, targeted solely to Brazil’s voting age population, to assess how the platform’s ad moderation systems treated election-related content ahead of the election on 4 October 2026.
To help ground the ads in real-world election narratives that were circulating in Brazil, Amnesty International analyzed online conversations and public sentiment on social media, as well as Portuguese-language content on the Facebook and X platforms between January and May 2026.
14 ads contained disinformation and one ad was a neutral ad that contained no disinformation. This analysis uses the term ‘disinformation’ to remain consistent with Amnesty International’s terminology, but in the experiment itself, Meta’s definition of “misinformation” is applied in the construction and analysis of the ads. As outlined in its policies and Community Standards, this definition covers false or inaccurate information, including content that is likely to contribute to interference with the functioning of political processes.
The 14 disinformation ads were designed to reflect three tactics that are often used by politicians and candidates to support authoritarian practices: “electoral delegitimization”, which refers to content that seeks to undermine trust in elections, voting systems, or election results; “enemy construction” which portrays political opponents and courts as threats to the nation or as illegitimate actors; and “security-focused authoritarianism” which presents force, military intervention, or strongman rule as necessary responses to crime or political disorder.
While some ads were designed around a single category, others incorporated narratives from multiple categories. All ads except the neutral ad violated Meta’s policy on misinformation, namely the section focusing on voter or census interference. The neutral ad was included to test Meta’s identity verification requirement for all election-related content.
Seven of the ads designed by Amnesty International focused on intentionally misleading claims about candidates and electoral institutions, including allegations that certain candidates were rigging the election and questioning the integrity of the voting system. The other seven ads included false information that could interfere with people’s ability to vote, such as incorrect details about when to vote, how to vote, or which candidates were running in the election.
The Facebook account used to submit the ads had not completed Meta’s “Confirm Your Identity” process. Identity verification was not completed as part of this research, in order to maintain a neutral test account and avoid any influence from prior account history or activity on ad moderation outcomes. Dedicated research accounts were used rather than personal accounts to mitigate the risk of account usage history impacting outcomes.
Researchers were not physically located in Brazil and did not use a VPN to create the appearance that the ads were being submitted from Brazil. The ads were submitted from London.
All ads were scheduled to run at a future date. This allowed Amnesty International to test the platforms’ ad review processes while ensuring that any ads accepted by the platforms could be cancelled before publication, preventing them from going live and avoiding potential human rights harms or other ethical risks.
Amnesty International wrote to Meta on 21 July 2026, seeking its response to allegations that Facebook’s advertising moderation systems failed to detect election-related disinformation, and raising concerns about whether the company has adequate systems to identify, assess and mitigate related human rights risks. Meta has not responded at the time of publication.
Findings
Facebook approved eight ads that contained disinformation, and none of the seven rejected ads were explicitly rejected on the basis of disinformation.
Of the eight ads containing disinformation accepted for publication, four focused solely on “electoral delegitimization”, two were solely from the “security-focused authoritarianism” category, including disinformation advocating military intervention or non-participation in elections. The other two overlapped between the three categories.
The seven rejected ads, including one neutral ad, were declined on the basis that they concerned “Ads about social issues, elections or politics”. In these cases, Facebook’s Ads Manager stated that, because the ads appeared to relate to a social issue, election or politics, the account would need to complete identity verification before the ads could be published. It is important to note that these rejection notices did not indicate that the ads had been rejected because of their content. Therefore, the notices do not provide any indication of how the ads would have been assessed had the account been verified.
Amnesty International also identified weaknesses in the safeguards applied when election-related ads were submitted. The ads were allowed to be submitted without declaring that the ads fell within Facebook’s Special Ad Categories as required by electoral law in Brazil as well as Meta’s own policies regarding election-related ads. Given the account was not identity-verified, the ads were also allowed to be submitted without the “Paid for by” disclaimer as required by Meta for election-related content. These are ads that Facebook should not have allowed to be submitted in the first place without identity verification.
The fact that the ads could be submitted from outside Brazil raises concerns that inadequate verification and disclosure controls may create vulnerabilities that could be exploited by domestic or foreign actors seeking to influence electoral processes. This failure to apply legally required electoral disclosures, and the submission of the ads from outside Brazil raise serious concerns about the risk of disinformation campaigns, both by domestic and foreign actors, interfering with electoral processes, as well as broader questions about Meta’s moderation systems to identify these risks.
Meta’s enforcement system uses artificial intelligence technologies to proactively identify content in ads that potentially violates its policies. Content is then assessed either automatically or by human reviewers and, where a violation is confirmed, enforcement actions such as removal, restriction, or rejection of ads are applied under Meta’s Community Standards.
“The investigation indicates that Facebook’s moderation systems may be failing to reliably detect election-related disinformation content. While Facebook rejected seven of the 15 ads, they were flagged under its social issues, elections, or politics policy, not specifically for electoral disinformation. This raises serious concerns about whether Facebook’s election safeguards are being consistently applied,”
Ummar Bashir, Researcher and Advisor on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights.
Amnesty International found that Facebook’s moderation systems appeared more effective at recognizing ads portraying political opponents as “criminals”, “traitors” or “illegitimate actors”. For example, one tested ad claimed that “The election will be stolen by Lula [the president of Brazil]”. Five out of seven ads containing this type of content were rejected. By contrast, three out of four ads containing military rhetoric that went against the rule of law and called for the military to take power, passed through Facebook’s moderation systems. One such ad stated: “We need a military revolution, do not vote in the elections, and the military will take back power if less than 50% votes!”
“Instead of safeguarding electoral participation, access to accurate information and human rights, these systems risk approving harmful content,” said Ummar Bashir, Researcher and Advisor on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights.
Business and human rights standards
Under international standards, companies have a responsibility to respect human rights and to avoid causing, contributing to, or being directly linked to adverse human rights impacts. This includes taking proactive measures to identify, prevent and mitigate human rights impacts.
For platforms such as Meta, this includes ensuring moderation practices do not allow false or inaccurate content to circulate that may affect individuals’ rights to information and participation in public affairs. The responsibility to respect human rights exists independently of state regulation and requires continuous risk assessment, transparency and effective mitigation measures.
Meta’s surveillance-based business model relies on the large-scale collection and analysis of user data to keep people engaged on its platforms and to enable highly targeted advertising. These ads are delivered using a complex combination of user profile characteristics, including location, demographics, interests, and online behaviour. Meta’s ability to offer advertisers finely tuned prediction and microtargeting tools is central to this model. In the first quarter of 2026, 98% of Meta’s revenue was derived from advertising.
Ahead of Brazil’s presidential election, Amnesty International is calling on Meta to ensure adequate Brazilian Portuguese language resourcing for content moderation including ad approvals and to immediately strengthen its capacity to identify and respond to election-related harms.
Meta should also conduct and publish updated, country-specific human rights due diligence, assessing how its systems, including content moderation and advertising, may contribute to risks to participation and access to information, and take effective, transparent steps to mitigate those risks.
“With the election just over five weeks away, Meta still has time to urgently address risks with its ad moderation systems and prevent the use of its platform to spread dangerous disinformation. Allowing such content to circulate unchecked could mislead voters, erode trust in electoral processes, and compromise people’s ability to freely and meaningfully exercise their right to vote,” said Jurema Werneck, Executive Director of Amnesty International Brazil.
Background
In recent years, Brazil has implemented several measures to tackle election-related disinformation. During the 2022 presidential election, Brazil’s national electoral authority, the Superior Electoral Court, introduced stricter measures requiring online platforms to rapidly remove false or knowingly decontextualized information regarding the electoral processes, with platforms facing fines and potential suspension for non-compliance.
The use of artificial intelligence (AI) was also restricted in advance of the municipal elections in 2024 to prevent disinformation and the manipulation of the elections. In 2024, Brazil’s Supreme Court also ordered the suspension of X, formerly Twitter, after the company failed to comply with court orders, including orders linked to accounts accused of spreading disinformation.
In March 2026, a new resolution outlined the specific content platforms are required to remove, including false or decontextualized content about the electronic voting system, the Electoral Court and other electoral processes, while also prohibiting the use of generative AI to rank, recommend, suggest or prioritize candidates, campaigns, political parties.

Armenia Signals Break With Russia-Led CSTO as Kremlin Says Yerevan Is ‘Free to Leave’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
02:57:56 UTC
11:57:56 KST

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan on Monday said he would be “very happy” if the Russia-led Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO) expelled Armenia, declaring that Yerevan’s interest in the military alliance had been exhausted.
The blunt statement drew an immediate response from the Kremlin, which said Armenia was free to leave the bloc if it no longer considered membership to be in its national interest.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Pashinyan told parliament that his government had no intention of resuming active participation in the CSTO during the next five years.
“We have raised questions with the CSTO, but we have not received answers to any of them,” Pashinyan said.
“I can say with confidence that we will not intensify our activities within the organization.”
He then went further, saying he would welcome a decision by the alliance itself to remove Armenia.
“I would be very happy if the organization decided to expel the Republic of Armenia from the CSTO, as this would free us from the dilemma of whether or not to leave,” Pashinyan said.
He added that Armenia had already put its concerns to the organization without receiving satisfactory answers and that Yerevan’s “interest in the CSTO has been exhausted.”
Armenia formally froze its participation in CSTO activities in 2024 after repeatedly criticizing the Russian-led alliance for failing to meet what Yerevan regarded as its security obligations.
Zelensky Meets With Coalition of the Willing Leaders, Says Ukraine Faces $27B Defense Budget Shortfall
Armenia is “free to leave”
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov responded that Armenia could formally withdraw if it no longer saw a reason to remain in the organization.
“If Yerevan, based on its national interests, no longer needs membership in such an important organization for ensuring regional security, then it is free to make the appropriate decision and leave the organization,” Peskov said.
Peskov noted that Armenia had until now frozen its participation without formally withdrawing.
The exchange underscored the widening rupture between Yerevan and Moscow, once Armenia’s dominant security partner.
Russia maintains a military base in Armenia, while Yerevan remains a member of the Moscow-led Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU).
But Armenia has steadily deepened ties with Europe amid anger over Russia’s perceived failure to protect the country during conflicts with neighboring Azerbaijan.
EU membership
On the same day, Pashinyan said Armenia would soon begin preparing a formal application to join the EU – another major step away from Moscow’s traditional sphere of influence.
“We may begin this process in the near future, especially given the urgent requests from our EAEU partners,” he said.
Pashinyan said a referendum on EU membership would follow once Armenia had formally applied and had greater clarity about its accession prospects and the reforms required.
Armenia’s parliament passed legislation in 2025 launching the process of seeking EU membership.
Pashinyan also pointed to Russian restrictions on Armenian exports, saying they contradict EAEU rules and have created what he described as a crisis within the Moscow-led economic bloc.
Russia has repeatedly warned Armenia that membership in the EU would be incompatible with remaining in the EAEU.
On Monday, Peskov said that EU and EAEU rules on trade, customs, and sanitary standards do not align and argued that moving toward European standards would create “deep contradictions” for Armenia.
He also pointed to Turkey’s decades-long stalled EU membership bid as a warning to Yerevan.
“I always recommend here that we keep in mind the experience of Turkey and a number of other countries, whose applications were submitted decades and decades ago, yet they’re still in the same situation today,” Peskov said.
Turkey has been an EU candidate since 1999, with its accession negotiations effectively frozen for years.
Moscow has increased pressure on Yerevan as Armenia moves closer to Europe, including through restrictions on Armenian imports.
Russian President Vladimir Putin also invoked Ukraine when warning Armenia in June against pursuing deeper European integration, saying the “Ukrainian scenario” had begun with Kyiv’s EU ambitions.
Pashinyan, who first came to power following mass protests in 2018, was re-elected in June after increasingly positioning Armenia toward closer cooperation with the EU and other Western partners.
His latest comments suggest that the distancing from Moscow is no longer limited to freezing Armenia’s participation in Russian-led institutions: Yerevan is openly discussing a future outside the CSTO while preparing its next formal step toward the EU.

What are tariffs and how do they work?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
02:53:02 UTC
11:53:02 KST

What are tariffs and how do they work?
What are tariffs and how do they work?
WASHINGTON (AP) — Tariffs are in the news at the moment. Here’s what they are and what you need to know about them:
Tariffs are a tax on imports
Tariffs are typically charged as a percentage of the price a buyer pays a foreign seller. In the United States, tariffs are collected by Customs and Border Protection agents at 328 ports of entry across the country.
U.S. tariff rates vary: They are generally 2.5% on passenger cars, for instance, and 6% on golf shoes. Tariffs can be lower for countries with which the United States has trade agreements. For example, most goods can move among the United States, Mexico and Canada tariff-free because of Trump’s US-Mexico-Canada trade agreement.
Mainstream economists are generally skeptical of tariffs, considering them a mostly inefficient way for governments to raise money and promote prosperity.
There’s much misinformation about who actually pays tariffs
President Donald Trump, a proponent of tariffs, insists that they are paid for by foreign countries. In fact, it is importers — American companies — that pay tariffs, and the money goes to the U.S. Treasury. Those companies, in turn, typically pass their higher costs on to their customers in the form of higher prices. That’s why economists say consumers usually end up footing the bill for tariffs.
Still, tariffs can hurt foreign countries by making their products pricier and harder to sell abroad. Foreign companies might have to cut prices — and sacrifice profits — to offset the tariffs and try to maintain their market share in the United States. Yang Zhou, an economist at Shanghai’s Fudan University, concluded in a study that Trump’s tariffs on Chinese goods inflicted more than three times as much damage to the Chinese economy as they did to the U.S. economy.
What has Trump said about tariffs?
Trump has said tariffs will create more factory jobs, shrink the federal deficit, lower food prices and allow the government to subsidize childcare.
“Tariffs are the greatest thing ever invented,’’ Trump said at a rally in Flint, Michigan, during his presidential campaign.
As president, Trump imposed tariffs with a flourish — targeting imported solar panels, steel, aluminum and pretty much everything from China.
“Tariff Man,” he called himself.
Trump has promised even more and higher tariffs in his second term.
The United States in recent years has gradually retreated from its post-World War II role of promoting global free trade and lower tariffs. That shift has been a response to the loss of U.S. manufacturing jobs, widely attributed to unfettered tree trade and an increasingly powerful China.
Tariffs are intended mainly to protect domestic industries
By raising the price of imports, tariffs can protect home-grown manufacturers. They may also serve to punish foreign countries for committing unfair trade practices, like subsidizing their exporters or dumping products at unfairly low prices.
Before the federal income tax was established in 1913, tariffs were a major revenue driver for the government. From 1790 to 1860, tariffs accounted for 90% of federal revenue, according to Douglas Irwin, a Dartmouth College economist who has studied the history of trade policy.
Tariffs fell out of favor as global trade grew after World War II. The government needed vastly bigger revenue streams to finance its operations.
In the fiscal year that ended Sept. 30, the government collected around $80 billion in tariffs and fees. That’s a trifle next to the $2.5 trillion that comes from individual income taxes and the $1.7 trillion from Social Security and Medicare taxes.
Still, Trump wants to enact a budget policy that resembles what was in place in the 19th century.
Tariffs can also be used to pressure other countries on issues that may or may not be related to trade. In 2019, for example, Trump used the threat of tariffs as leverage to persuade Mexico to crack down on waves of Central American migrants crossing Mexican territory on their way to the United States.
Trump even sees tariffs as a way to prevent wars.
“I can do it with a phone call,’’ he said at an August rally in North Carolina.
If another country tries to start a war, he said he’d issue a threat:
“We’re going to charge you 100% tariffs. And all of a sudden, the president or prime minister or dictator or whoever the hell is running the country says to me, ‘Sir, we won’t go to war.’ ”
Economists generally consider tariffs self-defeating
Tariffs raise costs for companies and consumers that rely on imports. They’re also likely to provoke retaliation.
The European Union, for example, punched back against Trump’s tariffs on steel and aluminum by taxing U.S. products, from bourbon to Harley-Davidson motorcycles. Likewise, China responded to Trump’s trade war by slapping tariffs on American goods, including soybeans and pork in a calculated drive to hurt his supporters in farm country.
A study by economists at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, the University of Zurich, Harvard and the World Bank concluded that Trump’s tariffs failed to restore jobs to the American heartland. The tariffs “neither raised nor lowered U.S. employment’’ where they were supposed to protect jobs, the study found.
Despite Trump’s 2018 taxes on imported steel, for example, the number of jobs at U.S. steel plants barely budged: They remained right around 140,000. By comparison, Walmart alone employs 1.6 million people in the United States.
Worse, the retaliatory taxes imposed by China and other nations on U.S. goods had “negative employment impacts,’’ especially for farmers, the study found. These retaliatory tariffs were only partly offset by billions in government aid that Trump doled out to farmers. The Trump tariffs also damaged companies that relied on targeted imports.
If Trump’s trade war fizzled as policy, though, it succeeded as politics. The study found that support for Trump and Republican congressional candidates rose in areas most exposed to the import tariffs — the industrial Midwest and manufacturing-heavy Southern states like North Carolina and Tennessee.

Türkiye and Qatar aim to increase their bilateral trade volume to $5 billion, Turkish Trade Minister Omer Bolat said Monday.
Bolat met with Qatar’s Minister of State for Foreign Trade, Ahmed bin Mohammed Al-Sayed, at the Trade Ministry in Ankara.
“Türkiye-Qatar relations have truly made tremendous progress. Our total annual foreign trade increased 53-fold over the past 21 years, reaching $1.3 billion last year,” Bolat told reporters after the meeting.
Trade between the two countries climbed as high as $2.5 billion during preparations for the 2022 FIFA World Cup in Qatar, largely due to construction projects, he added.
Bolat said the Trade and Economic Partnership Agreement between Türkiye and Qatar, which entered into force last year, would make a significant contribution to achieving the $5 billion trade target.
Turkish contractors have undertaken 206 projects worth a combined $21 billion in Qatar, he said.
Around 250 Qatari companies have investments totaling $7.8 billion in Türkiye, spanning sectors including finance, banking, energy, logistics, media and agriculture.
Meanwhile, approximately 1,116 Turkish companies of various sizes operate in Qatar’s construction, services and manufacturing sectors.
Alternative trade routes amid Hormuz disruption
Bolat said the closure of the Strait of Hormuz due to the war in the region had created logistics and supply bottlenecks, highlighting the need for alternative routes.
“The current circumstances have shown that alternative routes are greatly needed to avoid dependence solely on maritime transport and the Strait of Hormuz,” he said.
Türkiye is working to meet Qatar and other Gulf countries’ demand for consumer goods, Bolat noted.
Under a transit transportation agreement with Saudi Arabia that took effect on April 15, Turkish carriers have been conducting intensive shipments to Gulf countries through Syria, Jordan and Saudi Arabia, as well as via Iraq and Saudi Arabia.
“We will work together to establish these transit and trade corridors on a stronger and more stable basis,” he said.
Bolat added that Al-Sayed conveyed the Qatar Investment Authority’s desire to expand its investments in Türkiye and said initiatives were underway in this regard.

Apple gears up to launch its first new Mac Mini in two years
LOS ANGELES – Apple is gearing up to launch a new version of its Mac mini desktop computer for the first time in almost two years, according to sources familiar with the matter.
The new desktop will debut as soon as the coming days, potentially putting the unveiling ahead of a September event to introduce the next iPhones, said the sources, who asked not to be identified because the plan is not public. Apple has tested versions with both the M5 and M6 generations of its processor line.
The upgrade follows a surge in demand for the current Mac mini, which has become a popular tool for running artificial intelligence applications locally. At the same time, memory-chip shortages have made it harder for Apple to keep the product in stock.
A spokesperson for Cupertino, California-based Apple declined to comment.
The updated machine is part of a wave of new products coming in the second half of 2026.
Later this week, Apple is poised to send out invitations for its iPhone launch presentation. That event, which is likely to be held on Sept 9, will introduce the company’s first foldable smartphone, as well as the iPhone 18 Pro line.
The company is also preparing a range of new Apple Watches with minor changes, including upgrades to fitness tracking and a ceramic-case option for Series 12 models. And it is planning to debut fresh AirPods as early as the September product launch event.
The roll-out will include new AirPods 5, an update to Apple’s entry-level earbuds, the people said. That model was last refreshed in 2024. A camera-equipped version of the AirPods, meanwhile, is not expected until 2027.
Apple is also on track to debut its first-ever smart home device with a screen in 2026. The product will rely on facial recognition to identify users and display personalised content. The company is readying a new Apple TV set-top box and HomePod mini smart speaker as well.
Other new products in 2026 include a revamped iPad mini with an OLED screen. That technology, short for organic light-emitting diode, offers a crisper picture than the tablet had before and brings it closer in line with more premium iPads. The new model is due to arrive by the end of October.
Additional Macs are coming as well, though they are likely to be further out. That includes an iMac with new colour options, as well as a refreshed entry-level MacBook Pro. They will use M6 chips, the upcoming generation.
The most significant Mac introduction in the pipeline will be Apple’s first touch-screen computer. The company will add that capability to new MacBook Pro models, in 14-inch and 16-inch sizes, that will also include redesigned cases and OLED screens.
The Mac mini will likely be the last new product to launch under the watch of chief executive Tim Cook, who is handing the reins to John Ternus on Sept 1. Ternus will oversee the roll-out of the foldable iPhone and the other major new products in the company’s pipeline.
Looking ahead to 2027, Apple is planning updates to the entry-level iPad and iPad Air; new MacBook Air and MacBook Neo models; second-generation versions of the touch MacBooks that use chips from the upcoming M7 series; a second-generation foldable iPhone; and an iPhone with curved glass to mark the device’s 20-year anniversary.
It is also planning a push into AI wearables, starting with the AirPods with cameras. As part of that effort, the company aims to introduce smart glasses that would put it in competition with Meta Platforms. And it has been testing a pendant with cameras that can feed visual data into iPhones for AI processing.
The Mac mini has been a particular pain point for Apple’s supply chain in recent months, with deliveries to customers taking weeks or months to be completed. Cook said the problem would take a while to resolve, and it is unclear how the new model will affect wait times.
The computer is also central to Apple’s pledge to bring more manufacturing to the US. Earlier in 2026, Apple vowed to start producing the Mac mini in Houston later in the same year. Cook toured the factory in August with officials from the Trump administration, which has made domestic manufacturing a key piece of its agenda.
The company had previously assembled the Mac Pro in the US, but that model was discontinued earlier in 2026. BLOOMBERG

China is the biggest buyer of Iran’s oil. Could US sanctions threaten those ties?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
02:44:59 UTC
11:44:59 KST

An oil refinery in Binzhou in eastern China's Shandong province. Chinese independent refiners have been the main buyers of Iranian crude oil, attracted by what has typically been a steep discount to mainstream barrels. Photograph: CFOTO/Future Publishing/Getty Images
An oil refinery in Binzhou in eastern China's Shandong province. Chinese independent refiners have been the main buyers of Iranian crude oil, attracted by what has typically been a steep discount to mainstream barrels. Photograph: CFOTO/Future Publishing/Getty Images
China is the biggest buyer of Iran’s oil. Could US sanctions threaten those ties?
The US has put the world on notice to cease doing business with Iran, but experts say Washington is wary China could retaliate against any sanctions
The US has unveiled an expansion of sanctions that it says will cut off Iran’s economic lifeline but stopped short of the most punishing measures, instead putting the world on notice to cease doing business with the Islamic republic.
Treasury secretary Scott Bessent warned other countries would need to sever business ties with Iran or risk being forced out of the dollar-based financial system. He previously urged cooperation from China – the biggest buyer of Iranian oil for several years – although the US blockade of Iran’s ports, renewed in mid-July, has already cut much of the Iranian oil flows to China.
Experts say Washington is wary of Chinese retaliation for any sanctions on its banks ahead of expected talks next month between US president Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping, with any curbs on China’s exports of critical minerals especially sensitive.
What do the new moves by the US mean for China and oil and how might Beijing respond?
How much oil does China buy from Iran?
Through the early weeks of the war Iran continued to ship to China, with Beijing’s imports of Iranian crude slipping only marginally, according to Kpler ship-tracking data, from 1.57m barrels a day in February to 1.47m barrels a day in March.
Since then imports have dropped dramatically. The US renewed its blockade of Iran’s ships and ports in July in an attempt to cut off oil sales, as a deal to halt their war broke down.
Shipments fell to 785,000 barrels a day in June – the lowest since February 2023 – but then rose slightly in July to 823,000, provisional Kpler data showed. The intake so far in August has dropped to 534,000.
Who are the Chinese buyers?
Chinese independent refiners have been the main Iranian crude buyers, attracted by what has typically been a steep discount to mainstream barrels. Known as “teapot” refineries, they survive by buying cheap crude wherever they can, turning it into petrol and diesel for neighbouring provinces.
China’s big state refiners have shunned Iranian oil since 2019, when the US reimposed sanctions on Tehran, because they do not want to be cut off from the US dollar-based international financial system. But the teapots, which cater to a domestic market, have no such qualms.
Iranian oil delivered to China has long been branded as Malaysian, and more recently Indonesian, and is settled in Chinese currency, trading in a tight loop involving a chain of difficult-to-track intermediaries, according to refinery sources and traders involved in the business.
Have previous US sanctions been effective?
Washington has intensified its efforts to clamp down on Chinese purchases of Iranian oil since Trump returned to the White House early last year, imposing sanctions on mostly smaller Chinese refiners and other participants in the supply chain, which have in some cases proven disruptive.
The US treasury department has also warned two larger Chinese banks they could face secondary sanctions if Iranian funds were found moving through their systems, but has stopped short of designating them.
In April, Washington imposed sanctions on Hengli Petrochemical (Dalian) refinery, along with about 40 shipping firms and vessels, accusing Hengli of buying billions of dollars’ worth of Iranian oil, escalating its efforts to curb Tehran’s oil revenue. Hengli has denied buying Iranian oil.
In the past, however, sanctions themselves have done little to slow overall flows of Iranian oil into China.
Asked about Chinese banks on Monday, US treasury secretary Scott Bessent said: “We want to make clear here today that no one is above the reach of US sanctions.”
What have China and Iran said?
The Chinese foreign ministry said sanctions and pressure tactics did not help and Beijing would do what was necessary to protect China’s interests.
China, which has said it rejects unilateral sanctions, has called for a resolution through diplomatic and political means.
Iranian economy minister Ali Madanizadeh told state television that neither China nor Russia had “accepted” the US measures, and predicted other countries would resist them.
He said: “Naturally, the enemies intend to launch an economic terrorist attack on us, but we also have our own tools and know how to play the game.”

Major NSW property developer enters administration

Major NSW property developer Bathla Group falls into administration
Major Sydney residential developer Bathla Group has fallen into administration after months of mounting financial pressure.
Administrators from Teneo were appointed on Tuesday to its main corporate entity, Universal Property Group, as well as Raj & Jai Construction, a company linked to the Bathla Group, documents lodged with ASIC show.
Voluntary administration is when an independent administrator takes control of a company in financial trouble and assesses its future.
Creditors then generally decide whether the company can be restructured or should be wound up.
Bathla Group is a major developer of lower-cost homes, townhouses and apartments, particularly in Western Sydney suburbs such as Schofields, Marsden Park and Tallawong.
According to its website, 22,000 apartment dwellings and 3,500 homes are in the developer's "project pipeline".
In an Instagram post, managing director Bhart Bhushan said the developer was dealing with a "perfect storm" of softening sales, tax change impacts and higher construction costs.
As at June 30 last year, Universal Property Group had $3.2 billion in liabilities, the majority of which was reportedly owed to private credit funds.
The collapse is likely to intensify scrutiny of Bathla's extensive use of private credit to finance its property developments as administrators begin assessing the financial position of the affected companies.
Teneo appointed as voluntary administrator
In a statement, the administrators said their immediate priority was to "stabilise the Group's operations" and work with lenders and other stakeholders to support employees and the continued delivery of projects.
"Our priority is to stabilise the business so that construction activity and property settlements can continue in the ordinary course," Teneo Australia Financial Advisory head Stephen Longley said.
Bathla chief executive Robert Loader said the business has been through a period of "declining sales and falling property prices, while construction costs have increased".
Bathla Group operates through a highly complex corporate structure, with Universal Property Group, its main corporate entity, sitting at the top of a network of hundreds of separate companies, according to ASIC records.
Many are numbered UPG entities that extend as high as UPG 460. Others operate under different company names.
ASIC records Universal Property Group as the ultimate holding company for many of these entities.
Buyers in limbo
Kate, who does not wish to use her real name, bought an off-the-plan freestanding house in Lochinvar, in regional New South Wales, for $709,990 in the middle of last year.
Documents seen by ABC News confirm the purchase.
Kate told ABC News that, as a renter, she had been relying on the property becoming her family home.
"I am very worried and just scared this could jeopardise the completion of the house," the single mother said.
Kate said Bathla employees had previously told her the house would be ready by June, then August, but that the expected completion had since been pushed back to the end of this year.
"I have been nervous for some time, to be honest, as there seems to be no-one there working on the property on many days," she said.
"It seems like a ghost town."
Kate said she had hoped the house would help provide security for her two young daughters.
In a contract for sale seen by ABC News, Janice Cahill bought a two-bedroom apartment off the plan in a new development at Kembla Grange, near Wollongong.
She said she was initially told the apartment would be ready in September last year. The expected completion date was then pushed back repeatedly, to December 2025, March 2026, April, August and September.
She said the latest date she was given was December 31 this year.

She said the continuing delays had become an "absolute nightmare", particularly with a double knee replacement surgery approaching.
Ms Cahill said she had received no contact from Bathla since news of the company's voluntary administration emerged this morning.
"I'm starting to feel hopeless. It feels like they don't want to know."

Sudan’s government intensifying efforts to support civilian dialogue: UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
02:32:23 UTC
11:32:23 KST

Adel Abdelrheem and Mohammad Sio
25 August 2026•Update: 25 August 2026
Sudan’s government is stepping up efforts to support civilian dialogue in the country, UN Under-Secretary-General for Political and Peacebuilding Affairs Rosemary Dicarlo said Monday.
Dicarlo made the remarks during a briefing to the UN Security Council in New York on the situation in Sudan.
“Thirteen million people have fled their homes, including around 8.7 million who are displaced internally across all 18 states,” she said, referring to a country with an estimated population of around 50 million.
Dicarlo said there were “around 1,400 civilian deaths from January to June this year, including 1,100 people killed by drone strikes.”
Fighting in Sudan in recent weeks “has been characterized by the heavy use of drones and localized ground combat in areas less affected by rainy season conditions,” she said.
Dicarlo said fighting near Sudan’s border with Ethiopia in Blue Nile state “is also a serious cause for concern.”
“The sophisticated weaponry used continues to point to ongoing external support to both parties,” she added.
She noted that Sudanese authorities “have also stepped up their own efforts to support civilian dialogue” and welcomed “all efforts to foster meaningful political discussions regarding Sudan’s future.”
Sudanese Sovereignty Council Chairman Abdel Fattah al-Burhan said during an address on Aug. 14 that a group of Sudanese citizens had proposed an independent national mechanism to prepare for an inclusive dialogue led from within the country and involving political and community forces.
Burhan said the group had asked the government to provide guarantees for the dialogue and participation by its various parties. He said he had agreed to provide logistical support as well as legal, political and security guarantees.
He stressed at the time that the government will not organize the dialogue or determine its agenda or outcomes.
UN Undersecretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator Tom Fletcher, meanwhile, told the Security Council that “more than two-thirds of the people of Sudan are in desperate need of lifesaving support.”
“The people of Sudan need food, water and medicine. Yet the world sends drones, weapons and mercenaries,” Fletcher said.
“The people of Sudan need sustained, courageous diplomacy. Yet the world is too often indifferent and distracted,” he added.
Sudan has been embroiled in a war between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) since April 2023. The conflict has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced about 13 million, according to UN and international estimates.

Hottest ocean temperature recorded as ‘super’ El Nino forms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
02:30:07 UTC
11:30:07 KST

Hottest ocean temperature recorded as ‘super’ El Nino forms
Average surface waters reached 21.1 degrees Celsius, months ahead of when peak global ocean temperatures typically occur
Scientists have recorded the highest temperature ever measured in the world’s oceans, as climate change combines with a powerful El Nino in the tropical Pacific.
The global average sea-surface temperature hit a record 21.1 degrees Celsius (70 Fahrenheit) on August 22, according to Europe’s Earth observation agency Copernicus, which has been tracking the metric daily since 1979. The previous single-day record of 21.09 degrees was measured in March 2024.
“El Nino is adding heat to the system, but it is doing so on top of decades of human-driven warming,” said Samantha Burgess, strategic lead for climate at Copernicus’ European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts.
“As ocean temperatures continue to rise, the risks to marine ecosystems and coastal communities also increase,” she said.
Higher ocean temperatures contribute to sea level rise and increase the chance of extreme weather events, as warmer water transfers more heat and moisture to the atmosphere, intensifying storms and heat on land. Warmer oceans also have a reduced capacity to absorb carbon dioxide.

‘We’re going to keep going’: Venezuelan quake rescuers soldier on
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
02:30:00 UTC

‘We’re going to keep going’: Venezuelan quake rescuers soldier on
LA GUAIRA, Venezuela – Two months after two huge earthquakes struck Venezuela and killed thousands, volunteer rescuer Domingo Pacheco still faces a mountain of work.
The 53-year-old reached the worst-hit coastal state of La Guaira in the immediate aftermath of the quakes and has been picking through the rubble ever since.
The magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 tremors hit within a minute of each other on June 24, killing more than 6,500 people.
Pacheco has the unenviable task of looking for an unknown number of lifeless victims still buried under the debris, although he avoids thinking about the emotional impact.
The work is physically challenging, too.
One evening, after one of many exhausting days of digging through the detritus, he lost his breath and blacked out for a few seconds.
“The oxygen was slowly taken away from me until I kind of lost consciousness,” Pacheco told AFP.
“Everything went blurry and I thought of my young son before asking myself, ‘What’s going on?’”
‘Where I was needed’
When the volunteer arrived in June, he went straight to work, searching for a little girl buried under a collapsed social housing complex.
He recalls a trapped family who had lived on the top floor, begging to be rescued during those first hours of confusion.
“There were people screaming, asking us to help them,” he said. “I went where I was needed.”
Pacheco volunteers with the Unified Rescue Group of Venezuela (GRUV), which depends on donations and has rescued 21 people alive and recovered 56 bodies.
Witnessing the determination of families who refuse to give up on loved ones still trapped under the impenetrable rubble has “profoundly impacted” him, he told AFP.
There are no official figures to show how many people remain missing after the quakes.
“When to close this chapter?” Pacheco asked.
“God willing, as soon as possible, so that everyone, so that those family members too, can find relief from the suffering they are going through, from not being able to recover their loved ones.”
‘I can vouch for them’
Frank Viloria met Pacheco and his GRUV colleagues in Playa Grande, where entire residential complexes crumbled against a backdrop of stunning sea views.
Viloria’s sister and niece died when their eight-storey building fell to pieces.
“When I see him, I’m happy,” he said with a smile, shaking hands with Pacheco, who calls him “son”.
“I’m very grateful to them. I feel a lot of respect and admiration; I can vouch for them because I saw how they work,” the 38-year-old added.
The men hug when they say goodbye.
Located north of Caracas, La Guaira is usually a favourite weekend getaway spot for residents of the capital.
Its once touristy atmosphere has been replaced by tragedy these past few months, and thousands of people made homeless by the quakes now live in makeshift camps under difficult conditions.
“Sometimes I’m very sad; my mind is here... it’s never at home” in Caracas, said Pacheco.
“We’re going to keep going for as long as the body allows,” he said. AFP

US Commerce Secretary Lutnick’s intervention in Canada talks draws praise and blame

- The talks collapsed amid disagreements over tariff reductions, with Lutnick and trade hawk Peter Navarro opposing concessions seen as too generous to Canada.
- The breakdown triggered a trade war, angering US steel and aluminium sectors and leaving Canadian officials frustrated by shifting US demands and internal US administration conflicts.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – US-Canada trade talks collapsed after last-minute pressure from Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, according to people familiar with the matter, leaving President Donald Trump to impose new tariffs and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney vowing retaliation.
With the countries spiralling into a full-blown trade war, the spotlight is on Lutnick’s role in the last-minute talks.
Lutnick viewed a framework deal as too generous to Canada and emerged as a champion for US metal producers who wanted to claw back concessions, the people said, speaking anonymously to discuss the negotiations.
The Canadians blame him for moving the goalposts, some of the people said, while some business leaders credit Lutnick with derailing what they saw as a threat to US metals industries Trump has vowed to protect.
Trump on Aug 18 announced a deal was in sight and delayed imposing 50 per cent tariffs on a range of Canadian goods.
Battle lines, however, had formed as Lutnick and Peter Navarro, a pro-tariff trade hawk, criticised the framework from US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer’s weeks of talks with Canada.
Lutnick’s 11th-hour intervention, taking him deeper into the talks, marked the latest example of how he’s functioned as a disruptive force inside Trump’s administration, often seizing on trade files where he senses the US can squeeze more leverage.
A White House official disputed any notion Lutnick derailed the talks, insisting instead that they imploded after Canada made last-minute demands outside the agreed scope of discussions.
The official added that while there was likely debate among US officials about the magnitude of tariff relief, Lutnick and Greer are aligned and working under Trump.
While Lutnick was unhelpful and a major contributor to the breakdown of talks, his arrival wasn’t the cause, according to a Canadian official.
The official said there were fundamental problems with the US objectives over the final days.
USTR and the Commerce Department didn’t respond to requests for comment on the negotiations. The Canadian prime minister’s office also didn’t respond.
Lutnick’s shifting public comments on auto and steel levies in 2025 fuelled market volatility.
Deals he helped strike with Japan and South Korea – which saw the countries pledge hundreds of billions in investments in exchange for tariff relief – were initially met with caution and have continued to face questions, though some major projects have been announced.
With Canada in particular, Lutnick has sometimes played the role of spoiler, including helping delay the planned opening of the Gordie Howe International Bridge, actions viewed in Canada as an attempted shakedown.
US officials have blamed Canadian counterparts for the impasse.
“The USTR did a fine job negotiating. Canada was very foolish not to take the deal,” Navarro said. “It won’t get better. Carney chose politics over the Canadian people.”
After a conversation between Trump and Carney on Aug 18, the US president touted the prospect of resurrecting the Keystone XL oil pipeline and blessed the framework publicly, extending talks by three days to tie things up.
However, tensions continued to mount.
The US steel and aluminium sectors, typically staunch Trump allies, were outraged, saying they were caught off guard by a proposal that would weaken the tariff wall around their businesses and profit margins, the people said.
The industries pressured Greer’s office. Some turned to Lutnick and allies in Congress for help.
People familiar with the matter described a torrent of calls and frenzied meetings as they sought to warn the administration against the move.
Domestic aluminium extruders, which shape raw aluminium into value-added goods, told administration officials and key lawmakers that widespread discounts on aluminium tariffs could destroy their profit margin.
The Coalition for a Prosperous America emphasised that aluminium extruders are critical to support domestic production of the metal itself.
Lutnick and Greer cut vastly different figures within the administration.
Greer is seen as a restrained, details-focused trade lawyer at heart; Lutnick a more colourful, outspoken figure, like Trump.
Both have key roles implementing Trump’s trade policy.
While Greer led the talks with Canada, Lutnick’s Commerce portfolio includes the Section 232 tariffs targeting industrial sectors.
While some people familiar downplayed the divide, saying the two officials are united under Trump, the dynamic led to something of a dual-track negotiation.
Lutnick spoke directly with Carney repeatedly in the final days of negotiations even though Greer had been the Canadian delegation’s point person.
Canadian ambassador to the US Mark Wiseman declined to discuss Lutnick’s impact on negotiations.
“You’d have to ask the Americans how they were operating behind the scenes,” he said in an interview on Aug 23. “Our counterparty in our discussions was USTR.”
Meanwhile, Carney faced his own divisions with the provincial premiers he would need to lift bans on US alcohol sales to seal any deal.
One premier in particular, Manitoba’s Wab Kinew, had publicly criticised the tentative agreement.
Greer acknowledged on Aug 24 on CNBC that Canada sought guarantees he couldn’t unilaterally give, but called reports of a divide between him and Lutnick “a red herring.”
Still, he admitted “it could be frustrating for Canadians that we have tariff authorities in two different agencies, but that’s how Congress set it up.”
As the haggling continued, the terms shifted.
By the morning of Aug 21, the prospect of largely straight tariff reductions on aluminium and steel had been replaced by a push for more limited, nuanced relief.
The industry pressure campaign had persuaded some officials to dial back a planned concession to Canada that would have lowered the tariff to 25 per cent from 50 per cent on a quota of Canadian metal imports, alongside reductions for some derivative products.
As talks continued, the US told some stakeholders it would appreciate them speaking publicly about the benefits of a deal, one of the people said.
Both the US and Canada were signalling as of the afternoon of Aug 21 that officials believed they were on track to finalise everything, some of the people said.
As of the night of Aug 21, the Canadians thought they had a deal.
Lutnick focused on preserving the scope of the auto-sector concession.
While Canada thought the countries agreed to lower vehicle tariffs to 15 per cent from 25 per cent the US said the reduction applied only to light vehicles, not medium- and heavy-duty trucks.
The distinction would have imperilled a General Motors Co plant and a Ford Motor Co. plant in Ontario.
It’s unclear whether Lutnick’s goal was to derail the pact or reshape it.
One person said it appeared Lutnick and Navarro were betting that Canada would accept the terms and not walk away.
But Carney said the US demands were too much.
US steel and aluminium companies are privately pleased with the collapse.
“The breakdown of these negotiations should put an end to proposals to weaken” Section 232 tariffs, said Jon Toomey, president of the Coalition for a Prosperous America.
Other groups, including Business Roundtable and Autos Drive America, representing foreign companies that do business in the US, called for a return to talks.
There’s little sign of an immediate revival of negotiations.
Carney, speaking on Aug 22, sidestepped a question on whether Lutnick killed a deal.
“It’s a question for the US,” he said.
Carney called the Canadian approach “unified,” adding: “You cannot say that about the United States administration.” BLOOMBERG

Peru court hands lengthy prison terms in killing of Indigenous Amazon defender
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
02:23:01 UTC
11:23:01 KST

Peru court hands lengthy prison terms in killing of Indigenous Amazon defender
BOGOTA, Colombia (AP) — A Peruvian court on Monday evening convicted four men of murder-for-hire and sentenced them to between 15 and 35 years in prison for the 2023 killing of Indigenous rainforest defender Quinto Inuma Alvarado, in a closely watched case seen as a test of accountability for violence against Indigenous and environmental defenders in the Amazon.
Genix Saboya Saboya and Limber Ríos Ruiz were each sentenced to 35 years in prison. Segundo Juan Villalobos Guevara, a timber operator whom prosecutors accused of ordering Inuma’s killing, was sentenced to 28 years and four months. Jerly Saboya Saboya, who was convicted as an accomplice, was sentenced to 15 years.
Inuma, a 50-year-old Kichwa leader, was shot and killed on Nov. 29, 2023, as he traveled by boat back to his community, Santa Rosillo de Yanayacu, in Peru ’s northern Amazonian region of San Martin. He was returning from a national meeting of environmental and land defenders. A woman traveling with him was also shot and wounded.
The ruling came nearly 1,000 days after Inuma’s killing. Tom Younger, Peru program coordinator at the Forest Peoples Programme, called the sentences a “decisive step towards justice” and said they showed that impunity for killings of Indigenous defenders “is not inevitable.”
Prosecutors said Inuma was targeted because of his efforts to stop illegal logging on his community’s land. They accused Villalobos, whom Inuma had denounced over illegal logging, of ordering the killing and the other men of planning and carrying out the attack.
Cristina Gavancho, a lawyer with the Lima-based Legal Defense Institute who has accompanied Indigenous organizations and the victims’ families since Inuma’s killing, called the ruling an “exemplary sentence” and said the lengthy prison terms could set an important precedent for other cases involving environmental defenders in Peru.
Gavancho said it was the first case in Peru involving the killing of an Indigenous defender to result in sentences this severe.
Inuma had repeatedly warned authorities of threats
The trial began Jan. 20 and continued for nearly eight months. In March, judges traveled from Lima to the Amazonian city of Tarapoto for three days of hearings, where they heard testimony from Inuma’s relatives, other witnesses and a survivor of the attack.
Inuma had spent years denouncing illegal logging, drug trafficking and encroachment on his community’s territory. Between 2016 and 2023, members of Santa Rosillo de Yanayacu filed 13 complaints with prosecutors over environmental crimes and drug trafficking, according to the Legal Defense Institute.
Peru’s Justice Ministry classified Inuma as being at high risk in 2021 and ordered police protection for him and his brother. Local authorities also granted him protection measures against illegal logging groups. But police later acknowledged they were unable to carry out preventive patrols in the remote territory because they lacked money for boats and faced difficult geography, according to documents cited by the Legal Defense Institute.
Kevin Arnol Inuma, the murdered leader’s 30-year-old son, said his family received the verdict with a mixture of happiness and sadness after waiting nearly three years for justice.
“Before, there was no response from the state, so they were not afraid to kill,” he told The Associated Press on a phone call just after the verdict. “Now this sets a precedent for Indigenous peoples, a precedent for environmental defenders.”
Another Indigenous leader killed a day before verdict
Inuma’s death became emblematic of the dangers faced by Indigenous people protecting forests and ancestral lands in Peru’s Amazon, where illegal logging, drug trafficking, mining and land grabbing have pushed into remote territories with limited state presence.
Those dangers were underscored again just a day before Monday’s verdict. Américo Pascuala Tomisha, a 57-year-old Ashéninka Indigenous leader and former head of the Onconashari Indigenous community, was shot dead Sunday while patrolling his community’s territory in Peru’s Amazonian Ucayali region, according to the regional Indigenous organization ORAU.
ORAU said Pascuala encountered outsiders allegedly extracting oil from copaiba trees inside the community’s territory and was shot after a confrontation. The organization said he had previously reported incursions by settlers and other outsiders and called on authorities Monday to investigate his killing and strengthen protection for Indigenous leaders.
Pascuala’s killing came weeks after Asháninka communities along the Peru-Brazil border raised alarms about armed incursions into Indigenous territories. In July, Indigenous leaders in neighboring Brazil sought government protection after five men carrying machine guns entered their territory, threatened families and searched for community leaders. Brazil and Peru subsequently agreed to increase cooperation to protect Indigenous territories along their shared Amazonian border.
Family says risks remain despite convictions
The court also ordered 750,000 soles (about $223,500) in compensation for Inuma’s legal heirs and 250,000 soles (about $74,500) for Axeldina Barbarán Tapullima, who was wounded in the attack. The payments would take effect only if the ruling, which can be appealed, becomes final, Gavancho said. The defendants have five days after receiving the court’s full written judgment to file an appeal.
For Gavancho, the ruling was significant not only because of the prison terms but also because of the compensation the court recognized for Inuma’s family and the woman who survived the attack.
“I think this emblematic case can serve as a precedent for other cases involving environmental defenders in Peru,” Gavancho said.
But Inuma said his family still does not feel safe and fears what could happen if those convicted were eventually freed.
His father, he said, had spent years defending the territory that earlier generations had left to the community, and that responsibility had now passed to his family and others.
He said he hoped other families of murdered defenders would not have to wait as long for their cases to move through Peru’s justice system.
“Although they can no longer give us our family members back, we want justice for the other defenders whose cases are still going on,” he said. “Now my father can rest in peace because justice has been done.”

Colombia begins post-earthquake reconstruction as president pledges major investment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
02:22:03 UTC
