Diyar Guldogan
25 August 2026•Update: 25 August 2026
Colombian President Abelardo De La Espriella formally launched the reconstruction phase Monday following the country’s devastating Aug. 10 earthquake, announcing financial assistance for affected families and a major rebuilding effort centered on the hardest-hit Choco department.
De La Espriella visited Quibdo, the capital of Choco, to deliver aid and oversee the start of reconstruction efforts two weeks after the 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck western Colombia. The quake affected hundreds of municipalities and caused extensive damage to homes, schools, hospitals and other critical infrastructure.
"Today, from Quibdo, we took a decisive step: the reconstruction of Colombia has formally begun," De La Espriella said.
"After two weeks of grief, humanitarian care and tireless work, we are entering a new phase: rebuilding what nature destroyed and doing it better, safer and with lasting results."
The president said the first 480 tons of construction materials had begun arriving in Choco.
"We announced direct economic support for families who lost their homes; we launched the Milagro Fund to lead a reconstruction that will require more than 30 trillion pesos ($9.7 billion); and we continue to bring the private sector into this great national endeavor."
De La Espriella said he would return to Quibdo on Sept. 7 with business leaders committed to advancing a special plan for Choco.

Lockerbie bombing trial postponed by US judge days before start
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
02:18:40 UTC
11:18:40 KST

Lockerbie bombing trial postponed by US judge days before start
WASHINGTON – A US federal judge on Aug 24 postponed the trial of the man authorities allege built the bomb that blew New York-bound Pan Am flight 103 out of the sky over Lockerbie, Scotland, killing 270 people in 1988.
Jury selection had been scheduled to begin on Aug 26 in the trial of Abu Agila Mohammad Mas’ud Kheir Al-Marimi, a Libyan intelligence operative who prosecutors allege once confessed to his role in the 1988 bombing.
In the decision to postpone the trial, US District Judge Dabney Friedrich cited the discovery of new evidence that defence attorneys want to examine.
The judge said “the newly discovered evidence, as well as evidence located in other countries” and “the need for the defence to determine how best to defend this case” made her reach the decision.
Friedrich did not schedule a new trial date but set a court hearing on Sept 1 to discuss next steps.
Mas’ud, now in his mid-70s, has pleaded not guilty to two criminal charges related to the destruction of the aircraft resulting in death and faces a maximum of life in prison if convicted.
The Boeing 747 exploded minutes after take-off from London on Dec 21, 1988, killing all 259 people on board, including 190 Americans, and 11 people on the ground in Scotland.
The bombing made former Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi, whose government accepted responsibility for the attack in 2003, an international pariah.
Mas’ud has denied wrongdoing and his lawyers have challenged the credibility of evidence gathered by prosecutors, including Mas’ud’s alleged confession to a Libyan police officer in 2012, a year after rebel forces toppled Gaddafi’s government.
Mas’ud’s trial in Washington, D.C. federal court has been delayed by years of legal wrangling over the alleged confession and other issues that have exposed the complexities of a US prosecution over a decades-old attack in Britain with crucial evidence gathered in Libya.
Mas’ud, who was arrested in Libya and brought to the US in 2022, is accused of building a time-delayed bomb that was packed into a suitcase and placed in checked baggage in Malta. The explosive-laden suitcase eventually made its way to London Heathrow Airport, where it was stored in the hold of Pan Am flight 103. REUTERS

Gaza kites not used to carry weapons or incendiary materials: Board of Peace source
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
02:17:26 UTC
11:17:26 KST

Zein Khalil and Tarek Chouiref
25 August 2026•Update: 25 August 2026
Kites reaching Israel from the Gaza Strip have not been used to carry weapons or incendiary materials, an unnamed source in the US-led Board of Peace said Monday amid Israeli threats to sharply escalate attacks on the enclave.
Israel’s Channel 15 quoted the source as describing the issue as a “complex challenge.”
“It is extremely difficult to deal with something that any child can make on their own,” the source said.
The remarks came after the Israeli public broadcaster KAN reported that Israel had given the Board of Peace three days to stop kites from reaching its territory from Gaza, threatening to intensify strikes on the enclave if they continued.
KAN cited an Israeli security source as saying that the army would “significantly increase” the pace of attacks in Gaza if the kite launches persisted.
The broadcaster also cited Israeli security officials as claiming that Hamas was behind the launches in an attempt to test Israel’s response, without providing evidence.
Israeli media has reported several kites reaching communities near Gaza in recent days, with no explosives found on them.
Field information obtained by Anadolu indicates that the kites are recreational and flown by children in Gaza. If their strings break, wind currents can carry them toward nearby Israeli areas.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz threatened Sunday to escalate assassinations in Gaza and evacuate residential neighborhoods in response to the kites.
The Israeli army said Saturday that four kites found near Nahal Oz contained no suspicious materials and “posed no danger to the public.”
Hamas spokesman Hazem Qassem said the Israeli threats were based on “fabricated pretexts” aimed at justifying further attacks, describing the kites as “children’s toys in displacement camps.”
He called on the US administration, mediators, guarantor states and the Board of Peace to pressure Israel to halt attacks and preserve the ceasefire.
Israeli forces have carried out daily violations of a ceasefire in place since Oct. 10, 2025 which have killed 1,288 people and wounded 4,290, according to Palestine Health Ministry data.
Israel launched a war on Gaza in October 2023, killing more than 73,000 Palestinians, wounding over 174,000 and devastating about 90% of the enclave’s civilian infrastructure.

UN chief urges renewed global action over Rohingya crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
02:15:20 UTC
11:15:20 KST

Diyar Guldogan
25 August 2026•Update: 25 August 2026
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres called for renewed international attention and action to address the plight of the Rohingya, his spokesman said Monday.
"Nearly a decade since the horrific events of 2017, the Secretary-General calls for renewed global attention and action to the plight of the Rohingya.
"Rohingya people in Myanmar, Bangladesh and across the region face deepening insecurity, shrinking protection space and diminishing prospects for durable solutions, exacerbated by funding cuts impacting life-saving assistance," Stephane Dujarric said in a statement.
In Myanmar, Rohingya and other communities remain caught in conflict and displacement, facing "grave human rights violations and other abuses," including by the Myanmar military and the Arakan Army, Dujarric said.
"Hundreds of civilians continue to be killed every year, while movement and humanitarian access remain restricted. Rohingya are also exposed to forced recruitment, arbitrary arrests and sexual violence," he added.
Guterres reiterated his call for the protection of civilians in accordance with international law, including international human rights law, international humanitarian law and international refugee law, the statement said.
The UN chief also expressed appreciation for Bangladesh and other countries hosting refugees from Myanmar, urging all states to provide protection to those fleeing the crisis.
"He is alarmed by the increasing number of Rohingya perishing at sea and urges regional cooperation on search and rescue, safe disembarkation and action against human trafficking.
"He is deeply troubled by rising misinformation, disinformation and hate speech targeting Rohingya in Myanmar and other countries in the region," Dujarric said.
Dujarric said Guterres urges the international community to strengthen collective action to support an "inclusive and comprehensive" political solution that addresses the root causes of the protracted crisis in Myanmar.
His special envoy on Myanmar, Julie Bishop, continues to engage all stakeholders toward the cessation of violence and advancing an inclusive Myanmar-led and Myanmar-owned political process, he said.
"Until conditions allow for voluntary, safe, dignified and sustainable returns of the Rohingya, he calls for the international community to continue to provide humanitarian assistance, alongside livelihood opportunities and self-reliance support," he added.

Israeli basketball legend Mickey Berkowitz’s severe dementia diagnosis revealed in documentary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
02:15:17 UTC
11:15:17 KST

Mickey Berkowitz, widely regarded as Israel’s greatest basketball player and one of the country’s greatest athletes, is suffering from severe dementia, it was officially revealed Monday evening during the Channel 12 documentary Mickey Berkowitz’s Last Shot. His condition is considered complex.
In the documentary by Niv Raskin, the Berkowitz family agreed to reveal the secret they had kept for more than two years, shortly before Berkowitz received the Israel Prize for Outstanding Sports Achievement, regarding the illness affecting one of Israel’s biggest sporting icons.
Berkowitz has been living in a care facility away from his home in recent months, and the film documents his family’s efforts to cope with his condition.
Berkowitz's basketball career
Berkowitz, whose parents immigrated from Romania, joined Maccabi Tel Aviv’s youth team at the age of 11, where he was discovered by legendary coach Yehoshua Rozin, who has since died. At 17, he joined Maccabi Tel Aviv’s senior team, and a year later led Israel’s youth national team to fourth place at the European Championship.
At age 21, Berkowitz spent a year at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, before returning to Maccabi Tel Aviv. In 1977, at the age of 23, he led Maccabi Tel Aviv to its first European Cup championship, helping secure a historic 78,77 victory over Mobilgirgi Varese in the final.
Two years later, Berkowitz led the Israeli national team to a silver medal at the 1979 European Championship, where he was named tournament MVP. After the tournament, he received an offer from the New Jersey Nets, but Maccabi Tel Aviv refused to release him.
In 1981, Berkowitz won another European Cup title with Maccabi Tel Aviv, scoring the game-winning basket in the team’s 80,79 victory over Sinudyne Bologna in the final. He also reached four additional European finals with Maccabi, though the team fell short in each of them.
Berkowitz represented Israel at the 1986 World Championship after his decisive basket against Czechoslovakia in the qualifying tournament secured the team’s place in the competition.
During 16 seasons with Maccabi Tel Aviv’s senior team, Berkowitz won two European Cups, 16 Israeli league championships and 13 State Cups.
In the summer of 1988, after making his final European Cup final appearance with Maccabi Tel Aviv, Berkowitz moved to Maccabi Rishon Lezion, where he played for five seasons. Alongside his close friend Motti Aroesti, who spent 13 seasons with him on Maccabi Tel Aviv’s senior team, Berkowitz helped lead the club to the playoff finals against Maccabi Tel Aviv.
He later played one season for Hapoel Jerusalem and half a season for Hapoel Tel Aviv before retiring. At the time of his retirement, he ranked second on the all-time Israeli Premier Basketball League scoring list, behind Doron Jamchi.

Providence voters to decide Israel-linked divestment measure in November referendum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
02:15:09 UTC
11:15:09 KST

As pro-Palestinian progressives find some success at the 2026 ballot box, the long-gestating Israel divestment campaign is looking to capitalize in Rhode Island.
Voters in Providence, the state capital, will vote on a referendum this November saying the city should refrain from investing in “foreign countries conducting ethnic cleansing, apartheid, illegal military occupation, or genocide.”
The language of the actual ballot petition does not mention Israel, nor any other country, by name. But the signature campaign was led by Providence for Palestine, a local activist coalition, and both its proponents and opponents have framed the measure as a referendum on Israel and the global Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement.
With the referendum’s ballot placement secured, Providence has become the largest American municipality ever to place divestment before the voting public.
“We’re in this moment when the general public at large, and particularly Democratic voters, very much understand what’s going on in Gaza and Palestine as genocide, as apartheid, and want their leaders to take action on it,” Zack Kliger, a lead organizer of the ballot initiative and member of the Rhode Island chapter of the anti-Zionist group Jewish Voice for Peace, told the Jewish Telegraphic Agency.
Israel has rejected accusations of genocide as baseless
Kliger described the current divestment campaign as having “definitely been led disproportionately by Jewish organizers.”
To determine which countries are “conducting” any of its list of human rights abuses, the referendum would rely on “resolutions” from various bodies, including the United Nations Security Council, International Court of Justice and “any” US court ruling or UN body. Some, though not all, of those bodies have reached conclusions that would implicate Israel in the ballot language’s divestment campaign.
Both Israel and the Trump administration have strongly rejected all genocide accusations leveled against the country. “Apartheid” can be considered an independent crime under international law, while “ethnic cleansing” has no formal legal definition.
Divestment from Israel has seen some success on the municipal level since the Oct. 7, 2023 attacks and Israel’s military response in Gaza, which has sunk the country’s popularity across the American electorate.
Last year a non-binding divestment resolution in Somerville, Massachusetts, a Boston suburb with less than half of Providence’s population, became the first such initiative to win at the ballot box. Over objections from Jewish groups, the city this summer began exploring the question of how to enact the measure into law.
Critics of divestment measures argue that they force local governments to put undue focus on international issues; could prompt division and backlash against local Jewish communities, and jeopardize public pension programs.
The Providence campaign’s decision to avoid mentioning Israel in the ballot language sets it apart from similar initiatives, while also neutralizing claims, made against other resolutions, that such measures unfairly single out Israel.
Yet local Jewish groups say the risk to the community remains.
“All this will do [is] stoke more division in our community, and potentially make Jewish people here feel more unsafe,” Stephanie Hague, chief strategy officer of the Jewish Alliance of Greater Rhode Island, told JTA.
Hague noted that the ballot language, as written, prompts questions about the authority of the international bodies making judgments about what constitutes genocide, ethnic cleansing and other terms in in the initiative. She said that the Alliance would campaign against the ballot measure and, if it passes, explore legal options for putting up roadblocks to it.
Providence passed divestment proposal against Sudan in 2006
A 2024 proposal to the city council urged Providence, whose approximately 15,000 Jews make up around 7% of the population, not to invest in Israel bonds. The measure failed to make it out of committee.
Likewise, the board of Brown University, the Ivy League school located in Providence, voted on a divestment resolution as part of the demands of the school’s pro-Palestinian encampment movement in 2024. It failed.
Activists are more confident this time, citing the success in Somerville, where, unlike in Providence, Israel was mentioned by name as the target of the winning ballot measure. Also unlike Somerville, whose measure was non-binding, Providence’s initiative would mandate city action.
Supporters also note that Providence joined a 2006 divestment initiative against Sudan to protest ethnic cleansing in Darfur, a divestment campaign that was spearheaded by American Jewish groups.
“We’re really proud of the legacy of the American Jewish community and standing up on social issues,” Kliger, who grew up in the Conservative movement, attended a Jewish day school in Brooklyn and has family in Israel, told JTA.
Unlike in Pittsburgh, where a similar 2024 initiative was undone before the election following legal challenges to the signatures, the Providence activists were able to collect and verify more than enough signatures to qualify for the ballot.
The initiative’s supporters said they had identified around $2.5 million in city funds that would be affected by a divestment order. They cited American companies frequently targeted by pro-Palestinian activists, such as construction equipment manufacturer Caterpillar and weapons firm Axon Enterprise.
The city council of Portland, Maine, also passed a divestment proposal in 2024, though that city’s mayor, after initially endorsing the plan, later said he regretted having done so because of the divisiveness it spurred.
Democratic primaries in Rhode Island have become centered on Israel
Some progressive Jewish professionals in Providence say the initiative is in keeping with their values.
“I know there are others out there who think that this is a situation where one would need to choose between their Jewish principles and other principles. I don’t perceive it that way,” Lex Rofeberg, senior Jewish educator with the alternative Jewish engagement network Judaism Unbound, told JTA about his support for the ballot campaign.
Rofeberg, a Providence resident, said it would be wrong for non-Jews to conclude that “it is a Jewish value to support human rights violations.”
“For those who see a ballot initiative that does not name Israel at all, but simply says we should not invest our dollars in atrocities, for people who see that as somehow threatening to Judaism, why would they think that?” he asked.
Hague, the Jewish Alliance staffer opposing the initiative, sees just such a threat to Jewish interests. She acknowledged that it can be hard to communicate to non-Jews, who would understandably oppose genocide and apartheid, the ways in which her group sees the BDS movement as “a calling card for antisemitism.”
She outlined what she saw as her group’s mission: “We have to do so much education in a short period of time, and helping people understand the Jewish community’s relationship to Israel, and then understanding this initiative’s relationship to the BDS movement and how those things are connected, and the real fear and isolation many Jewish Americans are already feeling, particularly after Oct. 7.”
The political environment, though, may be unfriendly to such efforts. Following broader national trends, the city’s Democratic mayoral primary, set for Sept. 9, is also pivoting to a large degree around Israel.
Incumbent Mayor Brett Smiley, who converted to Judaism and held a bar mitzvah while in office, is a vocal Israel supporter who opposes the ballot initiative. His progressive challenger, state Rep. David Morales, has backed the ballot initiative.
So too have some local elected officials with Jewish heritage. “For any community that we are identified with, and for the sake of our soul and our humanity, we have to be able to say, ‘This is not OK,’” Rachel Miller, city council president, told JTA.
Miller, who has a Jewish father and Catholic mother, said she considers herself “culturally” Jewish and objected to the idea that there is a single Jewish voice on the issue. She believes, she said, in “disconnecting the actions of a state against a group of people from my personal Jewish heritage, from my personal Jewish identity.”
Even if passed, it’s possible the ballot initiative could run afoul of a statewide ban on working with government contractors who openly boycott Israel, a so-called “anti-BDS law,” one of many such measures enacted in a range of states.
Those laws themselves have been debated for years. This fall a ballot initiative in Oak Park, Illinois, a liberal Chicago suburb, will ask voters to register a formal objection to that state’s anti-boycott law. The initiative, which is opposed by local Jewish groups, survived a legal challenge on Monday.
Hague acknowledged current Jewish divisions on Israel, and the difficult political climate for pro-Israel Jewish groups. Facing down a ballot initiative like this, she said, takes work.
“I think we know public opinion is not supportive of Israel right now. I think it’s not an issue that people understand implicitly when they just read a ballot question,” she said. “So yes, of course, there’s reason for concern, and I think no matter what happens at the ballot, I still think it’s an important moment.”

China moots at least 100 standards for humanoid robots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
02:14:52 UTC
11:14:52 KST

China has proposed formulating at least 100 key standards for the humanoid robot industry by 2028, according to a draft guideline from the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology.
The draft guideline for developing a national standard system for the humanoid robot industry will be open for public comment from August 25 to September 23.
The proposed standards would cover areas such as methods for capability testing and evaluation, key technologies, platforms and systems, application scenarios and safety governance. 
By 2028, the draft also aims to establish a systematic, science-based and coordinated standard system, with more than 200 enterprises promoting and implementing these standards.
Humanoid robots are defined in the draft as a new generation of artificial intelligence-driven intelligent terminals with human-like forms and capabilities that can autonomously perform complex tasks.
Rapid development of the sector has created an urgent need for common standards covering terminology, interfaces, testing and evaluation to guide technological innovation, product development and large-scale application, according to the draft. 
More than 100 humanoid robot-related standards are already under development or preliminary research in China and abroad.
The draft calls for standardising methodologies for grading humanoid robot capabilities. It also proposes standardising the definition of unique identifiers, coding rules and identification mechanisms for humanoid robots.
The push for standards comes as China steps up efforts to deploy humanoid robots in real-world settings. 
Beyond technical and industrial specifications, the draft calls for standards governing ethical requirements and social-impact assessments in the development and application of humanoid robot technologies, placing safety and ethics alongside performance and commercialisation in the proposed standards system. (Xinhua)

Wildfire in western U.S. state of Nevada destroys dozens of homes, injures 7
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
10:14:23 CST
11:14:23 KST

LOS ANGELES, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- Authorities said Monday that dozens of homes had been destroyed or damaged and at least seven people injured as a fast-growing wildfire spread rapidly toward Reno, a city in northwestern Nevada near the Nevada-California border.
The Hawk Fire, which broke out Saturday, had burned more than 15,000 acres (about 60.7 square km) and was 27 percent contained, local fire officials said.
Truckee Meadows Fire Protection District Chief Richard Edwards said at a news conference Monday afternoon that the blaze had destroyed at least 32 homes and damaged six others.
Four civilians and three firefighters were injured in the fire, he added.
About 90,000 residents were in areas affected by evacuation warnings and orders, according to InciWeb, a U.S. interagency all-hazard incident information management system.
The Reno Police Department said in a Facebook post on Monday that evacuation conditions had improved in some nearby communities, with evacuation orders downgraded from "Evacuate Now" to "Get Set to Evacuate."
Officials cautioned that while the change was encouraging, the situation remained dynamic and conditions could change rapidly. Residents in affected areas were urged to stay alert, monitor official updates and be prepared to evacuate if necessary.
Nevada Governor Joe Lombardo declared a state of emergency for Washoe County on Saturday night. Reno is the county seat and the most populous city in Washoe County. ■

‘Have a problem, call the PM,’ says Netanyahu as he gives out his number in campaign video
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
02:14:22 UTC
11:14:22 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday posted what he described as his personal phone number and invited Israelis to contact him with their questions and problems.
It was an election-season stunt that drew such a flood of responses that the number’s WhatsApp account was blocked within minutes and those calling received a busy signal.
It also drew suspicions that it was a ploy to collect voter data.
In a video posted to social media, Netanyahu is seen with longtime adviser Topaz Luk, who asks the prime minister whether he can publish his phone number. Netanyahu initially reacts with disbelief, saying, “Topaz, have you gone crazy?” before agreeing.
“I want to hear from you. Your suggestions, your questions, your problems. I want to hear, so leave me a message,” Netanyahu said. He added that he could not promise to answer everyone but would respond to as many people as possible.
Hundreds of messages and calls arrived within minutes and the WhatsApp account associated with the number was blocked. Luk later posted on X/Twitter that the account had been disabled because of the volume of calls and said Netanyahu’s team was working to restore it, directing people to Telegram in the meantime.
Some suggested the number was used to get phone numbers of voters
Kan political correspondent Michael Shemesh questioned whether the number belonged to Netanyahu at all and suggested on X that the exercise was “probably designed to harvest the phone numbers of potential voters.”
Other users pointed to another clue that the handset seen in the video was unlikely to be Netanyahu’s personal phone. One of the WhatsApp groups visible in Luk’s video was a synagogue updates group whose latest message appeared to back political rival Naftali Bennett, the former prime minister who now heads the Beyachad party.
“Something tells me that Bibi isn’t signed up to the ‘Menachem’s House Main Shul Updates’ group,” one X user wrote, “especially not when the latest message there is ‘yalla, it’s time for Bennett.’”
The Likud spokesperson had not responded to a request for comment on the accusations by the time of publication.
Netanyahu has handed out his number in previous election campaigns
It was not the first time Netanyahu handed out what he presented as his personal number during an election campaign. In August 2022, little more than two months before the vote that returned him to power, the then-opposition leader published another number and invited Israelis to video call him.
“Why should only some people have my phone number? Everyone should have it,” Netanyahu said at the time, joking that the move was a “dramatic, world-changing decision.” He told supporters who sent proof they had joined his Telegram channel that they would have a better chance of receiving a video call from him.
The response was similarly intense. Likud said Netanyahu received 9,420 calls within the first 30 minutes, while follow-up videos showed calls and messages flooding the phone.
Netanyahu’s rivals mocked the stunt. Then-Finance Minister Avigdor Liberman released a parody video saying Netanyahu “has not picked up the phone in 12 years,” while Yair Lapid’s Yesh Atid dismissed it as a “fictional phone operated by Netanyahu’s aides.”
Difficult reelection campaign for Netanyahu
The episode comes as Netanyahu faces a difficult reelection campaign, with roughly 20% of voters remaining undecided, many of whom are disillusioned Likud voters, according to pollsters and researchers cited by Reuters.
A Channel 13 poll released earlier this month put Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party at 23 seats, ahead of Likud with 21, and Netanyahu’s current coalition projected to win just 49 of the Knesset’s 120 seats. Eisenkot also led Netanyahu 47% to 34% when respondents were asked who was better suited to serve as prime minister.
The phone-number appeal is the latest in a series of efforts to put Netanyahu directly in front of voters, including a blitz of highly publicized appearances. Last week, the prime minister visited a restaurant in Hadera, a Likud stronghold, where owner Simo Shtivi said his arrival was “like hoisting the World Cup,” as diners lined up for photos and a chance to speak with him.
Netanyahu also made a surprise appearance with his wife Sara at a concert by Israeli pop star Eden Ben Zaken. A few days earlier, he filmed a campaign video at Jerusalem’s Malha Mall meeting shoppers, including children. The Central Elections Committee later ordered the video removed because election law bars the use of children in campaign propaganda.
Likud also rolled out billboards showing New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani alongside the leaders of Iran, Turkey and Hezbollah under the slogan, “They want Netanyahu to lose. Don’t let them win.”

RIJEKA, Croatia, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- China won the mixed team event at the 2026 World Aquatics Junior Diving Championships here on Monday, securing its second gold medal and fourth medal overall of the competition.
The Chinese team of Xie Jianyi, Nie Jun, Kan Zilong and Yuan Qingcheng finished with 414.55 points, 38.70 points ahead of Mexico, while Russia took bronze.
China was third after the springboard section, behind Russia and Mexico, before surging into the lead on platform. Nie produced a forward four-and-a-half somersaults worth a team-high 90.65 points after contributing 72.00 points on the 3m springboard.
"This medal is comforting; it represents a teamwork spirit," Xie said after the win.
After four days of competition, China has collected two gold medals, one silver and one bronze, sitting second in the medal table.
Russia leads the medal tally after winning two titles on Monday. In the boys' synchronized platform, Kirill Kosimov and Miroslav Kiselev rose from sixth place to win with 301.14 points, just 1.38 ahead of Australia's Archie Forsyth and Hayden Brinckley. Britain's Jorden Fisher-Eames and Robbie Wood took bronze with 298.71 points.
Kiselev, 14, claimed his second junior world title after winning the boys' Group B platform on Sunday.
Russia's Viktoria Kazantseva won the girls' Group A 3m springboard ahead of teammate Nadezhda Trifonova, while Ukraine's Kseniia Bochek took bronze.
The girls' synchronized 3m springboard and boys' Group A 1m springboard competitions will take place on Tuesday. ■

MADRID, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- The third stage of the Vuelta a Espana cycling race was abandoned on Monday due to a torrential thunderstorm.
The storm, with thunder and lightning accompanied by heavy rain and hail, saw race leader Tadej Pogacar ride to the front of the peloton and wave for the riders to stop and seek shelter less than 20 kilometers from the finish at the top of Font-Romeu.
"For the security of the riders, stage three has been cancelled due to hail and severe weather. There will be no winner and no podium ceremony," the race organizers said.
Tuesday's fourth stage is a 104.8-kilometer route starting and finishing in Andorra la Vella, featuring three first-category climbs and one third-category climb before a downhill run to the finish. ■

Mexico’s Sheinbaum calls Sinaloa governor’s return to his post ‘imprudent’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
02:12:29 UTC
11:12:29 KST

Maryam Ashalem de Andres
25 August 2026•Update: 25 August 2026
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum called Sinaloa Governor Ruben Rocha Moya’s return to office while being investigated for alleged criminal links “imprudent,” saying personal interests should not take precedence over those of the people of Sinaloa and Mexico.
“I thought it was, to put it mildly, imprudent, because this is not a personal matter; it is a matter concerning the government of Sinaloa and the people of Sinaloa. What was the need to return?” Sheinbaum said Monday at her daily morning press conference.
“I had no prior knowledge that he wanted to return,” she added.
She said her criticism of Rocha Moya’s decision was political rather than judicial, adding that Mexico’s Attorney General’s Office (FGR) is responsible for providing information on ongoing investigations.
Sheinbaum said the investigations include allegations raised by US authorities concerning Rocha Moya, as well as the killing of Hector Melesio Cuen, a former rector of the Autonomous University of Sinaloa and a former political figure in the state.
Rocha Moya returned to the governorship Friday after more than three months on leave, despite criticism from Sheinbaum and members of the ruling Morena party. He subsequently requested another leave of absence after spending less than two days back in office.
The Sinaloa state congress unanimously approved his request Sunday and is due to consider the appointment of an interim governor Monday.
Rocha Moya, a member of the Morena party, initially took leave in May amid allegations of links to the Sinaloa Cartel.
The US Justice Department indicted him and nine current and former Sinaloa officials in April over alleged ties to Los Chapitos, a faction of the cartel. US prosecutors accused Rocha Moya of conspiring with cartel leaders to import narcotics into the United States in exchange for political support and bribes and alleged that cartel members helped secure his election.
Rocha Moya has denied the allegations, describing the US charges as politically motivated.
Sheinbaum reiterated that any potential criminal responsibility must be determined by the competent authorities, while defending her criticism of Rocha Moya’s decision as a political matter.
The controversy comes as Sinaloa continues to face violence linked to a power struggle within the Sinaloa Cartel, one of Mexico’s most powerful criminal organizations.

Syria's removal from US terrorism list opens door to 'brighter future' — Turkish envoy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
02:12:03 UTC
11:12:03 KST

Türkiye's Ambassador to Damascus has said that the US' decision to remove Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism paves the way for a "brighter future" for the country and contributes to regional stability.
"The last obstacle standing in the way of our friend and brother Syria's integration with the world has finally been removed," Nuh Yilmaz said on X on Monday.
Yilmaz said Syria's removal from the US State Department's State Sponsors of Terrorism list was important not only for the country's normalisation, stability and development but also for peace and stability across the region.
"I congratulate all parties that contributed to the decision," he said. "I hope this decision, which promises a bright future for Syria, will bring benefit to the entire Syrian people and the Syrian state."
Syria is no longer subject to prohibitions under the Terrorism List Governments Sanctions Regulations, according to the Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control.
Syria had held the designation since 1979, a status shared only with Cuba, North Korea and Iran.
The terrorism label imposed significant barriers on security assistance, financial transactions and foreign investment.
President Ahmad al Sharaa made a historic visit to the White House last November, the first by a Syrian leader since the country gained independence in 1946.
This followed a meeting with US President Donald Trump in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, in May 2025, which took place shortly before Washington lifted the Caesar sanctions.

sordo madaleno sinks open-air art gallery four meters below ground in los cabos
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
02:10:09 UTC
11:10:09 KST

sordo madaleno sinks arte abierto baja into los cabos
At Ánima Village in Los Cabos, a long ramp slips away from the plaza and drops four meters into the ground. The descent leads to Arte Abierto Baja, a 180-square-meter open-air gallery designed by Sordo Madaleno for large-scale sculpture and site-specific installations. Above, the mixed-use development continues around terracotta pavilions and planted squares. Below, the architecture reduces itself to tall walls, rough concrete and open sky.
The 17-meter ramp is partly covered, keeping the arrival compressed until the gallery opens at its base. Walls rise more than five meters around the space, enough to give large works a real sense of enclosure while leaving the roof completely open. Fernando Sordo Madaleno describes the sequence as a shift from compression to exposure, with the landscape entering the room once visitors reach the bottom.
Pigmented bush-hammered concrete runs across the walls of Sordo Madaleno’s Arte Abierto Baja, which lends a coarse surface that catches the hard light of Baja California Sur. The material keeps the space visually close to the rocky, arid terrain surrounding Los Cabos, while its thickness gives the gallery enough weight to stand apart from the lighter architecture above.
The simplicity of the architecture leaves plenty of room for the work itself. Arte Abierto Baja opens with an installation by Mexican artist Abraham Cruzvillegas, whose practice often works through found materials and improvised structures. Here, the architects harness the scale of the enclosure to give sculpture room to occupy the open air. Sunlight, heat and changing shadows enter the viewing experience along with the work.
Arte Abierto Baja sits four meters below the plazas of Ánima Village in Los Cabos
the gallery sits beneath ánima village
Arte Abierto Baja forms part of Sordo Madaleno’s wider masterplan for Ánima Village, a six-hectare development arranged around public plazas and desert-adapted planting. Six terracotta pavilions sit across the site, with shaded pedestrian areas connecting retail spaces and open-air squares. The landscape strategy responds directly to a climate that can reach 36 degrees Celsius, thus using planting to bring shade and cooling into the public areas.
The gallery takes a different approach within that larger composition. Its walls stay largely out of view from the plaza, and the shift below grade creates a distinct space without cutting it off from the village around it. Visitors can arrive specifically for an exhibition or come across the entrance while moving through the development, with the ramp acting as the threshold between the activity above and the more contained space below.
a 17-meter ramp creates the transition from the mixed-use development into the open-air gallery
Sordo Madaleno enclosed the 180-square-meter space with walls rising more than five meters
pigmented bush-hammered concrete gives the gallery a dense tactile surface against the desert
the roofless gallery keeps the sky and arid landscape present around each installation
the inaugural installation is by Mexican artist Abraham Cruzvillegas
Arte Abierto Baja forms part of Sordo Madaleno’s larger Ánima Village masterplan

Israeli occupier attacks in West Bank surge 63%: Palestinian agency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
02:09:44 UTC
11:09:44 KST

Awad Rjoob and Tarek Chouiref
25 August 2026•Update: 25 August 2026
Attacks by Israeli occupiers across the West Bank surged 63% from January through July compared with the same period last year, a Palestinian government agency said Monday.
The Wall and Settlement Resistance Commission said it recorded 4,113 attacks during the seven-month period, up from 2,524 a year earlier, an increase of 1,589 incidents.
The commission said the surge coincided with the expansion of illegal settlement outposts, particularly pastoral ones, as well as the arming of Israeli occupiers and the incorporation of some into security formations.
It also cited Israeli military protection and declining accountability as factors behind the rise.
The agency said weak international deterrence and accountability had helped turn attacks by Israeli occupiers from isolated incidents into an organized tool to impose new realities on the ground and push Palestinian communities toward displacement.
On Saturday, the commission said the occupied West Bank had 592 illegal Israeli settlements and outposts, while Israel controlled about 42% of the territory.
It put the number of Israeli occupiers living in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, at around 780,000 as of the end of July, including 333,600 in illegal settlements in Jerusalem and 446,400 elsewhere in the West Bank.
Israel’s escalation in the West Bank, including attacks by the army and occupiers since the start of the Gaza war, has killed 1,182 Palestinians and injured more than 12,000 others, in addition to the arrest of around 24,000, according to official Palestinian figures.

Greece seeks to cash in on Odyssey ‘hype’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
02:02:00 UTC
11:02:00 KST

ATHENS — Greece’s government and tourism officials are determined not to squander the opportunities created by a resurgence of interest in everything Greek kindled by Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster movie version of Homer’s epic poem, the Odyssey.
Conservative Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis was quick to organize a videoconference with Nolan to thank him and praise the film’s “contribution to stimulating global interest in ancient Greek culture.”
Since a significant part of the filming took place in Greece — showcasing some of the country’s most iconic sites like Nestor’s Cave, Voidokilia Beach, Methoni Castle and Acrocorinth — he also noted that “such productions bridge Greece’s rich cultural heritage with contemporary creativity.”
Advertisement
Perhaps most crucially for the Greek economy, officials are now seeking to translate that renewed interest in the Cyclops and man-eating Laestrygonians into tourist revenue.
The Greek National Tourism Organization organized a press trip to Odysseus’ home island of Ithaca — to which he struggled to return after the Trojan War — that resulted in a 162-page publication by Le Figaro magazine, titled “In the Footsteps of Odysseus.”
The Peloponnese region is creating a thematic travel program, called “The Odyssey Route — Homer’s Peloponnese,” which will likely be ready by November. The regional authorities are currently designing the signs and website that will guide tourists.
“The aim is to link Homer’s epics and the film production, connect the production locations with other locations in the Peloponnese, associated with the myth itself,” said the deputy regional governor for tourism in the Peloponnese region, Thanasis Michelongonas.
Such locations include the islet of Cranae, where, according to legend, Paris of Troy took Helen for their first night after abducting her from Sparta. Or the tiny islet of Pefnos, where Zeus took refuge in the form of a swan and seduced (or assaulted) Leda, who subsequently gave birth to the famous egg from which Helen of Troy hatched.
“We want to capitalize on the hype created,” Michelongonas said. “Expectations are probably greater than reality. Of course, that doesn’t change the fact that we’ve received a great deal of publicity, worth millions and it’s up to us to make the most of it.”
Advertisement
A statue of Homer, the Greek epic poet who is credited with the “Iliad” and the “Odyssey,” circa 850 B.C. | Hulton Archive/Getty Images
The initial signs are that Greece is indeed enjoying an Odyssey surge.
Data from easyJet holidays in early August revealed a spike, with overall bookings to the Greek mainland and island breaks rising 18 percent week-on-week. Unforgettable Greece, a tour operator, told Travel Weekly that bookings to Greece increased 76 percent year-on-year. The company launched 22 new thematic itineraries linking Athens, Corfu and Ithaca.
The film has also sparked renewed interest in Homer’s classics, with a 70 percent increase in U.K. sales and a 76 percent rise in the U.S. since the start of the year, according to data from Circana BookScan. According to Google Trends data, analyzed by language-learning platform Preply, online searches for “learn Greek” surged by as much as 5,000 percent in the fortnight following the film’s release.
Still, Angelos Chaniotis, professor in the school of historical studies at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, noted that Greece needed to look beyond the “quick wins” from a blockbuster movie to develop a more sustained strategy.
“Of course, there are instances where a film has led to the discovery of Greece, as happened with ‘Boy on a Dolphin’ and ‘Hydra’ in 1957, but often the impact of films is short-lived,” he said.
“To ensure sustained interest in Greek culture, Greek archaeology and classical studies, Greece needs a long-term strategy linked, for example, with the internationalization of relevant study programs, the strengthening of the archaeological service, and a specific policy to improve the presentation of archaeological sites and museums.”

Unknown Publisher

Hong Kong to revamp senior secondary science and maths curriculum from 2029-30
Authorities aim to encourage more students to take science subjects at the senior secondary level
Hong Kong’s education authorities will revamp the senior secondary school science and extended maths curriculum by providing additional syllabus options from the 2029-30 academic year in a bid to attract more students and nurture talent in the field.
Edith Tse Yuen-ching, principal assistant secretary for innovation technology education at the bureau, said in a blog post that the city was “strengthening the cultivation of innovation and technology talents to respond to the development needs of the country and Hong Kong”.
The circular said a draft of the updated curriculum and assessment for the science subjects – physics, chemistry and biology – had been released for consultation. It said the bureau would brief educators early next month before finalising the draft in the next academic year.
Schools have been invited to give their views on the revamp by the end of next month.

====================================================================================================

Trump’s Arctic saber-rattling boosts Iceland’s pro-EU campaign
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

REYKJAVÍK — Pro-EU campaigners have a handy boogeyman to win over Icelandic voters ahead of a crunch referendum on Saturday: U.S. President Donald Trump.
Trump’s threats to annex Greenland — Iceland’s closest neighbor — have added a strong geopolitical dimension to a referendum on resuming membership talks with the EU, which might otherwise have focused on long-standing gripes with Brussels, such as mackerel quotas.
And Trump is not the only security risk in the North Atlantic.
Advertisement
With Russia and China both pushing to secure Arctic resources, questions about global alliances are becoming increasingly vital to the 270,000 Icelandic voters heading to the ballot boxes across the weather-beaten volcanic island.
Reykjavík’s former mayor, Dagur Eggertsson, a prominent figure in the pro-EU “Yes” campaign, said that Trump’s threats to Greenland were weighing on voters’ minds and sparking debate about Iceland’s strategic position.
“This issue is not settled,” the Social Democrat member of parliament said of U.S. ambitions to control Greenland, whose coast is less than 300 kilometers from Iceland. “Trump has been quite outspoken, not only last year, but again and again. This is something that people on the streets think about.”
While Trump has rowed back on some of his more bellicose posturing to seize Greenland at the beginning of the year, he still insisted at a NATO summit in Ankara in July that the territory “should be controlled by the United States, not by Denmark.”
Facing that kind of regional tension, Eggertsson, who also chairs Iceland’s delegation to the NATO Parliamentary Assembly, echoed Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney in mapping out the stakes: “Small and middle powers need to stick together.”
In the case of Iceland, he insisted this meant closer ties to Europe. “The matter is more urgent now than before,” he said.
Advertisement
A question of sovereignty
The key theme looming over the Icelandic referendum is sovereignty. But it’s an issue that cuts two ways, and polls suggest the referendum is on a knife-edge. A Gallup poll in mid-August gave the “Yes” camp a wafer-thin advantage, with 51.5 percent support.
While “Yes” campaigners like Eggertsson stress the regional implications of threats to Greenland’s sovereignty, the “No” camp argues the EU could impinge on Icelandic sovereignty, particularly within the politically crucial spheres of fisheries and farming policy.
Indeed, it was fisheries quotas that were key to scuppering Iceland’s previous bid to join the EU, which was definitively halted in 2015.
Thirty-five-year-old musician Tumi Árnason says he will vote “yes” in the referendum. He’s worried about the international situation the country finds itself in. | Carlo Martuscelli/POLITICO
Eiríkur Bergmann, a professor of politics at Bifröst University, explained that national sovereignty has been the core issue animating political debate in Iceland since its independence from Denmark in 1944.
“There are two camps, both tapping into the same heritage,” said Bergmann. “One is arguing that Iceland needs to join the European Union to enhance its sovereignty and guard its heritage of its independence struggle. Another camp, equally vocal, is cautioning against EU membership on the exact same grounds, arguing that it threatens Iceland’s sovereignty.”
Those sentiments on national independence and identity have a long pedigree. Iceland’s parliament, the Althing, is one of the oldest electoral assemblies in the world, dating back more than a millennium.
Advertisement
Strategically, the island is a NATO member and has a bilateral defense agreement with the U.S. dating back to 1951.
At the same time, Iceland is a member of the European Economic Area, and it’s estimated that it already adopts about three-quarters of the EU’s rules through this. It’s also part of the Schengen Area, allowing for passport-free travel with most EU countries.
The core consideration, then, for the referendum is whether it is worth moving beyond that EEA relationship.
Tumi Árnason, a 35-year-old musician living in the capital, said he was planning to vote in favor of entering into talks for EU membership.
“I am for seeing what kind of deal we can get,” said Árnason, citing the economy as his primary concern.
But the international situation did worry him: “I think that at this point siding with the EU would be preferable in this political climate. With the U.S. on one hand, and then Russia on the other, it’s a bit of a precarious situation.”
Advertisement
Hannah Sigurðardóttir, a 68-year-old employee of Iceland’s medicines agency, also raised concerns about the reliability of the U.S. as an ally.
“We can’t count on the U.S., like we did for a long time. I think we should [have] better ties to our friends and allies in Europe. We have a similar history, culture,” she said.
‘Forward Iceland’
Not everyone agrees with the need to gravitate toward Brussels.
A statue of Icelandic independence movement leader Jón Sigurðsson in Reykjavík. Sovereignty is a key concept in Icelandic politics. | Carlo Martuscelli/POLITICO
Guðlaugur Þór Þórðarson, an MP with the conservative and pro-“No” Independence Party, thought that EEA membership was sufficient and that any swing closer to the EU would be misguided.
Sporting a pin reading Áfram Ísland, or Forward Iceland, the slogan of the “No” campaign, on the lapel of his gray suit jacket, Þórðarson condemned the U.S. president’s comments on Greenland.
“I think it’s, of course, outrageous what Trump is saying about Greenland,” said Þórðarson, who was Iceland’s foreign minister during Trump’s first term in office.
Advertisement
But he cautioned that U.S. administrations come and go.
“When it comes to defense and security, then the key things are the bilateral defense agreement with the U.S. and also being a member of NATO,” he said.
Former Reykjavík Mayor Eggertsson from the “Yes” campaign stressed that the concerns about Arctic security were not just about Trump.
“The Arctic has traditionally been described as a low-tension area when it comes to defense. This is changing because of climate change and melting ice caps, the possibility of new shipping routes opening up,” he said.
While this newfound perception that Iceland could be more vulnerable than previously thought has entered the public consciousness, it is more prosaic concerns that continue to dominate the debate.
Outside of the Reykjavík area, where about two-thirds of the country lives, voters are more likely to put a “No” on their ballots.
Advertisement
Selfoss is a town of 10,000 people about an hour’s drive southeast of Reykjavík. Farmers cultivating the black volcanic soil along the road to the town adorn their bales of hay with the “No” campaign’s Áfram Ísland slogan.
Ari Hrafn Elíasson, an 18-year-old builder from Selfoss, said he would vote against the accession talks.
“I’m going to vote no because the farmers want to vote no. In my opinion, they are the backbone of this country, farmers and fishermen. I’m going to listen to them,” he said.
Another Selfoss resident, 19-year-old fast food worker Dagmar Isabella, said she was in favor of the EU talks but stressed that foreign policy was not her main concern.
She said she was worried about the cost of living, particularly for rents and mortgages. She thought joining the euro could help get galloping inflation under control. Iceland’s July inflation was running at an annual rate of 5.6 percent, nearly double the euro area’s.
Talking about the euro, she said: “It’s a much more stable currency than the Icelandic krona.”

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Monday that Iran had attempted to assassinate one of his two sons, without offering further details.
“Something incredible happened: Iran targeted one of my sons. Iran tried to kill one of my sons,” Netanyahu said during a phone interview with Israel’s Channel 14.

South Korea pledges to help Trump revive talks with North Korea’s Kim
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
01:54:10 UTC
10:54:10 KST

Advertisement
South Korea pledges to help Trump revive talks with North Korea’s Kim
Trump’s recent olive branch to Kim and criticism of Seoul have raised concerns of a strain on long-standing Asian alliances
2-MIN READ2-MIN
3
South Korea and the US agreed to maintain close coordination on efforts to revive dialogue with North Korea, days after Pyongyang rebuffed President Donald Trump’s overtures and launched a barrage of short-range ballistic missiles.
South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun told US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in a phone call late on Monday that Seoul would work to ensure that Trump’s recent messages lead to renewed US-North Korea discussions and peace on the Korean peninsula, Seoul’s Foreign Ministry said in a statement on Tuesday.
The US State Department issued only a brief statement on the phone call, which comes at a period of tension between the allies. Trump recently announced a scaling back of joint military exercises and praised nuclear-armed North Korea, while saying that Seoul had not helped his efforts to try to denuclearise Iran.
The State Department said Rubio and Cho discussed “a range of issues in the US-ROK Alliance”, referring to South Korea by the initials of its official name, the Republic of Korea.
“The secretary noted the need for the two countries to remain in close coordination on matters that are integral to the alliance,” it added.
In its statement, South Korea’s Foreign Ministry did not mention whether the diplomats reaffirmed their usual commitment to North Korea’s denuclearisation, despite their emphasis on the importance of cooperation on the North Korean nuclear issue.

The NRL has changed its interchange rules to allow Jai Arrow to start the Rabbitohs' final two games of the 2026 regular season, taking him to 100 games for South Sydney.
The 31-year-old Arrow was forced to medically retire after being diagnosed with motor neurone disease.
What's next?
The Rabbitohs finish the regular season against Arrow's former club, the Titans, on the Gold Coast, before a clash with rivals the Roosters in Sydney.
Jai Arrow will make cameo appearances in the final two rounds of the regular season in order to reach 100 games for South Sydney.
In one of the feel-good stories of the NRL season, the forward who retired with motor neurone disease in May has been approved to start on the field in rounds 26 and 27.
Arrow will then be substituted out in the opening seconds before any active involvement in play.
Arrow, in jersey number 23, has been named co-captain with Cameron Murray, who is listed to come off the bench.
It came after the Rabbitohs made an appeal to the NRL to grant the former Queensland representative an on-field swansong while still able to walk and run.
The initiative gives Arrow two final chances to farewell an NRL career that featured a grand-final appearance in 2021 and 12 State of Origin caps.
The NRL has granted Souths special dispensation to name Arrow as an extra player on today's team list and an extra substitution in their rotation.
The matches, against Gold Coast and the Sydney Roosters, will bring Arrow's tally to 180 career games and 100 for the Rabbitohs.
Arrow will lead the team out on both occasions and sit on the interchange bench in Souths kit after being substituted out.
The Titans and Roosters have both approved the plan, as have the Rugby League Players Association.
"We are very grateful to Peter [V'landys] and the NRL, and Clint [Newton] at the RLPA, for supporting our proposal," Souths chief executive Blake Solly said.
"We believe this will provide great inspiration for everyone watching the game from the stadium or at home, showing that MND will not hold Jai, or anyone else, back from achieving what they want to achieve in life."
The NRL world has rallied around Arrow since his shock diagnosis and immediate retirement in May.
The league threw Arrow "the world's biggest birthday party" on the day Souths beat Newcastle in July, rolling out a birthday cake in the shape of the 31-year-old's jersey and presenting him with a commemorative jersey.
Fundraising efforts have already passed $1 million in support of Arrow, who is the father of a young daughter.
Players from all clubs have shown their support by marking tries with arrow celebrations throughout the month of July.

- Storms caused power outages for 2,800 homes, transport disruptions, and the cancellation of a Vuelta a Espana cycling race stage in the Aude department.
AI generated
POMAS, France - A tornado tore through a village in south-western France on Aug 24, injuring 41 people and damaging hundreds of homes, the authorities said.
The French authorities had placed swathes of the country’s south-west on orange alert for storms, and numerous areas were hit by power outages and transport chaos.
In the Aude department, officials cancelled the third stage of the Vuelta a Espana cycling race, which was being held in the area, when a hailstorm forced riders to seek shelter.
The tornado hit hardest in the village of Pomas, population 1,000, damaging an estimated 300 homes, in some cases ripping their roofs off.
More than 120 emergency workers were deployed to the scene, the local authorities said.
Fifteen of the injured were taken to hospital.
They included a pregnant woman who was hurt when her house collapsed on her, her husband told AFP.
The national weather service, Meteo-France, said winds had reached up to 117km hour in the nearby village of Arquettes-en-Val.
Storms across southern France upended the transportation network, delaying trains, forcing road closures, and causing delays and cancellations at airports in Bordeaux, Marseille, Nice, Toulouse and even Paris to the north, said Transport Minister Philippe Tabarot.
An estimated 2,800 homes were left without electricity across 10 villages, officials said.
France sees several dozen tornadoes per year on average.
The impact of global warming on their frequency and intensity is unclear, according to Meteo-France. AFP

The state will be able to seize physical and financial assets, and assume formal ownership rights, if entities responsible for such facilities are judged to have failed to protect them and are too slow to repair them after any attack. It applies to fuel, energy, industrial, communications, transport and logistics facilities and other objects regarded as critically important for security and economic stability.

The US wants to make the fee for new H-1B visas permanent at $103,000
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
04:34:58 EEST
10:34:58 KST

The US wants to make the fee for new H-1B visas permanent at $103,000
Kyiv • UNN
The US Department of Homeland Security is proposing to make the fee for new H-1B visas permanent. Its legality is being challenged in court.
The administration of U.S. President Donald Trump has proposed making permanent a fee of $103,265 for new H-1B work visas for highly skilled foreign workers. Reuters reports, UNN writes.
Details
Trump first introduced this fee temporarily last year. Its validity expires in September, but the U.S. Department of Homeland Security has proposed making it permanent. The rule could be finalized by the end of the year.
The H-1B program allows U.S. employers to hire foreign professionals in specialized fields. Each year, 65,000 such visas are provided, plus another 20,000 for workers with higher education degrees. Before Trump's decision, obtaining an H-1B visa usually cost between $2,000 and $5,000.
The fee will not apply to people who are already in the United States on student visas, or to extensions of existing H-1B visas.
The decision is being challenged in court
In June, a federal judge ruled that the fee was unlawful and barred the administration from collecting it. The decision is being appealed in an appeals court.
The U.S. Chamber of Commerce, several states, and a coalition of labor unions and employers are also opposed to the fee. They argue that the administration lacks the authority to impose such charges without congressional approval.
Supporters of H-1B, in turn, say that the program is necessary for U.S. companies to attract qualified professionals in fields where the United States is experiencing a labor shortage.

AI generated
KYIV – British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he and other European leaders plan to travel to the US in September to lobby President Donald Trump to let Ukraine access some of its Patriot air defence missile stocks ahead of the winter.
“I’m looking forward to going to New York in September,” Burnham said in an interview with Bloomberg in Kyiv on the evening of Aug 24, referring to the upcoming UN General Assembly meeting in New York.
It would be his first trip to the US since becoming prime minister.
“I’ve not fully confirmed the details yet, but it’s likely I will go, particularly after today’s discussion,” he said. “Leaving today, I’m quite clear what I need to do in the next few weeks.”
Burnham’s comments came on his first international visit since becoming premier, after chairing a meeting of Ukraine’s allies for the first time and holding a bilateral meeting with Ukraine’s President, Volodymyr Zelensky.
Zelensky has made repeated pleas to European nations and the US to help Ukraine obtain Patriot missile interceptors and to replenish its stocks in time for winter, when Russia is expected to ramp up attacks on energy infrastructure again.
The interceptors are the most potent weapons to shoot down Russian cruise and ballistic missiles.
Burnham said he left feeling “really optimistic” that Ukraine’s current struggles defending against Russian ballistic missile strikes due to its low stockpile of interceptors is “fixable.”
He said European leaders were considering holding another Coalition of the Willing meeting around the UN General Assembly meeting with a view towards securing American interceptors and stocks from other countries.
“That would seem to be the most likely pace of direction,” Burnham said. “Not confirmed yet, but that seemed like where most people’s minds were going.”
He stressed that while Britain did not use the Patriot missiles required by Ukraine, other European nations needed to step up.
“There are other players who could help in the mix who we have influence with,” Burnham said. “It’s probably going to be a solution that involves a lot of layers and a lot of negotiation.”
A ‘hard thing’
Trump has backtracked on an earlier promise to provide or let Kyiv build interceptors for US-made Patriot missile defence systems.
The war in Iran has also seriously depleted global stocks of Patriot missiles, leading to delays in supplies and making allies reluctant to provide them to Kyiv.
Trump in July told reporters he hadn’t yet agreed to Ukraine’s request to build Patriot missiles.
“We’re talking about it, but it’s a hard thing to give away that kind of technology,” he said at the time.
Burnham, in contrast, has moved aggressively to allow Ukraine access to closely-guarded British defence technology.
The British prime minister will allow Ukraine access to classified information on British components for the long-range missile, called SCALP, allowing Kyiv to assemble the cruise missile in Ukraine.
“We value the fact that the UK’s course remains unchanged – full support for Ukraine and our defence,” Zelensky said in a post on X late on Aug 24 outlining his discussions with Burnham.
Zelensky told reporters on Aug 22 that he’s seeking 300 Patriot missiles for the winter.
He’s said previously that if Kyiv could buy 5 per cent of the US’ Patriot missile stockpile it would survive the winter, and if it could purchase 10 per cent it could destroy all of Russia’s ballistic missiles.
Ukraine has already been struggling with an onslaught of Russian ballistic attacks that have led to a rising death toll among its population.
At least 437 Ukrainian civilians were killed in July 2026, a 30 per cent increase on a year earlier, according to the United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine.
August has seen several Russian attacks with high civilian death tolls, with 15 killed in ballistic missile strikes on Kyiv on Aug 20 and 16 killed in a drone attack on a shopping centre in Kryvyi Rih on Aug 21. BLOOMBERG

The Kyiv Independent cannot immediately verify the reports. Ukraine's military has not yet commented on the reported attack.

Ukraine has targeted oil refineries and other energy facilities in Russia as a means to disrupt fuel supplies to the Russian military and reduce revenues financing Moscow's war against Ukraine.

Gang members have attacked displaced people huddling inside a church near Haiti's capital, killing around 40, some of them execution-style, according to the AFP news agency.
"We have counted around 40 bodies. Searches are continuing. Some people are still missing" after the attack on Sunday night in the town of Kenscoff in the hills above the capital, its mayor Massillon Jean told AFP on Monday.
He described "a night of terror" in a town plagued for months by gang violence.
Jean said that among other places, the assailants targeted a site housing people who had already fled violence.

The government also announced that reinforcements would be sent to restore security in the area.

Haiti, the poorest country in the Americas, has for years suffered from chronic political instability, natural disasters, corruption and violence from powerful gangs that carry out rampant killings, rapes, looting and kidnappings. The gangs control much of the capital city.
Nearly 1.5 million Haitians are currently displaced in a country of about 11 million, and more than five million are facing severe food insecurity, according to UN figures.
The crisis worsened in early 2024, when gangs launched a wave of violence that forced the unelected prime minister to resign.
Haiti has not held any elections since 2016. Its last president, Jovenel Moise, was assassinated in July 2021 and was not replaced.
A general election is scheduled for December of this year.

Reflections of a reformed grammar Nazi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
01:30:10 UTC
10:30:10 KST

Reflections of a reformed grammar Nazi
The evolution of English is an unstoppable force and resisting its ‘dumbing down’ may be futile
“Nothing bad can happen. It can only good happen.” Donald J. Trump
It would be easy to write off the regular word salads of America’s 47th president as the increasingly incoherent ramblings of an elderly man in obvious mental and physical decline.
However, one can also argue that Trump’s seemingly dyslexic struggles with the English language reflect a deliberate disregard for grammar rules that resonates with his support base. It’s the level of language that up to half of Americans happily use and identify with, if you think about it.
Laugh if you will at his limited vocabulary, disrespect for formal syntax and contempt for punctuation, but they have never been detrimental to getting his message across as an effective public speaker and communicator.
His very lack of linguistic sophistication – simple words, short sentences, constant repetition, blunt delivery – makes maximum impact with minimum polish, grammar rules and hoity-toity talk be damned.
Trump’s dumbing down of the language is but a microcosm of a global shift towards hyper-simplified English usage, stripped bare of formalities and tuned to resonate on digital platforms. All without the encumbrance of archaic or arbitrary rules and the rigid structure that we are expected to adhere to without even remembering why we have to in the first place.

Tornado tears through French village leaving dozens injured
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
02:27:21 BST
10:27:21 KST

Tornado tears through French village, leaving dozens hurt and homes ravaged
- Published
A tornado has torn through the village of Pomas in south-west France, injuring 39 people and damaging hundreds of homes.
Authorities said 15 people were taken to hospital. One man said his pregnant wife was injured after their house collapsed on her.
More than 120 emergency workers were deployed to the village south of Carcassonne after winds reaching 117km/h (73mph) tore roofs off houses and damaged an estimated 300 homes on Monday.
"Half the village has been destroyed," said one resident called Pierre, who described the tornado as swirling like a "huge red and yellow chimney".
"There's a huge castle and a third of it is has collapsed - even though these are stones that have stood for 1,000 years," Pierre told Ici Occitanie.
The third stage of the Vuelta a España cycle race, which was taking place in the Aude area of south-western France, had to be cancelled when a hail storm forced the riders to take shelter about 15km from the finish line.
The extreme weather has left about 2,800 homes across 10 villages without electricity, according to officials.
Local sub-prefect Emmanuelle Plantier-Lemarchand told French radio that she was not aware of anyone missing. She lowered the number of victims from 41 to 39, and said 15 of them had been treated in hospital.
"I heard this massive noise... then I saw everything flying around in the air and my roof collapsed," shocked resident Chantal told French radio. "I've got no house left, that's for sure."
French authorities had issued an orange alert for thunderstorms in large parts of the country's south-west, which have already been hit by power outages and transport disruptions.
Eyewitness footage from the region captured the swirling vortex of the tornado looming in the horizon above houses and trees.
Images from the small village of Pomas, which was the hardest hit, showed uprooted trees, damaged cars and rubble from destroyed homes.
Meanwhile there were flight delays and cancellations at airports in Bordeaux, Marseille, Nice, Toulouse and north of Paris to the north, said Transport Minister Philippe Tabarot.
On average, France experiences several dozen tornadoes per year, according to the country's national weather service Météo-France.
It comes after Europe's summer of unprecedented heatwaves and wildfires, with France's south-west region among the worst affected with an area of 42,000 hectares burnt in one of the largest forest fires since World War Two.

Wife of active-duty Army sergeant is deported to Honduras under Trump’s immigration crackdown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
01:23:01 UTC
10:23:01 KST

Wife of active-duty Army sergeant is deported to Honduras under Trump’s immigration crackdown
The wife of an active-duty U.S. soldier was deported Monday to her native Honduras, according to her family and the U.S. Department of Homeland Security.
Cristy Maryori Villafranca-Trejo is at least the seventh spouse or parent of an active-duty U.S. military service member to be deported under President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown.
The Associated Press has found more than 50 cases in which immediate family members of U.S. troops were placed in federal immigration detention after the Trump administration rolled back protections for military families. In some instances, DHS has released military spouses following media attention and advocacy by congressional leaders.
Villafranca-Trejo’s husband, Army Sgt. Hedar Leonel Turcios Juarez, said he has been struggling to manage his military duties since she was detained July 11 outside a Walmart near Fort Bliss, Texas, where he is stationed. Since then, he’s had to care for their 6-year-old daughter without his wife’s help. Instead of training in the mornings, he takes his daughter to first grade, and he said he has already had to postpone a planned assignment at another base.
“I don’t know if I will be able to continue with this,” Turcios Juarez told AP of his Army career. “I have to make a plan to make sure I can still fulfill my military responsibilities — but also take care of my family.”
DHS confirmed Villafranca-Trejo’s deportation, saying she had “received due process.”
Villafranca-Trejo, who has no known criminal record and entered the U.S. in 2016 at age 18, was issued a final order of removal by an immigration judge in 2017 after failing to appear at a hearing, according to DHS. Villafranca-Trejo’s husband said she had not received a notice for the hearing she missed and did not realize she had been ordered deported until they went to apply for her green card after marrying in 2022.
Originally from Honduras, Turcios Juarez became a U.S. citizen in 2024 after enlisting two years earlier.
Villafranca-Trejo’s motion to reopen her case was denied last May and an appeal before the Board of Immigration Appeals remained pending, according to her attorney. She had also been waiting for about a year for a decision on her application for military parole-in-place, a program that allows the immediate family of U.S. troops to remain in the country to apply for a green card.
“We were following the rules -- we did everything we could on our side to fix this problem,” Turcios Juarez told the AP.
Prior to Trump’s second administration, U.S Immigration and Customs Enforcement would typically allow immediate family members of U.S. troops to adjust their legal status even if they had been issued a final order of removal, according to Dan Gividen, who served as ICE deputy chief counsel from 2016 to 2019 under Trump.
“If you’ve got an active-duty military member that’s married to someone now, and that’s going to give her the opportunity to get a green card, you wouldn’t detain them, much less execute the removal order,” Gividen said.
JP Caballero, a spokesperson for U.S. Rep. Veronica Escobar, a Democrat representing El Paso, said Escobar had opened a congressional inquiry into Villafranca-Trejo’s case and visited her at the Camp East Montana detention facility in Texas earlier this month.
“My heart breaks for her, her children and the soldier who must feel so betrayed by the country he is sacrificing for,” Escobar told AP in a statement. “There are far too many families like theirs who are being targeted instead of supported.”
Turcios Juarez said he is unsure how he will care for his daughter without his wife. He still hasn’t figured out how to tell his daughter what has happened. But he says he still wants to keep serving his country.
“I love what I do, I want to keep doing this,” he said of the Army. “I just don’t know how I am going to keep doing this.”
