Japan enlists 1,800 people to drag a 360-tonne castle keep using ropes and rollers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
01:10:44 UTC
10:10:44 KST

To chants of “so-re, so-re”, about 1,800 people came together in northern Japan over the weekend to pull a 360-tonne castle keep a little more than two metres closer to its original resting place as part of ongoing renovations.
The keep – a fortified tower within a castle – had to be moved to repair a wall that was damaged in a major earthquake.
Rotating teams of 80 people heaved on 30-metre ropes as the keep of Hirosaki Castle in Aomori prefecture edged closer to its destination. On Saturday participants towed the building – which has been set on rails – 1.13m, while on Sunday it was shifted another 1.09m.
“We had about 8,000 applications for the 1,800 slots over the last two days, roughly four times oversubscribed, so not everyone could participate,” Kensuke Hayasaka, head of the parks and green spaces division at Hirosaki City, told the Guardian. “Not only from the city, but from across Japan and overseas; a fair number from south-east Asia and from Europe and North America.”
In order to preserve the historic structure, a technique known as hikiya – whereby buildings are put on rollers and moved rather than dismantled – was used. In 2015 the city put out a call for people to come and participate directly. The result was the first citizen-driven hikiya, and the first time the method has been used in any form to move a castle for a century.
“Because the keep is a nationally designated important cultural property, we didn’t take it apart,” Hayasaka said. “We’re using hikiya, a building-relocation method that has existed in Japan since ancient times.”
Work to preserve the castle has been going on since. The wall was completed in December 2024, with all 2,185 stones restacked in their original positions.
With that task completed, this year officials again asked for the public’s help to pull the keep back to its original position.
Motoharu Nakata, 61, travelled from Hiroshima at the other end of Japan. “I pulled it 11 years ago too. It’s very moving to be able to participate again. There’s absolutely no other opportunity to pull a castle – it was fantastic,” Nakata told the Sankei Shimbun.
Pulling the keep by hand will continue until the end of August, with about 4,100 people scheduled to move it a total of 5m. It is a symbolic, community-building effort and the rest of the about 73m will be carried out using machinery by the end of the year.
The keep at Hirosaki Castle is one of 12 such structures left in Japan, and the only one in the north-eastern Tohoku region. Seat of the Tsugaru clan, the castle was completed in 1611 but the original keep burned down after a lightning strike ignited a gunpowder store in 1627. The current structure was rebuilt in 1810 and the castle is now the centrepiece of a park that draws about 2 million visitors each year during cherry-blossom season.
Major renovations mean the keep will not be accessible to tourists for years.
“Once it’s back on the original base, the preservation work on the keep begins and the whole structure will be covered over,” Hayasaka said. “As things stand, we expect it to reopen to visitors in 2033.”

CAIRO/WASHINGTON – Iran promised to retaliate against expanded US economic sanctions that the Americans said would cut off Iran’s economic lifeline, with Tehran expressing confidence that major trading partners would resist Washington’s pressure campaign.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent unveiled the measures on Aug 24 but stopped short of the most punishing sanctions, saying countries that continued trading with Iran risked being forced out of the dollar-based financial system.
Bessent declined to identify the countries that would be targeted or reveal when those penalties would take effect, saying he would instead provide them time to comply with the new directive.
The Treasury Department did announce new sanctions on 60 individuals, entities and vessels, but the list did not include any of the Chinese financial institutions suspected of facilitating Iran’s oil trade.
Iran and the United States signed an interim deal in June aimed at ending the war that began with US and Israeli attacks on Iran, but the Islamabad memorandum, as it is known, quickly faltered.

After they were unveiled, Iranian Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh said, “We are fully prepared for the US sanctions.”

Neither China nor Russia had “accepted” the US measures, he added, predicting that other countries would resist them.
Brigadier-General Hossein Mohebbi, a spokesperson for Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, vowed heavy blows to US vital interests and energy chokepoints if Iran’s infrastructure is threatened, Press TV reported.
Little sign of diplomatic solution
Struggling to resolve an unpopular war that has pushed energy prices higher, the administration of President Donald Trump appears to be counting on further economic pressure even though Iran has spent decades under layers of US and international sanctions that have battered its economy but have not deterred its leadership.
Despite no major strikes by either side in weeks, the war shows little sign of reaching a diplomatic solution. The US is seeking new ways to end Iranian attacks on ships in the Gulf and, more recently via its allies, in the Red Sea.
Just two commodity vessels transited the key energy chokepoint of the Strait of Hormuz on Aug 24, for the lowest daily tally since early May, shipping data showed.
Before the conflict, the strait carried about a fifth of global flows of crude oil and liquefied natural gas.
Almost six months have passed since the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran. Thousands of people have died, most of them in Iran and Lebanon.
While the war has degraded much of Iran’s conventional military capacity, inflicted economic pain and killed then Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, Iran has preserved enough missile and drone capability to attack its Gulf neighbours and threaten oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz.
The exact state of Iran’s nuclear programme, which the Americans and Israelis aim to wipe out, remains unknown.
Oil prices steadied on Aug 25, having fallen more than US$2 a barrel a day earlier.
Chinese oil trade
Asked why he stopped short of actually imposing penalties on Iran and declined to identify the countries that would be targeted, Bessent responded: “Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?”

Bessent previously urged cooperation from China, the biggest buyer of Iranian oil for several years, although the US blockade of Iran’s ports, renewed in mid-July, has already cut Iranian oil flows to China.

The Heartbreaking True Story of Mica Miller and Netflix's Death of the Pastor's Wife
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
01:02:00 UTC
10:02:00 KST

From the outside, the Myrtle Beach-based Millers appeared to have a picture-perfect marriage. Mica Miller was a beautiful pastor’s wife whose husband, church leader John-Paul Miller, led a devout congregation. But the Solid Rock Church community did not know that behind closed doors, Mica and John-Paul had a tumultuous relationship, and Mica would ultimately be found dead in a state park with a gunshot wound to her head, after telling authorities she planned to take her own life. The next day, on April 27, 2024, John-Paul took the stage at Solid Rock to share the news: The congregation was now without a creative director to lead the worship, youth, and women’s ministry, and he was without a wife.
It wasn’t long before the Solid Rock patrons began to ask questions about what led to Mica's death.
The new three-part Netflix docuseries, Death of the Pastor's Wife, charts the now infamous—and ongoing—case against John-Paul, who has been charged with cyberstalking and making false statements to federal investigators, and seeks to uncover what really led to Mica’s death at age 30. Co-directed by showrunner Mike Gasparro and Julia Willoughby Nason (Murdaugh Murders, American Murder: Gabby Petito), the series looks back on Mica’s life with never-before-seen footage and firsthand accounts from her friends and family, many of whom are speaking out for the first time.
Showrunner Gasparro tells TIME that Mica’s story is “complex and deeply resonant.” The responsibility of bringing what really happened to her to light was key to making the docuseries. “We met with Mica’s family and made sure they felt comfortable entrusting us with her story,” Gasparro says.
Here’s everything we learned about Mica’s story from the new series.
A whirlwind romance
John-Paul Miller first saw Mica Francis when she was a teenager attending Solid Rock Church. The Francis family had recently relocated to Myrtle Beach and soon became regulars at the evangelical parish. At the time, Pastor John-Paul was a married father of five. Mica worked as his nanny, according to an affidavit filed by Miller’s first wife, Alison Williams.
Mica got married at 18 to her first husband, who was also a member of Solid Rock Church. Mica and John-Paul began having an affair in 2015, when Mica was 20 and John-Paul was 35, according to the Francis family; the couple then divorced their respective spouses and wed each other on Nov. 7, 2017 when Mica was 23 and John-Paul, 38.
“Their 15-year age difference was significant, but even more important was the fact that Mica first met John-Paul ‘JP’ when she was at such a young age,” Nason tells TIME. “She grew up in the church, dedicated much of her life to it, and spent an enormous amount of time around JP and the congregation during some of her most formative years. Mica looked up to JP as both a pastor and an authority figure. As we examined their relationship, it became clear how deeply that imbalance influenced its development. He held a position of tremendous power in her life long before they became romantically involved.”
Mica’s sister, Sierra Francis, alleged to the Myrtle Beach Sun News that she believed John-Paul “had his sights set on [Mica] from a young age,” and that he had groomed her. John-Paul always maintained that they had a "great marriage" and an "amazing" relationship. Mica Miller’s father, Michael Francis, echoed that their family was never supportive of Mica’s relationship with John-Paul. “I had lunch with her with a minister friend of mine and we talked with her extensively about how it is very, very unwise to be in a relationship with John-Paul,” Michael told the Sun News.
A tumultuous marriage
According to the Francis family in the docuseries, Mica was fully wrapped up in John-Paul’s world: She even had gotten John-Paul’s signature tattooed on her body, a choice that seemed “possessive” to her sister Sierra Francis at the time, especially since Mica and John-Paul allegedly had a dynamic others describe as toxic—one that culminated in numerous filings for divorce and legal separations from both sides.
Mica first filed for divorce from John-Paul after almost exactly six years of marriage, on Oct. 8, 2023, according to court documents. Yet just in time for Valentine’s Day, on Feb. 13, 2024, the divorce was dismissed. Ten days later, John-Paul filed for separation from Mica, which was subsequently dismissed without prejudice on March 12, 2024.
The legal merry-go-round continued, but as it did, it escalated: Mica contacted Horry County Police for a report of a razor blade being placed in her tire on March 11, 2024, telling police this was the second time her tires were slashed in the past week. Police were dispatched at 1:30 a.m. and Mica named who she believed was responsible for the actions; the name was redacted from the public report. Mica added that she had witnessed “strange activity and what she believes as people following or watching her,” the report said. She even told the officer that “she was afraid for her life.”
This wasn’t the first time Mica had expressed this fear: After her death, her sister Sierra expressed in an affidavit that Mica had voiced her fears of being followed and even allegedly told Sierra, “If I end up with a bullet in my head, it was not by me, it was JP [John-Paul].”
Sierra continued, “I know my sister to have expressed the abuse and violence against her by her husband to others, including family members and members of the church congregation.” Mica had additionally sought a restraining order against her husband in the days prior to her death.
Yet John-Paul was adamant that he and Mica had a happy family and home life at their Coldwater Circle house in the Azalea Lakes neighborhood near Myrtle Beach. “We were good for each other. She was incredibly affirming. She was a great pastor’s wife,” John-Paul told the Sun News. “She always wanted me to look in the very best light possible.”
John-Paul and Mica also worked closely professionally: Mica served as the church’s creative director and his personal assistant. The duo wanted to keep their marriage and work separated like church and state, and went so far as to include in a joint postnuptial agreement that they would not speak negatively of Solid Rock Ministries and would keep their personal life confidential. The document additionally saw them both waive their rights to seek alimony or financial spousal support in the case of divorce, and that their shared family home—which was owned by Solid Rock—would not be considered marital property.
The final straw
Mica filed for separation for the last time on April 15, 2024. A hearing for the separation was scheduled for June 5. Mica also moved out of her home with John-Paul and began living in an apartment during this time. According to the affidavit, John-Paul was served the papers on April 25, 2024, notifying him of the hearing. Mica was found dead two days later, on April 27, 2024.
The timeline of Mica’s last day goes as follows: At 11:38 a.m., Mica left her residence, as seen on her ring camera. At 12:12 p.m., Mica was seen purchasing a firearm and ammunition at Dick’s Pawn Shop in Myrtle Beach. She left the store by 12:34 p.m. and drove to a North Carolina state park. At 2:54 p.m., Mica called 911 to announce that she was going to kill herself and asked operators to trace her call so her family would be able to find her body.
Law enforcement officials began investigating the area where the phone call had been made. A witness told the police that they had heard a person crying and then a gunshot. Mica’s body was found in a river by a kayaker. She died from a gunshot wound to the head.
The next day, John-Paul returned to the Solid Rock lectern and gave a sermon, announcing Mica’s death at the end. He told the audience that her death was self-inflicted and cited Mica’s alleged ongoing mental health struggles.
John-Paul told the press that he was grateful to have the sheriff’s department investigating his wife’s death. “I want them to find out every detail,” Miller said. “I want to know everything, every detail.”
The case goes viral
John-Paul’s immediate return to public work was one of the first things that raised flags in the Myrtle Beach community. Many found it a bit odd for a grieving husband to not take time away from his parish to cope with the sudden loss of his wife. His sermon was recorded and shared on the church’s website and YouTube page (the video has since been deleted) and included the details of Mica’s service: Solid Rock Church in Market Common was to host the memorial on May 5.
Mica’s family took to social media to speak out against John-Paul and publicly share their concerns over Mica’s well-being before her death. The Francis family began posting about Mica’s experiences, alluding to the alleged abuse that Mica had suffered at the hands of her husband. (John-Paul has denied any wrongdoing and claims they had a loving marriage.)
Mica’s mother posted on the Facebook page Voices in the Wilderness that her daughter had “a no contact order and a divorce was filed just days before this tragedy.” Mica’s own past Facebook posts, which detailed abuse and leaving a dangerous situation with the hashtag #abuseawareness, were also recirculated.
The Robeson County Sheriff’s Department was investigating the case, with Chief Deputy Damien McLean taking the lead. Following a New York Post article about Mica, the story went viral on TikTok, with both Solid Rock church members and strangers from outside the community using the hashtag #JusticeForMica. Protesters stood outside of Solid Rock church wearing shirts that read “Break the silence and end domestic violence #JusticeForMica.”
John-Paul began posting TikTok videos to share his side of the story and refute allegations that he was involved in Mica’s death. Some protesters set forth the theory that John-Paul had murdered Mica; that claim was determined to be unfounded by investigators who proved that John-Paul had an alibi: He was in Charleston, South Carolina, on the day Mica died. John-Paul was at his children’s school for a soccer tournament, the police confirmed.
“When we first became involved, there was an enormous amount of public speculation surrounding Mica’s death. Many people we spoke with questioned what had happened, and media coverage was actively discussing the possibility that she had been killed,” Gasparro told TIME. “We knew it would be impossible to tell Mica’s story responsibly without examining those questions thoroughly. We followed the evidence and spoke with the people closest to the investigation so that we could understand how authorities reached their conclusion.”
Gasparro added, “Once we had done that, our focus shifted from questioning the official ruling to examining the much more complicated question of why: How a 30-year-old woman who was actively trying to reclaim control of her life reached a point where she felt she could no longer go on. To us, understanding everything that preceded Mica’s death was the heartbeat of the story.”
The viral nature of the case, and the doubt it seeded, contributed to the closure of Solid Rock in November 2024. John-Paul originally set out to start a new ministry, but instead created a nonprofit, Living Water Church.
The battle between Mica’s family and her widow
John-Paul publicly pointed to Mica’s mental health issues immediately after her death, citing that he believed she had a mental breakdown at the start of 2024. He claimed that Mica had previously attempted to take her own life, and that she had been diagnosed with bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, and dependent personality disorder. A toxicology report from the North Carolina medical examiner’s officer listed Mica as having had bipolar disorder and a history of suicide attempts.
Mica was open about working through mental health struggles, and even posted social media videos about her journey and offered testimonies at church. But Mica’s family was convinced that her stress and diagnoses were only caused by her strained marriage with John-Paul.
Mica was hospitalized for mental illness multiple times over the course of the marriage. The most recent time was in February 2024; Mica never permanently returned to the home shared with John-Paul after being discharged.
John-Paul claimed to Sun News that Mica had told him she wanted to live with him again but was afraid her family would be upset with her since they disapproved of him. “When she was with me for seven years, she was happy, healthy, whole and lived her life and loved it. Apart from me for three months, she committed suicide,” John-Paul said. John-Paul added that he believed Mica’s family convinced her not to take her medications, including lithium, which could have contributed to her decision to end her life.
Meanwhile, Mica’s family alleged that John-Paul abused Mica for years. Regina Ward, Mica’s family lawyer, said that Mica was never prescribed medications for her mental health and accused John-Paul of forcing her to take his own lithium prescription, even sneaking pills into her food or forcing her to swallow them against her will. There was no lithium prescription for Mica noted on any medical records that surfaced during the investigation.
“She was mentally healthy until she got snared in his web,” Ward said of Mica on July 15, 2024. “[There has been] no evidence or incident or evaluations or diagnosis of her having any mental health problem until after she gets involved with John-Paul.”
John-Paul, in turn, claimed that the Francis family was so religiously devout that taking medications was against their beliefs, and that they instead encouraged Mica to undergo holistic medical practices. “If her family had simply looked at her and said, ‘Mica if you love him, you can go home and we’ll support you,’ she’d be alive today,” John-Paul told Sun News. “The fact that we had such a great marriage that we did was pretty amazing. It’s very amazing, considering the stress of my job, considering the mental illness, considering her family. I mean, we did very, very well.”
Generations of controversy
John-Paul’s father, Reginald Wayne Miller, is also a pastor. Reginald founded the Cathedral Bible College, which offered degrees in theology, ministry, and other Christian studies. Reginald also once led one of South Carolina’s largest charismatic churches, rooted in the religious movement that emphasizes speaking in tongues, prophecy, and faith healing.
In 2014, Reginald pleaded guilty in federal court to felony charges relating to the treatment of Cathedral Bible College international students ranging from visa fraud to hourly wage violations. He further was at the center of a controversy about sexual improprieties that forced him to move his ministry from Florence to Myrtle Beach, where his son John-Paul later led Solid Rock. In a lawsuit filed by “Jane Doe #1” in February 2025, Reginald and John-Paul were both accused of using their positions within their church communities to engage in “sexual abuse and predatory conduct -- often targeting minors.” Father and son filed a counterclaim in which they "expressly denied" all of the allegations in the lawsuit.
Mica’s belief that she was being stalked
In the time leading up to her death, Mica’s tires were slashed multiple times and she told officers that she was being followed. John-Paul originally denied being involved in this alleged stalking. But in December 2025, the FBI determined that John-Paul had not been telling the truth to officials. A federal grand jury indicted John-Paul on charges of cyberstalking and making false statements to the FBI.
Prosecutors claimed that John-Paul admitted to hiring a private investigator to “protect Mica from buying firearms,” but that he had actually hired people to follow her and and cyberstalk her over alleged adultery. The indictment also stated that John-Paul lied when he denied damaging Mica’s tires; the FBI later learned that he had purchased a tire deflation device online.
The federal indictment further alleged that John-Paul had a pattern of abusive behavior toward Mica that began in November 2022. John-Paul tracked her car via surveillance devices, called her excessively at more than 50 times in a single day, and anonymously posted nude images online without her consent. Department of Justice documents cite that John-Paul began harassing Mica while they were estranged and interfered with her finances to exert control when they were apart. .
John-Paul was arraigned on Jan. 12, 2026 in federal court in Florence, South Carolina. The case has been continued to October 2026 for a court date. The pastor pleaded not guilty to the federal charges and has maintained that he has no responsibility for Mica’s death, per ABC News. If he is found guilty, he could face a maximum penalty of five years in prison for cyberstalking and two years in prison for making false statements, plus a fine of up to $250,000.
"The FBI, as well as our local partners that helped us solve this case, were incredibly thorough, detail-oriented; they left no stone unturned. And when they were ready and we were ready, we brought the charges as soon as we could," said Assistant U.S. Attorney Elle E. Klein. "We're in constant contact with the victim's family. We're trying to respect them as they're going through this, because while Mica's gone, she's certainly not forgotten, and we want to stand by them through this whole process."
The legacy of Mica’s Law
While the Francis family awaits John-Paul’s trial, they are focusing on helping people who have suffered from spousal emotional violence and domestic abuse. Ward, their lawyer, told supporters to turn their attention away from protesting John-Paul and instead work to get a coercive control bill passed; they intend to call it Mica’s Law. The bill will modify the domestic violence law to include coercive control behaviors like isolating victims from their family, depriving them of basic needs, and stalking.
“There are still major gaps in how coercive control is understood—not only by the public, but within our legal system,” Nason tells TIME. “ It can be difficult to recognize and even harder to legislate because it often involves a sustained pattern of behavior rather than one isolated incident.”
Nason continues, “I think audiences are becoming more aware that domestic abuse does not always begin as physical violence. Technology has created additional ways for someone to exert control over another person…Stories like Mica’s are important because they give audiences a fuller understanding of what abuse can look like. When these behaviors are viewed individually, they may be minimized or dismissed. When you see the entire pattern, the danger becomes much clearer.”
Death of the Pastor's Wife showrunner Gasparro has a stark message for viewers: “Our role as filmmakers is not to predict or control what happens legislatively. Our responsibility is to tell Mica’s story as honestly and effectively as possible, raise awareness, and help viewers recognize patterns that can otherwise be difficult to see. That is the kind of impact we hope Mica’s story can have. If it helps even one person recognize a dangerous situation in their own life, or in the life of someone they love, we would consider that incredibly meaningful.”
If you or someone you know need help, call or text 988 to reach the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline or go to SpeakingOfSuicide.com/resources for a list of additional resources.

US plans to revoke business, tourism visas of 200,000 asylum seekers

Trump administration plans to revoke B1, B2 visas of 200,000 asylum seekers
If the action happens, it will be the largest single mass revocation of visas in US history, AP reports.
The United States is preparing to cancel business and tourism visas of up to 200,000 foreigners who have applied for or are seeking asylum in the country, according to the Associated Press news agency.
The AP, citing State Department documents and interviews with two US officials, reported on Monday that if the plan goes ahead, it would be the “largest single mass revocation of visas” in the country’s history.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Trump administration has revoked over 175,000 visas: US State Department
- list 2 of 3US judge strikes down Trump immigrant visa ban affecting 75 countries
- list 3 of 3Trump administration seeks to formalise H-1B fee of more than $100,000
It said the State Department is expected to announce the action within the coming weeks, working in coordination with the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).
It would target so-called B1 and B2 visas issued between 2016 and 2026, whose holders have sought asylum or are now seeking asylum.
“We are coordinating with DHS to identify and revoke the nonimmigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the United States claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently,” said State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott.
Officials cited by the AP said the revocations would not automatically trigger deportations.
Instead, most people with pending asylum cases would be shifted into a different immigration category, effectively stripping their business or tourist designation while their cases proceed.
In a social media post on Monday, Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau called out people who he said try to use tourist and business visas to get into the US and then apply for asylum.
“People in the US and all over the world are fed up with bogus asylum claims,” Landau wrote on X. “Asylum isn’t supposed to be a loophole to circumvent immigration law.”
Since President Donald Trump took office for his second term last year, his administration has steadily ramped up restrictions on visa applicants – demanding more information about their social media histories, requiring the posting of expensive bonds for the processing of visas, and outright banning the issuance of visas to citizens of certain countries.
In the past 18 months, the State Department has also revoked about 175,000 visas for people who have been convicted or accused of crimes ranging from drunk driving to rape and robbery, as well as for people who have spoken out publicly against US policies, particularly in the Middle East.

Ukraine’s UN Envoy Demands Action Against Russia’s ‘Ballistic Terror’ at Security Council
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
00:58:36 UTC
09:58:36 KST

Ukraine’s UN Ambassador Andriy Melnyk demanded decisive international action against Russia’s escalating ballistic missile campaign on Monday, telling the Security Council that words of condemnation alone cannot protect Ukrainian civilians from Moscow’s attacks.
Speaking as Ukraine marked the 35th anniversary of its independence, Melnyk said Russia was “already losing” the war it launched against Ukraine and would ultimately be defeated despite intensifying attacks on Ukrainian cities and civilian infrastructure.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Despite all the barbaric attacks against civilians in Ukraine, Russia is already losing and will ultimately lose this war,” Melnyk said.
He pointed to the mounting economic and military cost Russia is paying for its invasion, including weakening state finances, falling energy revenues, battlefield losses, and Ukraine’s expanding strikes against infrastructure supporting Moscow’s war effort.
Melnyk said Russia cannot indefinitely sustain a war of attrition while spending enormous resources on its invasion and absorbing growing damage to the infrastructure that enables its military campaign.
He also pointed to warnings from inside Russia’s own economic establishment that the country faces increasingly serious consequences from the prolonged war.
Russian war infrastructure is a legitimate target
Melnyk also laid out Ukraine’s legal position on strikes against Russian facilities used to support Moscow’s invasion.
Zelensky: Ukraine Can Produce 200–300 Long-Range Drones Daily, With Reach Up to 3,000 Km
He said infrastructure that makes an effective contribution to Russia’s military operations and whose destruction offers a definite military advantage may qualify as a military objective under Article 52, paragraph 2, of Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions.
“The same legal test applies to Russia’s dual-use infrastructure,” Melnyk said.
“Ukraine’s position is absolutely clear: our armed forces only target military objectives that contribute to Russia’s war effort, never civilians.”
He said Ukrainian forces act under the country’s inherent right to self-defense and follow the requirements of necessity, proportionality, distinction, and international humanitarian law.
“Ukraine takes all feasible precautions to minimize civilian harm,” he said.
“The only person responsible for any damages, for any casualties in Russia, is Mr. Putin alone.”
Melnyk contrasted Ukraine’s approach with Russia’s repeated strikes on Ukrainian civilian areas.
“And this is where the fundamental difference between Ukraine and Russia lies,” he said.
He rejected Russian claims at the Security Council that Ukrainian air defense was responsible for civilian deaths in Ukraine, pointing instead to attacks in which Russian drones were seen striking civilian targets.
“Deliberately genocidal, barbaric nature”
Melnyk cited the recent Russian attack on Kryvyi Rih, where a drone struck the city’s largest supermarket and a second strike hit after rescuers arrived.
He stressed that there was no military objective near the supermarket.
“Intentionally – I repeat, intentionally – hitting the city’s largest supermarket with no military objective anywhere nearby,” Melnyk said.
“And when rescue operations began, Russia sent a second drone to strike the rescuers at the scene.”
At least 16 civilians were killed and more than 100 injured, including 23 children, he said.
“This is the deliberately genocidal, barbaric nature of Russia’s war against the Ukrainian people.”
Melnyk said Ukrainians were marking Independence Day with sharply contrasting emotions – pride in their sovereign state and grief over the destruction Russia continues to inflict.
“On the one hand, we feel an extraordinary sense of happiness that for 35 years now Ukrainians have had the blessing of living in a free and sovereign state,” he said.
“For us, it is truly a gift from God, but it is also the result of the struggle of generations of Ukrainians over the course of centuries – generations who dreamt of, fought for, and sacrificed for the fundamental right to live freely in their own independent country.”
For Ukrainians, he said, independence is not symbolic.
“For us Ukrainians, statehood and independence are not some abstract formalities. They are our greatest national value, the very foundation of our existence as a people.”
But Ukraine is celebrating that anniversary, Melnyk said, during “the most barbaric phase of Russia’s war of annihilation against our nation.”
He highlighted the mounting toll of Russian attacks, noting that July 2026 was the deadliest month for Ukrainian civilians since the first months of the full-scale invasion.
At the same time, Ukraine continues to face critical shortages of the air defense systems and interceptor missiles needed to protect its cities.
Putin’s campaign of “ballistic terror”
Melnyk described Russia’s intensified ballistic missile attacks as a deliberate campaign of terror against Ukraine’s population.
“Putin has unleashed the most cynical and the most brutal campaign of ballistic terror in modern human history, deliberately targeting ordinary people across Ukraine,” he said.
He emphasized the speed and destructive force of ballistic missiles and the almost nonexistent reaction time they leave civilians.
“For those beneath its murderous trajectory, there is no time to react and almost no warning,” Melnyk said.
“What arrives from the sky is more than a missile; it is a deadly mass of explosives descending with enormous kinetic energy.”
He described Russia’s Iskander-M ballistic missile, which can carry a warhead of up to 700 kilograms and plunge toward its target at several times the speed of sound.
Melnyk said the danger was not theoretical for him.
“Believe me, believe me, I know what I’m talking about. I just arrived from Kyiv.”
During his stay in the Ukrainian capital, he said, Kyiv was repeatedly attacked at night with Russian ballistic missiles.
“I can assure you, it is a truly terrifying feeling when you simply have no time to reach a bomb shelter.”
The interval between an air raid alert and the impact of a ballistic missile on a residential neighborhood can be only a few minutes, he said.
“All that remained for me and my family, my parents-in-law, was to hide in the corridor of our apartment, praying that the missile would not hit our building.”
Melnyk compared Russia’s ballistic attacks on Kyiv to “the most atrocious form of Russian roulette imaginable.”
“Except that in Putin’s distorted version, the gun is a ballistic missile and the target is a peaceful city.”
“God spared us during those horrifying attacks. But many other Ukrainians were not so fortunate.”
On one of the nights following his arrival, Melnyk said, Russian missiles killed 17 civilians in Kyiv alone.
“And it is against this hellish reality that Ukrainians are marking the 35th anniversary of the restoration of our independence today.”
Melnyk then challenged the Security Council and the wider international community to move beyond declarations of concern and take measures capable of weakening Russia’s ability to continue its attacks.
“Distinguished members of the Council, all this resembles the most appalling and abhorrent theater of the absurd imaginable in history,” he said.
“Day and night, Ukraine, a great European nation, is being brutally destroyed before the eyes of the entire international community by Russian ballistic missiles and killer drones.”
He said the international response too often stops at meetings and condemnations while Russia continues killing Ukrainians.
“And all that the world community seems capable of doing is to convene a meeting of the UN Security Council and at best condemn Russia’s war crimes and crimes against humanity being committed on a staggering scale.”
Melnyk also criticized governments that avoid directly naming Russia when discussing the invasion.
“And some choose instead to hide behind abstract formulas, avoiding even mentioning Russia, the country that launched this war of extinction against Ukraine and continues to wage it with impunity.”
Melnyk reserved some of his strongest criticism for the Security Council’s failure to halt Russia’s aggression.
“What a disgrace that to this day the UN Security Council has failed to take effective action to hold Russia to account and to prevent a daily genocide of the Ukrainian people carried out in plain sight of the world,” he said.
Ukraine values the fact that Russia’s war remains on the Council’s agenda, Melnyk said, but diplomatic statements do not stop Russian missiles.
“Words alone, even the strongest words of condemnation of Russia’s criminal actions uttered in this chamber, cannot stop the killing force of Russian ballistic missiles.”
“Only decisive action – not words, not even the strongest words – can stop this deadly Russian war machinery.”
Ukraine demands sweeping sanctions
Melnyk called for the toughest possible sanctions against Russia, particularly companies directly involved in producing the missiles, drones and other weapons Moscow uses against Ukraine.
“It is time for the Security Council to impose the most painful and far-reaching sanctions against Russia, against foremost those enterprises which produce deadly weapons, so that Mr. Putin is compelled to stop this war.”
He also called for an end to Moscow’s ability to use its permanent seat on the Security Council to shield itself from consequences for its own invasion.
“And it is time to put an end to Russia’s abuse of its veto power as a fig leaf, as an excuse for inaction,” Melnyk said.

Türkiye, Qatar target $5B in bilateral trade amid expanding economic ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
00:53:42 UTC
09:53:42 KST

Türkiye and Qatar have set a target of increasing their bilateral trade volume to $5 billion, Turkish Trade Minister Omer Bolat said following talks in Ankara.
Bolat met with Qatar's Minister of State for Foreign Trade, Ahmed bin Mohammed Al-Sayed, at the Trade Ministry to review bilateral commerce and investment ties.
"Türkiye-Qatar relations have truly made tremendous progress. Our total annual foreign trade increased 53-fold over the past 21 years, reaching $1.3 billion last year," Bolat told reporters after the meeting.
Trade between the two nations previously climbed to $2.5 billion during preparations for the 2022 FIFA World Cup in Qatar, driven largely by construction projects, he added.
Bolat noted that the Trade and Economic Partnership Agreement, which entered into force last year, will make a significant contribution towards achieving the $5 billion target.
Corporate investments
Turkish contractors have undertaken 206 projects worth a combined $21 billion in Qatar, Bolat said.
Approximately 1,116 Turkish companies currently operate across Qatar's construction, services, and manufacturing sectors.
Meanwhile, around 250 Qatari companies hold investments totalling $7.8 billion in Türkiye, covering finance, banking, energy, logistics, media, and agriculture.
Bolat added that Al-Sayed conveyed the Qatar Investment Authority's desire to expand its investments in Türkiye, with related initiatives underway.
Addressing regional logistics challenges, Bolat stated that the closure of the Strait of Hormuz due to regional conflict has created supply bottlenecks, underscoring the urgent need for alternative trade routes.
"The current circumstances have shown that alternative routes are greatly needed to avoid dependence solely on maritime transport and the Strait of Hormuz," he said.
Under a transit transportation agreement with Saudi Arabia that took effect on April 15, Turkish carriers are conducting intensive shipments to Gulf countries through Syria, Jordan, and Saudi Arabia, as well as via Iraq and Saudi Arabia.
"We will work together to establish these transit and trade corridors on a stronger and more stable basis," Bolat noted.

Serena Williams and Carlos Alcaraz start US Open mixed doubles vs. team with women’s doubles champ
NEW YORK (AP) — Serena Williams and Carlos Alcaraz will open the U.S. Open mixed doubles tournament against a team that features the reigning women’s doubles champion.
Williams and Alcaraz will face Erin Routliffe and Lloyd Glasspool on Tuesday in the first round of the championship, which will be Williams’ first match at the U.S. Open since 2022.
Aryna Sabalenka and Novak Djokovic might have an even tougher draw. The top seeds, based on having the lowest combined singles ranking in the 16-team field, face the team of Katerina Siniakova and Henry Patten — who are the No. 1-ranked doubles players on their respective tours.
The first round and quarterfinals are Tuesday. The semifinals and final are Wednesday.
Williams and Alcaraz were drawn to face one of the teams that emerged from the qualifying tournament that was held Monday. That ended up being Routliffe and Glasspool, who won two matches, both requiring match tiebreakers, to secure their place in the main draw.
Routliffe teamed with Gabriela Dabrowski to beat Siniakova and Taylor Townsend for last year’s U.S. Open women’s doubles title. They also won the championship in 2023.
Sabalenka and Djokovic had been slated to play Leylah Fernandez and Frances Tiafoe. But Tiafoe withdrew from mixed doubles Monday after losing to Arthur Fils in the Cincinnati Open final on Sunday, opening the door for a team that lost in qualifying to nevertheless earn a spot.
Siniakova and Patten won both their matches to reach the main draw. Kristina Mladenovic and Marcelo Arevalo, who lost to Routliffe and Glasspool in their second match, got the remaining spot and will play Karolina Muchova and Jakub Mensik.
The eight-team qualifying tournament was added this year to give the traditional doubles specialists an opportunity to compete for the U.S. Open title. When the tournament was overhauled last year — with a $1 million prize for the winners — in an effort to get top singles players to compete, direct entry was based on singles rankings, essentially shutting out the players who largely focus on doubles.
Williams is not planning to play singles in New York. Alcaraz, who has been sidelined since April with a right wrist injury, will return to defend his singles title.

Colombia’s new president Abelardo de la Espriella announces immigration crackdown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
00:34:47 UTC
09:34:47 KST

Colombia’s far-right president, Abelardo de la Espriella, has announced a crackdown on immigrants, ordering authorities to detain and deport people who are in the country irregularly or have committed crimes.
In office for just over two weeks, the millionaire former lawyer made the announcement on Sunday as the country continued to grapple with the aftermath of a 7.4-magnitude earthquake on 10 August that killed more than 300 people and destroyed more than 30,000 homes.
De la Espriella said the first joint operations involving the police and the migration authority should begin “this very week”.
“Let the coordinated operations begin to track down illegal immigrants: first, those committing crimes; second, those who have not regularised their status and who will have to be deported immediately,” de la Espriella said during a cabinet meeting held on Sunday in Barranquilla, the Caribbean city that has in effect been turned into an alternative capital.
He echoed the “Americans first” rhetoric of his ally, US president Donald Trump, saying that from now on it would be “Colombians first, Colombians second and Colombians third”.
The Colombian president has joined other Trump-aligned leaders in the region who have also tightened migration rules, including Argentina’s Javier Milei and Chile’s José Antonio Kast.
De la Espriella’s order is facing criticism from the opposition and human rights activists, who say it will end a migration policy that endured for more than a decade under both rightwing and leftwing governments and benefited above all migrants fleeing the humanitarian crisis in neighbouring Venezuela.
Although he used the anti-immigration rhetoric characteristic of other far-right candidates during his campaign, his platform focused chiefly on his promise to pursue an iron-fist policy against criminal groups.
In the same announcement, he also declared that all gangs involved in drug trafficking, illegal mining, extortion and smuggling were “terrorists and we will treat them as such. Whatever happens, we will defeat them, by reason or by force.”
The president did not directly mention Venezuelans when discussing immigration, but they account for roughly 90% of all migrants in the country. Of the 2.8 million Venezuelans living in Colombia, about 848,000 are in an irregular situation, including 193,000 children and adolescents.
The leftwing senator María José Pizarro Rodríguez reposted the president’s announcement and asked whether he was “proposing a Colombian ICE against fellow Latin Americans”, in reference to the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). She added that the “order to deport irregular migrants is pure xenophobia and aporophobia”.
“Instead of persecuting people fleeing poverty and violence, regularise their status. There are thousands of migrants who work hard and contribute to the economies of the countries that receive them,” she wrote.
The Colombian newspaper El Tiempo reported that sources within the migration department believe the agency does not have enough staff to carry out the operations De la Espriella has promised.
Analysts have also noted that under Colombian law there is no such category as an “illegal” immigrant, as De la Espriella said, but rather migrants in an “irregular” situation, since being in the country without the proper documentation is not a crime.

DRC’s constitutional battle: The fight over the 2028 vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
00:34:29 UTC
09:34:29 KST

DRC’s constitutional battle: The fight over the 2028 vote
President Tshisekedi’s reform push is fuelling a battle over DRC’s 2028 succession.
Kinshasa, DR Congo – President Felix Tshisekedi is due to leave office in 2028 under the current Constitution of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Yet with more than two years to go, a battle over the rules governing what happens when his mandate ends is already reshaping Congolese politics.
In May, Tshisekedi said he had not sought a third term but would accept one if the Congolese people wanted him to continue. The remarks revived opposition fears that constitutional reform could eventually open a path beyond the existing two-term limit.
Under the current constitution, the president is elected for five years, renewable once, while the number and length of presidential terms are protected from constitutional revision.
Tshisekedi’s camp says the country needs institutional reform. Opponents of the reform fear the process could ultimately be used to change the rules governing presidential succession.
The dispute is unfolding as the DRC fights a rebellion in the east led by M23, an armed group that operates within the broader Alliance Fleuve Congo (AFC), a political-military coalition that controls Goma and Bukavu, the capitals of North Kivu and South Kivu.
With an opposition mobilisation planned for September and Tshisekedi preparing to outline an inclusive national dialogue, the confrontation is entering a critical phase.
The referendum battle
The confrontation accelerated in June when the Parliament of the Democratic Republic of the Congo passed legislation setting out conditions for organising a referendum.
The Constitutional Court ruled in July that the law complied with the constitution, while raising concerns about some of its provisions. On August 10, Tshisekedi formally asked the presidents of the National Assembly and Senate to reconsider the legislation in light of the court’s observations. The National Assembly said the fresh deliberation would be placed on the agenda for its September session.
The legislation provides for a constituent assembly followed by a referendum in the event of what it describes as a “major dysfunction” of state institutions.
Critics of the process say the mechanism could eventually be used to alter provisions that currently prevent Tshisekedi from seeking a third term. The government, meanwhile, has presented constitutional reform as a broader institutional issue rather than an explicit bid to extend the president’s tenure.
The main opposition group campaigning against the process is known as C64, or the Article 64 coalition. Its name refers to Article 64 of the DRC’s constitution, which calls on citizens to oppose anyone who takes power in violation of the constitutional order.
C64 says it will resist any attempt to use constitutional reform to extend Tshisekedi’s mandate beyond 2028. The coalition announced a nationwide mobilisation for September 15, with demonstrations in Kinshasa expected to converge on the Palais du Peuple, the seat of parliament.
Taking the fight to parliament
The dispute has already spilled onto the streets.
Thousands demonstrated in Goma and Bukavu on July 28 against proposed constitutional changes and any attempt to extend Tshisekedi’s time in office.
In Kinshasa, protesters are expected to converge on the Palais du Peuple.
For C64, the destination is deliberate: the coalition wants to take its protest to the institution at the centre of the constitutional process.
Jean-Marc Kabund, a Congolese opposition politician, told Al Jazeera that no constitutional revision, referendum or legal manoeuvre should be allowed to circumvent the current constitution.
He warned that this happening while the country is at war could deepen divisions and threaten national cohesion.
A constitutional fight during a war
The constitutional dispute is unfolding alongside a conflict that has transformed eastern Congo.
M23 and the AFC have seized large areas of territory, including Goma and Bukavu. The Congolese government accuses Rwanda of supporting M23, a charge that Kigali denies.
The war is also raising questions about the 2028 elections.
Tshisekedi has warned that elections may not be possible if the fighting continues, arguing that it would be difficult to organise a credible vote while parts of the country remain outside government control.
Emmanuel Bugama, a Congolese political analyst based in Bunia, told Al Jazeera that national interests should come before political disputes.
“The nation’s best interests should take precedence over these political squabbles,” he said.
The view from Goma
In Goma, the argument is being watched from a city no longer under Kinshasa’s control.
Gentil Mulume, a civil society activist in Goma, told Al Jazeera that any constitutional change extending Tshisekedi’s mandate would not be recognised in territory controlled by M23 and the AFC.
“If Tshisekedi dares to amend this constitution to extend his term of office, it will not be recognised here,” he said.
Mulume said the dispute was part of a deeper divide between Kinshasa and the east. He argued that continued Tshisekedi rule could be viewed there as a form of domination and that self-determination should be part of the political debate.
His comments illustrate how a constitutional confrontation in Kinshasa is being interpreted in territory already beyond the government’s effective control.
What do ordinary Congolese know?
There is also a more basic question: how much do ordinary citizens understand about the proposed changes?
Kevin Kalala, a 30-year-old mobile-credit retailer in Kinshasa, told Al Jazeera that he does not know enough about the constitution to take a position.
“We do not know what our constitution entails,” he said. “The Congolese state should start by teaching us about our constitution.”
Kalala said citizens should first be shown which provisions need changing, why they need changing, and what the benefits would be.
“I am neither for nor against amending the constitution,” he said.
An offer of dialogue
As tensions rise, Tshisekedi has proposed an inclusive national dialogue involving political parties, civil society and religious groups.
While in Libreville, Gabon, on August 16, he said he would soon address the nation to set out his vision and the contours of the talks. The date and format of the dialogue have yet to be announced.
Tshisekedi has ruled out sitting with people he accuses of siding with Rwanda or the armed rebellion.
Martin Fayulu, who challenged Tshisekedi in the 2018 presidential election, has called for former President Joseph Kabila and Corneille Nangaa, the political leader of the AFC, to participate.
For now, the constitutional dispute is running alongside the war in the east and the uncertainty over the 2028 elections.
The question is no longer only whether the constitution will change. It is whether Congo’s political forces can agree on the rules for what happens when Tshisekedi’s current mandate ends.
“We are certainly heading towards one of the most decisive periods in our recent history,” Bugama told Al Jazeera. “The country is under the control of an armed group, whilst the government in Kinshasa is posturing over constitutional reform instead of tackling what matters most.”

Want to keep a big dog in Hong Kong? Experts share what you should know
Concerns about responsible handling of big dogs raised after attacks last week
Heat, humidity and crowded living spaces could pose challenges for Hongkongers hoping to keep large or aggressive dogs as pets, experts have said, urging potential owners to consider the needs of such animals before deciding to house them.
They issued the warning after a woman and two small canines were mauled in two separate attacks last week.
The woman was found collapsed in Ping Yeung Tsuen, hours after she was attacked at a dog training centre by a canine suspected of being a mixed-breed fighting dog. She was certified dead at the scene.
The smaller dogs were mauled to death in Yuen Long by an unleashed 60kg (132lbs) mastiff-type canine earlier that week.
Discussing the importance of correctly caring for big dogs, Lau Yun-yu, chairman of the Hong Kong Society for Pet Nutrition, said large canines, particularly those with thick coats, could face greater challenges in Hong Kong’s hot and humid climate.
“Dogs rely primarily on evaporative cooling through panting rather than sweating,” he said, adding that sustained high humidity could significantly reduce their ability to cool themselves.

“More than 100 people were injured in the attack, 70 of whom were hospitalized with injuries of varying severity,” the SSU said.
More than 20 residential buildings in different districts of Kyiv also sustained significant damage.
Based on the evidence collected, SSU investigators served Gerasimov with a notice of suspicion in absentia under Part 2 of Article 438 of Ukraine’s Criminal Code, concerning war crimes resulting in deaths.
The SSU recalled that, based on evidence gathered by the Ukrainian security service, the International Criminal Court in The Hague issued an arrest warrant for Gerasimov in June 2024 over war crimes against Ukraine’s civilian population. At the time, the evidence established the Russian general’s direct involvement in missile strikes against Ukraine’s energy system between 2022 and 2023.
As Gerasimov remains in Russia, comprehensive measures are under way to bring him to justice.
As reported, on July 2, Russian forces launched a massive drone and missile attack on Kyiv, with damage recorded in every district of the city. The heaviest destruction was reported at a residential building in Kyiv’s Darnytskyi district.
Thirty people were killed in the Russian attack overnight on July 2.

California lawmakers vote to increase transparency over influencers’ paid political posts

California lawmakers vote to increase transparency over influencers’ paid political posts
SACRAMENTO, Calif. (AP) — The California Senate passed a bill Monday that would fine content creators who don’t disclose they were paid to post in support of a political candidate or issue on the ballot.
California, along with Texas, already requires content creators to include payment disclaimers on their political posts. The goal of this year’s bill is to better enforce the law. The legislation, which was authored by Democratic Assemblymember Marc Berman, will need a final vote in the Assembly before it can reach Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom’s desk. Newsom has until the end of September to sign or veto it.
“Voters should have a right to know whether or not campaigns are paying for the messaging that they’re seeing,” Berman said in an interview last month.
Under current law, the state’s campaign watchdog can seek a court order compelling an influencer to disclose that they were paid, but that process can take months. Berman’s bill would give the state’s Fair Political Practices Commission, which supports the proposal, the power to fine influencers and political committees if they are found to have violated the law, allowing the commission to bypass the court process. Content creators could face fines of up to $5,000 per violation, according to the commission.
The bill’s passage comes as federal efforts to pass disclosure requirements for influencers have yet to advance. Sen. Adam Schiff of California introduced a bill in Congress last month, but it hasn’t received a vote.

Nevada sues US government over cuts to Colorado River access
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
00:21:00 UTC
09:21:00 KST

Nevada sues US government over cuts to Colorado River access
- Nevada has sued the US government to block planned cuts to its Colorado River water allocation, which could reduce its share by two-thirds and threaten Las Vegas's water supply.
- The federal plan cuts water use for lower-basin states Arizona, California, and Nevada by up to 3.7 billion cubic metres annually, while upper-basin states keep their current levels.
- The cuts respond to ongoing drought and overuse, with federal officials warning that without agreement, hydropower dams on the river could fail, and other states like Arizona may also file lawsuits.
AI generated
LOS ANGELES - Nevada on Aug 24 launched legal action against the administration of US President Donald Trump over a plan that would cut the state’s access to the vital Colorado River.
The river, which originates in the Rocky Mountains, makes farming possible in large tracts of the arid American south-west, and provides drinking water to the 40 million people who live there, including in cities like Phoenix.
But decades of over-use, coupled with years of drought, have put crippling strain on a watercourse whose management has always been based on an over-allocation of available resources.
Last week the federal government announced it was imposing cuts on the amount of water the so-called “lower-basin states” – Arizona, California and Nevada – can use, while leaving the allowances for the “upper basin states” of Colorado, New Mexico, Utah and Wyoming unchanged.
The plan envisages slashing the three states’ collective water consumption by up to 3.7 billion cubic metres per year until 2036 – the equivalent of 1.5 million Olympic-sized swimming pools.
Now Nevada has launched legal action seeking to block the change, which state officials say could reduce their allocation by two-thirds, potentially devastating the desert city of Las Vegas, which depends on the river for 90 per cent of its water.
“This isn’t about political posturing,” Nevada Governor Joe Lombardo, a Republican, said on Aug 24.
“This is a matter of survival for a community that represents about two-thirds of our state’s citizens and the lion’s share of its economy.”
Federal officials say their plan to cut usage is necessary because the seven states that lie on the river have been unable to agree amongst themselves.
They say without an agreement, dams on the river that are used to generate hydropower could cease to function.
Experts say Nevada’s lawsuit, lodged in a US district court, is unlikely to be the only legal action, with Arizona – which faces the deepest cuts – expected to launch its own challenge.
The federal government directive and the resulting legal action come after Lake Powell and Lake Mead, America’s two largest reservoirs, and which are fed by the Colorado River, fell to record low levels.
Scientists say human behaviour, including the unchecked burning of fossil fuels, is warming the global climate and interrupting weather patterns.
This leads to more sustained droughts in some parts of the planet, and more ferocious storms in others. AFP

Tunisia protesters march after deadly migrant boat sinks
Volunteers in Tunisia have continued the search for two people still missing after a boat carrying 15 migrants sank off the country’s southeastern coast, as the city of Ben Guerdane reeled from violent protests sparked by the tragedy.
Footage, verified by Al Jazeera, showed volunteers in the city of Zarzis heading out to sea on fishing boats on Monday to search for the missing.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Tunisia recovers 11 bodies after boat carrying migrants sinks, 3 missing
- list 2 of 3Antigovernment protesters take to Tunisia’s streets for second month
- list 3 of 3Tunisia sees protests after migrant boat sinking kills eight
The migrant boat, believed to be headed towards Italy, sank late on Friday after setting off from a location between Zarzis and Ben Guerdane with 15 mostly young people on board. It sank about 14 nautical miles (26km) off the coast of Zarzis.
Only one person survived, having drifted at sea for about 48 hours before being rescued by a commercial vessel, according to Tunisian media.
The bodies of 12 people were recovered by Sunday, the Tunisian National Guard said.
The deaths have sparked a wave of grief and anger, triggering violent protests in Ben Guerdane on Sunday night. According to the Tunisian National Guard, some 14 people on the boat were from Ben Guerdane, and one was from Zarzis.
The protesters burned tyres and blocked roads, while police responded by firing tear gas to disperse the crowds. The protesters demanded better living conditions and economic development, saying a lack of opportunities and years of marginalisation are pushing young people to undertake dangerous sea crossings to Europe in search of a better life.
Mostafa Abdelkebir, the head of the Tunisian Observatory for Human Rights, said those on board included seven members of the same family. He told the Reuters news agency on Monday that a hospital in Ben Guerdane has received at least 19 bodies of migrants recovered from the sea over the past two days.
It was not clear if all the bodies were from the boat that sank. Abdelkebir told Reuters that genetic testing was being carried out to identify the bodies and determine how many had been on board the boat.
Some in Tunisia have called for a national day of mourning over the deaths.
Imad Oulad Jibril, a lawmaker, on Sunday called it “the tragedy of a nation that sees its youth fleeing the hardships of the land only to be swallowed by the sea”.
The opposition Democratic Bloc party tied the sinking to Tunisia’s economic strains, saying: “When crossing the sea becomes easier than living in Tunisia, we must ask: Who is at fault?”
Tunisia has seen similar tragedies in recent years, including the Kerkennah disaster, in which more than 100 people died or went missing in 2018 after the sinking of a migrant boat. The incident led to the dismissal of the then-interior minister. In Zarzis in 2022, at least 18 people died after another migrant boat sank, sparking weeks of protests.
Tunisia’s southeastern coast lies just 145 km (90 miles) from the Italian island of Lampedusa.
The central Mediterranean is considered the deadliest migration route in the world, according to the International Organization for Migration, which says at least 821 migrants have died or gone missing on the route this year – more than double the toll over the same period last year.
Across the Mediterranean as a whole, at least 1,065 people have died or gone missing, according to the group.

US state probes OpenAI over rogue AI hack
WASHINGTON – ChatGPT-maker OpenAI faces an investigation by the US state of Alabama after the company revealed in July that its models went rogue and hacked an artificial intelligence (AI) platform during testing.
In mid-July, two OpenAI models escaped their confined testing environment and gained access to the internet, where they found and attacked Hugging Face, a site AI developers use to store and share models and data sets.
The incident raised alarm about the dangers of AI systems acting autonomously and breaking guardrails set by human programmers to prevent safety violations.
In a 14-page order, the office of Alabama Attorney-General Steve Marshall demanded OpenAI hand over internal records about the July incident, along with a long list of other material, including the identity of every employee involved in the intrusion or in the testing that led to it.
The investigation comes in response to “the company’s complete lack of oversight and adequate safeguards”, Marshall’s office alleged in a statement.
It is the first known state investigation into whether an AI system attacking another company’s infrastructure amounts to a violation of consumer protection law – a finding that would expose the company to major litigation across the US.
On Aug 3, Alabama and 14 other states wrote to OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman asking the company to preserve records on the incident and halt any internal cybersecurity evaluations of its models.
OpenAI has not responded to that August request, a spokesperson for the Alabama attorney-general’s office told AFP.
OpenAI did not immediately respond to an AFP request for comment.
However, OpenAI said in a statement to the tech news site TechCrunch that it was “conducting a thorough review along with external advisers”.
“Once the review is complete, we will share a technical report with relevant government authorities and publish our findings publicly,” it added. AFP

'Rushed effort'
In June, Judge Indira Talwani ruled that the president lacked the authority to order changes in how states administer federal elections, noting that under the US Constitution, states have the role of determining voter-eligibility requirements.

The states contend that their claims are not hypothetical and that the administration's "rushed effort to change the rules of mail voting on the eve of the November midterms risks disenfranchising a substantial number of voters."
The judge rejected the administration's arguments, finding that the suit was not filed too soon and that the states had legal standing because they would face election administration disruption, compliance costs and a credible threat of criminal prosecution.

Viral false claims about quakes, Hiroshima expose Japan’s online conspiracy problem
Claims that a deadly quake was artificial and Hiroshima was not hit by an atomic bomb have alarmed experts tracking Japan’s online spaces
In the aftermath of the July 28 earthquake in Kumamoto prefecture in southern Japan, a social media user claimed that seismic data from the National Research Institute for Earth Science and Disaster Resilience showed the tremor was “not an earthquake but an artificial explosion waveform”.
The post, published about 30 minutes after the magnitude 7.1 quake, was later listed by Yahoo Japan’s real-time search as a popular post, with more than 2,100 reposts and 6,300 likes. Other posts pushed a related claim that the quake had been triggered by HAARP, a research facility in Alaska that has long been a target of disaster-related conspiracy theories.
Days later, as Japan marked the August anniversaries of the Hiroshima and Nagasaki bombings and the end of World War II, NHK reported that false claims denying the atomic attacks were gaining traction online, with some posts on X and TikTok drawing more than 1 million views and one YouTube video claiming the bombing was a lie attracting more than 300,000 views.
“Both the theory that the earthquake was artificially triggered and the denial of the atomic bombings lack scientific basis, but the contexts in which these conspiracy theories take root differ,” said Yuzuru Kido, a former J-CAST News deputy editor and internet media researcher who tracks Japanese social media discourse.

US State Dept. sanctions Iranian military activities, fuel export in Operation Economic Outcast
Unknown

2026-08-25

09:10:21 KST

The US State Department implemented sanctions against Iranian military activities, cyber threats, and illicit oil trade, according to a statement from US State Department Spokesperson Tommy Pigott on Monday evening.
"Today, the United States took sweeping action against multiple entities, individuals, and vessels enabling the Iranian regime’s destabilizing activities," Pigott said.
"The measures target Iranian military officials responsible for procuring weapons and directing attacks against US servicemembers and regional partners, Iran-based entities that gathered intelligence for targeting US forces and allies, and a procurement ring supplying Iran’s military and missile programs," he added.
"The US will continue to disrupt, expose, and dismantle Iran’s military and proliferation activities, procurement schemes, malicious cyber operations, and illicit oil trade that sustains the regime’s malign behavior."
Sanctions target groups for supporting Iranian military actions
The sanctions targeted two Iran-based groups that were involved in procuring images used to attacks US forces and bases located across the Middle East.
DadeNegar Startup Studio and the Iranian Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Cyber-Electronic Command (IRGC-CEC) were named in the sanctions package.
DadeNegar was sanctioned for supporting the "targeting of US and partner facilities in the Middle East for the Iranian military during Operation Epic Fury." The State Department said DadeNegar used commercial Chinese satellite imagery to support Iran's military in its efforts to target and damage US forces and bases in the region.
The IRGC-CEC was sanctioned due to obtaining information about US forces and bases that was used to support Iran’s targeting of US assets during the conflict.
Both groups were designated "for having engaged, or attempted to engage, in any activity that materially contributes to, or poses a risk of materially contributing to, the proliferation of arms or related materiel or items intended for military end-uses or military end-users, including any efforts to manufacture, acquire, possess, develop, transport, transfer, or use such items, by the Government of Iran."
Individuals also sanctioned by US State Department
Monday's announcement also targeted seven individuals responsible for directing the use of conventional weapons against US forces.
Sanctions targeted members of Iran's Supreme National Council, several commanders of various military branches of the IRGC, the country's deputy defense minister, and the spokesperson for Iran's Defense Ministry.
Former Secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, was targeted for having "an active role advocating for Iran’s continued support of its so-called Axis of Resistance."
Zolghadr "was designated by the UN Security Council in Annex I of UN Security Council resolution (UNSCR) 1747 (2007), reimposed on September 27, 2025, in response to Iran’s 'significant non-performance' of its nuclear commitments," the statement added.
Ahmad Vahidi, Commander-in-Chief of the IRGC, and Ali Abdollahi, Commander of the Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters, the Iranian government branch responsible for wartime operations were sanctioned for their roles in driving military decisions made by Iran during Operation Epic Fury.
Sanctions also targeted Commander of the IRGC Aerospace Force Sayyid Hossein Mousavi Eftekhari, and Amir Hatami, Commander Iran's conventional military. Both were sanctioned due to their responsibility for Iran’s ballistic missile and drone programs.
Deputy Defense Minister for Industrial and Research Affairs Seyyed Mahdi Farahi was sanctioned by the US for "directing the procurement of arms and related materiel and has demonstrated in-depth knowledge of various missile systems, including those that Iran has reportedly used against US forces and allies."
Reza Talaei-Nik, spokesperson for Iran's main defense ministry body was sanctioned for "engaging in activity that materially contributes to the supply, sale, or transfer, directly or indirectly, to or from Iran, or for the use in or benefit of Iran, of arms or related materiel, including spare parts."
US sanctions also target fuel exports, shadow fleet
The Department of State also sanctioned companies that "engaged in the illicit trade of Iranian petroleum and petrochemical products, activities that have generated millions of dollars in revenue for the Iranian regime," the statement said.
"These Iranian petroleum, petroleum products, and petrochemical cargos," the statement added, "are frequently transported by shadow fleet operators, including vessel management companies that regularly engage in dark activity and other deceptive shipping practices, endangering other vessels and trade flows."
Sanctions targeted both Iranian and international companies that facilitated the trade of petroleum and petrochemical products with Iran.
Implications of the sanctions
The sanctions coming following US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's announcement of the start of Operation Economic Outcast and the implementation of an "economic D-Day" against Iran.
Monday's sanctions mark the start of US action aimed "to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone," said Bessent.
"We are no longer managing the Iranian threat," he emphasized. "We are ending it."
Iran promised to retaliate to sanctions
Before the announcement, Iran threatened both a possible military response and further reduction in oil exports from the Gulf in response to any US economic measures. Afterward, Iranian Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh said, "We are fully prepared for the US sanctions."
"Naturally, the enemies intend to launch an economic terrorist attack on us, but we also have our own tools and know how to play the game. Our defense is no longer so defensive; the enemies should wait for an attack," Madanizadeh told state television.
He also said neither China nor Russia had "accepted" the US measures, and predicted other countries would resist them.
Brigadier General Hossein Mohebbi, a spokesperson for Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, vowed heavy blows to US vital interests and energy chokepoints if Iran's infrastructure is threatened, Press TV reported.
