Tens of Thousands of Nevadans Evacuated in Latest Wildfire of Record-Breaking Year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
23:01:47 UTC
08:01:47 KST

The ongoing “Hawk” fire outside the city of Reno, Nevada, has prompted the evacuation of tens of thousands of people in yet another devastating blaze contributing to one of the worst U.S. wildfire seasons in recent history.
Roughly 42,000 people have been evacuated around Reno, while an additional 45,000 were warned that they may also have to flee. The evacuation is among the largest prompted by a U.S. wildfire this year, following the fires around Spokane, Washington, in early August during which roughly 60,000 people were evacuated.
The Reno evacuations mark another flashpoint of a record-breaking fire season. The fire is dwarfed in acreage by larger blazes from this year, at roughly 15,000 acres burned so far, but its direct effect on civilians is one of the largest in recent years, and demonstrates the potential risk that worsening wildfires may have on people and their communities in years to come.
Here’s how fires around the U.S. have set new records, and why they have been so bad this year.
More acres burned and more entrapments
Compared to the past 10 years, more acres have been burned this year in the U.S. to date.
The National Interagency Fire Center (NIFC) posted on Monday that firefighters have responded to 50,784 wildfires that have scorched over 7.8 million acres this year: 168% of the 10-year average for acres burned, and 129% of the average for total fires.
Around the same time last year, roughly 4 million acres had been burned, around 50% of the current acreage for 2026 so far, according to NIFC tracking.
The U.S. has also been at the highest level of “fire preparedness” for 38 days, since July 18th, at a five out of five, which means that federal resources are strained and may not be available to address every new fire.
The 10-year average for fire preparedness in August is four. The last time the fire preparedness level was at a five for the entire month of August was in 2021.
Meanwhile the 10-year annual average for days spent at level four and five combined is 48 days, and so far, the U.S. has already spent 57 days within that range, after reaching level four in late June.
There has also been a 20-year high of firefighter entrapments, life-threatening situations in which firefighters’ safety zones and escape routes are compromised. According to a Reuters report, there had been 12 entrapments in 2026 as of Aug. 13, more than the year-total average of nine in the last 20 years. This year’s entrapments also marked the highest year-to-date figure since 2006.
Six out of 13 firefighter deaths have involved entrapments, the report shows. An average of 17 firefighter fatalities occur each year from wildfires.
Hotter, drier, and windier conditions
Wildfire trackers often use the “30-30-30” rule to identify conditions that can lead to extreme wildfires. The rule refers to when the temperature is at least 30 degrees Celsius (86 Fahrenheit), humidity is at 30% or lower, and wind speeds are at 30 kilometers per hour or more (roughly 19 miles per hour). When combined, these hot, dry, and windy conditions can produce extremely large and destructive fires, as they have this year.
Reno has experienced an average daily high temperature of 92.8 degrees Fahrenheit (33.7 Celsius), 27% humidity, and 18 miles per hour (29 kilometers per hour) daily maximum wind speed over the last 10 days, including the week before the “Hawk” fires began on Saturday and the three days since as the blaze continues.
Although the 30-30-30 rule is a metric for local weather conditions’ effect on wildfires, increases have been exhibited this year compared to past years across the U.S. in each of its categories—temperature, dryness, and wind speed.
When it came to temperature, the average in the contiguous U.S. from January through July was the second warmest in 132 years, at 4.2 degrees Celsius (55.5 Fahrenheit), according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).
July in particular was the hottest month on record in the U.S., with an average of 76.9 degrees Fahrenheit (24.9 Celsius). Nevada specifically had one of its warmest July’s on record, according to NOAA.
Wind speeds generally fluctuate the most by region, but from January through June of this year, they averaged 0.5% above the 20-year average during 2005-2024, according to an S&P Global analysis.
These hotter, drier, and windier conditions have set the stage for an active wildfire season.
One underlying explanation for increasingly fire-prone conditions is climate change, which has contributed to longer-lasting fire seasons, now lasting for six to eight months in some areas, compared to what used to be roughly four months in past decades.
“Generally we're having drier summers and higher winds,” Peter Sunderland, professor of fire protection engineering at the University of Maryland, previously told TIME. “We are seeing more and more climate extremes.”

‘Immense drop-off’ in support contributing to care leaver deaths in England, review says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
23:01:41 UTC
08:01:41 KST

Profound isolation contributed to the deaths of more than 100 care leavers in England in a year, with a dramatic drop-off in support from social services at 18 leading to catastrophic consequences, a review has found.
A government-commissioned report into the early deaths of young people who left care described the problem as a national tragedy and said many were left on their own “at the height of vulnerability” before they died.
Josh MacAlister, the children’s minister, said: “Care leavers have been left so isolated, so lonely, and that is the core of the problem. Both adult and children’s social care need to be humanised and need to focus on building those enduring, loving connections. This is a stain on society because all of us have failed.”
The review, led by the social work leader Clare Chamberlain and the broadcaster Ashley John-Baptiste, looked at the deaths of 112 care leavers aged 18 to 24 in 2025.
It found that the death rate among this group was three to four times higher than among the general population, and suicide rates among female care leavers were potentially 15 times higher.
In total, 36% of the care leavers probably died by taking their own lives, including 24 women. One-fifth of the deaths were at age 18, which the review said highlighted the “immense drop-off in support services” when care leavers reach adulthood.
John-Baptiste, who grew up in the care system, said the review was the “most emotional and triggering piece of work I’ve ever had to do”.
He said: “I remember being in a meeting at 17 where my foster parents said: ‘If we’re not getting paid, we don’t want to look after him.’ Why do services change when children reach 18 and should they have to change?
“I think there is certainly a case for a 0-25 service. If 112 deaths doesn’t compel us to try and reform things quickly, there’s a big problem in our society.”
Among the deaths examined were care leavers in custody, mothers whose children had been removed, people undergoing gender transition, young asylum seekers, murder victims and people who died from medical conditions.
One case was that of David (not his real name), who died in the summer of 2025 from a lack of insulin after he lost access to the children’s diabetes nurse who had been helping him keep track of his condition since he entered the care system at 14.
The care leavers’ hub he socialised in was closed for refurbishment and his personal adviser was on leave. After his death, his body wasn’t found for two weeks. The review found that when he turned 19, many of the connections he had made “fell away and he was left on his own”.
Young people leaving care are assigned a personal adviser to help them transition into independent adulthood up to the age of 21. The review found many of these advisers “hardly knew” the young people they were working with and were only required to see them once every two months. It said many were untrained, ill-equipped and “avoided the emotional side of the transition”.
It called for a “major national review of the knowledge and skills” of the workforce tasked with monitoring care leavers, including better mental health expertise.
The review found that young people were often attracted to the “lure of living alone and being free of constraints” but were unprepared for the significant drop in support, which “no amount of transition planning will compensate”.
In response to the review, the government said it was investing £25m in connected housing options for care leavers, which would include supported housing and shared housing for groups of care-experienced people.
MacAlister said this was part of the government’s strategy to make “loving, trusted relationships around care-experienced people the central focus of the care system”.
Since December 2023, local authorities must report the deaths of care leavers through a serious incident notification system. MacAlister said “the same thing happening over and over again” compelled him to commission the review.
He said it should be a call to action not just for the government and the social care sector. “We need more foster carers, we need mentors for care leavers, we need neighbours to show an interest in a young care-experienced person who might have got their first tenancy and to extend the hand of friendship,” he said.
“This is about connections and relationships, and you can’t pay people to do that – it has to be grown organically and nurtured over time.”

‘He was left on his own’: the care-leaver lives lost to a system that abandons them at 18
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
23:01:41 UTC
08:01:41 KST

David* spent most of his childhood in and out of care after experiencing abuse and neglect, and spent his teenage years in a children’s home, where a nurse helped him keep track of his type 1 diabetes.
But as he approached 18, things changed: he was moved into supported accommodation on his own, and then, at 19 years old, his diabetes nurse stopped working with him because of his age.
He lost a lot of connections, including a personal adviser who moved out of the area, and the monitoring of his insulin levels declined. David loved swimming and ice skating, qualified as a lifeguard, and spent lots of time in a local care leavers’ hub where he enjoyed chatting to other young people.
Then, in the summer of 2025, the hub closed for three weeks for refurbishment and his new personal adviser went on leave. It was during this time that David died from a lack of insulin. His body wasn’t discovered for two weeks.
David’s death is one of a number examined in a landmark review into the deaths of more than 100 care leavers aged 18-24 in 2025. The review findings suggest the death rate of this cohort is about 3-4 times higher than the death rate of the general population.
One-fifth of all these deaths occurred at age 18, with experts saying a “care cliff” means young people experience an “immense drop off in support” as they transition from being a child to an adult.
The review said: “It is notable that there was no one in David’s life who was connected enough to notice his absence [when he died] and, in the end, it was neighbours who alerted the police. Those who knew David talked about him fondly, and he clearly made connections with a number of them in children’s services.
“They said that when he turned 19, all those connections fell away and he was left on his own.”
The children’s minister, Josh MacAlister, said: “In all of these stories, one person could have been the difference.
“A young man who wasn’t getting the support with his diabetes medication should never have died. But it was a system that left him not seen for two weeks. If he had his own people, his own tribe, that wouldn’t have happened.”
There were similar failings in the case of Michael* who suffered “trauma, rejection and hardship” throughout his childhood, including sexual abuse, and he was placed into care at six years old.
He built a solid relationship with a foster carer, with whom he lived for four years, but when she became unwell and could no longer care for him, he went to more than 10 foster placements before he turned 18.
When he was moved into semi-independent accommodation outside his local area, he was frequently reported as missing and started taking drugs. Social workers had long raised concerns about his vulnerability and fears he could be exploited.
After several skirmishes with police, including having to be brought down from the roof of his accommodation, he was sent to an adult prison aged 18. He was reported to be very agitated, shouting and repeatedly pressing the emergency bell in his cell – he was then placed into segregation after getting into a fight with his cellmate.
After being deemed “medically unfit” for segregation he was moved back into the main prison wing and was found dead in his cell after taking his life, just two weeks after he first walked through the prison doors.
Of the 112 care leavers who died in 2025, six were in prison and died as a result of a drug overdose or suicide, and Ministry of Justice officials report care leavers are disproportionately more likely to self-harm in prison.
However, care leaver status is not reported in custody deaths data, meaning there is no way of knowing exactly how adversely affected they are.
Another risk factor highlighted in the review was care-experienced women who had their own children removed: six of the deaths recorded were young women killing themselves in these circumstances.
Janey*, who came into care aged 15 after being rejected by her mother, thrived in the home of her foster family until the age of 18.
After leaving home, she ended up in a volatile relationship and intermittently taking drugs, leading to her three children being taken into care.
She killed herself soon after, aged 23, leaving a letter behind for each of her children to read as adults, saying how sorry she was and how she missed cuddling them.
Staff involved with Janey said if there had been a more formal role for her foster carer in her adult life, or if she had been supported to rebuild her relationship with her sister, things could have turned out differently.
*Names have been changed for anonymity.

Trump administration to revoke visas of foreigners seeking asylum in US, officials say

Trump administration to revoke hundreds of thousands of asylum visas
US President Donald Trump’s administration said on Monday it plans to revoke non-immigrant visas held by foreigners who applied for or are seeking asylum in the United States. The move could affect up to 200,000 people, the Associated Press reported, potentially making it the largest mass visa revocation in US history.
US President Donald Trump's administration said on Monday it planned to revoke the non-immigrant visas of foreigners who have applied for or are currently seeking asylum status in the US, marking its latest step in a sweeping immigration crackdown.
A State Department spokesman said it was coordinating with the Department of Homeland Security "to identify and revoke the non-immigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the United States claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently."
The State Department statement did not specify the number of visas that will be revoked in the process.
The Associated Press put the number of foreigners whose business and tourism visas is planned to be revoked at up to 200,000, which if materialised, would be the largest single mass revocation of visas in US history. The AP cited State Department documents and two US officials.
The State Department will revoke so-called B1 and B2 visas issued between 2016 and 2026 whose holders have sought asylum or are now seeking asylum, the AP report added. The B1 and B2 non-immigrant visas are issued for business and tourism travel.
Read more'Contrary to law': US judge strikes down Trump's 75-country visa ban
The visa revocations would not necessarily result in immediate deportation, the AP report said, adding that most of those with asylum cases currently pending would be re-categorised but would lose their status as business or tourism travelers.
Earlier on Monday, Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau alleged on X that the American immigration system "has long been swamped by frivolous asylum claims."
The State Department said earlier this month that under the Trump administration, it has revoked more than 175,000 visas of foreign nationals.
Trump has pursued an immigration crackdown that includes revocations of visas and green cards and an aggressive deportation drive.He says the crackdown aims to improve domestic security.
Rights groups say the crackdown has violated free speech and due process rights and created an unsafe environment, particularly for ethnic minorities, who have raised concerns about racial profiling.
While Trump campaigned in 2024 on a platform of stopping illegal immigration, his administration has also made legal immigration more difficult - for example, by imposing new and expensive fees for applicants of certain work visas. The government's crackdown has faced legal challenges.

US vows 'economic asphyxiation' of Iran with new sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
22:53:54 UTC
07:53:54 KST

Breadcrumb
US vows 'economic asphyxiation' of Iran with new sanctions
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday laid out plans for the "economic asphyxiation" of Iran, expanding Washington's secondary sanctions threats and warning of dire consequences for countries that do not join the campaign.
The announcement comes almost six months into a war on Iran that has ground to a stalemate, with stalled peace talks and Tehran blocking most traffic through the crucial Strait of Hormuz.
Bessent earlier said the US was declaring an "economic D-Day" on Iran, but his announcement named no specific countries beyond Iran and gave no timelines.
"Around the globe, our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone," Bessent told journalists.
"We are going to hold everyone accountable, and this is economic asphyxiation of this regime."
He added that countries not joining US sanctions would "share in the isolation" of Iran, and noted that President Donald Trump was making phone calls to world leaders with requests to stop interactions with Tehran.
The Treasury Department said expanded secondary sanctions would target Iran's digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping sectors.
It also issued new sanctions against 60 individuals, companies and vessels that allegedly aid Iran in oil revenue generation, weapons procurement and cyber operations.
The sanctions hit entities around the world, including in the United Arab Emirates, Hong Kong, China, Singapore and in Europe.
Bessent vowed that any entity "that facilitates money laundering on behalf of Iran will be removed from the US dollar system."
Iran had been dismissive of the threat of additional sanctions, and on Monday its economy minister predicted "another defeat" for Washington.
"We've been waiting for these plans for a long time, and the government is and was ready and has a two-year plan to manage these events," said Ali Madanizadeh.
Decades of sanctions
Iran has weathered decades of crushing international sanctions, and before the war it continued to export millions of barrels of oil, mostly to China, and to evade sanctions through complex international financial networks.
Asked on Monday if Chinese banks would be targeted by the new sanctions, Bessent said "no one is above the reach of US sanctions."
Ali Vaez of the International Crisis Group said Washington was seeking to impose maximum economic pressure through various levers, but that Iran "has faced all of these before."
"While there is little doubt in Washington's ability to impose substantial pain, Tehran believes that it has a high threshold for absorbing it, as well as the potential to respond to financial pressure with military counterpressure," he said.
The US naval blockade of Iran has seen its oil exports via the Strait of Hormuz fall from two million barrels a day pre-war to just 0.4 million by mid-August, according to maritime tracker Kpler.
Speaking to reporters on Monday, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said that the pivot to applying economic pressure did not mean that military strikes were off the table.
"Economic pressure, we know, hurts them the most right now," he said. "But by no means are we foreclosing using kinetic strikes anywhere in the Strait of Hormuz or around Iran."
For ordinary Iranians, the standoff is likely to bring only more economic pain after years of rampant inflation, which in December and January fueled massive anti-government protests.
Sarah Hassanbeigi, a 32-year-old pharmacist in Tehran, said: "I don't think people can really take this much longer."
Pakistani delegation
Last week, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, considered a relative moderate, said Tehran should "bring the war to an end now as we are in a position of power."
That followed Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei's appointment of hardliners to key security positions.
On Monday, Pakistan's army chief Asim Munir -- a key mediator in the conflict -- visited Iran and met separately with Iran's president, chief negotiator and the head of its highest national security body.
The meetings took place after Trump spoke last week with Munir, a US source familiar with the matter told AFP earlier on Monday.
Islamabad was a leading mediator in talks that helped secure an April ceasefire that later fell apart. It is also a major trading partner of Iran, possibly opening it up to the threat of the new sanctions.
Oman's foreign minister was due in Iran on Tuesday, as Muscat and Tehran seek a deal on regulating passage through Hormuz.

US urges new UN sanctions to spur rivals in Sudan to negotiate an end to war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
22:53:02 UTC
07:53:02 KST

US urges new UN sanctions to spur rivals in Sudan to negotiate an end to war
UNITED NATIONS (AP) — The United States is urging beefed-up U.N. sanctions against the warring parties in Sudan to build pressure on them to negotiate an end to the fighting that has killed at least 59,000 people, displaced some 13 million and pushed many parts of the African nation into famine.
President Donald Trump’s senior adviser for Arab and African affairs, Massad Boulos, told the U.N. Security Council on Monday that financial, military and political support given to either the government forces or the rival paramilitary group, Rapid Support Forces, remains a driver of the conflict, now in its fourth year.
Boulos did not name any countries providing that support. Egypt has been a vocal supporter of Sudan’s military, while the United Arab Emirates is accused by U.N. experts and human rights groups of providing arms to the RSF, which it has repeatedly denied.
He said the Security Council has the tools to curtail the provision of “a tremendous and increasing amount of military support to both warring parties” from “numerous external actors.”
U.N.-backed human rights investigators two years ago called for the expansion of an arms embargo on Sudan’s long-restive western Darfur region — scene of mass atrocities between 2003 and 2005 — to cover the entire country.
Boulos said a proposed U.S. resolution before the U.N. Security Council would expand the arms embargo throughout Sudan. It also would apply “to all parties operating in the territory” and reaffirm that drones and related technologies are part of the arms embargo.
Experts say Sudan’s army and the RSF are competing to obtain new drone models. Rights groups have said the use of unmanned aircraft has become increasingly common in the northeast African nation’s war.
The U.S. draft resolution, obtained by The Associated Press, deplores “the continuous influx of external military assistance, weapons, and ammunition to the warring parties, which is prolonging the conflict and undermining mediation efforts,” including launching drones and unmanned aerial systems from third countries.
The proposed resolution demands that all countries “cease any direct or indirect support to the warring parties, be it logistical, financial or military, which enables conflict to continue.”
The conflict exploded from a power struggle that emerged following Sudan’s transition to democracy after an uprising forced the military ouster of longtime autocratic President Omar al-Bashir in April 2019.
Tensions boiled over three years later between Sudan’s military chief Gen. Abdel-Fattah Burhan, who chairs the ruling sovereign council, and RSF commander Gen. Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, who was Burhan’s deputy.
Burhan said Monday that new sanctions would not deter his troops from carrying on with their war until all RSF-controlled areas are captured, according to the army-controlled SUNA news agency.
“Our souls and destiny are in God’s hands,” he said while attending the graduation ceremony of new police officers in the capital, Khartoum. “Our message to those staying in hotels abroad and cheering at sanctions that are meant to subjugate the Sudanese people is the following: The people will not be broken, but we will break and defeat you.”
U.N. political chief Rosemary DiCarlo told the Security Council that despite numerous diplomatic efforts to get government and paramilitary leaders to start negotiations and end hostilities, “the parties remain locked in a zero-sum military logic.”
“Greater international attention and action are urgently needed for them to change that calculus,” she said.

Associated Press writer Noha Elhennawy in Cairo contributed to this report.

cool blue tones meet a vivid red counter inside hubarch’s new optics boutique
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
22:50:36 UTC
07:50:36 KST

For Bazilio Optics Boutique, Hubarch works with a restrained palette of pale blue and white, then interrupts it with a single flash of red. Set on the ground floor of a residential building, the 100-square-meter store occupies a raw, open shell framed by two oversized windows and a glazed entrance. The existing openness gave the studio a useful starting point: plenty of morning light, few spatial obstacles, and room to give the optics brand an architectural identity of its own.
Rather than filling the interior with competing gestures, the design keeps almost everything deliberately quiet. Pale blues wash across walls and textured plaster, while the exposed concrete ceiling is lacquered and left visible overhead. Minimal display units recede into the background, allowing rows of eyewear to read clearly against the cool-toned surfaces. The effect sits somewhere between clinical precision and domestic calm — appropriate, perhaps, for a space devoted to seeing things more clearly.
all images by Dmitry Suvorov | courtesy of Hubarch
A RED COUNTER BREAKS THE BLUE
At the center of this controlled palette, a custom red counter introduces the project’s only major chromatic interruption. Designed and produced according to the studio’s drawings, the piece cuts through the otherwise cool interior with a saturated point of warmth. Its angled shelving takes cues from the balconies of the surrounding residential architecture in Saint Petersburg, translating an element of the city outside into the store at furniture scale.
The counter is not simply there to look photogenic, although it manages that rather efficiently. Its upholstered upper surface adds tactility to an otherwise hard-edged environment, while the structure accommodates fittings, consultations and purchases, making it both the visual anchor and working core of the boutique. Instead of spreading color throughout the space, Hubarch concentrates it in one object, allowing the contrast to do considerably more work with considerably less paint.
pale blue tones define the optics boutique interior
DAYLIGHT SHAPES THE 100-SQM RETAIL INTERIOR
Behind the main retail area, the studio arranges the more functional spaces — an optometrist’s office, lens-fitting workshop, staff room and restroom — in a compact strip along the rear wall. This organization keeps the storefront open and allows daylight from the two large windows to travel deep into the customer-facing area. The plan remains visually straightforward, with the technical functions tucked away without fragmenting the principal volume.
Material choices are similarly economical. Painted surfaces and textured plaster sit alongside exposed concrete and Italon porcelain tiles, responding to a limited budget and construction timeline without turning austerity into the main event. Instead, the project directs its attention toward proportion, daylight and bespoke furniture. The finished boutique is defined by a simple visual equation: a cool-toned shell, restrained displays and one conspicuously red object holding everything together.

WASHINGTON, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- The U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) on Monday proposed a 103,265-U.S.-dollar fee for H-1B cap-subject petitions, marking the agency's newest move to restrict the visa program on new grounds.
The move came after previous efforts to charge 100,000 dollars for the visa were struck down by the courts.
"The proposed fee would generate revenue to recover a portion of the federal government's costs for administering the lawful immigration system," the DHS said in a news release.
The new fee is designed to recover a portion of the full costs of providing immigration adjudication and naturalization services incurred by multiple federal agencies in processing, adjudicating and supporting the lawful immigration system, according to a document scheduled to be published in the Federal Register on Tuesday.
The DHS estimates the proposed fee would generate approximately 8.8 billion dollars annually, based on a projected annual volume of 85,000 H-1B cap-subject petitions, according to the release.
Under the proposed rule, the additional fee would not apply to H-1B petitions that are not subject to the cap, such as petitions filed by certain nonprofit research organizations, governmental research organizations, and institutions of higher education, the release added.
The public will be given a 30-day period to submit comments on the proposed rule before it can take effect.
"If finalized, the new proposal would place a significant new burden on the technology and finance sectors, which rely on the H-1B visa to hire top international graduates from U.S. universities," The Wall Street Journal reported.
The latest proposal came two months after the Trump administration's 100,000-dollar fee on new H-1B visas was struck down by a federal judge in Boston, Massachusetts. The judge ruled that the executive branch exceeded its authority and violated the Administrative Procedure Act.
In September 2025, U.S. President Donald Trump signed a proclamation raising the fee that companies pay to sponsor H-1B applicants to 100,000 dollars, saying the move was intended to ensure that the United States brings in highly skilled talent whom American workers cannot replace.
Earlier reports from U.S. media noted that the hefty fee would affect tech giants such as Amazon, Microsoft and Google, which have long relied on the H-1B visa program to hire foreign employees, including software developers.
CBS reported that the plan could backfire by encouraging U.S. companies to shift jobs overseas, especially in specialized fields such as research and development. It could also further deter international students from studying in the United States.
Since Trump returned to the White House, his administration has tightened immigration policies, cracking down on undocumented immigrants and increasing scrutiny of U.S. visa holders.
On Aug. 10, the U.S. State Department announced that it had revoked more than 175,000 visas since January 2025, when Trump began his second term.
The Trump administration is preparing to revoke the business and tourism visas of up to 200,000 foreigners who have applied for or are currently seeking asylum status in the United States, according to a report by The Associated Press.
"If it happens, the move would be the largest single mass revocation of visas in U.S. history and would likely face legal challenges," the report said. ■

How US sanctions on Iran ripple through global markets and consumers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
22:46:02 UTC
07:46:02 KST

How US sanctions on Iran ripple through global markets and consumers
New sanctions hit Iran’s aviation, tech, and shipping sectors, amplifying pressure on global markets and energy prices.
The administration of United States President Donald Trump has announced new economic sanctions on Tehran, describing the measures as an “economic D-Day” as the US war on Iran approaches the six-month mark.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced the sanctions on Monday, alongside a naval blockade of Iranian ports.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4US threat of ‘economic D-Day’ for Iran tests Trump’s China detente
- list 2 of 4Trump slams Canada with new 50 percent auto tariffs from January
- list 3 of 4What to expect as Iran braces for new US economic measures amid war
- list 4 of 4Trump administration seeks to formalise H-1B fee of more than $100,000
Bessent said the sanctions target key sources of Iran’s revenue, including its oil and gas industry, and called on countries around the world to cut economic ties with Tehran.
What are the sanctions?
The Treasury Department said the sanctions will target Iran’s aviation, digital assets, gold, technology and shipping sectors, as well as impose sanctions on 60 specific individuals and vessels.
“The main point is that Iran seems to have much less room than it did in previous years to simply work around sanctions,” Peiman Salehi, a Tehran-based geopolitical analyst, told Al Jazeera.
Bessent also said on Monday that the new sanctions expose Tehran’s trade partners to secondary penalties. According to a Treasury Department release on Monday, the targets include ships based in or associated with countries including Singapore, China, and Hong Kong.
“Today’s sanctions are mostly incremental, but are part of trying to intimidate remaining trading partners into cutting ties [with Iran],” said Rachel Ziemba, an adjunct senior fellow at the Center for a New American Security think tank.
“There’s a lot of signalling and bluster aimed at getting other countries to crack down on entities involved in grey-zone trade, but new measures are mostly incremental for now,” she said. Grey-zone trade refers to both illegal, underground trade and trade that is unsanctioned but difficult.
The Treasury Department said Iran has used cryptocurrency to circumvent its longtime sanctions and facilitate transactions involving the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and members of the Iranian regime. The department also said Iran has used gold to help prop up the value of its currency amid economic instability.
The new shipping sanctions target Iran’s state-linked shipping fleet, which the Treasury Department alleges is being used to transport oil as well as “sensitive weapons components”.
The technology sanctions are intended to restrict Iran’s acquisition of materials that could be used in its weapons programmes. The aviation sanctions target Iranian airlines that the Treasury Department alleges are being used to transport weapons and military personnel, as well as financial resources to Iran’s proxies.
Washington also indefinitely suspended several broad exceptions to its ongoing sanctions on Iran, including those covering academic exchanges, personal money transfers and certain sporting activities. Organisations currently engaged in those activities have until September 8 to wind down their operations.
Ziemba says these measures “will have more effect on Iranians, not just the regime”.
What sanctions were already in place?
Washington’s sanctions on Iran have been in place since 1979, after students took hostages at the US Embassy in Tehran, and increased over the next 45 years. Sanctions were briefly paused, however, after the administration of President Barack Obama and world powers signed a nuclear deal with Tehran in 2015. But the Trump administration withdrew from the deal during its first term, in 2018, bringing back old penalties while adding new ones.
Washington imposed new sanctions during Trump’s second term, many of them before the US and Israel first struck the country on February 28.
In February 2025, the Treasury Department sanctioned 30 individuals and vessels involved in the “brokering [of] the sale and transportation of Iranian petroleum-related products”, according to a department release. The targets were based in several countries, including India and China.
In December 2025, Washington sanctioned 29 vessels it accused of being part of a so-called shadow fleet used to transport Iranian petroleum. It also sanctioned Egyptian businessman Hatem Elsaid Farid Ibrahim Sakr over his businesses’ alleged ties to seven of those 29 vessels. The measures continued the 1979 sanctions campaign against Iran’s oil industry.
The Treasury Department stepped up the sanctions again in April 2026, targeting another two dozen individuals, companies and vessels operating within the network of Iranian oil shipping magnate Mohammad Hossein Shamkhani, the son of now-deceased senior Iranian security official Ali Shamkhani.
Later that same month, the Treasury also targeted what it described as “regime-linked cryptocurrency” and said it had seized nearly half a billion dollars from so-called “shadow banking networks”.
How have sanctions affected US consumers?
Pressure on the Iranian oil market, both through existing sanctions as well as the current war, has tightened the rest of the globe’s oil supply and affected countries that buy Iranian oil.
China, for example, is the primary destination for Iranian oil, buying roughly 90 percent of Iran’s crude oil exports. Beijing bought 1.4 million barrels per day in 2025.
At the same time, Asian markets, China included, also heavily rely on oil travelling through the strategically vital Strait of Hormuz, where roughly one-fifth of the globe’s oil transited before Iran choked off the route.
This has put pressure on the global oil supply, meaning the benchmark for crude oil has ticked up, translating to higher prices on fuel and food.
For US consumers, that has been most apparent at the petrol pump. The average price for a gallon of petrol (3.78 litres) is $4.09, up from $2.98 on February 28 when the US and Israel first struck Iran, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA), which tracks daily petrol prices.
Experts warn that if Iran retaliation accelerates, it could hit Americans hard.
“If sanctions provoke Iranian retaliation against Gulf shipping, materially reduce oil exports, or cause insurers and shipping companies to avoid the region, then Americans could feel it very quickly through gasoline, diesel, airfares, freight costs and ultimately inflation,” John Deal, managing director of capital markets at Post Oak Group investment bank, told Al Jazeera.
The economy and Iran are emerging as key issues heading into the US midterm elections, with voters expressing dissatisfaction on both fronts. That could put pressure on Republicans in competitive races, including in traditionally red states such as Texas.
A late-July Reuters/Ipsos poll suggested that only about a third of Americans supported the war, while just 28 percent of respondents in a CNN poll approved of Trump’s handling of Iran.
On the economy, an AP/NORC poll suggested that 32 percent of Americans approved of Trump’s performance. A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll, meanwhile, suggested that Democrats were narrowly ahead of Republicans on which party voters trust more to handle the economy—the first Democratic advantage in roughly a decade.
How are the sanctions affecting markets?
The latest sanctions announcement is weighing on Wall Street as well as the oil and gold markets.
On the heels of the announcement, the price of gold, largely considered a safe investment during times of economic uncertainty, jumped by 0.8 percent to $4,639.49 per ounce (28 grams) in midday trading, ticking up to its highest level since mid-May.
As for oil, prices pulled back on Monday after two weeks of gains. The price of the global benchmark Brent crude tumbled by more than 2 percent on Monday to $85.22 a barrel.
On Wall Street, the major indices are mixed amid the latest sanctions news as well as Trump’s announcement of new tariffs on Canada. The Nasdaq is down 0.5 percent, and the S&P 500 is down 0.2 percent. The Dow Jones Industrial Average, however, is trending in positive territory, 0.2 percent higher than the market open on Monday.
The oil sector is taking a hit. Chevron is down 0.8 percent, ExxonMobil tumbled 0.9 percent, BP fell more than 2 percent, and Shell is down 0.2 percent.

Details

The package also includes documentation, helmets and gear, spare parts, necessary tools, logistical support, and maintenance services.
The cost of the Black Hawk was compared with European counterparts
Defense Express notes that the cost of the Norwegian deal makes it possible to estimate the potential price of new Black Hawks for Ukraine. At the same time, Ukraine is primarily considering the possibility of obtaining used aircraft.
For comparison, Romania purchased 12 H225 helicopters for $993.8 million, or approximately $82.8 million per aircraft. The United Kingdom ordered 23 AW149 helicopters for $1.34 billion, which amounts to about $58.3 million each.
The publication emphasized that a direct comparison of costs is conditional due to differences in configuration and additional equipment. In addition, the $2.3 billion figure is the maximum estimate under the U.S. approval for the sale, and the final contract value may be lower.

US Supreme Court sides with Trump administration on mail voting
Unknown

US Supreme Court allows Trump’s mail voting restrictions to proceed
Mail balloting has long been a favourite target of US President Donald Trump.
The United States Supreme Court has cleared the way for President Donald Trump to move ahead with his executive order restricting mail voting, though it remains unclear how much his administration can implement before the fast-approaching midterm elections in November.
The decision on Monday appears to leave room for additional court challenges that could further slow Trump’s order. The court has a 6-3 conservative majority. The three liberal justices dissented from the decision.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3US Vice President JD Vance holds midterm election rally in Ohio hometown
- list 2 of 3Trump seeks to block the BBC’s attempt to subpoena Ivanka Trump, Trump Jr
- list 3 of 3US public support for Iran war falls as Trump approval at record low: Poll
The US Postal Service laid out how it would implement the order last week, but time is running short to impose major changes with some states beginning to send mail ballots to voters in just a few weeks.
Voting by mail has long been a favourite target for Trump, who has claimed that it breeds fraud despite strong evidence to the contrary and his own use of the voting method.
The case could be one of multiple voting-related challenges before the justices. The US Justice Department had filed an emergency appeal asking the high court to allow work on implementing the changes before the midterms.
Trump’s executive order, signed in March, calls on his administration to create lists of eligible voters and orders the US Postal Service to deliver mail ballots only to people on those lists.
Democratic officials in 23 states and the District of Columbia sued to block the order. They argued that the US Constitution gives states and Congress the power to run elections, and Trump’s changes could lead to chaos and partisan abuse.
“The consequences of allowing such transformative changes to take effect so close to this fall’s elections would be extreme,” lawyers for the states wrote. Dozens of state and local election officials weighed in, asking the justices to leave the order frozen while election preparations are already underway.
A judge in the US state of Massachusetts blocked the plan for the midterm elections in those states. An appeals court upheld her decision. She later granted a second order blocking it nationwide.
The Trump administration appealed to the Supreme Court on procedural grounds in late July, arguing that the states sued too soon. They also pointed to another ruling out of Washington, where a judge allowed Trump’s order to proceed. An appeals court backed that decision, while still leaving room for future court action if the changes are implemented.
Federal attorneys argued that the Massachusetts order “blocks the government’s ability to finalize and implement the President’s proposed policies to promote election integrity for the upcoming federal elections in November.”
A dozen Republican-leaning states supported the federal government in their own appeal before the high court, saying states would have input on the final voter lists.
The Supreme Court has previously ruled against Trump-backed arguments on mail-in ballots, finding in June that states can count ballots that arrive after Election Day. That case was decided after full briefing and arguments, rather than on the court’s emergency docket.
Trump, who has made false claims of widespread fraud in U.S. elections including his 2020 loss to Democrat Joe Biden, has pressed the Republican-controlled Congress to pass a contentious package of voting restrictions called the SAVE America Act.
He’s also repeatedly pressed for the passage of the legislation that requires proof of citizenship to vote. Noncitizen voting has been shown to be rare, and is a felony that can be punishable by deportation.
Using mail ballots has become increasingly popular with voters of both parties, with about 30 percent of all ballots cast that way during the 2024 presidential election, according to federal data. The process also is secure. A 2025 Brookings Institution study found only about four cases of fraud out of every 10 million mail ballots cast.

US Supreme Court removes judicial decision blocking Trump's mail-in ballot restrictions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
22:38:06 UTC
07:38:06 KST

The US Supreme Court on Monday lifted a judicial decision blocking President Donald Trump's administration from implementing his executive order to restrict the use of mail-in ballots ahead of the November midterm elections that will decide control of Congress.
But the fate of Trump's order remains uncertain, as a separate injunction blocking a key part of the plan remains in place.
Monday's ruling from the Supreme Court's 6-3 conservative majority applied to a June injunction from Boston-based US District Judge Indira Talwani.
The justices granted a Justice Department emergency request to put on hold an injunction that Boston-based US Judge Indira Talwani's imposed in June preventing the Republican president from proceeding with his directive in a coalition of 23 mostly Democratic-governed states and Washington, DC that had sued to stop it.
The court did not act, however, on another injunction issued by Talwani on August 11 that blocked the US Postal Service nationwide from enforcing the directive's tighter rules for voting by mail. The judge issued that order in a separate lawsuit filed by several voting-rights groups.
The Supreme Court's action leaves open the door to the states suing again in the coming months as the midterm contest approaches.
The Justice Department had urged the Supreme Court to make clear that its action applied to both of Talwani's injunctions, but the justices did not do so on Monday.
Both lawsuits had challenged Trump's order as unconstitutional.
Trump's March executive order
Trump's executive order, issued in March, directed the Department of Homeland Security to compile and transmit to the states a list of US citizens eligible to vote in each state, and the Justice Department to prioritize investigating and prosecuting state and local election officials who issue ballots to people deemed "not eligible" to vote in federal elections.
It also required the US Postal Service to deliver ballots only to voters on each state's approved mail-in ballot list. The Postal Service recently moved to implement Trump's directive.
Trump has vowed to end the use of mail-in ballots nationwide before the midterms, and has long cast doubt on the security of such ballots, although evidence of voter fraud is rare.
Republicans are seeking to retain control of Congress in the hotly contested midterms. Restricting mail-in ballots would stand to disproportionately benefit Republicans given that Democratic voters traditionally have been more likely to use mail-in ballots than Republican voters.
Justice Department deemed Trump lacked authority
In June, Talwani ruled that the president lacked the authority to order changes in how states administer federal elections, noting that under the US Constitution, states have the role of determining voter-eligibility requirements. The judge also noted that federal agencies lack the ability to compile accurate citizen lists for each state.
The Justice Department had said the lawsuit challenging Trump's directive was premature and that the states did not have the required legal standing at this stage to sue. The agencies have not yet taken any concrete actions that impact the states and so any harm they allege is speculative, the administration said.
The states contend that their claims are not hypothetical and that the administration's "rushed effort to change the rules of mail voting on the eve of the November midterms risks disenfranchising a substantial number of voters."
The judge rejected the administration's arguments, finding that the suit was not filed too soon and that the states had legal standing because they would face election administration disruption, compliance costs and a credible threat of criminal prosecution.
Trump's executive order is part of his wider efforts to make fundamental changes in US elections. Trump, who has made false claims of widespread fraud in US elections including his 2020 loss to Democrat Joe Biden, has pressed the Republican-controlled Congress to pass a contentious package of voting restrictions called the SAVE America Act.

US removes Syria from ‘state sponsor of terrorism’ list

The United States has removed Syria from its list of “State Sponsors of Terrorism”, a decision Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa hailed as “historic” and said would help the country’s recovery after 14 years of civil war.
The removal on Monday took effect after a 45-day congressional review period, triggered when US President Donald Trump formally notified Congress on July 8 of his intention to rescind the decades-old designation.
Recommended Stories

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement that the action was “taken in recognition of the positive actions taken and further commitments” by al-Sharaa to “fully distance Syria from acts of international terrorism”.
Al-Sharaa welcomed the decision in a statement on X.
He thanked Trump and said Syria was tearing a “page from its painful past, in order to launch itself into the realm of development, reconstruction, and building”.
Syria had been on the list since 1979, when Washington accused the government of former President Hafez al-Assad of supporting armed groups. The designation remained throughout the rule of his son, Bashar al-Assad, who was toppled by rebels led by al-Sharaa in December 2024.
The designation carries restrictions on US foreign assistance, defence exports and sales, certain dual-use items (which can have civilian and military applications) and financial transactions. It had remained a major deterrent for banks and investors even after Washington dismantled its broader sanctions programme on Syria.
Iran, Russia influence
Al Jazeera’s Kimberly Halkett, reporting from Washington, DC, said the US move ends five decades of Syria’s isolation.
“Only Cuba, Iran, and North Korea remain on that list. This will open up an opportunity for international legitimacy – something al-Sharaa’s government has been seeking. But it also paves the way for commercial investment, not only in the form of US financial assistance, but also defence sales,” she said.
“Strategically, there’s another goal of the United States in all of this: to try to pull Syria away from the clutches of both Iran and Russia, and end the formal pariah status Syria has previously found itself in,” she added.
Monday’s announcement also revoked the designation of al-Nusrah Front – the group formerly led by al-Sharaa, also known as Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS) – as a global “terrorist” organisation. HTS was once al-Qaeda’s official branch in Syria.
It represents a further vote of confidence in al-Sharaa, who has launched what many experts have described as a charm offensive aimed at Western powers, including meetings with Trump and French President Emmanuel Macron.
“Today’s action will help foster additional investment in Syria to promote political and economic stability,” US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement, adding that it is “in line with President Trump’s promise to deliver sanctions relief to Syria”.
‘A new chapter’
Syria’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said the US action “represents an important shift that opens a new chapter in international relations with Syria”. It said the move “will contribute to supporting economic recovery efforts and creating suitable conditions for reconstruction and enhancing stability in Syria and the region”.
The governor of Syria’s central bank, Safwat Raslan, said on X that this is “a historic step that restores the country to its natural place in the global economic system”. He added that the bank is “working to build a modern and reliable financial system”.
Syrian Finance Minister Mohammed Barnieh, meanwhile, described Washington’s move as “a major and historic success for Syrian diplomacy”, according to the country’s official news agency SANA.
It “opens a major and long-awaited door to strengthening Syria’s integration into the global economic and financial system, attracting investment and modern technologies, and supporting development opportunities”, he said.
The US envoy to Syria, Tom Barrack, also hailed the move.
He called the end of the designation a “decisive step in Syria’s remarkable journey from isolation to partnership, and from a source of terrorism to a committed partner in the global fight against it”.

The contract was signed by the Armament Agency of Poland’s Ministry of National Defence with the Polish company Mesko S.A. More than 80% of the order is intended for the Polish military, with the remainder for Lithuania, Latvia, and Norway.
The total value of the deal is 8 billion Polish zlotys, or approximately €1.86 billion. In addition to the missiles and launchers themselves, the contract also includes simulators, training, and logistics packages.
Poland, Lithuania, Latvia, and Norway have formed a four-country consortium for joint procurement. The parties plan to sign the agreement to implement the contract within several days, while arms deliveries are to continue until 2030 under the European SAFE program.
The Piorun is used by the Armed Forces of Ukraine
Piorun man-portable air-defense systems have been in service with the Defense Forces of Ukraine since 2022. Ukrainian troops have used these systems against Russian aircraft and other aerial targets, including airplanes, helicopters, and cruise missiles.
In addition to Poland and Ukraine, Piorun systems are in service with Latvia, Norway, Sweden, Belgium, Estonia, and North Macedonia. Following the new procurement, Lithuania is expected to join the system’s operators.
This order became Poland’s first joint procurement under the SAFE program and the largest contract for Piorun man-portable air-defense systems in history. Earlier, preparations for a similar agreement worth 7 billion zlotys had been reported, but the contract’s final value increased to 8 billion zlotys.

Largest review of its kind confirms benefits of tai chi and other Chinese exercises
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
22:30:40 UTC
07:30:40 KST

Traditional Chinese exercises such as tai chi can offer wide-ranging benefits for people with musculoskeletal disorders, improving physical function, pain, mental health, sleep quality and bone mineral density, according to the largest review of its kind.
More than 1.7bn people have musculoskeletal conditions worldwide. While prevalence varies by age and diagnosis, people of all ages in every country and every continent are affected.
Musculoskeletal conditions significantly limit mobility and dexterity, leading to early retirement from work, lower levels of wellbeing and reduced ability to participate in society. They are also the leading contributor to disability worldwide, with low back pain being the single leading cause of disability in 160 countries.
There was already evidence indicating traditional Chinese exercises were associated with beneficial health outcomes in people with musculoskeletal disorders, but much of it was fragmented and contained inconsistencies.
The overarching review of pooled data analyses of systematic reviews by researchers at hospitals and universities in China, published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine, drew on 92 data syntheses from 1,744 randomised controlled clinical trials.
It found “high certainty evidence” for the effectiveness of traditional Chinese exercise – such as tai chi, qigong, baduanjin, wuqinxi and yijinjing – for a range of health outcomes for people with musculoskeletal disorders.
These included improving movement in knee osteoarthritis, mental health associated with neck pain and knee osteoarthritis, and sleep quality associated with fibromyalgia.
Tai chi, in particular, significantly eased chronic musculoskeletal pain and stiffness in several conditions while increasing bone mineral density in participants with osteopenia or osteoporosis, the research found.
Maximum benefits were achieved when people did these exercises for longer than six months, at least three times a week, clocking up a total of at least 150 minutes a week.
“This comprehensive [umbrella review] provides a definitive, high-level evidence synthesis supporting [traditional Chinese exercises] as effective interventions for a range of musculoskeletal conditions],” the researchers concluded.
“The evidence, particularly for tai chi, reaches high certainty for improving key outcomes such as physical function in knee osteoarthritis, mental health in neck pain, sleep in fibromyalgia and bone density in osteoporosis.”
The findings suggested traditional Chinese exercises should be included in clinical guidelines and rehabilitation programmes worldwide, the researchers added.
“[These] exercises represent a safe, accessible, and cost-effective strategy that can complement conventional therapies, reduce pharmacological reliance, and empower patients in self-management.”
While the prevalence of musculoskeletal conditions increases with age, younger people are also affected, often during their peak income-earning years.
And with global population growth and ageing, the number of people living with musculoskeletal conditions and associated health problems is rapidly increasing.
“For healthcare systems and policymakers, promoting the adoption of traditional Chinese exercises, particularly in community and primary care settings, could be a strategic component of public health initiatives aimed at healthy ageing and chronic disease prevention,” the researchers said.

US set for largest mass visa revocation in history targeting up to 200,000 foreigners — report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
22:29:19 UTC
07:29:19 KST

The Trump administration is preparing to revoke the business and tourism visas of up to 200,000 foreigners who have applied for or are currently seeking asylum status in the US.
If it happens, the move would be the largest single mass revocation of visas in US history and would likely face legal challenges.
Unless challenged or revised, the State Department is expected to announce in the coming weeks the revocation of so-called B1 and B2 visas issued between 2016 and 2026 whose holders have sought asylum or are now seeking asylum, according to State Department documents obtained by The Associated Press and two US officials.
The action will be taken in coordination with the Department of Homeland Security.
"We are coordinating with DHS to identify and revoke the nonimmigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the United States claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently," said State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott.
He declined to comment on the number of visas that might be revoked, saying "as the process will be ongoing, the number of revocations remains dynamic and will be done on a rolling basis."
Most of those with asylum cases currently pending would be recategorised but would lose their status as business or tourism travellers, according to the officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
“Circumventing immigration law”
In a social media post on Monday, Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau called out people he said try to use tourist and business visas to enter the US and then apply for asylum.
"People in the US and all over the world are fed up with bogus asylum claims," Landau wrote on X. "Asylum isn't supposed to be a loophole to circumvent immigration law." Landau cited the case of a Colombian citizen who came to the US in 2015 on a tourist visa and then applied for asylum.
He argued that the system has long been swamped by asylum claims, a process that takes years, during which applicants put down roots in the country.
B1 visas are generally issued for business trips and B2 visas are generally issued for tourism, family visits or medical care. It was not immediately clear from the documents or the officials how many of these visa holders are seeking or have sought asylum in the United States and would be affected by the revocations.
Current applicants for B1 and B2 visas are asked to affirm that they will not apply for asylum in the US and prove that they intend to return to their home countries.

S+DLH and VASTO gallery bring contemporary art and collectible design under one roof
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
22:26:28 UTC
07:26:28 KST

S+DLH AND VASTO SELECT OBJECTS TO LIVE INSIDE ARCHITECTURE
Madrid-based studio SIERRA+DELAHIGUERA (S+DLH) joins forces with Barcelona’s VASTO Gallery for Capsule 04 · Selected to live inside architecture, an exhibition bringing together contemporary art, collectible design and objects from the studio’s own archive. Installed at S+DLH Gallery on Calle Orellana in Madrid, the project looks beyond the usual art-versus-furniture divide, instead considering how objects, artworks and architecture can comfortably occupy the same room — without anyone needing to stay on their designated pedestal.
The exhibition marks the beginning of an ongoing collaboration between S+DLH and VASTO, the Poblenou-based home gallery founded by Carmen Riestra. Rather than approaching art as a finishing touch added once an interior is complete, the partnership proposes a more integrated relationship: works represented by VASTO will continue to appear within future residential and commercial projects by the Madrid studio. Capsule 04 serves as an initial experiment in this shared language, connecting the two practices through materiality, atmosphere and an interest in how objects influence the perception of space.
capsule 04 unfolds inside S+DLH in Madrid | images: courtesy of S+DLH
POL AGUSTÍ, MAX MILÀ SERRA AND ESTHER GATÓN ENTER THE ROOM
Three artists from VASTO’s programme shape the exhibition. Pol Agustí, born in Barcelona and based in Mexico City, works between object, ritual and presence, often using clay and recovered materials to create forms that feel simultaneously familiar and difficult to place. Fired at low temperatures, his ceramics preserve traces of gesture, irregularity and fire, giving the material a deliberately direct quality while allowing apparently everyday forms to drift towards something more symbolic.
Barcelona-based Max Milà Serra takes a more precise route, bringing engineering, light and perception into minimal structures capable of shifting the atmosphere around them. His works are less concerned with simply illuminating a room than with quietly recalibrating it. Esther Gatón, meanwhile, works across sculpture, installation, audiovisual media and text. Her recent pieces use hand-dyed linen produced through slow, non-repeatable processes, turning variations of pigment, time and gesture into part of the work rather than imperfections to be corrected.
contemporary art meets collectible design throughout the exhibition
ARCHIVE PIECES JOIN NEW DESIGNS BY SIERRA+DELAHIGUERA
Alongside the artists represented by VASTO, S+DLH introduces pieces from its own design practice, including objects presented publicly for the first time and others recovered from an archive accumulated over the years. Removed from the logic of a conventional showroom, the works are arranged as part of a broader spatial composition in which authorship and category become somewhat less important than proximity, scale and material conversation. A lamp can behave almost like sculpture; a sculpture can begin to feel suspiciously at home.
This deliberate ambiguity sits at the centre of Capsule 04. Under the subtitle Selected to live inside architecture, the exhibition proposes collecting not as the accumulation of isolated statement pieces but as a way of constructing environments over time. Art, furniture, light and found objects are allowed to coexist without a strict hierarchy, forming interiors that feel assembled rather than styled.

ALBAWABA- Saudi Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman and French President Emmanuel Macron on Monday chaired the inaugural meeting of the Saudi-French Strategic Partnership Council in Paris, marking a new institutional phase in relations between Riyadh and Paris as the Middle East faces mounting security and economic pressures.
The meeting took place during Mohammed bin Salman’s official visit to France at Macron’s invitation. The two leaders signed the minutes of the council’s first meeting and witnessed the exchange of a series of agreements and memoranda covering defense, investment, infrastructure, artificial intelligence, culture, tourism and economic cooperation. Macron said the visit represented an important step in strengthening bilateral ties and reaffirmed the two countries’ commitment to peace and regional stability.
Among the agreements was an extension and amendment of the Saudi-French agreement governing the development of AlUla, covering cultural, environmental, tourism, human, economic and heritage projects. The expanded agreement extends bilateral cooperation on AlUla until 2035 and includes archaeology, heritage preservation, tourism, training, innovation and sustainable development. France has been a key partner in Saudi Arabia’s long-term effort to transform AlUla into a major international cultural and tourism destination.
The two countries also signed a declaration of intent between Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Defense and France’s Ministry for the Armed Forces and Veterans’ Affairs to strengthen their defense partnership. The cooperation is expected to include emerging defense technologies, cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, military training and education, and the development of defense-industrial capabilities.
The broader package reflects Riyadh’s strategy of diversifying its international partnerships while pursuing major economic transformation projects under Vision 2030. One of the most prominent announcements was a €6 billion Saudi-backed Qiddiya project near Paris, involving three theme parks, accommodation and other facilities and expected to create about 22,000 jobs. Other agreements covered Riyadh Metro expansion, ports, nuclear technology, artificial intelligence, aviation, mining and investment financing.
Against the backdrop of escalating regional tensions, the meeting comes as Saudi Arabia faces renewed security pressure from the Houthis in Yemen, who on Monday claimed a ballistic-missile attack on a vessel off the Saudi Red Sea port of Yanbu. The Houthis said the attack was part of their declared blockade of Saudi maritime traffic, while the vessel’s crew was reported safe.
Saudi Arabia and France used the visit to discuss wider regional crises, including Iran, Lebanon, Syria and maritime security. In a joint statement, Riyadh and Paris called for diplomacy over Iran and stressed the importance of freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, while reaffirming their broader positions on Palestinian statehood and regional stability.
