Trump’s Iran ‘economic D-Day’ lands as another threat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
22:24:59 UTC
07:24:59 KST

For days, U.S. President Donald Trump and his administration had raised expectations of a dramatic announcement, promising an “economic D-Day” against Iran, invoking the term associated with the Allied invasion of Normandy during World War II. In a Truth Social post last Thursday, Trump promised unprecedented economic warfare in an effort to isolate Iran and force it into submission. His Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, said the objective was to bring about the regime’s collapse.
Hours before Monday’s news conference, which he had announced several days earlier, Bessent further raised expectations in an opinion article for the Financial Times. “At dawn begins an economic D-Day — the single greatest financial offensive ever marshalled against an adversary,” he wrote.
But it was not Trump who stepped up to the podium in Washington on Monday. It was Bessent, and the reason soon appeared clear: in practice, the announcement amounted largely to another threat, one of many made since the war began.
Bessent did announce new sanctions targeting around 60 individuals, entities and vessels with links to Iran, but such sanctions announcements are not in themselves unusual. The centerpiece of his announcement was instead a warning to countries around the world: cut all economic ties with Iran or face punishment yourselves.
In prepared remarks before taking reporters’ questions, Bessent said the campaign would intensify gradually until Iran was economically isolated and forced to choose between near-total isolation and compromise in negotiations to end the war. The Treasury Department described the objective as severing Iran’s economic lifelines until Tehran stood alone.
But when Bessent was asked why Washington was not immediately punishing countries that continue to do business with Iran, he effectively acknowledged that doing so could carry severe consequences for the world economy.
The question came from a reporter who noted that the original D-Day was not merely a threat and that the United States had not warned Nazi Germany in advance of the Allied invasion. Why, the reporter asked, were the sanctions not being imposed immediately? “We are giving everyone the opportunity to remedy bad behavior. Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?” Bessent replied.
He said Washington wanted to give countries a short period to change course before deploying secondary sanctions, which he described as an extremely powerful tool. Bessent said the administration believed “a warning shot” was appropriate, while making clear that countries that refused to meet U.S. expectations could ultimately find themselves outside the dollar-based financial system.
“We know who they are, they know who they are,” Bessent added, referring to countries that he said continue to provide Iran with a financial or commercial lifeline. He warned that when the “hammer of U.S. Treasury actions” came down on them, they would have only themselves to blame.
But he gave no explicit deadline and did not identify the countries concerned. He also declined to say whether the threat applied to China, which for years has largely ignored U.S. sanctions and continued buying Iranian oil.
China is currently unable to import Iranian crude as it did before because of the U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports. Still, international media noted that the roughly 60 entities targeted in Monday’s sanctions did not include major Chinese financial institutions accused of helping Iran circumvent previous restrictions.
If Trump follows through and imposes sanctions on China, he risks triggering another trade war with Beijing. Analysts believe he would prefer to avoid that for now, particularly with Chinese President Xi Jinping expected to visit Washington next month.
Trump hopes during that visit to extend the temporary agreement reached with Beijing last November, which ended the trade war he had been waging against China. Turkey and Russia also maintain significant economic ties with Iran.
Trump himself made no public reference to the new sanctions campaign on Monday and did not mention it during an event later at the White House. Hours before Bessent’s announcement, however, he posted a brief message on Truth Social about the plunge in Iran’s currency: “IRAN IS COMPLETELY COLLAPSING!!!”
In his announcement, Bessent said the United States would focus its new campaign, dubbed “Operation Economic Outcast,” on five sectors that Washington says Iran uses to sustain its economy: digital assets, gold, technology, aviation and shipping.
He indicated that a “major” announcement involving sanctions against a financial institution was expected by the end of the week, although he did not identify it.
During the news conference, however, he specifically mentioned Bank Melli, the Iranian state-owned bank with branches and subsidiaries around the world, including in Britain, France, Germany, Hong Kong and Russia. Bessent said those overseas operations must be shut down or risk exclusion from the U.S. dollar system.
Washington has previously accused Bank Melli of providing financial services to entities involved in Iran’s nuclear and ballistic missile programs.
Markets were unimpressed too
The relatively muted impact of Monday’s announcement was also reflected in the way it was received by the U.S. media. The New York Times portrayed Bessent’s promised crippling sanctions campaign as having ultimately produced another round of warnings rather than an immediate economic strike.
Financial markets also showed little reaction. Oil prices had risen in the days before the announcement but fell after Bessent spoke, suggesting investors had expected something more consequential.
Market commentary noted that there was little in the announcement that required investors to immediately reassess the economic picture.
Iran, meanwhile, responded dismissively to the announcement. On Monday, Tehran did not repeat the particularly sharp threats of attacks against countries joining what it calls the U.S. “economic war” that had been voiced a day earlier by Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council.
Even before Bessent began speaking, Iranian parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf dismissed the measure. “The Americans know that no one believes their bluster,” Ghalibaf wrote on X. “The United States is not in an economic position to restrict its relations with other countries any further.”
He said Iran’s trading partners had indicated, both publicly and privately, that they attached little importance to Washington’s statements.
Shortly after the announcement, Iranian Economy and Finance Minister Ali Madanizadeh said the country had prepared in advance for the new measures. He said the latest U.S. sanctions would fail to sever Iran’s economic lifelines just as previous attempts had failed, adding that Tehran had been preparing for such measures for a long time and arguing that the era of a unipolar world had ended.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who on Monday said Iran had tried to assassinate one of his sons, welcomed Bessent’s announcement. In an English-language statement published by his office, Netanyahu congratulated Trump and Bessent on the new sanctions and said they were right to impose a heavy price on the Iranian regime and those enabling its continued aggression.
Trump has shifted strategy in recent weeks after negotiations with Iran reached an impasse and Tehran refused to fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz, the oil artery of the global economy, without U.S. recognition of its control over the strategic waterway. Rather than restart large-scale military action, Trump has opted for an increasingly severe economic blockade.
For now, however, that means global oil prices, and particularly fuel costs for American consumers, are likely to remain high. That in turn is increasing domestic political pressure on Trump to end the war, particularly ahead of the U.S. midterm elections in November.
Trump has insisted that he is in no hurry despite that pressure, arguing that Americans should understand the economic cost as a price worth paying to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. Polls, however, show that the war remains deeply unpopular in the United States and that Trump’s approval ratings have fallen to new lows.
So far, only the United Arab Emirates, once a critical hub for Tehran’s sanctions-evasion networks, has formally announced the suspension of trade with Iran.
But many analysts question whether economic pressure, even if other countries join the effort, can force Tehran into a rapid capitulation. Iran is now operating what has been described as a “survival economy,” designed to minimize the effect of sanctions that it has lived under for decades and repeatedly found ways to circumvent.
In line for dollars in Tehran, spending his last savings: ‘There is no hope’
Still, Iran’s economic crisis has worsened considerably following the two most recent wars. According to the International Monetary Fund, inflation in Iran is expected to approach 70% this year. Since the latest war began, the prices of some foods, including meat, have risen by as much as 150%, while the economy as a whole is expected to contract by a massive 5.4%.
Unemployment has surged, with at least 1 million people losing their jobs since the war began in late February.
Iran’s currency, the rial, had already fallen to a record low of 1.9 million to the U.S. dollar at the beginning of the month and continued to slide ahead of Monday’s announcement. On Sunday it crossed the threshold of 2 million to the dollar, and on Monday it reached 2.02 million. The naval blockade is also depriving Iran of oil-export revenues, with some estimates putting the loss at $435 million a day.
New accounts from inside Iran describe mounting frustration among residents struggling to afford basic food. “We have virtually given up on many things,” Ahmad Karimi, a 52-year-old taxi driver and father of two, told the Associated Press. Karimi works 15-hour days to make ends meet.
“We’re cutting out fruit, we’re cutting out protein, we’ve given up leisure, we even work on weekends,” he said.
Karimi said Iran’s leaders would ultimately have to act to ease the hardship facing him and millions of others. In his view, people cannot continue living under those conditions indefinitely and are increasingly focused simply on getting through each day.
Sadegh Mahmoudi, a 73-year-old Tehran resident, was equally pessimistic about the prospects of an agreement that could bring sanctions relief. “There is no hope for a deal and peace,” he told AP as he waited in line to buy U.S. dollars with what remained of his savings.
Although senior officials in Tehran repeatedly say they recognize the seriousness of the crisis and the hardship facing ordinary Iranians, they insist the Islamic Republic will not surrender.
Ahead of the U.S. sanctions announcement, Iranian officials again threatened escalation, including possible attacks on countries that join the U.S.-led economic blockade.
There have so far been no signs of renewed mass protests against the government, against the backdrop of continued harsh repression and warnings that participation in anti-government demonstrations could be treated as an act of treason punishable by death.
At the beginning of the year, tens of thousands of Iranians were killed by regime forces during nationwide mass protests that erupted amid the economic crisis.
Meanwhile, mediators continue trying to prevent another escalation. Pakistan’s Field Marshal Asim Munir made a brief visit to Tehran on Monday, meeting Ghalibaf, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and later President Masoud Pezeshkian.
Munir, who left Tehran within hours, has emerged as a central figure in mediation efforts. A visit he made to Tehran in May helped pave the way for the breakthrough that produced a memorandum of understanding between Washington and Tehran in June, an agreement that later collapsed.
Qatar’s Al Jazeera reported Monday that Trump had spoken with Munir last week about Iran. Citing a source familiar with the matter, it said Trump asked the Pakistani military chief to use Pakistan’s influence to help restart negotiations.

Enes Kanter Freedom and Royce White are not eligible for the WNBA draft, AP source says

Enes Kanter Freedom and Royce White are not eligible for the WNBA draft, AP source says
NEW YORK (AP) — Former NBA players Enes Kanter Freedom and Royce White are not eligible for the WNBA draft, a person familiar with the decision said Monday.
The person spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity because of the sensitive nature of the situation. The person did not elaborate on the reasons for declaring the two men ineligible.
Freedom and White have declared their intention to enter next year’s draft, but the WNBA has not publicly addressed their eligibility.
The WNBA has been the subject of recent debates on whether transgender women — people assigned male at birth who transition to align with their gender identity — should be allowed to participate in the league. There has never been such a player in the WNBA.
Although the league’s collective bargaining agreement says the WNBA is restricted to women, it contains no more specific language about gender identity or sex assigned at birth. When they announced their intention to enter the draft, Freedom and White said they identified as women.
The 6-foot-10, 250-pound Freedom played 11 seasons in the NBA. White played in three NBA games.
Freedom was ejected from Sunday night’s Indiana-Chicago game after he was confronted by Sky guard Natasha Cloud late in the third quarter.
Freedom was sitting along the baseline wearing a black shirt that read “WOMAN noun. adult human female.”
The Fever called for a timeout after Cloud scored inside with 1:22 left in the third. Cloud then did a chest bump with teammate Aicha Coulibaly before turning around and walking in Freedom’s direction.
Cloud, 34, started yelling and pointing at Freedom, 34, as she approached him. A standing Freedom held his arms out and took one step on the court as security and a handful of Sky players moved in between the two.
Freedom stopped near the basket to plead his case to security as he was escorted from the court area. He spun around while holding his shirt out and encouraged the crowd to respond as he walked toward the front lobby.
He had a conversation with a group of police officers before departing Wintrust Arena.
“I just got kicked out of a @WNBA game for supporting WOMEN!” Freedom wrote on social media Sunday night. “Let that sink in, AMERICA!”
Cloud met with team and league security after the game. She did not speak with the media.
Fever guard Sophie Cunningham said in an ESPN profile published last month that she was opposed to transgender girls and women competing in girls’ and women’s sports, and since then the league has been embroiled in debates about transgender participation. Freedom joined a small rally in support of Cunningham outside the arena before the game.

Judge postpones US trial for Libyan man charged in 1988 bombing of Pan Am Flight 103
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
22:23:02 UTC
07:23:02 KST

New evidence prompts trial delay for Libyan man charged in 1988 bombing of Pan Am Flight 103
WASHINGTON (AP) — A federal judge on Monday postponed a trial in the U.S. for a former Libyan intelligence official charged in the 1988 bombing of Pan Am Flight 103, citing the discovery of new evidence that defense attorneys want to examine in the nearly 40-year-old case.
Jury selection was scheduled to begin Wednesday for the federal trial of Abu Agila Mohammad Mas’ud Kheir Al-Marimi in Washington, D.C. His trial will be the first in the U.S. for the Dec. 21, 1988, bombing over Lockerbie, Scotland, which killed 270 people, most of them Americans.
U.S. District Judge Dabney Friedrich’s order didn’t specify the nature of the newly discovered evidence.
Al-Marimi’s lawyers say prosecutors disclosed the new evidence to them on Saturday and added that their “constitutional and ethical obligations require the defense to investigate this development.” Defense attorney Laura Koenig, an assistant federal public defender, declined to elaborate in response to an Associated Press inquiry.
The judge scheduled a Sept. 1 hearing in Washington to discuss the status of the case. Friedrich’s brief order cited the complex nature of the case, the newly discovered evidence and “the need for the defense to determine how best to defend this case” as reasons to postpone the trial.
Al-Marimi is charged in the U.S. with making the bomb that downed the airplane.
Flight 103 was 31,000 feet (9.45 kilometers) over Lockerbie when a bomb in the plane’s forward cargo area exploded 38 minutes after takeoff from London Heathrow Airport. The flight was bound for John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York.
The blast killed all 259 passengers and crew members and 11 people on the ground in Lockerbie, where the wreckage destroyed an entire city block. Citizens of 21 countries were killed, including 190 Americans and 43 from the United Kingdom. The passengers included 35 Syracuse University students returning home from a semester abroad.
Kara Weipz, board president of the nonprofit Victims of Pan Am Flight 103, said her organization had received no details about the new evidence that prompted the trial delay. Weipz’s brother Richard Monetti was among the Syracuse students killed.
She called the delay a shock and noted that some victims’ relatives were already packing to head to the trial.
“At the same time, for almost 38 years we’ve been seeking the truth of what happened,” Weipz said. “If that’s what this is, then that’s a good thing, and this delay is worth it. ... It’s important to hear all the facts.”
Prosecutors allege Al-Marimi and others carried out the bombing at the direction of Libyan leader Moammar Gadhafi, who was ousted and killed during a 2011 civil war.
Two other Libyan intelligence agents were tried by a panel of Scottish judges on a former U.S. military base in the Netherlands in 2000. The tribunal convicted one official and acquitted the other, but the bombmaker’s possible identity remained a mystery for years.
Al-Marimi, now in his mid-70s, is charged with two counts of destruction of an aircraft resulting in death. He faces a maximum penalty of life in prison if convicted.
Al-Marimi worked for the Libyan intelligence service from approximately 1973 to 2011, rising to the rank of colonel, according to prosecutors.
Prosecutors believe he brought a suitcase containing a bomb to an airport in Malta and gave it to co-conspirators for a flight to Frankfurt, Germany. The suitcase traveled from Frankfurt to London, where it was loaded onto Flight 103, according to investigators.
___
Associated Press reporter Gene Johnson in Seattle contributed.

Trump moves toward levying new tariff on China for flooding market with cheap goods, AP sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
22:23:02 UTC
07:23:02 KST

Trump moves toward levying new tariff on China for flooding market with cheap goods, AP sources say
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump is moving toward levying a new tariff on China that would penalize the world’s second-largest economy for flooding the global market with underpriced goods, according to three people familiar with the matter.
Two of the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal deliberations still being finalized, said Trump is considering setting the new tariff at 7.5%. It’s a level administration officials believe would not endanger the one-year trade truce between Washington and Beijing or a planned White House meeting between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping expected to take place in late September.
The move, if finalized, appears to be a calibrated effort by the White House to work around a Supreme Court decision earlier this year that struck down Trump’s plan to implement a sweeping, high-tariff scheme not seen since the 1930s.
After that decision, the Trump administration announced in March it was launching formal investigations targeting excess industrial capacity and forced-labor regulations in China and other nations.
It isn’t clear if the U.S. administration is also nearing its decision in its probes of the other economies that it announced it was investigating for unfair trade practices, including the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Norway, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, South Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Mexico, Japan and India.
The White House and the U.S. Trade Representative’s office did not respond to requests for comment on the tariff deliberations, which Bloomberg News reported earlier Monday.
The Chinese embassy in Washington said in a statement that economic and trade issues should be resolved through bilateral talks rather than unilateral tariff actions, and rejected the idea that it has an issue with overcapacity.
The excess industrial capacity probe of China was initiated under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which allows the president to levy tariffs against nations that discriminate against U.S. companies or commerce.
The new tariff would come on top of existing tariffs on China
The people familiar with the deliberations stressed that Trump could still change his mind on the new tariff on China.
It would come on top of tariffs of 10% to 12.5% announced last month for 60 economies around the globe that the Trump administration accused of failing to effectively enforce a ban on goods produced with forced labor.
Many countries, including China, protested that move, which took effect just as the clock ran out on temporary tariffs Trump had turned to after the Supreme Court in February struck down sweeping “reciprocal” tariffs he levied on nearly every U.S. trade partner.
China last month pushed back against claims of overcapacity, anticipating that the U.S. would soon release results of its probe and impose new tariffs.
Massive capacity in a slew of Chinese industries, from autos to solar panels, cement and steel manufacturing, has drawn increased attention from Beijing’s trading partners in recent years.
Although China’s own leaders have prioritized rebalancing the economy, slowing domestic demand has prompted companies to expand into overseas markets. Surging exports pushed China’s trade surplus to a record of nearly $1.2 trillion last year.
China has never sought a large trade surplus, the Ministry of Commerce said in a recently published report titled “China’s Position on the So-called Excess Capacity Issue.”
The deliberations come as the Treasury Department on Monday warned countries doing trade with Iran that new secondary sanctions are in the pipeline aimed at ostracizing nations that continue to do business with Tehran. China is Iran’s biggest trade partner.
Washington has promised the new sanctions would put even more pressure on an Iranian economy already battered by previous sanctions and a U.S. naval blockade as the U.S. and Israeli war against Iran nears the six-month mark.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s announcement Monday provided little detail and did not name which countries could face secondary sanctions.
___
AP writer Paul Wiseman contributed reporting.

While You Were Sleeping: 5 stories you might have missed, Aug 25, 2026
US vows ‘economic asphyxiation’ of Iran
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Aug 24 laid out plans for the “economic asphyxiation” of Iran, expanding Washington’s secondary sanctions threats and warning of dire consequences for countries that do not join the campaign.
The announcement comes almost six months into a war on Iran that has ground to a stalemate, with stalled peace talks and Tehran blocking most traffic through the crucial Strait of Hormuz.
Bessent earlier said the United States was declaring an “economic D-Day” on Iran, but his announcement named no specific countries beyond Iran and no timelines.
“Around the globe, our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone,” Bessent told a press conference. “We are going to hold everyone accountable, and this is economic asphyxiation of this regime.”
Trump’s approval holds at record low
US public approval of the war with Iran fell to its lowest level since the conflict’s early days, helping to hold President Donald Trump’s popularity at a record low, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll that closed on Aug 24.
The four-day poll showed just 31 per cent of Americans support US military action against Iran, down from 37 per cent in a March Reuters/Ipsos poll and 34 per cent earlier this month.
The decline was driven by fewer self-identified Republicans backing the conflict. Some 69 per cent of Republican respondents support the war, compared with 77 per cent in March.
Netanyahu says Iran ‘tried to kill’ one of his sons
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Aug 24 that Iran had attempted to assassinate one of his two sons, without offering further details.
“Something incredible happened: Iran targeted one of my sons. Iran tried to kill one of my sons,” Netanyahu said, during a phone interview with Israel’s Channel 14.
The claim came during a discussion about reports that the Shin Bet domestic security agency had declined to provide a security detail for Gadi Eisenkot, the former army chief who is running neck and neck with Netanyahu ahead of elections on Oct 27.
S. Korea, US vow close cooperation on North: Seoul
South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio spoke on Aug 24, and Seoul said they agreed to maintain close communication and cooperation on resolving the North Korean nuclear issue, South Korea’s Yonhap news agency reported.
The US State Department issued only a brief statement on the phone call, which comes at a period of tension between the allies.
President Donald Trump recently announced a scaling back of joint military exercises and praised nuclear-armed North Korea, while saying that Seoul had not helped his efforts to try to denuclearise Iran.
Chelsea start Xabi Alonso era with exciting 3-2 win
Chelsea began life under new coach Xabi Alonso with a breathless 3-2 victory at West London neighbours Fulham in the Premier League on Aug 24 as their exciting front three of Joao Pedro, Morgan Rogers and Cole Palmer all found the net.
Chelsea got off to a dream start after 31 seconds when Palmer – looking back to his best after struggling with an injury last season – passed to Joao Pedro and the Brazilian flicked the ball over goalkeeper Bernd Leno.
It was the quickest goal scored in the opening round of fixtures in the 34-year history of the Premier League.

22 million hectares of degraded land restored during 2011 and 2020
Vishwa Mohan / TNN / Updated: Aug 25, 2026, 06:23 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small

India restores nearly 22 million hectares of degraded land, says Bhupender Yadav at UN conference
NEW DELHI: India has restored nearly 22 million hectares of degraded and deforested land during the 2011-20 period as against its target of restoring 26 million hectares by 2030, said Union minister Bhupender Yadav at a UN conference Monday.While addressing the 17th session (COP17) of the UNCCD conference in Ulaanbaatar in Mongolia, he also pitched for "diversified, adequate, predictable and sustained international finance" for land restoration and drought resilience, saying it is not a cost, but an investment in food, water, biodiversity, livelihood and long-term resilience.Underlining how the country's restoration efforts had generated approximately 1.2 billion person-days of employment during the 2011-20 period, he said these figures demonstrated restoration could deliver both environmental and socio-economic outcomes by reviving degraded landscapes while creating employment and supporting rural livelihoods.According to India’s second progress report on its land restoration efforts, covering the period 2011–2020, Telangana restored the maximum (4.2 million hectares) degraded area followed by Madhya Pradesh (3.8 million ha), Odisha (2.6 million ha), Gujarat (1.7 million ha) and Andhra Pradesh (1.6 million ha) through afforestation, water resource management, sustainable farming practices, agroforestry, mangrove restoration and natural regeneration of formerly forested land.
India’s Desertification and Land Degradation Atlas shows that 97.8 million ha of land, or nearly 29.8% of the country’s geographical area, are affected by land degradation and desertification. Around 82% of India’s degraded land falls in nine states/UT - Rajasthan, Maharashtra, Gujarat, Jammu & Kashmir, Karnataka, Jharkhand, Odisha, Madhya Pradesh and Telangana.
Highlighting India’s innovative and diversified financing architecture for land restoration and drought resilience, Yadav noted the ‘Sovereign Green Bonds’ as an avenue to mobilise capital and underlined the country’s ‘Green Credit Programme’, which enables public and private entities to finance restoration of degraded forest land.Though the minister during his address flagged India’s experience demonstrating what the committed domestic resources can achieve, he stressed that this cannot substitute for “additional, adequate and predictable international finance” for restoration and drought resilience.
Vishwa Mohan is Senior Editor at The Times of India. He writes on environment, climate change, agriculture, water resources and clean energy, tracking policy issues and climate diplomacy. He has been covering Parliament since 2003 to see how politics shaped up domestic policy and India’s position at global platform. Before switching over to explore sustainable development issues, Vishwa had covered internal security and investigative agencies for more than a decade.

Hakeem Jeffries, Jared Kushner meeting sparks speculation amid US midterms
Private meeting between Jeffries and Kushner fuels discussions amid contentious US midterm battle.
United States House Democratic Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has met privately with Jared Kushner, US President Trump’s son-in-law and a top outside adviser, in a signal that the White House is seeking ways to work with Democrats if they wrestle majority control from Republicans in the midterm elections.
Little is known about the details of the discussion, which was first reported on Sunday by the New York Times. The newspaper described it as a high-profile meeting with the hope of sparking bipartisan “common ground.”

The meeting reportedly touched on issues ranging from housing and immigration to the cost-of-living crisis. Americans are struggling under inflationary prices that Democrats fault Republicans and Trump for failing to curb.
In a statement reported on Sunday, Jeffries did not mention the private conversation but said the Republican administration needed to drop the GOP’s “my-way-or-the-highway” approach that has thus far “failed the American people”.
“To stop the madness, we have repeatedly made clear that an extremist approach will not work and will be met with forceful opposition”, the New York congressman said. “The question is whether Republicans will join us.”
Kushner also suggested that Jeffries meet with White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles as a follow-up.
The reported meeting comes in the final stretch of the contentious November midterm elections in which Democrats may have a chance to win back the House majority, a highly anticipated development that would elevate Jeffries to the powerful Speaker of the House role. If they win back the seat, Democrats are expected to use their oversight power to aggressively probe the Trump administration, including allegations of self-enrichment by the president and his family.
Jeffries’ office did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.
Congressional Republicans are unhappy about the matter. On Sunday, current House Speaker Mike Johnson dismissed the meeting and denigrated Kushner’s importance, telling Fox News, “I don’t know what that’s about. I know Jared has interest in lots of other things going on.”
Johnson added that Kushner “hedges bets” and is “not really directly involved in the admin, at least in the day-to-day in the White House”.
“I’m telling you what, you better not bet against the House Republicans”, the Louisiana Congressman added, saying that even if the war with Iran was not finished by November, Republicans will still turn up victorious.
The meeting also raised some eyebrows for those who worried that Jeffries was indulging one of Trump’s most corrupt cronies.
Tommy Vietor, previously an aide to former US President Barack Obama and now a co-host of the left-leaning podcast Pod Save America, noted, “Jared Kushner has no actual government job he just uses his family connections to get money from gulf autocrats and fund corrupt deals. The only way [Jeffries] should work with him is with demands for documents and subpoenas.”
Mehdi Hasan, the CEO of Zeteo, echoed Vietor, writing on social media, “The only meeting Hakeem Jeffries should be having with Jared Kushner is to tell him he’ll be subpoenaed by the House for a corruption investigation on day one of Democratic control of the House.” He added, “This is just pathetic stuff from the House Dem leader.”
William Kristol, a former neocon-turned-leading voice in the ‘Never Trump’ movement, posted, “Really? Or, as the kids say, AYFKM?” (The acronym stands for “Are you f****** kidding me?”)
During his time in Congress, Jeffries has remained a fierce critic of Trump’s bellicose foreign policy, repeatedly condemning the administration’s “reckless war of choice” against Iran and for what he called “a failure to adequately prepare for the consequences of launching a war on Iran”.
The meeting shows the depth of Republican Party angst over losing their congressional majority, particularly the House, and the need to make inroads with the opposing party as the White House seeks to stem any potential political fallout on the president.
“The American people want bold change and that’s what House Democrats will deliver”, wrote Jeffries in the statement on Sunday.
The White House did not immediately respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.
Jared Kushner is a familiar messenger between Donald Trump and Democratic politicians
Jeffries and Kushner are not strangers.
The two New Yorkers united during the first Trump administration on landmark legislation to allow sentencing flexibility for certain drug offenses as a way to curtail lengthy terms in the federal prison system.
While not necessarily close, they have maintained a professional working relationship despite the repeated punches Trump has inflicted against Jeffries and the Democratic leader’s rhetoric. In Trump’s second term, Kushner has wielded disproportionate influence within the administration despite holding no official White House title. He serves as a top outside adviser and Special Envoy for Peace, shuttling to foreign diplomatic missions as the US war against Iran inches toward its sixth-month mark.
Just last week, Kushner traveled to the Middle East to convene with Qatari, Turkish and Egyptian mediators before heading to Tel Aviv where he met with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu over the fate of the 15-point Gaza peace plan that Israel had rejected. The trip came after officials from Trump’s newly-created Board of Peace confirmed that Kushner would lead a delegation to break the diplomatic deadlock, via Egypt and Israel.
Trump has only met with Jeffries once since returning to the Oval Office. After the meeting, the president posted AI-generated deepfake content of Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer alongside Jeffries wearing a sombrero with a handlebar mustache. The image was widely viewed as a racist trope and a parody of the Democratic establishment just before what would become the longest federal government shutdown in US history.
Trump has thus far been able to discount Congress as he either relies on the unchecked force of executive power to implement his priorities or the lobbying of Republicans in the House and Senate, when needed, to fall in line behind his unilateral decisions.
That may soon change if Democrats control either the House or the Senate, or both, with lawmakers increasingly keen on flexing their own power in Congress as a coequal branch of government more willing to hold the White House in check.

A tornado tore through the southwestern French village of Pomas on Monday, injuring 41 people and damaging about 300 homes, authorities said. A tornado tore through a village in southwestern France on Monday, injuring 41 people and damaging hundreds of homes, authorities said.
French authorities had placed swathes of the country's southwest on orange alert for storms, and numerous areas were hit by power outages and transport chaos.
In the Aude department, officials cancelled the third stage of the Vuelta a Espana cycling race, which was being held in the area, when a hailstorm forced riders to seek shelter.
The tornado hit hardest in the village of Pomas – which has a population 1,000 – damaging an estimated 300 homes and in some cases ripping their roofs off.

Venice adds Gaza documentary by Oscar-winning team to main competition
A documentary examining Israel's killing of civilians in Gaza was added to the Venice Film Festival line-up on Monday, the second year running that a work about the conflict has competed for the prestigious Golden Lion.
Festival organisers said "NAZA", directed by the Israeli duo Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, will join the main programme for the September 2 to 12 event — the only documentary among this year's 21 contenders.
Last year, "The Voice of Hind Rajab", which tells the harrowing story of the brutal murder by Israeli forces of a five-year-old Gazan girl trapped in a car, won second prize at Venice after earning a record 23-minute standing ovation at its premiere.
According to a synopsis released by the festival, "NAZA" was shot at night on the rooftops of Tel Aviv and "reveals in detail the systems behind Israel's calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza".
Palestinian health authorities say more than 73,000 people were killed in Gaza after Israel launched its genocidal war against the coastal enclave in October 2023.
Abraham and Szor were two of the four co-directors of "No Other Land", which won the Academy Award for best documentary feature in 2025. The film chronicled the destruction of a Palestinian community in the Israeli-occupied West Bank and the relentless expansion of Jewish settlements.
"NAZA" was produced by Britain's Guardian newspaper and James Wilson, and executive produced by Jonathan Glazer, the Oscar-winning director of the 2023 Holocaust drama "The Zone of Interest".
Wilson and Glazer were also producer and executive producer respectively on "The Voice of Hind Rajab". Israeli authorities last week opened a criminal investigation into the girl's death.
"NAZA" will premiere in Venice on September 10. The film joins a high-profile field that includes new works from Martin McDonagh, Florian Zeller, Danny Boyle, Werner Herzog and Hirokazu Kore-eda.
(Reuters)

How China’s anti-corruption fight became Xi Jinping’s most important policy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
22:00:07 UTC

Advertisement
In FocusHow China’s anti-corruption fight became Xi Jinping’s most important policy
Far from a temporary crackdown, the campaign has proved to be a key tool for enforcing party discipline and driving economic strategy
7-MIN READ7-MIN
5
 Listen
Phoebe Zhangin Shenzhen
The South China Morning Post has launched a major data project diving into President Xi Jinping’s signature anti-graft campaign. In the first part of a series accompanying the data project, Phoebe Zhang looks at how the campaign became one of the Communist Party’s most important policies.
In the early years of President Xi Jinping’s first term, when graft fighters were taking down senior officials in ways that raised eyebrows, Chinese authorities constantly had to remind the public that the anti-corruption campaign was not “just a gust of wind”.
At that point, Beijing had already locked up dozens of senior officials, including Zhou Yongkang, a former member of the Communist Party’s Politburo Standing Committee, the highest echelon in China’s political hierarchy. Before his downfall in 2013, Zhou had been one of China’s most influential politicians.
Concerns were so widespread that the anti-corruption push would be a flash in the pan, especially at the local level, that Wang Qishan, then the party’s top anti-corruption chief, warned that local governments might fall back on temporary “movement-style” crackdowns.
A decade later, few need convincing as the anti-corruption fight expands, netting record numbers of senior officials and unearthing new types of graft involving cryptocurrency schemes and clandestine proxies.
A new analysis by the South China Morning Post found that the campaign has widened since its inception. Last year, anti-corruption agencies handed down punishments to 983,000 people, with the fallout ranging from mild warnings to investigations and criminal prosecution. The number of senior officials taken down last year was three times that of 2013.
The SCMP’s data bank project also found that from 2013 to 2025, 60 per cent of senior officials felled by China’s anti-corruption drive were serving in regional governments. The campaign has hit provincial administrations particularly hard, with resource-rich areas – notably Jiangxi, Liaoning, Shanxi and Hebei provinces, as well as Inner Mongolia, autonomous region – recording the highest number of dismissals.

Shame and fear of false accusations deter male victims of intimate partner violence from seeking help
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
22:00:05 UTC
07:00:05 KST

Men who experience abuse by a female partner encounter a range of shared obstacles when trying to seek help, but the specific challenges they face often vary depending on their racial and ethnic backgrounds. New research details how concerns like shame, fear of false accusations, and institutional bias shape the decisions of Black, Latino, and White men who have been victimized. The findings were published in Psychology of Men & Masculinities.
Intimate partner violence affects people across all demographics. A survey covered by PsyPost in 2024 indicated that a large majority of men have experienced at least one instance of sexual victimization by a woman. Despite high rates of abuse, men who are victimized are much less likely to ask for support than women.
When they do look for help, they often find themselves alienated in systems that were designed primarily with female victims in mind. These institutional structures can reinforce the idea that male victimization is rare, leaving men without tailored resources.
Earlier research identified the common hurdles that prevent male victims of abuse from seeking help. A 2019 study showed that male victims frequently avoid reporting abuse because they fear society will not believe them or will instead view them as the actual aggressor. That same year, a systematic review confirmed the widespread difficulties and stigma men face when trying to find support for domestic abuse.
Adding to this context, a study covered by PsyPost in 2025 found that societal sexism often leads people to outright deny or minimize the fact that men can be victims of relationship violence. These roadblocks can leave men trapped in abusive situations.
Most of the previous research on this topic focused on predominantly White samples or lumped all men together without looking at racial differences. This dynamic led a research team to investigate how these barriers might differ among specific groups.
The research, led by Lyric N. Russo of George Mason University, involved 1,194 men in the United States between the ages of 18 and 59. The participants were recruited through an online survey platform and were roughly divided into three groups: 596 Latino men, 299 non-Latino Black men, and 299 non-Latino White men.
To participate, all the men had to report having experienced aggressive, controlling, or coercive behavior from a female romantic partner at some point in their lives. The sample represented men who had endured high rates of abuse. Almost all the participants (95.8%) reported being subjected to coercive control, such as a partner keeping them from seeing friends and family, and 84.6% reported experiencing physical abuse.
The men answered questions from a 17-item scale designed to identify specific reasons why they might not have asked for help. The survey also included an open-ended question allowing the participants to describe their unique obstacles in their own words.
Across all three groups, the men reported similar core obstacles. Over half of the total sample (55.7%) viewed the abuse as a private or personal matter, making it the most common reason for not seeking help. Nearly half of the participants reported feeling shame or embarrassment (49.2%).
Similar numbers expressed concerns that their partner would falsely accuse them or seek revenge (47.8%), that they would be blamed (47.5%), or that they simply did not know how to tell anyone (47.3%). Nearly 40 percent doubted whether resources could actually help them.
The pattern of obstacles shifted when looking at specific racial and ethnic groups. Latino men reported a higher total number of barriers on average than Black men. They were more likely than both Black and White men to report that they did not know how to disclose their experiences.
They also expressed more concern about bringing shame or dishonor to their families. Compared to White men, Latino men were more likely to cite language difficulties, concerns about revealing their immigration status, and a fear that their partner was actively preventing them from seeking help.
Black men in the study were less likely than both Latino and White men to worry that others would not believe them or would be biased against them. The authors note that this finding requires context to be properly understood. Rather than feeling confident that they would be supported, the lower concern about bias might reflect societal stereotypes about Black women.
Because 73.2% of the Black men in the study reported that their abusive partner was a Black woman, racialized gender stereotypes portraying Black women as aggressive might cause society to find the men’s reports of abuse more believable, even if institutional support remains inadequate.
White men reported their own distinct challenges. Based on the open-ended responses, White men were more likely than Latino men to express difficulty recognizing or labeling their experiences as abuse. Traditional gender norms that emphasize toughness and self-reliance can make it hard for men to realize that a partner’s behavior is actually abusive, leading them to interpret the harmful actions as normal relationship conflict rather than mistreatment.
The study relied on a specific sample of men recruited through an online panel, meaning the results might not represent all men in these demographic groups. Men without internet access or those less comfortable sharing personal experiences online were likely not included. The research also captured a snapshot in time rather than tracking the men over a longer period. This approach makes it impossible to determine how barriers to seeking help might change as a relationship progresses or as a person’s life circumstances shift.
The data comes entirely from self-reported surveys, which can be influenced by a person’s willingness to disclose sensitive information. The study focused exclusively on men abused by female partners. Men who experience abuse from male or nonbinary partners might encounter a different set of obstacles, shaped by different social stigmas and available resources. Future research could explore how different types of relationships and community contexts alter a person’s ability to access support services.
The study, “Barriers to Help-Seeking Among Male Victims of Female-Perpetrated Intimate Partner Violence: Insights From Black, Latino, and White Men,” was authored by Lyric N. Russo, Denise A. Hines, Jennifer L. Mezzapelle, Chiara Sabina, Kerry A. Lee, and Emily M. Douglas.

Air Force ‘Closely Following’ Navy’s New Long-Range Air-to-Air ‘Malice’ Missile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
21:57:01 UTC
06:57:01 KST

A new Navy missile could fill a long-range air-to-air need for the U.S. Air Force’s fourth-, fifth-, and sixth-generation fighters.
The Navy’s portfolio acquisition executive for munitions posted information on the AIM-424 Long Range Air-to-Air Missile online on Aug. 22, the same day it unveiled the project at the service’s annual Tailhook Symposium in Reno, Nev.
The Raytheon missile is geared for Marine and Naval aviators’ fighter platforms, from the Boeing F/A-18 Super Hornet to the Lockheed Martin F-35 Lightning II, with a range “in excess of 250 nautical miles.”
“Also known as Malice, the LRAAM directly supports the Department’s contribution to integrated deterrence by increasing range, lethality, and combat effectiveness for Marine and Naval Aviation forces that are defending our fleets, our interests, and our homeland,” according to a Navy statement emailed to media. “Further details regarding specific capabilities and deployment timelines remain classified to protect operational security.”
Malice’s advertised range is well more than that of the Lockheed Martin AIM-260 Joint Advanced Tactical Missile, said to be beyond 120 miles, and the Raytheon AIM-120D Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missile, around 100 nautical miles. The Air Force is taking the lead in developing JATM for itself and the Navy.
“With increased range, lethality, and combat effectiveness for naval forces, the AIM-424 delivers a generational leap in long range air-to-air combat capability that can out range any threat,” Phil Jasper, president of Raytheon, said in an email statement.
Malice Data
- Contractor: Raytheon
- Propulsion: Solid-propellant rocket motor
- Length: 13.5 feet
- Diameter: 13.5 inches
- Wingspan: 26.2 inches
- Weight: 1,500 pounds
- Range: In excess of 250 nm
- Warhead: Blast fragmentation
Source: Navy
But while Malice represents a major increase in range over current missile programs, it falls short more ambitious efforts early in development like the Air Force Long Range Weapon, which seeks distances of more than 1,000 nautical miles. The Air Force first revealed plans for the AFLRW in June.
“The Air Force is closely following the progress of the Navy on the AIM-424 Long Range Air-to-Air Missile Program,” an Air Force spokesperson told Air & Space Forces Magazine on Aug. 24. The spokesperson declined to answer additional questions.
The two services often partner on missiles for their aircraft, such as JATM, AMRAAM, and the AIM-9X Sidewinder.
“The Navy and Air Force have different operational requirements, but in areas such as fighter-launched offensive weapons, each can benefit from the other’s technological advances, testing, and development,” said retired Air Force Col. John “JV” Venable, senior resident fellow at the Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies. “Malice appears to be another example of how parallel efforts can accelerate capability and produce benefits across the Joint Force.”
The Navy has also developed the AIM-174B Gunslinger, which has a range of 150-200 nautical miles, but that missile won’t fit in the internal weapon bays of the F-35 and F-22, limiting its usefulness to the Air Force.
The new Malice missile, on the other hand, is meant to go a wide range of aircraft, including sixth-gen fighters like the Navy’s not-yet-named F/A-XX and the Air Force’s parallel project, the Boeing F-47.
“The long-range missile fight is much like a jousting contest: the fighter with the longer lance has a major advantage,” said Venable, a former F-16 pilot and commander. “Chinese beyond-visual-range missiles are assessed to outrange many current U.S. weapons, potentially giving Chinese fighters the opportunity to shoot first by dozens of miles.”
The Malice missile would “extend U.S. engagement range, improve first-shot opportunities, and help restore our tactical advantage against peer adversaries,” he said.
Beyond the tactical level, Venable noted, having a missile like Malice in the fighter community’s quiver would give commanders greater flexibility in operational planning and offset numerical disparity with a potential peer fight.
“The People’s Liberation Army Air Force (PLAAF) already holds a significant advantage in the numbers of fighters it can generate over Taiwan compared with the U.S. and allied forces,” he said. “We need every technological advantage available to offset that numerical disparity.
Roots
Aviation Week reported that Malice has a two-stage design—reminiscent of a decade-old program known as the Long Range Engagement Weapon, developed in the mid-2010s under then-Secretary of Defense Ash Carter.
Flight Global reported at the time the LREW effort was also a two-stage design that would eventually transition to multiple services. The Air Force was known to be working on the weapon while also developing the JATM – both efforts sought to replace the decades-old AMRAAM, which debuted in the mid-1980s.
The JATM is seen as a direct replacement for fighters to carry instead of the AMRAAM. But the LREW’s two-stage design promised a far greater range.

Minimum wage in Slovakia to rise to 972 euros per month in 2027
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
05:56:12 CST
06:56:12 KST

BRATISLAVA, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- Slovakia's minimum wage will rise to 972 euros (1133.5 U.S. dollars) per month in 2027, up from 915 euros (1067.1 U.S. dollars) in 2026, Slovak Labour, Social Affairs and Family Minister Erik Tomas announced on Monday following a meeting of the tripartite council.
"The minimum wage next year will be 972 euros (1133.5 U.S. dollars), bringing it closer to the symbolic threshold of 1,000 euros (1166.2 U.S. dollars)," Tomas said. The minister also presented a qualified estimate for the minimum wage in 2028, when it is expected to exceed 1,000 euros (1166.2 U.S. dollars) per month and could reach 1,016 euros (1184.8 U.S. dollars). Extra payments for night and weekend work will also increase, as they are linked to the minimum wage.
The minimum wage in Slovakia is regulated under Act No. 663/2007 Coll. It is set annually for the following calendar year and applies as a monthly and hourly amount. Under the law, the minimum wage is set at 60 percent of the average nominal salary from two years earlier. According to Slovak Statistics Office, the average nominal salary in 2025 stood at 1,620 euros (1889.2 U.S. dollars).
Tomas added that approximately 120,000 employees are paid the basic minimum wage in 2026. If all six minimum-wage levels based on job difficulty are taken into account, the measure will affect approximately 160,000 people in 2026, some 6 percent of the country's labor force. ■

U.S. Homeland Security proposes H-1B fee exceeding 100,000 USD on new grounds
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
05:56:03 CST
06:56:03 KST

WASHINGTON, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- The U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) on Monday proposed a 103,265-U.S.-dollar fee for H-1B cap-subject petitions, marking the agency's newest move to restrict the visa program on new grounds.
The move came after previous efforts to charge 100,000 dollars for the visa were struck down by the courts.
"The proposed fee would generate revenue to recover a portion of the federal government's costs for administering the lawful immigration system," the DHS said in a news release.
The new fee is designed to recover a portion of the full costs of providing immigration adjudication and naturalization services incurred by multiple federal agencies in processing, adjudicating, and supporting the lawful immigration system, according to a document scheduled to be published in the Federal Register on Tuesday.
The DHS estimates the proposed fee would generate approximately 8.8 billion dollars annually, based on a projected annual volume of 85,000 H-1B cap-subject petitions, according to the release.
Under the proposed rule, the additional fee would not apply to H-1B petitions that are not subject to the cap, such as petitions filed by certain nonprofit research organizations, governmental research organizations, and institutions of higher education, the release added.
The public will be given a 30-day period to submit comments on the proposed rule before it can take effect.
"If finalized, the new proposal would place a significant new burden on the technology and finance sectors, which rely on the H-1B visa to hire top international graduates from U.S. universities," The Wall Street Journal reported. ■

Ceasefire verification team deployed in eastern DR Congo amid continued fighting

GOMA, DR Congo, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- A team tasked with verifying ceasefire violations between the government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and the rebel March 23 Movement (M23) arrived Monday in Minembwe in the eastern province of South Kivu, as fighting continued in several parts of the region.
The team arrived aboard two helicopters of the United Nations Organization Stabilization Mission in the DRC (MONUSCO). It includes military experts from member states of the International Conference on the Great Lakes Region (ICGLR), as well as representatives of the DRC government and the M23, with support from MONUSCO.
The mission marks the first field operation of the ceasefire verification mechanism and is tasked with documenting and reporting possible violations of the truce.
Its deployment came two days after the DRC government and the M23 announced that they had agreed on a roadmap for a peace initiative.
In a joint statement issued Saturday, the two sides welcomed progress in operationalizing an expanded joint verification mechanism, whose first ceasefire verification mission was scheduled for Aug. 24 in Minembwe.
Tensions, however, remain high on the ground in South Kivu. In recent weeks, clashes have continued between the M23 and government forces and their allies in several areas around Minembwe.
On Monday, the DRC government issued a statement accusing the M23 of serious human rights violations in areas under its control. According to the statement, more than 300 people were killed in summary executions, massacres and bombings in June and July.
Since January 2025, the M23 has intensified offensives in the eastern provinces of North Kivu and South Kivu.
Under Qatar's mediation, the DRC government and the M23 signed a declaration of principles in Doha in July and a framework agreement in November 2025, committing themselves to continued negotiations toward a comprehensive peace settlement. ■

WASHINGTON, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- The U.S. Department of State on Monday removed Syria from its list of State Sponsors of Terrorism, according to a notice from the U.S. Treasury Department.
The department also revoked the designation of Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), a former al-Qaida-linked rebel group that played a dominant role in the formation of Syria's new government, as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist organization. The Treasury Department concurrently removed HTS from its sanctions blacklist.
The Trump administration announced plans earlier this year to further ease restrictions on Syria. The decision to remove Syria from the terrorism list was subject to a congressional review period.
Syria had been designated a State Sponsor of Terrorism by Washington since 1979. The designation imposed restrictions on U.S. foreign assistance, defense exports and certain financial transactions.
The Trump administration ended the broad U.S. sanctions program on Syria in July 2025, while retaining sanctions on former President Bashar al-Assad and his associates. ■

Canadian politicians sharpen tone over U.S. tariffs
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
05:55:45 CST
06:55:45 KST

OTTAWA, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- Canadian political leaders stepped up their rhetoric on Monday in response to the latest U.S. tariff threats.
Speaking in Quebec, Prime Minister Mark Carney said Ottawa would be willing to talk if Washington changed tack. "When the Americans go to the negotiating table first, with the right attitude toward our industries and in a true partnership, of course we'll come to the negotiating table," he said.
Carney added that he would not accept the attitude that "Canada is a subsidiary of the United States," or that the country should be disadvantaged relative to the United States.
Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne urged a firm stance during consultations in Montreal. "At some point you have to say enough is enough," Champagne said, indicating that federal support is on the way for businesses hit by 50 percent tariffs.
Champagne emphasized ongoing work to build a resilient economy, stating, "Plan A has always been to build a strong Canadian economy, to remove interprovincial trade barriers, to diversify our economy and to do big things in our country."
Former prime minister Jean Chretien urged Ottawa to hit back with export taxes on critical commodities such as energy, oil, natural gas, and potash. "If we want to stay upright, we have to hit where it hurts," Chretien said. "That's where we should tax. The advantage of an export tax is it's not us who pays, it's the Americans."
Ontario Premier Doug Ford also took an assertive stance, calling for all available countermeasures to be deployed. Ford warned that Canada must be ready to cut off electricity and critical mineral exports to the United States if trade relations worsen.
"I'll cut them off," Ford said regarding mineral shipments. "You won't get a grain of sand out of Ontario."
The 50-percent U.S. tariffs on 20 billion U.S. dollars' worth of Canadian goods took effect just after midnight Saturday, after extended trade negotiations between the two countries collapsed. Carney earlier said retaliatory tariffs would take effect starting Sept. 8. ■

Botswana, Chinese-invested mining firm partner to establish technical training center
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
05:55:36 CST
06:55:36 KST

Botswana's Minister of Higher Education Prince Maele speaks at an event to sign a collaboration agreement in Gaborone, Botswana, Aug. 24, 2026. Botswana's Ministry of Higher Education and the China-invested Khoemacau Copper Mining company on Monday signed a collaboration agreement to establish a Mining Center of Excellence at Maun Technical College in North West District of the southern African country, to train technical workers for the local mining sector. (Photo by Tshekiso Tebalo/Xinhua)
GABORONE, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- Botswana's Ministry of Higher Education and the China-invested Khoemacau Copper Mining company on Monday signed a collaboration agreement to establish a Mining Center of Excellence at Maun Technical College in North West District of the southern African country, to train technical workers for the local mining sector.
Speaking at the event held in Gaborone, the capital of Botswana, Minister of Higher Education Prince Maele said the partnership shows "a new way of thinking about skill development, technical education, relationship of education and industry," to fill the industry skill gap.
The agreement is meant to produce graduates who are "skilled, employable, innovative, adaptable and globally competitive," bringing the classroom closer to the workplace so that "theory must meet practice," and knowledge translates into productivity, said Maele.
He said the goal is for young people to leave school ready to work, cultivating not just job seekers but problem-solvers and entrepreneurs equipped to enter the workforce with practical, industry-relevant skills. He noted that he is "looking forward to a productive, enduring, and mutually beneficial relationship" with the project.
Chen Dexin, chairman of China Minmetals Corporation, parent company of Khoemacau Copper Mining company's investor MMG, termed the mine project as a bridge of friendship between China and Botswana, and pledged the corporation's long-term commitment to the country's socio-economic development.
The mining center of excellence aims to build local capacity through world-class training and produce a substantial pool of skilled workers, he added, describing its purpose as extending far more than running training courses to include lasting community and regional benefit.
Minister of International Affairs Phenyo Butale said the country's relationship with China has evolved beyond financial assistance toward skills transfer, which is successful in China's development. He described the center as a step toward building a pipeline of Batswana technicians and engineers who will eventually lead, not just work in, the mining sector.
Minister of Minerals and Energy Bogolo Kenewendo said the government is focused on making work-based learning standard and letting industry help shape curricula, pointing to the Kalahari Copper Belt and other base-metal deposits as key to diversifying an economy long dominated by diamonds.
Botswana's Minister of Labor and Home Affairs Pius Mokgware and Chinese Ambassador to Botswana Fan Yong also attended the event, which featured traditional music and song performance of Botswana. ■

Feature: Polish farmers find cheer in harvest despite tough growing season
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
05:55:27 CST
06:55:27 KST

by Yue Yuanyuan, Guo Shuang
WARSAW, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- Folk music filled the air as people in traditional costumes danced, local residents sold agricultural products and handicrafts, and families wandered among stalls at a harvest festival in Warsaw over the weekend.
The festival is one of Poland's long-standing rural traditions, held after the main fieldwork and harvests are completed.
Traditionally, farmers give thanks for the crops they have gathered and celebrate the end of months of work in the fields.
Yet behind this year's festive atmosphere lies a difficult growing season marked by sharp weather swings.
Poland experienced unfavorable weather conditions for agriculture this year, according to Statistics Poland.
In its preliminary estimate released in late July, the agency put production of basic cereals and cereal mixtures at 25.3 million tonnes this year, down about 4.9 percent from 2025.
Rapeseed production was projected to fall 14.4 percent, while fruit harvested from trees was expected to decline by 18.6 percent and output from fruit bushes and berry plantations by 6.5 percent.
The Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development has said frosts in April caused temperatures near the ground to fall as low as minus 10 degrees Celsius in some areas, damaging sour and sweet cherries, raspberries and currants.
Drought added another layer of pressure.
Poland's agricultural drought monitoring system found drought conditions affecting a wide range of crops between March and July, including cereals, rapeseed, fruit bushes and maize.
Stanislaw and Barbara Wojcik, an elderly farming couple who grow wheat and rye and sell homemade bread at the festival, said "We harvested less wheat and rye than last year. There was too little rain at some stages, and the heat also affected the crops."
The picture emerging from the harvest festival, however, was not entirely bleak.
Alexander Sobolev, who sells bottled freshly pressed fruit juice and has lived in Poland for four years, said "apples are expected to be very good, and there were a lot of strawberries."
For beekeeper Krzysztof Tomkielski, the changing weather brought more gains than losses. Sunny weather was particularly favorable for buckwheat honey. "There was more honey than last year," he said.
The sector's resilience is also supported by government measures. Poland has 2.4 million bee colonies, the second-largest number in the European Union after Spain, and nearly 100,000 active beekeepers, according to the Polish government.
Funding for this year's beekeeping support programs has been increased by 20 million zlotys (about 5.4 million U.S. dollars).
The harvest may have been uneven, but the difficulties of the growing season did little to dampen the festive spirit. Music played, children watched folk performances, and farmers stood behind their stalls smiling and talking with visitors.
"It is not only about having a very good harvest," said Sobolev. "People come here to be thankful for what they have and celebrate the work of the whole season." ■

U.S. threatens "economic D-Day" sanctions on Iran
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25

This photo taken on Aug. 24, 2026 shows the U.S. Department of the Treasury in Washington, D.C., the United States. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday threatened Iran with "an economic D-Day," announcing a wave of new sanctions aimed at further isolating the country. (Xinhua/Li Rui)
NEW YORK, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday threatened Iran with "an economic D-Day," announcing a wave of new sanctions aimed at further isolating the country.
"We are launching an economic onslaught against Iran's financial connections around the globe," said Bessent at a press conference. "Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline" that sustains the country, he said.
The U.S. Treasury Department said in a press release that the new sectoral sanctions determinations target five critical sectors -- digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping -- that the U.S. says Iran has relied on to prop up its economy.
The measures marked the beginning of "a sustained and systematic campaign to close every financial resource" that supports Iran, the department said. It added that "any entity that facilitates money laundering or sanctions evasion on behalf of Iran risks being cut off from the U.S. financial system."
The department is expanding the categories of "Iran-related conduct" that the United States might sanction in the future, and said "every country will be given a defined timeline to shut down the Iran-related activity" the United States has identified.
Bessent disclosed that U.S. President Donald Trump has been calling world leaders with specific requests to cease their interactions with Iran.
Simultaneously, the department's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) sanctioned nearly 60 entities, individuals, and vessels in multiple jurisdictions that enable Iran's activities, including illicit nuclear and missile technology procurement, cyber operations, and oil-revenue generation networks.
OFAC also suspended several general licenses that previously authorized certain remittance payments to Iran and Iranian access to the U.S. cultural and academic system.
Additionally, the Treasury Department released additional guidance on the sanctions risks associated with complying with Iranian demands regarding shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.
In a post on X, Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf responded to U.S. economic threats against Tehran by saying that, "Iran's trading partners, both in the media and through messages sent to us, have made it clear that they don't take these statements into account anywhere."
"They cannot cut off our financial lifelines," Iran's Minister of Economic Affairs and Finance Seyed Ali Madanizadeh said in another X post, adding that Tehran has been "planning for some time to counter the sanctions." ■

US set for largest mass visa revocation, targeting up to 200,000 foreigners
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
21:53:42 UTC
06:53:42 KST

US targets up to 200,000 foreigners in largest-ever mass visa revocation
State Department prepares mass revocation of tourist and business visas for foreigners seeking asylum
The Trump administration is preparing to revoke the business and tourism visas of up to 200,000 foreigners who have applied for or are currently seeking asylum status in the United States. If it happens, the move would be the largest single mass revocation of visas in US history and would likely face legal challenges.
Unless challenged or revised, the State Department was expected to announce in the coming weeks the revocation of so-called B1 and B2 visas issued between 2016 and 2026 whose holders have sought asylum or are now seeking asylum, according to State Department documents obtained by Associated Press and two US officials. The action would be taken in coordination with the Department of Homeland Security.
“We are coordinating with DHS to identify and revoke the nonimmigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the United States claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently,” said State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott.
He declined to comment on the number of visas that might be revoked, saying “as the process will be ongoing, the number of revocations remains dynamic and will be done on a rolling basis”.
The revocations would not necessarily result in their immediate deportation, the officials said. Most of those with asylum cases currently pending would be recategorised but would lose their status as business or tourism travellers, according to the officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity because the revocations are not final yet.
Since US President Donald Trump took office for his second term last year, his administration has steadily ramped up restrictions on visa applicants — demanding more information about their social media histories, requiring the posting of expensive bonds for the processing of visas, and outright banning the issuance of visas to citizens of certain countries.
