Locals concerned as Trump admin fast-tracks public process for Wyoming rare earth mine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
21:53:02 UTC
06:53:02 KST

Locals concerned as Trump admin fast-tracks public process for Wyoming rare earth mine
The U.S. Forest Service in July began a 30-day public comment period on its plan to review a rare-earth element mining project in northeast Wyoming — the only opportunity for the public to weigh in on the federal process that is being fast-tracked by the Trump administration.
Colorado-based Rare Earth Resources plans to construct an open-pit mine at Bull Hill in the Black Hills National Forest 12 miles northwest of Sundance and about 22 miles from Devils Tower. Raw materials from the mine will be trucked to its “demonstration” processing plant near Upton.
People with concerns about the mine’s implications for health, wildlife, exemptions to the Black Hills Forest management plan, air and water quality have until Friday to submit comments.
Thirty days is precious little time to absorb a complex mining proposal and environmental review documents, Sundance resident Justin Johnson told WyoFile. He’s lived in the area for more than a decade, and the project’s fast-track nature came as a surprise.
“It was kind of hush-hush, in my opinion, as far as not much word about it around Sundance,” Johnson said. “All of a sudden, in July when it came to our attention, it’s like, ‘Holy cow. We got little time before the federal deadline to get our comments and concerns to the Forest Service.’”
Crook County Commissioner John Davis acknowledged that locals are caught off guard with the expedited process.
“We’re in favor of the project, and we hope it goes forward,” Davis told WyoFile. “We’ve got a lot of questions and a few concerns ourselves that we’re hoping get squared away, too.”
The commission is hosting a special meeting at 4 p.m. at the courthouse in Sundance to pose questions to staff from the Wyoming Department of Environmental Quality and the Wyoming State Geological Survey.
Rare Element Resources’ Bear Lodge Rare Earth Project is among more than 50 projects in queue for fast-track federal permitting under FAST-41 coverage — one tool the Trump administration is using to address what it describes as a national security priority to increase domestic production and curb U.S. reliance on China for rare-earth elements, or “critical minerals.” The metals are increasingly in demand as building blocks for everything from magnets to batteries in devices like cell phones and MRI machines. They’re also frequently used in military equipment such as radars and jet engines.
Last year, President Donald Trump issued the Immediate Measures to Increase American Mineral Production executive order while invoking the Defense Production Act to fast-track permitting and help finance mining and processing efforts.
Rare Element Resources touts “one of the highest-grade deposits for the critical magnet (rare earth elements) neodymium and praseodymium, as well as samarium and terbium,” according to the company’s website. “These elements are expected to see the largest demand growth and price support over the next 10 years due to their importance in permanent magnets used in defense systems, transportation, advanced energy and other high-tech applications.”
Regardless of the demand for rare-earth elements, there’s no excuse to rush a mining project that involves public natural resources, said Rachael Hamby, policy director for the Colorado-based conservation and advocacy organization Center for Western Priorities. Especially for hard-rock mining in a national forest.
“They (federal officials) know that their actions on national public lands, and related to our natural resources, are deeply unpopular with the public,” Hamby told WyoFile. “That’s why we see them trying anything they can to avoid and minimize taking public comment, because they know it’s not going to go their way.”
The company, meanwhile, says there will be additional opportunities for public participation — via other federal and state entities — later in the process.
Bear Lodge project
Rare Element Resources is headquartered in Firestone, Colo. General Atomics, a U.S. defense contractor, is a majority shareholder in the company, and its affiliates play a key role in the refining technologies that will be used to process critical minerals from the Bear Lodge mine.
The company has invested about $180 million in the project, it says, and could spend up to $250 million. The mine would support a combined 110 permanent jobs and contribute more than $75 million in state taxes over its 17-year operational life, it says.
The jobs and economic benefits of the processing plant in nearby Upton are less clear. However, Rare Element Resources received a $4.4 million Energy Matching Funds grant from the Wyoming Energy Authority in 2022 and $24.2 million in federal funding — both to support the processing facility in Upton. The plant is essentially built, but the company and its affiliates are still working out kinks to conduct full operational testing.
Rare Element Resources submitted its draft Bull Hill mine operations plan to federal officials in July as part of the federal permitting review. One of the key questions before the Forest Service is whether to “authorize deviation from existing visual standards and guidelines in the Black Hills Forest Plan,” according to the agency’s “notice of intent” published in the Federal Register.
In addition to the open-pit, the company proposes to build access roads, a power line and support infrastructure — some of which would be located on adjacent private land.
As with any proposed mining activity, locals have voiced concerns and posed questions about potential impacts to water and air quality, as well as what some feel is a rushed federal permitting process. The Bull Hill area is also a popular place for locals to hike before and after work, Johnson said.
“Where this mine is, the drainage basically goes through Cook Lake before it heads out of there,” Johnson said. “It’s at the headwaters of a lot of creeks that leave the Bear Lodge (area) and head somewhere.”
Fast-tracked
The FAST-41, or Fixing America’s Surface Transportation Act, was established under the Obama administration in 2015. Originally intended to increase transparency and expedite permitting for transportation infrastructure projects among multiple federal agencies, the program was expanded under the Biden and Trump administrations. President Trump, in his second term, has directed federal agencies to use the program to expedite mining projects, including for rare-earth minerals.
Though the Forest Service will conduct an “environmental impact statement” review, it “will not publish a draft environmental impact statement or conduct an objections process,” according to the agency’s notice in the Federal Register. That’s a major departure from public engagement typically required under the National Environmental Policy Act.
“As originally intended, the FAST-41 program is supposed to be about transparency in permitting,” Hamby said. “What I think we have seen a little bit more of is the Trump administration trying to treat it as a fast-track (tool), and that is certainly how the general public perceives it, and they don’t like that.
“People don’t like when things are rushed through,” Hamby added, “when they don’t feel heard or listened to, and they don’t have an opportunity to weigh in.”
Johnson confirmed that assertion.
“You would think there’d be a lot more time for the actual owners of public land — the citizens of the U.S. — to have a response to what’s going on,” Johnson said.
Despite the short public comment period, local and state governments will have additional opportunities to weigh in on the federal permitting process, according to Rare Element Resources.
“State and local agencies (and other federal agencies) are all part of the NEPA process (as cooperators and participating agencies), and do have inputs to the process post Aug. 28, for sure, through the EIS progression,” Rare Element Resources Vice President and General Counsel Kelli Kast told WyoFile via email.
State agencies — primarily the Wyoming Department of Environmental Quality — will also have a role in shaping the project’s regulatory parameters, she said. But, she added, the company “has not yet made applications for those permits and licenses, as we’re in the pre-application phase.”
Johnson said he and his neighbors are not against mining. “Mining for Wyoming is huge. I mean, a lot of towns in Crook County would not survive if the coal mines were not in operation.”
But, he said, hard-rock mining for rare-earth minerals in a national forest — that’s a new aspect that he and others have a lot of questions about, and they deserve to be more engaged in the process.
“We would actually like them to say, ’Yeah, we would like to extend the period of review, so we make sure that everything’s looked at.”

DC’s delegate candidate plans to target federal lawmakers challenging the city’s autonomy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
21:53:02 UTC
06:53:02 KST

DC’s delegate candidate plans to target federal lawmakers challenging the city’s autonomy
WASHINGTON (AP) — The District of Columbia’s presumptive incoming delegate to Congress unveiled a strategy Monday to counter Republican interventions in the city’s affairs by sending local residents to congressional districts in nearby states to stump for candidates who support greater autonomy for the nation’s capital.
Robert White Jr., the Democratic nominee to be the district’s sole delegate to Congress, unveiled the “Defend DC” mobilization effort, which he said will recruit, train and transport city residents and supporters to canvass for candidates who support the district’s independence. White will also launch a political action committee to support candidates that back D.C. statehood and local control.
“Congress has used its power over D.C. to attack us. So Washingtonians are banding together to use our collective power to change Congress,” White told a crowd of supporters in a downtown Washington plaza.
The Constitution gives federal lawmakers authority over the District of Columbia, while the Home Rule Act of 1973 lets residents elect a mayor, a council and neighborhood commissioners. But Congress maintains significant control, including approving the budget and all laws passed by the D.C. Council.
The D.C. delegate position is a nonvoting one, but it grants the nearly 700,000 people of the district, who have no other representation in Congress, a voice through speechmaking on the House floor and bill introduction.
Trump has squeezed Washington’s autonomy
White’s plan comes as Washington during the second Trump administration has faced multiple new challenges to its autonomy, most visibly the ongoing deployment of the National Guard which has been extended into 2029.
The plan will target U.S. House districts within driving distance of the nation’s capital in states like Pennsylvania, Virginia and New Jersey with members up for reelection who have backed President Donald Trump’s surge of federal agents into the district and who themselves have proposed efforts to overhaul the city’s governance.
“If politicians somewhere else believe they can come into our city and take away our rights without consequences, then we will go into their communities, the communities that determine whether those politicians keep their jobs,” White said.
The program’s first target will be Rep. John McGuire, a Virginia Republican who introduced legislation last year that would codify into law Trump’s executive order, “ Making the District of Columbia Safe and Beautiful.”
The order paved the way for the deployment of the National Guard and federal law enforcement agents onto the streets of Washington, D.C. Trump later also briefly federalized the city’s police force.
D.C. Council Chair Phil Mendelson called White’s strategy necessary to protect D.C. residents’ constitutional rights.
“Our current situation is one that was not imagined nor intended by the Founding Fathers,” Mendelson said.
Taking the fight to the district’s congressional opponents has been central to White’s platform. He spoke of the strategy during debates. He also spoke of his plan the night of the June primary when he won the Democratic primary for the district’s delegate to Congress, ushering in generational change for a position long held by 18-term delegate Eleanor Holmes Norton.
White’s win in the heavily Democratic city set him up to take the top spot in November’s general elections. Norton, 89 and a fixture of the Civil Rights movement, decided not to run again after facing growing concerns over her ability to forcefully push back against the Trump administration’s federal intervention into the city’s affairs.
One of Norton’s key roles has been to push back against incursions by Republicans in Congress who have grown increasingly willing to step into local affairs, despite the city’s Home Rule. In recent years, Congress members have tried to overturn the district’s motorcycle helmet law and ban the district’s use of automated traffic cameras.
White said he had spoken with House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., and Rep. Susan DelBene, the chair of House Democrats’ campaign arm, about the strategy.
A plan modeled after a former delegate’s
White modeled the strategy after one used by the district’s first delegate, Walter Fauntroy Jr., a civil rights legend who mobilized voters in several key races, most notably in 1972 in South Carolina. His efforts there were instrumental in defeating Rep. John McMillan, who chaired the House District Committee and routinely blocked the district’s efforts to govern itself.
Michael Fauntroy, Fauntroy’s nephew, and the founding director of the Race, Politics, and Policy Center at George Mason University, said the elder Fauntroy drew on a relationship he had built during his civil rights work, especially in the South when he sought office and visited targeted districts.
“His strategy was primarily to focus on those congressional districts in which the Black voters composed the margin of victory in a particular district,” said Michael Fauntroy, who authored “Home Rule or House Rule? Congress and the Erosion of Local Governance in the District of Columbia.”
“At one point, there were roughly 100-some-odd districts around the country, primarily in the South in which the Black vote was the marginal vote,” he said.
The situation is more complicated now. Gerrymandering has left few competitive districts, and Fauntroy said he doesn’t know what kind of network White has.
“If you don’t have those connections, it’s going to be difficult to take the fight to somebody,” he said.

El-Sayed distances himself from popular streamer’s comments on Israel and Jewish Americans
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate in Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed, distanced himself Monday from progressive commentator Hasan Piker, who suggested that some pro-Israel rhetoric may lead to backlash against American Jews.

El Sayed is one of several Democratic candidates this year who harnessed Piker’s online megaphone to appeal to younger voters, and they appeared together at campaign events during the primary, but last week’s comments may have cooled the relationship.
Wearing a suit and tie during one of his typically hours-long livestreams, Piker argued against the idea that opposing Israel is antisemitic. American Jews are not uniformly supportive of Israel, he said, but many “Jewish institutions” are “teaching people the idea that Jews are monolithic” and “its a very dangerous mode of propaganda.”
“If Jews in America keep putting this idea out there that they are singularly invested in Israel, eventually someone is going to come around and take action, not against the state of Israel mind you, but against American Jews,” he said.
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, a New York Democrat, issued a sharply critical statement.
“The malicious claim that American Jews are inviting violence against themselves is dangerous and antisemitic,” he said on social media. “There is zero justification for threats against the safety of our Jewish brothers and sisters at a moment of rising hate.”
El-Sayed issued his own statement later in the day.
“I believe all Americans deserve the right to advocate for what they believe without fear of violence,” he said. “This is particularly true for communities that have been intimidated for their beliefs in the past.”
He also said “antisemitism is a scourge, and we need to address it in all its forms” and “nobody speaks for this campaign besides me and my campaign spokespeople.”
“And while politicians and pundits try to make this race about a Twitch streamer, we’re going to be talking about gas, groceries, good schools and healthcare,” El-Sayed added.
While Piker was speaking on the livestream last week, he was displaying an X post with a photo of Jeremy Moss, a Jewish Democratic candidate for U.S. House in Michigan, on his screen.
Moss posted Monday, “I will not be lectured by a California podcaster about what Oakland County, Michigan’s Jewish community should and shouldn’t believe,” adding that “we certainly won’t be gaslit that we’re responsible for the antisemitic harm upon us.”
Piker’s spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment. On another livestream Monday, he called El-Sayed’s statement “neutral” and described the outrage as a “smear.” He argued that he wasn’t advocating violence but warning against the rhetoric that could.
El-Sayed’s Republican opponent, former congressman Mike Rogers, said El-Sayed’s response was inadequate.
“El-Sayed doesn’t have the guts to disavow his running mate,” Rogers said. He said the Democratic nominee is “unfit to represent our state.”
Piker’s previous statements has been controversial, including a past comment that “Hamas is a thousand times better” than Israel.
Some Democrats urged El-Sayed to go further in responding to Piker’s comments.
“I want Abdul to win desperately, but the most predictable thing in the world was that Piker would inevitably become a serious liability in a general election,” Tré Easton, a Democratic strategist, wrote on social media. “If you care about Abdul’s campaign succeeding, you should want him to distance himself from Piker clearly and directly.”

Burnham arrived in Kyiv for his first trip abroad since taking office, alongside other European leaders and European Council President António Costa.

EU releases €6.1 billion for Ukraine’s defense
On Monday, the EU said it had released another €6.1 billion ($7.1 billion) in military aid for Ukraine to boost its air defenses.
The funding is part of a €90-billion ($104 billion) loan, including €60 billion ($70 billion) in military aid, that the EU has said will go to Ukraine.
Ahead of the talks, Ukraine forged ahead with its campaign against Russia’s logistics sites, hitting multiple warehouses belonging to e-commerce giant Ozon.
Ozon reported fires early Monday at two warehouses in southern Russia, adding that two other sites had been evacuated over threats of drone attacks.
Russian authorities also said debris from a Ukrainian drone attack had killed three children and wounded eight others.
Russian leader Vladimir Putin on Saturday said Kyiv had “opened Pandora’s box” by targeting Russia’s economy and promised further escalation, including against Ukrainian agriculture.
UK clears Storm Shadow technology transfer
Burnham announced in Kyiv that the British government was authorizing defense firm MBDA to release classified information needed to help Ukraine and France set up local production of the long-range Storm Shadow/SCALP missile.
The Kremlin accused London of preventing peace in Ukraine by handing the information to Kyiv and threatened to target and “destroy” facilities producing the missile in Ukraine.
On Saturday, Macron pledged Paris would deliver new interceptor missiles.
The ballistic missiles Russia has been firing in their dozens are incredibly fast and travel with a high-arching trajectory, making them difficult for Kyiv to intercept.
Ukraine relies on advanced systems – chiefly, US Patriot interceptors – to protect its skies.
But it has reported a shortage of Patriot interceptors since the United States and Israel went to war with Iran in February, diverting supplies.
Ukraine reveals scale of Patriot shortfall
Ahead of the meeting, Zelensky revealed the extent of the deficit, releasing usually closely guarded numbers.
He said deliveries of crucial Patriot interceptors had halved since 2023.
“Over the entire of 2023, Ukraine received 675 missiles, and over all of 2025 – 364, even though Russian missile strikes have increased,” Zelensky said.
“For 2026, as currently projected, it is 264,” he added, saying Ukraine was seeking a package of at least 300 for the upcoming winter.

Israel bars two Swedish MEPs from West Bank visit
Israel said Monday that it had refused entry to two left-wing Swedish deputies in the European Parliament who wanted to visit the occupied West Bank.
Jonas Sjostedt and Hanna Gedin, members of Sweden's Left Party, were turned away Sunday at Israel's Ben Gurion Airport, the primary gateway for visitors to the Palestinian territory.
Israel's foreign ministry said the pair had "consistently acted against Israel", including by calling for international legal proceedings against Israelis.
"On various public occasions, they have spread false accusations against Israel, including allegations of genocide, deliberate starvation and the intentional targeting of children and medical personnel," the ministry said in a statement.
United Nations investigators, who do not speak for the global body as a whole, charged in June that Israel was deliberately targeting Palestinian children in an ongoing "genocide" in Gaza.
Israel fiercely rejected the finding and accused Hamas of using Palestinian children as human shields.
Sjostedt in a Facebook post said that the two MEPs planned to meet human rights and charitable organisations, including Save the Children, and to see refugee camps.
"We continue to work against Israel's illegal occupation, the displacement of Palestinians, and genocide," Sjostedt wrote.
He added that Sweden had issued a protest.
But Swedish Foreign Minister Maria Malmer Stenergard, while noting the Swedish embassy assisted the pair, said that every country "has its own entry regulations" and that Sweden has a travel advisory in place for Israel and the Palestinian territories.
"Why Jonas Sjostedt and Hanna Gedin nevertheless choose to travel there is something they themselves need to answer," she told the Dagens Nyheter newspaper.
Rawhi Fattouh, president of the Palestinian National Council, the West Bank-based legislative body, called on European parliaments to speak out against the exclusion of critical voices.
The denial of entry is "an attempt to impose silence by force and turn criticism of the occupation into an accusation, in clear disregard for international law and the moral immunity afforded to parliamentary work", he said.

US could carry out further strikes on Iran if needed: Hegseth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Ahmet Salih Alacaci
25 August 2026•Update: 25 August 2026
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Monday that Washington is not ruling out further military strikes on Iran, even as the Trump administration intensifies economic pressure on Tehran.
Asked whether kinetic strikes were currently on pause, Hegseth said: “No. If we need to use kinetic strikes, we'll use them.”
“If Iran is foolish enough to overplay their hand or mess with the American military, we'll do what we need to do,” he told reporters after a speech to defense industrial workers in Oshkosh, Wisconsin, where he urged US defense contractors to "pivot to a wartime footing."
Hegseth said economic pressure was currently hurting Iran the most but added that the US was “by no means” ruling out strikes “anywhere in the Strait of Hormuz or around Iran.”
He also claimed the US maintains control of the Strait of Hormuz, saying Washington’s blockade was “ironclad” and that Iran was unable to move oil through the waterway, while the US could protect shipping.
Hegseth said the administration expected Congress to provide the full $1.5 trillion sought for defense, even if approval came during a lame-duck session after November midterm elections but before the newly elected Congress takes office in January.
Asked whether munitions purchases could be cut if the full amount was not approved, he called them “pretty sacred,” saying the Pentagon had entered long-term agreements aimed at increasing supplies of some priority munitions two-, three- or fourfold.
Hegseth also declined to discuss reports that US stocks of ATACMS long-range missiles had been significantly depleted in ongoing conflicts, saying the military had “plenty” available.
- USS Abraham Lincoln heading home
Hegseth also confirmed that the USS Abraham Lincoln is returning home after an extended deployment.
“To the sailors and families of the Lincoln, I say godspeed on a historic mission. Congratulations, you're on your way home,” he said, describing the deployment as “tough” and longer than most.
The Lincoln has spent more than eight months without making a port call, setting a US Navy record. Families of sailors have reported worsening conditions and morale aboard the carrier, though Hegseth has said such claims have been “completely misrepresented.”

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Monday that Iran had attempted to assassinate one of his two sons, without offering further details.

Supreme Court allows Trump's plan to regulate but not block use of mail ballots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
21:38:04 UTC
06:38:04 KST

Supreme Court for now allows Trump to plan new mail ballot rules. California to sue again
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta said his office expects to sue again within days.
- About 30% of the nation’s voters — and 80% of Californians — cast their ballots by mail in 2024.
WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court cleared the way Monday for President Trump to continue seeking new limits on the use of mail ballots, though their implementation remains in dispute as the November election rapidly approaches.
California leaders immediately noted the limits of the high court ruling and said they would file a lawsuit to prevent Trump’s desired changes from taking effect.
“The Supreme Court just let the Trump administration move ahead (for now) with its plan to disenfranchise voters across the country. California will be suing AGAIN to block these Orwellian rules from being implemented,” Gov. Gavin Newsom said in a statement.
Acting by a 6-3 vote, the court’s conservatives granted an emergency appeal from Trump’s lawyers and set aside a lower judge’s order that blocked federal agencies — including the Department of Homeland Security and the U.S. Postal Service — from advancing new federal regulations on states and their use of mail ballots.
Trump called for those regulations in a March executive order directing Homeland Security to compile its own lists of eligible citizen voters in each state and the Postal Service to restrict its processing of mail ballots to those submitted by individuals on those Homeland Security lists.
The high court’s ruling allows those agencies to move forward with their work to comply with Trump’s order, but reaches no conclusions as to the legality of those pending rules.
Across California and the nation, Democratic leaders and voting rights advocates are ramping up coordination and gaming out responses to a raft of potential actions by the Trump administration to subvert the November vote or deny its outcome.
“The Court’s disposition of this application does not mean that any measure taken by the Government to implement the Order will necessarily be lawful. On that score, time will tell,” the high court wrote.
The unsigned order spoke for the six Republican appointees. The three liberals, all Democratic appointees, dissented in two separate opinions.
Lauren Bis, a White House spokeswoman, called the ruling a “major win for the security of American elections” in a statement to The Times.
“These are commonsense measures that protect the security of mail-in ballots and ensure only Americans are electing American leaders,” Bis said. “This Administration will continue to lawfully enact the agenda President Trump was elected on — which includes the safety and security of our elections.”
California officials stressed that the court’s ruling does not allow final implementation of the rules requested by Trump.
California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta, who helped lead the coalition of states challenging Trump’s order, called the ruling “somewhat disappointing” but “purely procedural” and far from the final word on the issue.
“It doesn’t address the merits. And we think that when the merits are addressed — and we will bring a lawsuit to address the merits of this case — that we will prevail, because the president has zero authority to determine the time, place and manner of elections, and he is through an executive order trying to exert a very significant amount of authority,” Bonta said.
He said the court found the state’s lawsuit was not “ripe” to bring because there was no final Postal Service rule in place implementing new controls on mail ballots. He said the Postal Service issued a final rule Friday — and “now that the final rule’s in place, we’ll sue, and we’ll start from the beginning.”
The 95-page new rule implements parts of Trump’s executive order by requiring a new design for mail ballots and the envelopes they go in, as well as procedures for how data are collected from them by the federal government.
Bonta said his office expects to sue again within days. He expects a lower court will block the Trump-ordered changes again, and for that ruling to stand through November. He said if the high court does weigh in again before the midterms, he expects it to acknowledge that the president has no authority to dictate election policy.
Dean Logan, registrar-recorder and county clerk for Los Angeles County, also said the issue is far from settled.
“As we approach the issuance of the first ballots for the November General Election, it is important to recognize that these regulations are still subject to active litigation and interpretation,” Logan said in a statement to The Times. “In response, we will intensify our voter outreach and educational initiatives to ensure individuals are fully informed and aware of any adjustments to the voting process.”
The Supreme Court found in part that the lower court order blocking the agencies from working toward Trump’s order was invalid because that work had yet to cause any harm to the states that sued, including California.
It wrote that Trump’s executive order “is internal directive from the President to his subordinates mandating that certain agencies pursue certain policies. It neither requires nor forbids anything of anyone outside the Executive Branch.”
About 30% of the nation’s voters — and 80% of Californians — cast their ballots by mail in 2024. Trump, however, has long maintained that voting by mail leads to fraud, including voting by noncitizens.
With the court’s ruling Monday, Homeland Security may compile state-by-state lists of citizens who are 18 and over and eligible to vote. However, California and other states “are not required to use the Lists,” the court said.
The Trump administration has acknowledged potential law enforcement applications for the lists and warned state election officials across the country that they could face legal consequences if they don’t work to ensure that noncitizens aren’t able to vote in their elections.
President Trump signed an executive order Tuesday purporting to place new federal controls on voting by mail in states such as California.
Such warnings from the administration were mentioned by Justice Sonia Sotomayor in her dissent as evidence of the harm suffered by the states already, and reason for the lower court’s ruling halting implementation to hold.
She wrote that the administration has acknowledged that a state’s “refusal to consider” the Homeland Security lists “could conceivably, depending on the circumstances, be relevant evidence of an intent to violate, or to facilitate the violation of, the federal laws prohibiting non-citizen voting.”
She also made the limits of the majority’s ruling clear.
“Today’s decision does not address whether the President’s attempts to interfere with States’ administration of the November 2026 elections are lawful,” Sotomayor wrote in a dissent joined by Justice Elena Kagan. “Nor does it suggest that the Executive Branch has any constitutional or statutory authority to implement the President’s directives. Instead, today’s decision merely postpones adjudication of those challenges.”
Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, in her own dissent, also noted the limits of the majority’s ruling and criticized it for failing “to explain when, exactly, is the right time to bring a meritorious election-rule claim challenging unconstitutional interference with electoral processes.”
Jackson wrote that the ruling “needlessly injects chaos and uncertainty into the upcoming midterm elections. It also lets another shoe drop in the Kafkaesque nightmare that our precedents have been steadily creating for certain plaintiffs who seek to bring election-related challenges.”
Trump’s executive order said it was aimed at “ensuring citizenship verification” in federal elections. California and 22 other Democratic-led states sued a few days later and said Trump sought to use the Postal Service to impose new restrictions on voting by mail. They also argued the Constitution gives states and Congress the power to regulate elections, not the president.
A federal judge in Boston and the 1st Circuit Court agreed with the challengers and blocked Trump’s executive order from taking effect for the November elections.
The case on appeal was Trump vs. California because Bonta was a leader of the Democratic state attorneys who sued.
Logan, of Los Angeles County, said the Trump administration’s “ongoing efforts to modify the electoral process amid an election cycle are deeply troubling and frustrating,” and that one of the “most significant risks we face” as a result is “the possibility of voter confusion and diminished participation — outcomes that run counter to the principles of free and fair elections.”
“Our team is dedicated to minimizing any adverse effects on voters, and we will work diligently to safeguard their ability to make their voices heard and ensure their votes are properly recorded,” Logan said.

US public support for Iran war falls as Trump approval at record low: Poll

US public support for Iran war falls as Trump approval at record low: Poll
Falling Republican support, rising gas prices, and fears of a long conflict drive a decline in backing for the Iran war.
Support in the United States for the war on Iran has fallen as President Donald Trump’s approval remains at a record low, a Reuters/Ipsos poll suggests.
Public backing for the war has dropped to its lowest level since the early stages of the conflict, with declining Republican support contributing to the shift, according to the poll released on Monday.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Trump’s approval rating sinks to new low at 33 percent
- list 2 of 3Trump’s ‘economic D-Day’ claims first victim: Not Iran, but US markets
- list 3 of 3Trump slams Canada with new 50 percent auto tariffs from January
Just 31 percent of Americans surveyed said they support US military action against Iran, down from 37 percent in March and 34 percent earlier this month. Support among Republican respondents fell to 69 percent, compared with 77 percent in March.
The war is also continuing to weigh on Trump’s standing with the public, the poll suggests. For the second consecutive Reuters/Ipsos survey, 33 percent of respondents said they approved of Trump’s performance as president, matching the lowest approval rating recorded in the polling series across his first and second terms.
Trump has defended the military campaign as necessary to prevent Iran from developing a nuclear weapon. The conflict began on February 28 with US and Israeli attacks on Iran.
But the economic effects of the war remain a concern for Americans. Iran has maintained a de facto blockade of oil exports from the region, contributing to a rise in US petrol prices to near record highs.
The Trump administration has also announced recent pledges to increase economic pressure on Iran. Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent said on Monday that the US would target all of Iran’s sources of revenue, including oil, with the aim of preventing other countries and companies from doing business with Tehran. The campaign is dubbed “Operation Economic Outcast”.
A growing majority of Americans expect the war to continue for some time, the poll suggests. Eighty-three percent of respondents said they believe the conflict will last for an extended period, up from 80 percent earlier this month.
The prospect of a lengthy war presents a challenge for Trump, who campaigned for the presidency in 2024 on promises to bring down inflation and to adopt an “America First” strategy of avoiding foreign military engagements.
Six months into the conflict, petrol prices are more than $1 per gallon (3.8 litres) higher than they were before the war, adding to economic pressure ahead of November’s midterm elections.
The higher fuel costs could also create difficulties for Republicans defending narrow congressional majorities.
The poll suggests that independent voters favour Democrats over Republicans when asked which party they would support in a congressional election held today. Among independents, 33 percent said they would vote for a Democrat, compared with 19 percent who said they would choose a Republican.
The Reuters/Ipsos survey questioned 1,215 adults across the United States over four days and has a margin of error of 3 percentage points in either direction.

US Supreme Court gives Trump temporary win on mail-in ballots as midterms loom
Decision permits Trump administration to enforce restrictions for now, leaving final judgment pending as Democrats vow new lawsuits
The US Supreme Court gave President Donald Trump a temporary victory on Monday, lifting a lower court block on his executive order curbing the use of mail-in ballots.
The Republican president signed an order in March seeking to restrict mail-in voting ahead of the November midterm elections but it was immediately met with multiple legal challenges.
Democratic-led states sued the administration on grounds that under the US Constitution, states – and not the federal government – retain broad control over the administration of elections.
A district court in Massachusetts blocked implementation of the executive order but the Supreme Court on Monday lifted the judge’s stay, allowing parts of Trump’s directive to go ahead for now.
“The District Court lacked jurisdiction to bar the Government from trying to implement” the executive order, the Supreme Court majority said in an unsigned opinion.
But the justices withheld final judgment on the merits of the case pending further litigation.

Burnham backtracks on spending housing fund only on building social homes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
21:30:39 UTC
06:30:39 KST

Andy Burnham has backtracked on his proposal to rip up the government’s housing plans and boost social home building.
Ministers laid out plans on Monday to spend an initial £10bn from the 10-year Affordable Homes Programme on a mix of subsidised housing types in England, in line with the Starmer government’s policy.
Burnham previously called for the programme to be spent entirely on social homes, which are more heavily subsidised and therefore more affordable than other types of government-funded housing.
He said when launching his campaign to become MP for Makerfield: “There’s £39bn allocated over a 10-year period … I’m saying that should be dedicated to council homes. Let’s not be coy any more … I’m saying council homes because control matters.”
Under the plans announced on Monday, however, £10bn will be spent helping to build 70,000 homes outside London, about 60% of which will be social rented houses. The rest will be other types of accommodation such as shared ownership schemes and sheltered housing.
London will get another £6bn, which will be allocated at a later date.
Ministers said the investment would help bring the government closer to its promise of building 300,000 affordable homes over the next 10 years. It will be spent by 33 “strategic partners”, who will be guaranteed funding for the next decade to help deliver their plans.
The Guardian has learned that for the first time in the history of the scheme, three of those partners will be local councils, as the government looks to deliver what Burnham has promised will be “the biggest council housebuilding programme since the postwar period”.
Angela Rayner, the housing secretary, said: “Growing up on a council estate and raising children as a young working mum, I know firsthand that access to a secure, affordable home can be a lifeline for families up and down the country.
“Guardian readers will know just how important council housing is too. You will know it’s so much more than just a roof over your head – it gives working parents a safe place to raise their family, offers kids the stability needed to thrive in school and wraps a community around those who need it most.”
She added: “This once-in-a-generation investment will help rewrite these stories, delivering the genuinely affordable homes our country needs, getting people off waiting lists and helping families put down roots so they can get on in life.”
Officials say that another £16bn is yet to be allocated, and that social rent homes and council houses will be prioritised in future funding rounds.
Sarah Elliott, the chief executive of the charity Shelter, said: “Today’s announcement puts councils back on the pitch in the fight to end homelessness. By giving local authorities some of the funding and support they need to start delivering social homes at scale again and ramping up the percentage of funds allocated to social homes, the government has laid the foundations for its council housing revolution.
“But there are still underlying obstacles which hold councils back from building. The government must use the autumn budget to finally remove these barriers, like unsustainable housing debt that councils are saddled with, to make the prime minister’s vision of a new generation of social homes a reality.”
The plans contrast with those announced by Reform UK on Monday, which is promising to boost the supply of social homes by evicting foreign tenants and allowing housing associations to borrow more.

Why all the fuss on a Triple Zero campaign from telcos?
Why are telcos sending us messages on how 000 works? Nobody cares how it works. If my network is down I just want to know if I dial 000 I’ll get connected. Sounds like they’re just going to give us all the excuses why it might not work .
- Phillip
Hi Phillip,
That's the whole point of the campaign — because in the event your network is down, they want you to know you can still dial Triple Zero (000) if there's an emergency.
Since outages are (thankfully) pretty rare, not everyone knows that they can still call Triple Zero and be connected to the relevant emergency service. But during an outage, the only difference is that the call can take slightly longer to connect to the other network (we're talking 40–50 seconds) due to how the "camp-on" process works.
In other words — if you called Triple Zero during an outage, you might not hear the usual or expected ringing initially, but the call is still going through.
Optus in particular has been leading the push for this campaign after their outage in 2023.
"This campaign provides Australians with practical information about how their phone connects to emergency services and what they should do if their usual network is unavailable," an Optus spokesperson said.
"By raising awareness of safeguards such as emergency camp-on and providing simple guidance people can use in a high-pressure situation, we're helping Australians better prepare for the moments when reliable access to Triple Zero matters most."
Key Event
AI brands seeing mounting distrust levels amongst Australians
Australians are increasingly distrustful of artificial intelligence brands like OpenAI and Palantir, according to Roy Morgan's latest risk monitor report.
The findings show that in the year to June, Optus is still the most distrusted brand, followed by Meta, Temu, Woolworths and Coles.
While their positions haven't changed, Roy Morgan's research shows that OpenAI (including ChatGPT) and Palantir have seen the "most consequential declines".
OpenAI is the 16th-most distrusted brand due to privacy concerns and personal data risks, while Palantir is now the 30th-most distrusted brand in the country.
"The latest results from the ongoing trust survey show distrust in both brands has grown quickly — despite neither facing a definable and definitive scandal," said Roy Morgan CEO Michele Levine.
"Australians are increasingly citing concerns about AI companies such that the customer interfaces don't protect users' privacy, the companies are unethical and dishonest, they're too motivated by profit and greed, and also that the large electricity requirements to run the data centres these companies rely on are environmentally irresponsible."
As for the brands Australians trust the most? There have been no changes there: Bunnings, Aldi, Kmart, Commonwealth Bank and Apple are still topping the list.
Key Event
eHarmony engaged in misleading conduct about pricing and subscriptions
The Federal Court has ruled that online dating site eHarmony misled customers about the "pricing, renewal and duration" of its memberships.
Almost three years ago, the ACCC announced it was suing the dating site over what it described as a "subscription trap" and alleged the company broke consumer law in the process.
But the Federal Court has today ruled that the dating site did breach Australian Consumer Law by engaging in misleading or deceptive conduct by:
- offering free dating when a consumer could not engage in ongoing communication with other people for free
- the automatic renewal of memberships
- one-month memberships, when the minimum period consumers could sign up for was six months
- consumers not being able to cancel their subscription early
- stating monthly subscription prices that did not mention an additional mandatory fee to pay monthly.
eHarmony was also found to have broken Australian Consumer Law by failing to display the minimum total amount a customer would pay for their subscription as a single price.
"The ACCC is committed to taking action against businesses that engage in misleading conduct in the digital economy, including by using subscription traps and other dark patterns that unfairly impact consumer choice," ACCC Commissioner Luke Woodward said.
"The Court's ruling underscores that when businesses advertise a price for a subscription divided into instalments, such as a price per month, the minimum total cost must also be clearly and prominently displayed."
In a statement, eHarmony says it has been cooperating with the ACCC throughout the case and is "carefully reviewing the Federal Court's judgment and considering [its] options".
The matter will return to court at a later date to determine penalties and compensation for customers.

Key Event
Telcos join forces for Triple Zero campaign after network outages
Have you gotten a reminder from your telco provider this week about reaching Triple Zero even when your phone doesn't have any connection?
Don't be alarmed, it's not a scam. It's a new campaign that the three main telco providers have started rolling out this week in the wake of recent Triple-0 outages.
In conjunction with the Australian Telecommunications Alliance (ATA) and the federal government's Triple Zero Custodian, Telstra, Optus and TPG Telecom (Vodafone's parent company) have launched a public information campaign "to help ensure Australians can reliably connect to Triple Zero (000) when needed".
You can expect to get direct emails and notifications from your provider about how to connect to Triple Zero in the event of an outage, how the backup systems work, and what to do if you're having trouble connecting.
"We've been working closely with the three major mobile network operators and the Triple Zero Custodian to develop this campaign," Luke Coleman, the CEO of the ATA said in a statement.
"Our priority is to ensure Australians are equipped with simple advice they can recall and use in a worst-case scenario if they need to call Triple Zero and find their usual network is unavailable."

Key Event
RBA considered rate hike at August meeting
The minutes from the RBA's latest monetary policy meeting earlier this month have just been released, and have revealed the central bank considered lifting interest rates by 0.25 percentage points.
That would have taken the cash rate to 4.6%, the highest level since late 2011, but unanimously voted to leave it on hold at 4.35%.
In explaining its consideration to potentially lift rates the minutes referred to the "assessment of the risks to the inflation forecast".
"Members noted that if the risks around the inflation forecast were judged to be significantly skewed to the upside it may be appropriate to mitigate those risks somewhat by tightening monetary policy pre-emptively," it said.
Those risks included:
"A prolonged conflict in the Middle East could cause oil reserves to dwindle to very low levels and oil prices to rise sharply; widespread cost pressures … could be passed into consumer prices more fully than assumed; the AI and data centre investment boom could prove to be larger than anticipated, globally and/or in Australia; aggregate demand in Australia more generally could be more resilient than forecast; and productivity growth might not pick up as assumed in the forecasts."
Ultimately though, the RBA "judged it appropriate to leave the cash rate target unchanged at this meeting, while remaining alert to the upside risks to the inflation outlook and being ready to act should they materialise".
That said, the RBA reiterated that it won't hesitate to lift rates again if it deems it necessary to "deliver price stability and full employment" and those upside risks to inflation materialise.
The RBA's next interest rates decision will be handed down on September 29.

Forcing women to drink at business dinners has no place in modern China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
21:30:06 UTC
06:30:06 KST

Forcing women to drink at business dinners has no place in modern China
The alleged assault of a female employee in Hangzhou exposes how such unsavoury practices persist amid Beijing’s anti-extravagance campaign
Reports of a female employee allegedly being assaulted at a drinking party in Hangzhou brought back a version of myself from more than a decade ago. Back then, I was one of those young women routinely invited to business dinners.
Seating followed an unwritten rule, with the most powerful person taking the seat of honour, flanked by two young women. Everyone knew what we were there to do: keep the conversation lively, entertain the guests and, above all, keep raising our glasses.
I’ve always been a terrible drinker. Yet under the familiar pressure – “Everyone else is drinking. Why aren’t you?” – I would force down a glass or two. I developed little tricks. Baijiu is clear, so I could sometimes discreetly spit it into a napkin without anyone noticing.
However, that didn’t always work. Once, I was told to drink what they called a “red apple”, or a full glass of red wine. There was nowhere to hide it. I drank it, blacked out later, vomited three or four times and spent the next day with a splitting headache.
What I remember most vividly is not the physical misery. It’s a strange sense of shame. Why could everyone else drink but I couldn’t?
The ability to drink was seen as an important professional skill. The women who could drink without flinching seemed admirable. They knew when to stand, whom to toast and, above all, how to manage the mood of the table. I felt that my own body and personality were holding me back.

Syria hails its removal from US terrorism list as ‘result of transformation brought by Syrians’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
21:30:01 UTC
06:30:01 KST

Abdulsalam Fayez and Mohammad Sio
25 August 2026•Update: 25 August 2026
Syria on Monday hailed its removal from the US list of state sponsors of terrorism as the “result of the transformation brought about by the Syrian people,” saying the decision reflects the new Syrian state’s commitment to international peace and security.
 
“We congratulate the Syrian people on this historic milestone,” Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani said on the US social media platform X, referring to the removal of Syria from the list after 47 years.
 
Shaibani said the designation was associated with the policies and practices of the former regime, which was toppled in late 2024, and “was never the choice of the Syrian people, nor was it befitting of Syria and its history.”
 
“This step is the result of the transformation brought about by the Syrian people,” he stressed, adding that it also reflects the new Syrian state’s commitment to international peace and security and to cooperation and partnership with the US and countries around the world.
 
Under President Ahmad al-Sharaa’s guidance, “we will continue our efforts to overcome the legacy of isolation and foster an environment based on transparency, mutual interests and respect, in support of development and stability in Syria and the region,” Shaibani said.
 
Shaibani thanked US President Donald Trump, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, US Envoy for Syria and Ambassador to Türkiye Tom Barrack, the US administration, members of Congress and others who contributed to the decision.
 
In a separate statement, Syria’s Foreign Ministry welcomed the US decision as opening “a new chapter” in the country’s international relations, saying it would support economic recovery, help create conditions for reconstruction and strengthen stability and security in Syria and the region.
 
Damascus also expressed hope for further US steps to lift remaining restrictions hindering its recovery and said it looked forward to deeper strategic partnerships and broader cooperation with Washington and the international community.
 
Hours earlier, the US State Department announced that it had removed Syria from the list of state sponsors of terrorism and revoked the designation of the al-Nusrah Front, also known as Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham, as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist Organization. The Treasury Department also endorsed the move.
 
Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham was one of the most prominent armed groups opposing Bashar al-Assad’s forces during Syria’s civil war. The group was led by Ahmad al-Sharaa, who became Syria’s president after Assad’s ouster in December 2024.
 
Syria had remained on the US list of state sponsors of terrorism since 1979, during the decades-long rule of the former regime.
 
Damascus sees the removal of the designation as opening the way for greater economic transactions, investment and international cooperation as well as eliminating restrictions linked to the designation. Other US restrictions remain subject to separate legal processes.

SC to decide on Tejpal’s plea against surrender after 10-year rape conviction
NEW DELHI: Supreme Court Monday said it would pass order on former Tehelka editor Tarun Tejpal's plea seeking exemption from surrender after Bombay High Court convicted and sentenced him to 10 years of imprisonment in a 2013 rape case, with Goa govt opposing his plea and contending that his appeal was not admissible since the convict had not filed a separate application seeking exemption from surrender or shown a certificate that he has already surrendered as per Order XXII Rule 5 of the Supreme Court Rules, 2013.The matter was heard by a single judge, Justice Alok Aradhe. Solicitor general Tushar Mehta, appearing for the state govt, contended that existence of the appeal was dependent on Tejpal either filing a certificate that he has surrendered or, alternatively, requesting the court to allow an exemption from surrender.
Senior advocate Kapil Sibal, representing Tejpal, said there was no need to surrender yet since the high court itself had granted him time to surrender. "This rule doesn't apply because this is a case where stay has been granted by the high court, so there is no question of applying this rule. Suppose the court says no stay, I will have to go to jail," Sibal said, requesting the court to list the appeal for Aug 31.After hearing both sides, Justice Aradhe said he would pass an appropriate order in the matter.The Goa bench of Bombay high court convicted Tejpal under multiple provisions of the IPC and sentenced him to 10 years rigorous imprisonment each under sections 376(2)(f) and 376(2)(k), with the sentences to run concurrently. It also imposed additional concurrent sentences for offences relating to outraging a woman's modesty, sexual harassment, disrobing, wrongful restraint and wrongful confinement. The fines imposed on Tejpal total Rs 10.1 lakh, which the court directed to be paid to the victim. tnn

'A dangerous individual': Ex-snooker champ convicted of child sex abuse
Unknown

06:24:01 KST

Former snooker world champion Graeme Dott has been found guilty of abusing two different children in the 1990s and early 2000s.
Dott was labelled "a dangerous individual" by a detective inspector from Police Scotland after the conviction.
What's next?
The judge has ordered Dott to be held in custody ahead of his sentencing on September 29.
Former world snooker champion Graeme Dott has been convicted of sexually abusing two primary school children in Scotland in the 1990s and early 2000s.
Dott, 49, was found guilty of abusing a girl from 1993-96 and a boy from 2006-10 after a five-day trial at the High Court in Glasgow. The judge ordered Dott to be held in custody ahead of his sentencing on September 29.
The woman, now in her 40s, testified that Dott sexually abused her on multiple occasions, "caressing" her bottom over her clothing, exposing himself and touching her with parts of his body, including his penis.
The man, now in his late 20s, said he was abused on multiple occasions, with Dott touching him inappropriately, kissing him and performing sexual acts.
"Dott is a dangerous individual, and I hope this conviction provides some measure of comfort to those impacted by his crimes," Detective Inspector Gary Smillie from Police Scotland said.
Snooker's governing body suspended Dott in April 2025 after he was charged in the case. The Scot was ranked number 56 in the world at the time and dropped from the rankings after the season.
On Monday, the World Professional Billiards and Snooker Association revoked Dott's membership following an emergency board meeting. The WPBSA also said it wrote to the World Snooker Tour to request his immediate removal from the WST Hall of Fame.
Dott won the World Snooker Championship in 2006 and was a runner-up twice.

An NFL player coming back to college? Yes, it could happen. Here’s why
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
21:23:02 UTC
06:23:02 KST

An NFL player coming back to college? Yes, it could happen. Here’s why
These used to be among the fundamental facts about going to college in America: College lasts four years. And though that timeline had been flexible when it comes to sports, there was never much debate over the notion that once a player moved on to the pros, their days as a college athlete were over.
A recent rule passed by the NCAA has resulted in confusion, lawsuits and the once unthinkable notion of players leaving college, signing with professional teams and now leaving those teams to head back to college.
Among this week’s headline grabbers are Dae’Quan Wright, an undrafted tight end out of Mississippi who had tryouts with the Eagles and Browns over the summer, but now has a deal in place to play this season at Ole Miss’ rival in the Southeastern Conference, No. 11 LSU.
Wright is among a number of college athletes who have sued for the right to return to college to play as the start of both the college football and NFL seasons approach. A quick look at how we got here:
NCAA passes a new rule allowing for five years of eligibility
This part happened in June, and by the NCAA’s plodding standards, it happened quite fast.
The rule now allows athletes to play five seasons over the span of five years. Most college athletes now see the “clock” start on their eligibility either when they enroll full-time in college or at the start of the regular school year immediately following their 19th birthday, whichever comes first.
The rule itself isn’t all that outlandish. A lot of players were taking redshirt years (and getting extensions due to the pandemic) to prolong their eligibility to five, six, seven years and more, so putting some guardrails around it made some sense.
But the NCAA’s decision to start applying this new rule to athletes who graduated high school in 2023 is what caused the chaos. By not including those from the Class of ’22, many of whom saw their fourth and final year of eligibility end after last school year, they opened themselves up to trouble.
The members of the Class of ‘22 are arguing they’re being deprived of education and potential NIL financial benefits by being excluded from the rule.
Meanwhile, college athletes are suddenly looking at unexpected competition for roster spots and playing time coming from a class of players they thought would be gone this season. And teams, most of which have locked in their football rosters, are seeing a potential influx of talent they didn’t expect.
A federal lawsuit filed by those who only got 4 years of college
A basketball player named Brock Wisne filed a federal class-action lawsuit, saying the NCAA violated antitrust law by excluding that Class of 2022 from the new rule. A judge in Denver ruled in favor of Wisne, opening the door for everyone in the class to come back to college, but only to their former college. The judge left NCAA transfer portal rules intact, meaning the players couldn’t come back, enter the (currently closed) portal and find a new school.
An appeals court last Friday temporarily halted that judge’s order, though that was hardly the end of the confusion.
State lawsuits pile up as a workaround to the federal case
Despite the federal court ruling, players across the country have filed lawsuits in state courts and many judges granted orders allowing them to come back to school. This “find a local judge” approach has generally been successful for the athlete over the past couple of years.
In some cases — including the case involving Wright in Louisiana — a judge not only said the players could come back, but also ordered a weeklong reopening of the transfer portal, which gave the players a chance to shop around.
Side note about Wright’s potential move from Ole Miss to LSU: The SEC forbids moves within the conference such as that one, unless they come when the transfer portal is open, which in football is January. There is no clarity on how the ruling impacts the SEC rule.
The issue prompted conference leaders to meet Monday and draft a statement saying that allowing players to move back and forth between the pros and college “will blur the line between college and professional sports, create significant equity concerns and reduce opportunities for high school and current college athletes.”
Sam Ehrlich, a former lawyer who follows college sports litigation at Boise State, said the state lawsuits were filed “just in case” the federal order got overturned. It did, and that federal case had no bearing on the various state lawsuits.
According to Ehrlich’s College Sports Litigation Tracker, at least 26 eligibility cases have been filed in state and county courts across the U.S. In at least 10 of those, judges have granted a restraining order or injunction favoring the players. In only one — involving basketball player Filip Borovicanin — has an appeals court overturned the initial decision, leading to a favorable outcome for the NCAA.
When will this all be decided?
Court cases move slowly, and in the Wisne case, odds are nothing will be final until long after football (and maybe basketball and baseball) season is over and there’s no relief left to give to the impacted players.
While football teams are madly scrambling, trying to make sense of it all, basketball teams are also feeling some pressure. Teams are allowed to start practice on Sept. 25. A notable instance of where confusion might set in is Gonzaga, which recruited two players from that Class of ’22 who (presumably) had their eligibility restored.
One, however, is Javon Bennett, who was part of the Borovicanin lawsuit that an Ohio court overturned. The other is Chauncey Wiggins, who comes from Florida State and was part of a case in Georgia, where the ruling favorable to the players remains in force.

Mexico outraged by the US decision to deport its citizens to third countries
Kyiv • UNN
Mexico was outraged by the deportation of its citizens to third countries without prior warning. The US has already transferred more than 2,000 Mexicans to Guatemala.
Mexico opposed the decision by the United States to deport Mexican migrants not directly to their homeland but to third countries, including Guatemala, while Washington does not inform the Mexican authorities about such transfers. LRT reports, UNN writes.
Details
Mexican authorities say they are ready to accept their citizens deported from the United States; however, the U.S. administration has already transferred more than 2,000 Mexicans to Guatemala. One of the goals of this policy, according to Washington, is to deter illegal migration.
At the U.S.-Mexico border, migrants continue trying to enter the United States despite the strengthening of the security system. According to LRT, Mexican cartels may demand up to $20,000 to smuggle people across the border, while attempts to cross the desert terrain often end in injury or death.
"They make these makeshift ladders, which are used by people who transport people across the border. The so-called \"coyotes\" build them so that people can climb over the wall. But on the other side, they do not always build ladders that people can use to climb down. Recently, people have been forced to jump down. In addition, it is obvious that the ladders are very primitive and cannot support people's weight. We have seen more than once how people fall from them, resulting in fatalities and very serious injuries
Migrants are increasingly being transported by sea
Tighter controls along the land section of the border have caused changes in illegal migration routes. According to LRT, Mexican cartels are increasingly using maritime routes to transport people.
Migrants from various countries in Central and South America travel through Mexico toward the U.S. border. Some of them say they cannot safely travel through Mexico by public transport because of the activities of criminal groups.
At the same time, the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump continues the practice of sending migrants to third countries. In particular, Mexicans are transported by plane to Guatemala, after which they are returned to Mexico. Representatives of the Mexican embassy and consulates accompany the citizens and provide them with information about the procedure.

US Supreme Court lifts a judicial hurdle to Trump's mail-in ballot curbs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
21:13:37 UTC
06:13:37 KST

US Supreme Court hands a win to Trump over mail-in ballot restrictions
NEW YORK – The US Supreme Court on Aug 24 lifted one court order blocking President Donald Trump’s administration from implementing an executive order restricting the use of mail-in ballots ahead of the November midterm elections.
But the fate of Trump’s order remains uncertain, as a separate injunction blocking a key part of the plan remains in place.
Republicans are locked in a tight battle to retain control of Congress in the midterms.
Restricting mail-in ballots would stand to disproportionately benefit Republicans given that Democratic voters traditionally have been more likely to use mail-in ballots.
The Aug 24 ruling from the Supreme Court’s 6-3 conservative majority applied to a June injunction from Boston-based US District Judge Indira Talwani.
A coalition of 23 mostly Democratic-governed states and the District of Columbia had sued to stop the executive order over mail-in ballots.
The Supreme Court on Aug 24 said it was too soon for the states to challenge the order but left the door open for them to sue again as the midterm contest approaches.
Trump’s March executive order
Trump’s executive order, issued in March, directed the Department of Homeland Security to compile and transmit to the states a list of US citizens eligible to vote in each state, and the Justice Department to prioritise investigating and prosecuting state and local election officials who issue ballots to people deemed “not eligible” to vote in federal elections.
It also required the US Postal Service to deliver ballots only to voters on each state’s approved mail-in ballot list.
Trump has vowed to end the use of mail-in ballots nationwide before the midterms, and has long cast doubt on the security of such ballots, although evidence of voter fraud is rare.
The court on Aug 24 did not act on another injunction from Talwani that blocked the US Postal Service nationwide from enforcing the directive’s tighter rules for voting by mail.
The judge issued that order on Aug 11 in a separate lawsuit filed by voting-rights groups.
Judge ruled Trump lacked authority
Trump’s executive order is part of his wider efforts to make fundamental changes in US elections.
Trump, who has made false claims of widespread fraud in US elections including his 2020 loss to former Democratic president Joe Biden, has pressed the Republican-controlled Congress to pass a contentious package of voting restrictions called the SAVE America Act.
In June, Talwani ruled that the president lacked the authority to order changes in how states administer federal elections, noting that under the US Constitution, states have the role of determining voter-eligibility requirements.
The judge also noted that federal agencies lack the ability to compile accurate citizen lists for each state.
Despite Talwani’s action, USPS on Aug 21 released a finalised rule to implement Trump’s order, which would require states to provide it with lists of voters who received mailed ballots, as well as unique barcodes on outbound and return ballot mail envelopes.
In the Aug 24 decision, the conservative majority agreed with the Justice Department that the lawsuit challenging Trump’s directive was premature and that the states did not have the required legal standing at this stage to sue.
The agencies have not yet taken concrete actions that impact the states and so any harm they allege is speculative, the court said. Trump’s order itself “does not harm the states”, the court added.
California Governor Gavin Newsom, a Democrat, said on Aug 24 : “The Supreme Court just let the Trump administration move ahead (for now) with its plan to disenfranchise voters across the country. California will be suing AGAIN to block these Orwellian rules from being implemented.”
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The USPS declined to comment.
Justice Sonia Sotomayor, joined by fellow liberal Justice Elena Kagan, said that the states should not have to wait to challenge the order.
“Today’s decision does not address whether the president’s attempts to interfere with states’ administration of the November 2026 elections are lawful,” Sotomayor wrote. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson also wrote a separate dissent.
The states contend that their claims are not hypothetical and that the administration’s “rushed effort to change the rules of mail voting on the eve of the November midterms risks disenfranchising a substantial number of voters”.
“This decision is a painful setback, but it will not be the final word,” New York Attorney-General Letitia James said in a statement. “The right to vote is sacred, and no administration should be allowed to put that right in jeopardy by making it harder for eligible voters to cast their ballots.”
In her June ruling, Talwani rejected the administration’s arguments, finding that the lawsuit was not filed too soon and that the states had legal standing because they would face election administration disruption, compliance costs and a credible threat of criminal prosecution. REUTERS

Ukraine to Produce French-British Storm Shadow Cruise Missiles Domestically

Ukraine to Produce French-British Storm Shadow Cruise Missiles Domestically
Ukraine will begin producing Storm Shadow long-range cruise missiles domestically after the United Kingdom approved the transfer of relevant technology. British and French defense companies will also participate in the effort, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said during a visit to Kyiv, according to RBC-Ukraine on August 24.
Burnham said Britain had been the first country to provide Ukraine with long-range weapons in 2023 and that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had since asked London to share Storm Shadow technology to enable Ukraine to develop the capability independently.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The Storm Shadow, jointly developed by Britain and France, is an air-launched cruise missile designed for precision strikes against high-value targets at long distances. France operates the missile under the name SCALP-EG.
Burnham said the decision was intended to further strengthen Ukraine’s ability to conduct long-range strikes as Russia continues missile attacks against Ukrainian cities and civilian infrastructure.
According to the British prime minister, Russian leader Vladimir Putin is seeking to prevail through what he described as a campaign of terror involving ballistic missile attacks against Ukrainian civilians.
Burnham said Russia must be prevented from launching missiles by imposing sanctions that disrupt its supply chains and by supporting Ukraine’s long-range strike campaign.
Several hours earlier, Britain had authorized missile manufacturer MBDA to share classified technical information on British-made components incorporated into SCALP missiles.
The authorization allows the Franco-British defense company to provide Ukraine with technical documentation covering UK-origin components used in the missile, paving the way for the establishment of local assembly and production capabilities.

A drone that flew in from Moldova after Russia’s overnight attack on Ukraine was found in Romania
Kyiv • UNN
Drone fragments were discovered in the village of Cișlia after Russia’s overnight attack on Ukraine. The aircraft did not carry an explosive charge; its origin is being established.
In Romania, near the border with Moldova, fragments of a drone were found that had presumably crossed the airspace of the neighboring country after a Russian attack on Ukraine. This was reported by Romania's Ministry of National Defence, writes UNN.
Details
The drone was discovered on August 24 in the yard of a house in the village of Chushlya, Vrancea County, not far from the border with Galați County. The area within a radius of 300 meters was evacuated, and specialists examined the device that had been found.
After the checks were completed, it was established that the drone did not carry an explosive charge
According to the ministry, the items found most likely belonged to a drone that entered Romanian airspace from Moldovan territory on the morning of August 24. Its exact origin and model have not yet been established.
Moldovan airspace was temporarily closed
Earlier, Moldova's Ministry of Defence reported that an unidentified drone entered the country's airspace at 05:55 from the direction of Odesa region. It was heading toward Vulcănești, and at 06:09 it left Moldova's territory in the direction of Romania.
Because of the drone's appearance, airspace in southern Moldova was restricted for approximately 15 minutes. Moldova's Ministry of Defence said that the device flew over the country's territory after Russian airstrikes on Ukraine overnight.
In Romania, after radar signals were detected, two F-16 fighter jets from the 86th Air Base in Borcea and an IAR-330 SOCAT helicopter were scrambled. At 06:12, a RO-Alert message was issued to residents of the area.
Christian Popoviciu, a representative of Romania's Ministry of Defence, said that the last radar contact with the drone was recorded at 06:37.
We cannot confirm either its origin or its model, but we are continuing the investigation, and when we have all the details, we will release the information
Residents of Galați County reported that a drone had flown over their homes. Some of them also recorded the device on video, and after the air-raid alert was announced, they saw Romanian aircraft and a helicopter taking part in the search for it.

Energy minister indicates single artificial intelligence package
The energy minister has indicated Labor will legislate minimum artificial intelligence standards and conditions for copyright, security and skills development in a single piece.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced plans to develop a national framework to bring together its response to artificial intelligence.
Chris Bowen says the federal government is looking at a "comprehensive package" for parliament.
He's confirmed the government would be looking to settle the laws despite objections from Queensland and the Northern Territory.
"Like all legislation, Commonwealth legislation which would apply across the country," Bowen says.
"The constitution is pretty clear about, if there's a dispute between Commonwealth legislation and state legislation, which legislation prevails."
Chris Bowen says he thinks Australia would be able to handle data centre demands
Energy Minister Chris Bowen has held a press conference in Perth where federal cabinet is convening today.
The minister has been asked whether he's confident Australia's energy plan can handle the demands of data centres.
Data centres are expected to draw as much power from the grid by 2036 as all homes in NSW and Victoria do today, the energy market operator has forecast.
Speaking to journalists in Perth, Bowen says he thinks Australia can handle the demands of data centres if the policy settings are correct.
"If we don't, then the answer to your question is no. But if we do, we can make sure that data centres work in the best interests of Australia and Australians," Bowen says.
"That's why we're requiring new data centres to bring their own new renewable energy, backed by gas firming. That's a sensible, commonsense approach."
He's taken a shot at the Queensland government, which has opposed federal Labor's plan to use renewables for new data centres.

South Australian Greens senator Barbara Pocock has announced she will not contest a second term at the next election in 2028.
