More than 500 diphtheria cases recorded, but experts warn real numbers likely higher
In short:
There have been 538 cases of diphtheria in 2026 across Australia as part of the largest outbreak of the disease since records began.
However public health experts warn a drop in testing means actual numbers could be higher.
What's next?
The federal government says it is delivering a $13 million package to support affected jurisdictions responding to the outbreak.
There have been almost 540 cases of diphtheria across the country so far this year, as experts caution a drop in testing could mean actual numbers of a disease once considered eliminated are much higher.
Federal and state governments continue to work to mitigate the largest outbreak of diphtheria since records began in 1991, with 538 cases recorded primarily in the Northern Territory and Western Australia, as well as in South Australia and Queensland.
That is more than 17 times the previous peak in 2022, when 31 cases were recorded.
The latest report from the Australian Centre for Disease Control (CDC) notes cases peaked between late May and early June this year, and have since declined across affected jurisdictions.
The CDC told the ABC that in the last fortnight 26 cases of diphtheria were reported, compared to almost 80 at the height of the outbreak.
However, Megan Campbell, a public health physician and medical adviser at the National Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Organisation (NACCHO), said while the lower case numbers were encouraging, testing rates had not been consistently high across affected areas.
"We're just a little bit cautious about how we interpret that data when we're hearing that testing is quite low in some parts of Australia," Dr Campbell said.
"So we do worry with that drop in numbers that part of that may be due to a lack of testing in some areas."
What is diphtheria?
Diphtheria is a highly contagious and dangerous bacterial infection that can affect the nose, throat, airways or the skin.
It is treated with antibiotics, and vaccination is considered the primary line of defence against the disease.
Diphtheria spreads through respiratory droplets from coughing or sneezing, or direct contact with infected wounds.
Most of the cases this year have spread through skin lesions, with the vast majority among Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in outer regional and remote areas.
Professor of epidemiology at Adelaide University, Adrian Esterman, said while the type of diphtheria which mainly affected the skin was generally milder, that could mean it sometimes went undetected or could be mistaken for something else.
"Unfortunately Aboriginal children and adults are prone to skin lesions, especially in crowded housing."
Loading...
He said if people had scabies or insect bites, that could increase the risk of diphtheria spreading.
Dr Campbell urged people in affected regions to remain vigilant and proactive in being tested.
"We still really want people to be coming in early for testing if they've got skin infections or skin sores or a sore throat," she said.
"Serious illness can occur from diphtheria, and the hospitalisation rate for this outbreak has been around 20 per cent … we really do want people to keep thinking about diphtheria and keep talking to their health professionals and coming in to get their vaccination."
How did this outbreak occur?
Once a leading cause of childhood deaths and historically known as the "strangling angel", diphtheria has been considered largely eliminated in Australia since the 1950s, on the back of routine vaccination use.
Governments and public health experts have attributed this outbreak to a complex cluster of factors, such as waning immunity and housing conditions.
The CDC report said a high proportion of people with diphtheria in 2026 had received at least three valid vaccine doses.
However, CDC epidemiologist Stephanie Williams said vaccine immunity wanes over time and urged people to stay up to date with vaccines and boosters.
"Whilst those antibody levels generally do decline over time, they are still providing some protection [and] when we look at the cases in this outbreak, we have seen mostly mild disease," Dr Williams said.
Experts note the outbreak has disproportionately affected people in lower socio-economic areas, where poor housing conditions and crowding have meant the disease has spread easily.
"What I'm talking about is overcrowded housing, housing that's not been designed or maintained for large families and where there's inadequate health hardware in the home," Dr Campbell said.
"So that's making sure there's enough space, enough beds and bedding, enough towels, consistent water, soap and so on so that people can maintain a healthy living situation."
Can diphtheria be eliminated again?
As the outbreak peaked in May, the federal government announced a multi-million-dollar package to build a surge workforce to administer booster vaccinations and treatments, as well as to procure additional vaccines and antibiotics.
A health department spokesperson said that package now totalled $13 million.
Professor Esterman said he believes Australia can stamp out diphtheria once again but only if meaningful improvements to Aboriginal housing are made.
"We can vaccinate until the cows come home, but it won't help unless they do something about housing and sanitation," he said.
Dr Campbell agreed improving living conditions needed to be a priority.
She said while there were "proactive partnerships" between governments and the community-controlled health sector to respond to the outbreak, more investment was needed in environmental health programs.
A Health Department spokesperson said the government's $13 million package was supporting affected jurisdictions to respond to the outbreak, and included $3 million for NACCHO to deliver community liaison and on-the-ground health supports.
A CDC spokesperson said the public health response was focusing on identifying and treating cases, tracing contacts and providing vaccination and treatment.
"Maintaining strong immunisation uptake remains the best way to prevent severe cases of diphtheria," they said.
"We encourage people in affected areas to continue to follow advice from their local public health authorities and Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Services."

How does H5N1 bird flu spread to humans and what are the health risks?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
18:37:03 UTC
03:37:03 KST

How does H5N1 bird flu spread to humans and what are the health risks?
The detection of a deadly strain of bird flu in seals in Australia may have you wondering about the risk to humans.
Although H5N1 has previously spread to mammals elsewhere in the world, the chance of people catching it is considered low by Australia's Centre for Disease Control (CDC).
Since a dominant new clade, H5N1 2.3.4.4b, emerged in Europe six years ago, there have been just 141 reported cases of H5N1 globally, including 24 deaths.
CDC director-general Zoe Wainer said bird flu was rarely transmitted from animals to people and spreading between people was also very rare.
While the current risk of being infected is low, with no human cases in Australia, scientists are studying the potential of the virus to mutate and cause a human pandemic in the future.
Raina MacIntyre, the head of the biosecurity program at the Kirby Institute, said flu viruses mutated rapidly and the H5N1 strain had already changed a lot since it emerged.
That's because the virus has been hopping around a lot of different species beyond birds.
"There's much greater opportunities for mixing between humans and infected birds or animals," Professor MacIntyre said.
So how can you catch H5N1, what are the symptoms and how can you help protect yourself if it takes hold in Australia?
How do humans get bird flu from animals?
So far, most infections have come from close contact with farm animals.
Seventy-one of the H5N1 cases in humans in the past six years have been in the US and mostly among poultry and dairy farm workers.
Only a handful of people in the US have been infected from contact with wild animals or unknown sources.
Professor MacIntyre said there were a couple of ways people could get bird flu from poultry.
"The virus can be transmitted from infected poultry by direct contact or aerosolisation of any poultry components including faeces, respiratory secretions, and contaminated dust in coops, as well," she said.
The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (US CDC) warns human infection may happen when someone touches the virus and then touches their eyes, nose or mouth.
Raw milk from infected dairy cows is also thought to be a key transmission risk if workers come into contact with contaminated milk and touch their face or it splashes their eyes.
Veterinary epidemiologist Jason Lombard, from Colorado State University, said how exactly the virus moved from cow-to-cow or to people remained unknown.
"Milk, which has the highest concentration of the virus, is believed to be a key component of disease transmission but studies evaluating transmission of disease during milking has not been able to replicate disease transmission," he said.
"Other routes of exposure, including aerosol exposure, has been documented but none of the possible modes of transmission has risen to the top as the most likely route."
Human-to-human transmission of bird flu viruses is rare.
But Professor MacIntyre said there was a report from Indonesia of this happening with a different clade of H5N1 in 2006.
"This occurred in Sumatra in a remote area, where a family cluster of eight cases occurred," she said.
"It was possibly because of the remote location that it died out."
Can you get bird flu from eggs or milk?
There have been no reported cases in the world of humans getting infected with H5N1 from consuming eggs or milk.
Australian CDC advice says it is safe to eat properly handled and cooked meat or eggs.
According to the US CDC, it could be possible to get infected by eating uncooked or undercooked poultry and eggs.
Loading...
But the watchdog also noted pasteurisation killed bacteria and viruses, including bird flu, in milk.
Although there aren't any examples of people getting bird flu from consuming eggs or milk, there is some evidence animals can be infected.
ViroEpiVet veterinary virologist and epidemiologist Robyn Hall said raw milk consumed by cats appeared to give them the virus.
"What we've seen in the US, where a lot of cats on dairies were dying, is often the virus goes to the brain in cats and there's a very high mortality in that species," she said.
What are the symptoms of bird flu in people?
Professor MacIntyre said many people in the US infected with bird flu had conjunctivitis (eye inflammation).
The Australian CDC highlighted several other symptoms, which usually start within one to 10 days of being infected, to watch out for:
- fever
- coughing
- sore throat
- runny nose
- muscle aches and pains
- headache
- fatigue
- nausea and vomiting
Diarrhoea is a less-common potential symptom.
Some people who are infected with bird flu could also be asymptomatic and show no obvious signs of infection.
How deadly is bird flu in humans?
Professor MacIntyre said the fatality rate of the 2.3.4.4b clade was much lower than other H5N1 clades in the past.
Out of the 71 cases of H5N1 in the US, there has been one death. A second US bird flu death in November was from a different strain, H5N5.
Most of the human cases in the US contracted from poultry and dairy herds have been from two different types of H5N1 2.3.4.4b known as D1.1 and B3.13.
The type of bird flu detected in Australia is known as B3.2 and entered Australia via Antarctic islands.
Are there treatments if you get bird flu?
The US CDC recommends people are treated with an antiviral drug, like baloxavir and oseltamivir, as soon as possible if they show flu symptoms after being exposed to infected birds or animals.
Antivirals are thought to work best within the first two days of symptoms and can reduce some complications from flu.
A study published in Nature Communications this year found mice infected with H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b didn't die when given a dose of baloxavir.
The researchers recommended baloxavir be considered in pandemic planning as a potential frontline therapeutic approach to treatment of humans.
Professor Wainer said Australia had access to antivirals and pandemic influenza vaccines through the National Medical Stockpile as part of preparedness planning.
What should you do about bird flu?
There are a few ways you can keep yourself safe while authorities continue to investigate.
The CDC recommends:
- Washing your hands thoroughly before and immediately after handling any bird, even if they are healthy.
- Staying away from sick or dead birds and their surroundings, droppings, body fluids, feathers and eggs.
- Not allowing pets to touch or eat sick and dead birds.
- Thoroughly cooking meat and eggs before eating.
There is currently no bird flu vaccine for the general public, but Professor MacIntyre urges people to stay up to date with their seasonal flu jab.
That's because it can reduce the chance of someone getting human and bird flus at the same time.
Could bird flu turn into a human pandemic?
The virus would need to mutate further for this bird flu outbreak to turn into a pandemic.
Professor MacIntyre said there were certain mutations in the different types of H5N1, associated with adaptation to mammals, that researchers were looking out for.
A particular mutation linked with mammal-to-mammal spread in the US is not present in the strain we know has arrived on Australian shores so far.
Loading...
The strain detected in Australia, the B3.2 genotype, is most closely related to an outbreak on Heard Island and McDonald Islands where thousands of birds and mammals, like southern elephant seals, were killed.
But this genotype, according to a pre-print study on bioRxiv, had several mutations that increased disease severity or aided virus replication in mammals.
Professor Wainer said the risk of a pandemic could increase if someone got both bird flu and seasonal human flu at the same time.
"The viruses could exchange genetic material and this may create a new strain that more easily infects humans," she said.
This is when you could get a pandemic, according to Professor MacIntyre.
"A flu pandemic, if it starts, will start quite suddenly and could start anywhere in the world," she said.
"It's not necessarily going to start in Australia."
Professor Wainer said there were currently no human cases of bird flu in Australia.
"Public health authorities are identifying and monitoring any individuals who may have had close contact with infected birds," she said.
If you find a sick or dead bird take photos or video, if possible, and report it to the Emergency Animal Disease Hotline on 1800 675 888.

Misogyny identified as biggest red flag for violent extremism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
18:34:58 UTC
03:34:58 KST

Misogynistic views are biggest red flag for violent extremism, report finds
In short:
Young men are more likely to hold hostile attitudes to women than their grandfathers' generation, according to a new survey.
The research identifies misogynistic views as a national security issue closely linked to violent extremism.
What's next:
The research recommends misogyny and anti-feminism be recognised as a form of violent extremism.
Hostile and violent attitudes toward women are the clearest warning sign of violent extremism, a study has found.
As national cabinet prepares to discuss how to combat family violence, the research identifies misogyny as not just a social issue, but a matter of national security.
The University of Melbourne survey of Australians as young as 13 found that misogyny could predict support for extremist violence "way beyond" where someone sat on the political spectrum, what religion they belonged to, or how much time they spent online.
Report author Sara Meger said the study was the first of its kind to show that misogyny was not an isolated prejudice, but a robust, cross-cutting predictor of violent extremism.
"The number one thing predicting whether or not somebody is going to hold extremist attitudes is whether they think violence against women is acceptable," Dr Meger said.
The research was funded by the Office of National Intelligence and put forward five recommendations, the first being that misogyny and anti-feminism should be recognised as a form of violent extremism in the national counter-extremism framework.
Teen boys most likely to hold hostile attitudes
Dr Meger's team surveyed 3,429 Australians about their attitudes toward women, gender roles, consent violence against women, and a range of extremist ideologies.
A significant minority of Australian men and boys shared beliefs that gender equality had gone too far, that feminism was a hate movement, that it was OK to pressure girlfriends into having sex, and that feminism should be resisted with violence if necessary.
Teenagers and young men were much more likely to express hostile views when compared with both young women, and with older men.
'Extraordinary' link between misogyny and extremism
The researchers also analysed associations between various types of extremist views.
The results revealed a consistent and robust pattern of positive associations between misogynistic attitudes and multiple indicators of extremist behaviour.
"If you take misogyny, violence against women attitudes and this idea that feminism's gone too far, if you combine them, they account for approximately 70 to 80 per cent of all the explained variants in how someone's answering the extremism questions," Dr Meger said.
"That's an extraordinary finding,"
Dr Meger's team looked at six extremist movements: incels; far-right; white supremacy; far-left; anti-feminism; and religious extremism.
Misogyny was the key ideology that cut across all of them.
"What they share is an ideology that men ought to dominate women, that transgression of the natural gender order deserves punishment and that violence in service of restoring the natural gender order is legitimate," she said.
A national security issue
Dr Meger said the findings meant intelligence agencies and police forces should take anti-feminist views into account in their work to combat violent extremism.
However, she cautioned against "securitising" misogynistic views.
"I don't think the policy solution is to try and criminalise people's beliefs and attitudes," she said. "It's more about recognising the creation of these rifts in the first place that's driving the political violence.
"And that means the solution has to be much more oriented around education and cohesion building."
The Australian Federal Police confirmed that "some individuals charged with possessing or creating violent extremist material have also had misogynistic material".
"The AFP is currently exploring how it can improve the capture of information specifically relating to gender, sexual orientation and/or identity to better inform the identification of matters arising in our work, and to support future investigations, analysis and reporting requirements," the AFP said in a statement.
The Office of National Intelligence, which funded the University of Melbourne research, did not specifically comment on the findings or whether it would take up the recommendations in its advice to government.
Lucy Nicholas, an associate professor in gender and sexuality at Western Sydney University, has completed studies on the manosphere, gendered violence and right-wing extremism.
They noted the University of Melbourne findings were in line with other research, such as their own study around misinformation.
"We found more men than women were likely to believe misinformation about gender equality, family courts and the system being against men and they were also more likely to have violence-affirming views or believe that violence can be used for a cause," Dr Nicholas said.
"We need to always realise that whilst young men might feel aggrieved, what they're aggrieved about is a loss of entitlement and privilege and that's not actually reasonable.
"We need to work with men to see that violence is not a reasonable response to the loss of that privilege and that there's other ways to manage it where they work on themselves rather than blaming."
It is about more than time spent online
Dr Meger's study also explored the level to which online environments were cultivating misogynistic and extremist attitudes.
What it found was that exposure to manfluencer content, online dating platforms and pornography were the behaviours most connected to attitudes that excused violence against women.
This was in contrast to the platforms government agencies has been focused on such as social media, gaming and online forums.
When testing if these environments drove extremism directly, they lost all predictive power.
"The online factors that the government's been really concerning themselves with, the only one that retains any independent relationship with extremism, the only online variable that still has any independent relationship with extremism, is pornography.
"And this is completely off our radar for countering violent extremism."
Dr Meger said while the research painted a picture of more hostile attitudes toward women from younger generations than might be expected, it was important to remember those views were not dominant.
"It feels dire, but some of the helpful elements that I think we can take away is that even if you just look at the tables on frequencies," she said.
"What it doesn't show is the vast majority of people responding on these attitudes questions are strongly disagreeing.
"It's a vocal minority, and they might be an influential minority that are expressing these really problematic attitudes, but most Australians don't harbour them.
"That gives me hope."

Russia’s Covert Mobilization Reaches at Least 17 Regions as Forced Recruitment Surges

- Category

Russia’s Covert Mobilization Reaches at Least 17 Regions as Forced Recruitment Surges
Reports of forced military recruitment are spreading across Russia, with residents of at least 17 regions alleging they were detained, threatened, or coerced into signing Defense Ministry contracts over the past six weeks, independent Russian outlet Verstka reported, citing several rights groups on August 24.
The complaints point to what activists describe as an expanding form of covert mobilization as Russian authorities face growing difficulties finding men willing to voluntarily join the military and fight against Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Rights organization School of the Conscript recorded complaints in July and August from Udmurtia, Primorsky Krai, the Irkutsk, Ryazan and Arkhangelsk regions, Buryatia and Russian-occupied Donetsk.
Another group helping Russians avoid military service, Get Lost, said it received 18 similar requests for assistance over the past two months. They came from locations including the Penza, Amur, Orenburg and Jewish Autonomous regions, Krasnodar and Khabarovsk krais, as well as Izhevsk, Omsk, Blagoveshchensk and Ulan-Ude.
Call to Conscience, another organization assisting people facing military recruitment, separately reported 18 complaints involving alleged forced enlistment during July and August.
Timofey Vaskin, head of the legal department at School of the Conscript, said the alleged recruitment efforts disproportionately target people who are particularly vulnerable to pressure.
“In most of the appeals we receive, people explicitly say that the victims are men from vulnerable social groups. That means people with alcohol or drug problems, mental health issues, as well as older people or those who are physically ill, live alone or have problems with the law,” Vaskin said.
Get Lost reported similar patterns and described several cases in which men were allegedly subjected to extreme pressure before being sent into military service.
In Novorossiysk, one man was reportedly taken to a police station, beaten, framed with drugs and forced to sign a military contract. In the Arkhangelsk region, another man was detained for drinking in public and subsequently sent to the front, according to the organization.
In Omsk, activists said a man was taken directly from his workplace, held against his will and eventually had a contract signed on his behalf. In Udmurtia, another man was reportedly removed from psychiatric registration before being sent to Ukraine’s Donetsk region.
Grigory Sverdlin, director of Get Lost, said Russian authorities are increasing pressure because attracting enough voluntary recruits has become increasingly difficult.
“They know who has debts, who is under investigation, who recently lost their driver’s license, and these are exactly the people they hunt,” Sverdlin said.
Previously, reports emerged that Russian authorities have introduced unofficial restrictions on foreign travel for men of mobilization age, with the practice emerging in several major cities.
The partisan movement Atesh said its agents among border service and airport employees in Moscow, St. Petersburg, and Yekaterinburg had reported an informal screening system for men seeking to leave the country.

Risks using AI in classrooms 'go beyond cheating', education expert says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
18:31:22 UTC
03:31:22 KST

How education departments across the country are cracking down on students using AI to cheat
Advances in artificial intelligence (AI) technology could have significant implications for the future of education, according to one of Australia's leading AI education experts.
A federal framework for ethical and responsible AI use was released by the Albanese government in 2023, which focused on protecting students and assisting educators.
While it was intended to set national standards for AI use, since then state education departments have adopted their own approaches in an effort to clamp down on AI-enabled cheating.
New South Wales
Recently, the New South Wales government proposed a major overhaul of the Higher School Certificate (HSC), pushing to ban unsupervised take-home assignments for year 11 and 12 students to combat AI cheating.
It was prompted by more than 1,000 recorded cheating cases in 2025 and rising concerns over AI in writing student essays.
University of Technology Sydney professor in AI and Education, Leslie Loble, said AI in learning spaces could have implications that "go beyond cheating".
"The process of learning relies on converting the working memory of new information into retained memory and knowledge.
"AI is disrupting that process and keeping us much more in surface learning, not the deep retained knowledge upon which we build understanding."
She said AI gives "short-term" boosts, keeping the user reliant on it for more answers.
"What we're seeing in the research is that we're increasing dependency, and it becomes a vicious cycle because we're not converting that information into long-term knowledge," she said.
Professor Loble said the NSW government's proposal was a step in the right direction but "we have to take the threats and risks seriously".
While warning there were a "basket of risks", Professor Loble said there was evidence that students who were falling behind in class could benefit from using AI-tools to catch up.
"For students, there is growing evidence that AI tools can be helpful for kids who are falling behind. On the other hand, there's definitely a basket of risks."
The NSW Education Standards Authority (NESA) developed a policy on the use of AI in schools in 2024, which states that unapproved use of AI in completing assignments is a breach of academic integrity.
Under that protocol, students must complete a learning unit called All My Own Work (AMOW) before they are eligible to take HSC courses and to be awarded the HSC.
South Australia
In South Australia, the approach to AI in schools stands out nationally. The SA government has embraced AI in public education rather than banning it.
They partnered with Microsoft to develop a ChatGpt-style AI tool for classrooms, called EdChat.
South Australia has rolled out 'EdChat', a large language model similar to Chat GPT or Claude, something no other state has done so far.
EdChat was delivered through a partnership with Microsoft and is branded as a custom, secure generative AI tool for public high schools.
After trialling the software, the SA government said a broader rollout would facilitate safe and productive technology use.
It was an example of how AI tools can be used to help students who need it, according to Professor Loble.
"The tool challenges the student through further questioning and providing some information but not the answer, to essentially have a much more robust approach to learning built into the tools.
"These are examples of how you can have design standards that will give us greater confidence of the technology in schools," she said.
A Department of Education spokesperson told the ABC that the state government recently announced a nation-leading royal commission into AI commencing in October this year.
"Our teachers are supported to use a range of assessment types including oral, written, multimodal and performance modes so that evidence of learning is collected in multiple ways.
"It is expected that teachers' professional judgement continues to be applied when assessing a student's work," the statement said.
Victoria
In Victoria, The Victorian Curriculum and Assessment Authority (VCAA) provides advice on how schools use AI, and sets standards for academic integrity.
Those standards state that students must submit work they have produced on their own, acknowledge the resources they used to complete it and must not plagiarise or otherwise cheat.
Individual schools are left to adjudicate on whether suspected cases of AI use have breached the VCAA standards.
A VCAA spokesperson told the ABC in a statement that the authority required work submitted for assessment to be the student's own, except where assistance was explicitly permitted and acknowledged.
"The vast majority of work students do to complete their VCE certificate is already completed under supervision in class.
"The best integrity control is our teachers — they know their students and monitor their progress as they complete take-home tasks to make sure their work is their own.
"We continue to explore ways to protect academic integrity with respect to AI," the statement said.
Professor Loble says Victoria is leading the way in screen time restrictions for primary schools.
Starting in term 1, 2027, the Victorian government has introduced strict daily screen time caps and device rules for all state primary schools.
The rules state that schools must not invite or allow families to purchase or bring their own student digital device to use at school from Prep to year 6.
It's "worth a conversation" if this should become a national standard, Professor Loble said.
"Screen time caps, age standards, should those be national standards? These are the sorts of things that ministers should be considering," she said.
Queensland
The Queensland Department of Education and the Queensland Curriculum Assessment Authority (QCAA) work together to protect the integrity of the state's Certificate of Education qualification.
The QCAA provides advice to schools about academic integrity, which includes a course on the subject that all students must complete during their senior years.
They work together to support schools and maintain the Queensland Certificate of Education qualification by supporting a balanced approach to teaching and assessment.
The Department of Education said in a statement that the QCAA provides advice to schools about academic integrity in its policy and procedures handbook and requires students to complete an academic integrity course during senior schooling.
"Digital tools, including emerging technologies such as AI, are used in the classroom where they add value to student learning. Schools continue to maintain an appropriate balance between digital and non-digital learning.
"Decisions about device use and how technology is integrated into learning and assessment are made by principals in consultation with their school communities," the statement added.
Western Australia
Western Australia has adopted the federal government's Australian Framework for Generative AI in Schools.
That was a "good place to start" but Professor Loble said there were gaps that needed to be filled to minimise risks.
In a statement sent to the ABC, the WA Department of Education said they were monitoring developments in generative AI.
"Developing an understanding of the ethical use of AI is an important part of the Western Australian Curriculum from pre-primary to year 12.
"Schools with year 11 and 12 students are required to implement a senior secondary assessment policy which provides information to those students, their parents/guardians, and teachers on authentication of student work, including cheating, collusion, plagiarism, appropriation, and unacknowledged use of artificial intelligence applications," the statement said.
Northern Territory & Tasmania
Like WA, education departments in Tasmania and the Northern Territory have adopted the federal government's framework.
The NT Council of Government School Organisations tracks AI deployment to balance equitable student access against risks such as bias and diminished human connection and has oversight.
AI use is permitted under the AI framework, but it empowers individual public schools to develop their own localised processes to meet territory expectations, according to the NT Department of Education.
The Tasmanian Department for Education, Children and Young People (DECYP) regulates AI tools via risk assessments, permitting low-risk systems like Microsoft Copilot for staff while restricting unvetted student apps, alongside managing recent safety and deepfake controversies.
A DECYP spokesperson told the ABC in a statement that AI apps and websites have been blocked for all students on DECYP devices and networks.
"The Department has policies, procedures and support resources for principals and teachers related to generative AI in schools, including an academic integrity guide," the statement said.
There are no take-home exams used as part of the end-of-year external assessment program for year 11 and 12 senior secondary courses in Tasmania.
Low-risk approaches can work to the student's benefit, but it's important not to miss out on using AI as an enhanced learning tool, Professor Loble said.
"What we are seeing now is widespread use of AI by teachers and students.
"So it's become so much more integral," she said.
Professor Loble called for consensus among state departments on AI in schools.
"Australia has taken the lead globally in setting standards in social media technology, we could certainly set standards for education technology."

Minors in Israel are being lured into criminal activities, recruited into gangs, and arrested or detained by police at an increasing rate, N12 News reported on Thursday.
"For an expensive night at a club and a hotel stay with all the luxuries, there are boys today who will be willing to cooperate and do whatever is required of them," one figure close to criminal organizations told N12.
"There are teenagers who are really excited to be close to well-known figures in criminal organizations. They want to be there. For them, being part of a criminal organization gives you a feeling that you belong to something, that you have their back, that you are no longer just a kid from the neighborhood."
According to N12, detention of minors has risen by approximately 23% each year, while indictments have risen by around 27%.
Police officers speaking to N12 said that, in many cases, adult gang members intentionally take advantage of minors' willingness to commit crimes for relatively little reward.
"Restaurants, a few thousand shekels, entertainment, vacation. There are those who would be willing to kill for a vacation in Eilat."
The advantage of taking on young gang members
This is extremely beneficial for the adult gang members, an investigator said. Younger gang members are less likely to be recognized by police, and can more easily carry out gang activity without attracting attention. If the operation goes south, the children are the ones who get caught most often, while the adults are left in the background, relatively free of police hassle.
Investigators told N12 how minors have become more aware of interrogation procedures and more difficult to get answers from.
"There used to be a perception that you would stop a child, separate him from his friends, and he would panic and tell everything," they described. "Today you can find yourself with several 14- or 15-year-old boys who know exactly what happened, and they all remain silent or tell you almost the same thing: 'I don't know, I didn't see, I didn't hear.'"
'Sophistication, silence, and lack of cooperation'
"You see a middle school student in front of you, but sometimes it feels like you are sitting in front of the head of a criminal organization," a senior investigator told N12. "The level of sophistication, the silence, the lack of cooperation. He knows what not to say; he knows not to bring his friends into the incident. He knows when to shut up. Sometimes you talk to him about a shocking act, and there is no mercy, no conscience. He doesn't even seem to understand what he did or why you are shocked by him."
Police noted that they came up against these issues while investigating the murder of 19-year-old Benayahu Razi, who was stabbed to death in a Jerusalem Airbnb in July. As a result of the investigation, two young adults and four minors aged approximately 15 to 17 were charged with murder and aggravated assault.
Maya Zanger-Shamir contributed to this report.

US removes Syria's designation as State Sponsor of Terrorism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
18:30:53 UTC
03:30:53 KST

The United States removed Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism on Monday, lifting what Damascus says was the last major impediment to investing in the country as Washington deepens ties to the new Syrian government.
The removal, posted on the US Treasury's website, took effect after a 45-day congressional review period triggered when Trump formally notified Congress on July 8 of his intention to rescind the designation.
“These actions were all taken in recognition of the positive actions taken and further commitments by the Syrian government under President Ahmed al-Sharaa to fully distance Syria from acts of international terrorism,” US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement.
Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shibani told Reuters on Saturday that the government hoped removing what he called the "last obstacle" would help reconnect Syria to the global financial and economic system and boost investment. "There is no longer any obstacle to investment, doing business and rebuilding economic life in Syria," he said.
Syria had been on the list since 1979, when Washington accused the government of former President Hafez al-Assad of supporting militant groups. The designation remained throughout the rule of his son Bashar al-Assad, who was toppled by rebels led by current President Ahmed al-Sharaa in December 2024.
Cuba, Iran, North Korea remain designated terrorist organizations
Monday's announcement also removed the designation of the Nusrah Front as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist organization, leaving Cuba, Iran, and North Korea as the three countries designated by Washington as state sponsors of terrorism.
The designation carries restrictions on US foreign assistance, defense exports and sales, certain dual-use items and financial transactions, and had remained a major deterrent for banks and investors even after Washington dismantled its broader sanctions program on Syria.
Trump's administration terminated comprehensive US sanctions on Syria in July 2025, while maintaining targeted sanctions against Assad and his associates, rights abusers, drug traffickers, Islamic State, and al Qaeda affiliates, and Iranian proxies.
The US Treasury has since said American financial institutions can provide services to Syria, process payments involving Syrian banks and establish correspondent banking relationships with them, provided sanctioned parties are not involved.
But the terrorism designation remained a source of legal and compliance risk for firms considering entering Syria, whose government is seeking billions of dollars in investment to rebuild after nearly 14 years of war.
Signs of interest had grown ahead of the removal. Syria's finance ministry said this month that Finance Minister Mohammad Yisr Barnieh held talks with Bank of America executives over potential cooperation and Syria's reintegration into the international financial system. Bank officials expressed willingness to visit Syria and continue discussions, according to the ministry.
Mastercard has gone further, announcing in May that it was working with QNB Group and Syria's central bank to prepare infrastructure for international card payments in the country. The company has described itself as an early investor in Syria and said it wants to help connect Syrian consumers and businesses to global payment networks.
US, Syria look forward to continued cooperation
Trump notified Congress of his decision after meeting Sharaa in Ankara in July, telling the Syrian president in a letter seen by Reuters that he had promised to "remove all barriers" preventing Syria from rebuilding.
The delisting also followed months of negotiations between Damascus and Washington over Syria's economic and foreign policy.
Reuters reported this month that Damascus agreed to drastically reduce imports of Russian oil during discussions with Washington over lifting the terrorism designation, according to three sources familiar with the talks.
Trump has increasingly embraced Sharaa, the former commander of al Qaeda's Nusra Front who broke ties with the global jihadist network in 2016 and led the rebel coalition that overthrew Assad.
Washington has praised cooperation by Sharaa's government against Islamic State and said easing restrictions is intended to give Syria an opportunity to stabilize, attract investment, and rebuild.
Syrian Foreign Ministry responds to change
"The Syrian Arab Republic welcomes the decision of the US to remove Syria from the list of State Sponsors of Terrorism," a statement issued by the Syrian Foreign Ministry on X/Twitter on Monday.
The Ministry affirmed the decision, saying that it "will support economic recovery, help create the conditions for reconstruction, and strengthen stability and security in Syria and the region."
"Syria hopes that further steps will follow to lift the remaining constraints that hinder its recovery and support its return to its natural and actie role in the Arab region and wider international community."
The country "looks forward to deepening strategic partnerships and broadening cooperation with the US and the ineternational community," the statement said.

Movement for Quality Government demands answers over Channel 14's Jerusalem relocation deadline
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
18:30:37 UTC
03:30:37 KST

The Movement for Quality Government in Israel on Sunday demanded that the Second Authority Council, which regulates Israel's commercial television and radio, clarify what steps it plans to take when an extension granted to Channel 14 to relocate its news operations to Jerusalem expires at the end of August.
The request was sent to the chairman of the Second Authority Council, the authority's acting director-general and its legal adviser, seeking clarification on the authority's planned response after the extension period ends.
At the center of the dispute is a provision in the Second Authority Law requiring that the headquarters of a news operation be located in Jerusalem. Under the law, a holder of a small-scale broadcasting license was granted a three-year exemption from this requirement. In Channel 14's case, the exemption period ended in February 2026.
Despite this, the Second Authority Council decided on July 7 to delay enforcement of the requirement until either the passage of the new Communications (Broadcasting) Law or the end of August 2026, whichever comes first.
The Movement for Quality Government argued that the decision effectively granted an additional extension after the statutory exemption had already expired, and said it was unclear what legal authority allowed such a move.
Dispute over enforcement of Jerusalem requirement
The Second Authority justified its decision, among other reasons, by citing progress in legislation of the new communications law, as well as the costs and complexity involved in relocating the news operation to Jerusalem. The movement, however, argued that provisions in the proposed law that could change the current situation have not yet taken effect, after their implementation was frozen as part of petitions currently being heard by the High Court of Justice.
According to the movement, as long as the existing provisions of the Second Authority Law remain in force, a future arrangement that has not yet taken effect cannot justify avoiding enforcement of the current requirements. The organization said Channel 14 continues to broadcast from Modi'in and, to the best of its knowledge, has not taken steps to move its news operation to Jerusalem.
The request follows a series of previous appeals by the Movement for Quality Government regarding the Second Authority's conduct toward Channel 14. Among other issues, the movement previously claimed that the channel had not yet submitted its 2025 revenue data, which it said was necessary to complete an examination of whether the channel remains eligible to be considered a "small-scale license holder" and continue receiving the benefits associated with that status.
The movement is now demanding that the Second Authority explain how it intends to act after the current extension ends at the end of the month. If the authority considers granting the channel another extension, the movement requested details of the legal basis for such a decision and the considerations behind it.
Movement threatens further legal action
The movement requested a unified response to all of its inquiries by August 31, 2026, and said that if no response is received by that date, it will consider further legal action, including an appeal to the relevant courts.
Attorney Yaniv Goldberg, head of the economic department at the Movement for Quality Government, said: "The law established a clear and time-limited exemption period, and it ended already in February. As long as the provisions of the existing law remain in force, the authority is obligated to enforce them."
"When this is combined with the failure to provide the revenue data required to examine Channel 14's status, there is a serious concern that the provisions of the law are not being enforced against the channel as required. The Second Authority is a regulatory body, and its role is to enforce the law equally, consistently, and in accordance with the powers granted to it by law," he added.

Israel's Project 720 brings Google, Microsoft, Amazon AI solutions to education system - feature
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
18:30:31 UTC
03:30:31 KST

Israel's Program 720, which aims to incorporate artificial intelligence into the education system, will be powered by key players in the AI world, such as Microsoft, Google, and Amazon, The Jerusalem Post learned, with the Education Ministry saying on Monday that these companies must comply with the highest security and privacy regulations.
"This process includes extensive reviews and compliance requirements covering information security, privacy protection, accessibility, and other regulatory obligations established by the ministry," Deputy Director-General and Head of the Innovation and Technology Administration at the Education Ministry, Meirav Zerbib, told the Post.
While privacy protection regulations are established by the government, one key requirement from the National AI Regulatory Sandbox initiative, which is a key aspect of the project, is that all the companies involved in this project need to offer "scalable, adaptive personalized learning capabilities," and not a solution that only offers an isolated function.
In other words, the project aims to be as personalizable as possible, with the objective of offering a unique learning experience to every Israeli student without compromising the national curricula and their learning experience.
"For the coming school year, the Program 720 includes schools from across Israel, from the north to the south, and represents the diversity of the education system, including Arab, Bedouin, Haredi, Religious Zionist, and general education schools," Zerbib added.
Israel's unique regulatory sandbox
The Post learned that the program's main selling point is this "regulatory sandbox," which allows for innovation and rapid iteration while maintaining safety and minimizing disruption to students or curricula.
While other countries like Germany have made slower progress because of heavier regulatory systems, Israel is using this agile framework to scale the project effectively.
The program had a pilot test during the 2025 school year with 28 schools and will expand to 180 schools in the next phase, with 300 interested in using it going foward.
The program moves from traditional AI solutions that focus on single situations to a wide solution that optimizes the learning experience of every student involved.
As the Post understands, the program will also change the role of teachers from only focusing on the materials to guiding every student and searching for the best academic path that they can follow given their strengths and weaknesses.
Both central, agentic AI used together
The models powering the system will work both in an agentic way, focusing on simple tasks in the day-to-day tasks, and in a central way, gathering data and creating a long-term plan for every student.
The AI agents used focus on monitoring progress, taking attendance, and updating all of the students' goals, while the system is able to adjust content, pace, and direction in real time.
The platform also works closely with people from every sector to offer personalized options that adapt to the requirements established by each community.
"The platform will be available in both Hebrew and Arabic, and in the 2026- 2027 school year we will continue our work to better understand the unique needs of each population," Zerbib told the Post. "These insights will enable us to continuously refine the platform and expand culturally and pedagogically appropriate support as the program grows."
Top-of-the-line software, hardware
"The platforms participating in the program are developed as cloud-based web applications. This architecture was chosen to support high standards of information security, system maintenance, reliability, and the ability to continuously improve and update the products," said Zerbib.
She also explained that, in the event of connection issues or hardware failure, the platform allows for limited work locally, meaning that it's not dependent on the cloud settings. "As a result, even in the event of a temporary connectivity issue, teaching and learning can continue," she said.
Nevertheless, she also pointed out that access to the platform's digital capabilities may be limited until connectivity is restored, even if the system doesn't depend on these functions.

The announcement comes almost six months into a war on Iran that has ground to a stalemate, with stalled peace talks and Tehran blocking most traffic through the crucial Strait of Hormuz.
Bessent earlier said the US was declaring an “economic D-Day” on Iran, but his announcement named no specific countries beyond Iran and no timelines.
“Around the globe, our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone,” Bessent told journalists.
“We are going to hold everyone accountable, and this is economic asphyxiation of this regime,” he said, adding that countries not joining US sanctions would “share” in Iran’s isolation.
US President Donald Trump was making phone calls to world leaders with requests to stop interactions with Tehran, Bessent said.
The Treasury Department said expanded secondary sanctions would target Iran’s digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping sectors.
It also issued new sanctions against 60 individuals, companies and vessels that allegedly aid Iran in oil revenue generation, weapons procurement and cyberoperations.
The sanctions hit entities around the world, including in the United Arab Emirates, Hong Kong, China, Singapore and Europe.
Bessent vowed that any entity “that facilitates money laundering on behalf of Iran will be removed from the US dollar system”.
Iran had been dismissive of the threat of additional sanctions, and on Aug 24, its economy minister predicted “another defeat” for Washington.
“We’ve been waiting for these plans for a long time, and the government is and was ready and has a two-year plan to manage these events,” Ali Madanizadeh said.
Decades of sanctions
Iran has weathered sanctions for decades, using complex international financial networks to evade restrictions.
Before the war, it continued to export millions of barrels of oil, mostly to China.
Asked on Aug 24 if Chinese banks would be targeted by the new sanctions, Bessent said that “no one is above the reach of US sanctions”.
Ali Vaez of the International Crisis Group said Washington was seeking to impose maximum economic pressure through various levers, but that Iran “has faced all of these before”.
“While there is little doubt in Washington’s ability to impose substantial pain, Tehran believes that it has a high threshold for absorbing it, as well as the potential to respond to financial pressure with military counter-pressure,” he said.
The US naval blockade of Iran has seen its oil exports via the Strait of Hormuz fall from two million barrels a day pre-war to just 0.4 million by mid-August, according to maritime tracker Kpler.
Underscoring the risks of transiting the strait, an oil tanker was struck by an “unknown projectile” off the coast of Oman, causing damage but no casualties, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations reported late on Aug 24.
Speaking to reporters on Aug 24, US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said the pivot to applying economic pressure did not mean that military strikes were off the table.
“Economic pressure, we know, hurts them the most right now,” he said. “But by no means are we foreclosing using kinetic strikes anywhere in the Strait of Hormuz or around Iran.”
For ordinary Iranians, the stand-off is likely to bring only more economic pain after years of rampant inflation, which in December and January fuelled massive anti-government protests.

US Postal Service issues new rule for mail ballots, but its impact on the midterms is uncertain
The U.S. Postal Service unveiled new requirements for mail ballots less than two weeks before some states begin sending them and in time for the conservative majority of the Supreme Court to clear the way for President Donald Trump’s executive order limiting the method to be used in November’s elections.
The provisions are still subject to additional legal challenges and may not go into effect in time to meet the tight deadline to change procedures for the midterm elections. They would forbid the Postal Service from sending mail ballots from any state that does not comply with Trump’s order and would require an overhaul of the envelopes containing the ballots.
Despite the high court’s initial clearance of the order, it did not decide on the constitutionality of the new regulation— only on whether the challenge was premature when Democratic-controlled states persuaded a federal judge in Boston to suspend them in June. A second ruling from the same judge would prevent the Postal Service from implementing any procedural changes before this year’s midterms and would likely need to be nullified, as well.
Time is running out for the administration to make any changes in the nation’s voting procedures. The first mail ballots are required to be sent to military and overseas voters from North Carolina on Sept. 4. At that point, it would be virtually impossible for all states to alter the formatting of their mail ballots to comply with Trump’s directive. The Postal Service rule also requires states to submit voter lists in order to get their mail ballots delivered.
The Postal Service said it could not comment on its rule given the litigation.
Lawyers from Democratic-run states and civil rights groups who sued to block the order argued that Trump doesn’t have the authority to change election regulations in states. The U.S. Constitution vests that power in the states or Congress, which has been unable to pass Trump’s desired election changes.
The Trump administration appealed to the Supreme Court last month to let it move forward with the executive order, which calls for the federal government to compile a list of eligible voters and send mail ballots only to those on the list.

Europe has become dependent on Norway as its largest supplier of natural gas since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The Scandinavian nation meets around 30 percent of gas demand in the EU and UK.
With the United States war against Iran also tightening energy markets, such consumers are starting to rethink policy.
Norway has argued to EU officials that the parts of the Barents Sea opened to oil and gas activity are ice-free, and therefore less prone to oil spills and other environmental impact.
“We would develop these areas, and then it will be up to the EU whether they should have a moratorium on buying that gas or oil,” Aasland said.
Anders Opedal, CEO of Equinor, Norway’s biggest oil firm, said oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) from the Barents Sea can be shipped anywhere in the world if rejected by the EU.
“The only thing that will suffer from this is European security. We have the flexibility,” Opedal told Reuters on the sidelines of the ONS conference.
Oslo’s approach is mirrored by the industry. French oil company Total will appoint a new exploration manager to examine new projects in Norway, CEO Patrick Pouyanne told Norwegian television.
Describing Norway as the natural energy supplier for Europe, he said Total hopes to expand its market share, as EU countries seek resources and new maritime routes closer to home in light of global trade disruptions due to the US-Israel war on Iran.

Mark Carney said on Monday that while American negotiators saw the French language in Canada as an “irritant … in Quebec, these are rights,” days after receiving widespread praise from political leaders for rejecting a US trade proposal that many perceived as weakening the country’s Francophone culture.
The prime minister’s remarks came hours after the US president, Donald Trump, showed little interest in retreating from the spat, posting on social media that Canada had been “ripping off the United States of America for years” and threatening a swath of new, economically devastating tariffs on cars and trucks.
Carney instructed his negotiators to walk away from trade talks last week. Tariffs on an array of Canadian products took effect over the weekend, affecting around 5% of Canada’s exports to the US, and Canada said it will retaliate in early September.
On Monday, Carney toured a shipyard with Quebec’s premier, telling attendees Canada “could not accept” a proposed trade deal that would have weakened French language protections after trade talks collapsed between the two countries last week, adding that his government “will not give what they have asked”.
The prime minister’s decision to abandon trade talks with the US spurred declarations from political leaders and pundits in Canada that the country is now fully locked into an economic war with its longtime ally.
Quebec, Canada’s predominantly French-speaking province, has long sought to protect its distinct identity, at times with laws that clashed with the federal government and the Canadian charter of rights and freedoms.
In recent years those rules have also frustrated US negotiators, who have framed them as trade irritants. Bill 96, for example, requires products sold in Quebec to have a French description and for trademarks using generic terms to be translated into French, while Bill 109 compels media services such as Netflix, Spotify and Apple to promote and prioritize French content for Quebec users.
Quebec’s premier, Christine Fréchette, said Carney had made the right decision in walking away from talks that looked to cross a “red line” for Francophones.
“Our culture, our language is central to our identity and it is important to exclude that from the negotiation table,” she told reporters over the weekend. “It’s something that is crucial for us and it won’t change, even though we are threatened with different tariffs, it won’t change. We will stay the way we are.”
Polling from earlier in the month shows that dislike for Trump is highest in Quebec. Separatists in the province have seen a sharp decline in support amid the economic wounds inflicted by the US.
Last week, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, the sovereigntist politician most likely to emerge victorious in upcoming provincial elections, said his party would delay a possible referendum into seceding from Canada until Trump is out of office. He wrote that deciding Quebec’s political fate “must not be hijacked by the upheaval of American politics, the outbursts of an unpredictable president or by a campaign of fear”.
The Quebec Federation of Chambers of Commerce (FCCQ) called the tariffs a “worst-case scenario” for the province’s businesses.
“Quebec, in fact, has been the most affected by these tariffs since the very beginning of this trade war,” Fréchette said. “In all our regions, businesses risk losing contracts. In fact, it has already begun.”
On Monday, Trump’s top trade representative, Jamieson Greer, called reports that French language protections were up for debate a “a funny fake story”.
“That is not true,” Greer told CNBC. “I like the Quebecois and I like that they speak French.” He said both he and his sons speak the language.
He claimed the issue at stake was that Americans did not like Canada “forcing” streaming giants in the US to pay some of their profits to support Canadian content. Canada had already dropped that position, however, previously abandoning elements of digital services tax.
“I understand why the Quebecois want to have French language content. We think that’s a really valuable thing and we encourage countries to really put their own country first and put their national identity first.”
Carney rejected that framing, telling reporters it was not “funny” and there was an “enormous spread” in perspectives.
Also on Monday, Trump redoubled his efforts to wage economic war against his country’s longtime political, security and economic ally.
“Canada has been ripping off the United States of America for years,” Trump wrote on social media. Criticizing Canada’s “ridiculously high tariffs” on American farmers, Trump wrote: “Not sustainable, and not anymore!”
The president, who faces mounting domestic unease over his trade spat with Canada, pledged to increase tariffs on cars, trucks, auto parts and steel beginning on 1 January . “We don’t need Canada, they need us!” he wrote, using capital letters.
The move has provoked an increasingly predictable backlash from political leaders.
The Conservative premier of Ontario, Doug Ford, told local media Trump can “kiss my ass”.
“We need to throw everything in the kitchen sink at him. He’s arrogant, he’s cocky, and you know, as Ronald Reagan said, if you come to a draw with a bully, what stops that bully from coming after you the next day and the next day. And that’s all Donald Trump is – is a bully,” said Ford. “Well, he’s going to have a rude awakening.”

“The Perm oil refinery, Russia's seventh-largest oil processing plant by volumes, stopped operations following a Ukrainian drone attack, which caused fire and damage to technological units on August 21,” two industry sources said on Sunday.
According to the sources, the refinery’s main CDU-4 crude distillation unit, which accounts for nearly 40% of the plant’s capacity, was shut down on August 21. The unit can process 14,000 metric tons of crude oil per day.

Another primary crude processing unit, CDU-5, which accounts for 34% of the refinery’s capacity, has been offline since a July 29 drone attack, the sources said.

Teachers Union chief urges reforms as Israel faces growing educator shortage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
18:13:39 UTC
03:13:39 KST

Teachers Union Secretary-General Yaffa Ben-David spoke on 103FM ahead of the start of the school year on Sunday, discussing the state of Israel’s education system and the growing shortage of teachers.
"According to our estimates, the system is currently short by nearly 5,000 teachers," Ben-David noted. "If we do not develop a strategic plan and continue to rely on slogans, we will see more people leaving the profession."
She questioned, "Where will we find new teachers? First and foremost, we need to transform the education system into a place where people want to work."
Ben-David noted that the teacher shortage reflects a broader global trend but urged that urgent attention is needed for Israel’s education system.
Loss of 'a sense of mission' in teachers
“In the past, people joined the teaching profession out of a sense of mission and trained to be educators. Today, however, it’s different, and this issue is widespread. You can see it in almost every country. It’s not just in teaching, but across various workplaces. Education is the heart of the State of Israel, and we need to direct our best and most qualified individuals to it.”
“If we do not address the deep-rooted problems, the situation will only worsen,” Ben-David warned.
Ben-David also stressed the need to tackle issues such as violence, the special education law, and the support, trust, and authority granted to principals and teaching teams in the system.
“Inclusion is a valuable, important, and moral objective, but the key is how we implement it.” She said.
She also addressed the issue of special education, stating, “The solution is not simply to legislate a law, and this is the biggest mistake we have warned against. Whoever introduced the law only considered the immediate small issue, which cannot address something so substantial and important, and it caused the system to collapse.”
The issue of ‘parental interference’
Ben-David also discussed the issue of ‘parental interference’ in education circles. “We issued a new, historic director-general's circular regarding the conduct between parents and education staff. Parents need to understand one thing: if you want quality educators to stay, you must give them the respect and treatment they deserve. They know what is best for the children.”
“The lack of training, where untrained individuals were brought in to fill the shortage, is problematic in itself.” She said, turning back to the issue of staff shortages.
“However, there are many excellent principals, kindergarten teachers, and educators who are trained and part of the system but receive disrespectful treatment from parents. Staff members' time is valuable, and just as every person has working hours and private time, so should teachers.”
Regarding overcrowded classrooms and the burden placed on educators, she remarked, “This situation is not normal, and it has persisted because we have been warning about it for decades. We said there would be issues within the system in kindergartens and schools, and many dismissed our concerns.”
“It is important to understand that salary is crucial, but on its own it will not resolve the teacher shortage. We need to provide fair salaries, status, and working conditions. Compared to OECD countries, we have many teaching hours in crowded classrooms and kindergartens. How can we expect better results? Teachers are not magicians,” according to Ben-David.
“I have to ask, where are the parents? Where is their leadership? All day, your leadership only responds to what I say. Why don’t you, as the parents’ leadership, take a stand and advocate for reducing the number of students in kindergartens?” she criticized.
'The Finance Ministry has no understanding of education'
Regarding the need for a council to coordinate efforts within the education system, she stated, “I can identify the real and pressing issues in the education system, including the central problem that there is no strategic plan. I support establishing a national public council for the education system, which would include professors from academia, field professionals, and representatives from teachers’ organizations, to prepare a strategic plan that will not depend on one minister or another.”
“I am committed to fighting for this cause, and it is essential to keep the public education system under state control. There are several systems that should remain with the state, and the education system is at the top of that list. We cannot shift responsibility onto someone else and replace one authority with another,” she added.
“Since when has the Finance Ministry been the one determining education policy?” Ben-David questioned. “ Where have we ended up? Let them focus on the real problems facing the country. They have no understanding of education; it is a paradox.”
“Since 2022, there has been an agreement, and personal contracts are not the solution to the teacher shortage. We need to address the real issues deeply, not seek cosmetic solutions,” she said.
In closing, Ben-David encouraged education teams and students excited to start the school year to welcome everyone with love and dedication.

Saudi Arabia to invest €6 billion in theme parks near Paris, Macron says
France and Saudi Arabia on Monday signed an agreement for the oil-rich Gulf kingdom to invest €6 billion to create three amusement parks near Paris, including one likely to be a manga-themed park, the French presidential office said. The announcement came during Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's visit focused on bilateral deals and the current crisis in the Middle East.

France and Saudi Arabia on Monday signed a memorandum of understanding for a €6 billion ($7 billion) Saudi investment to create three theme parks near Paris, including one likely to be manga-themed, the office of the French president said.
The French presidency's Élysée presidential palace said the agreement for the "colossal" project was signed during a two-day visit to France by Saudi Arabia's de facto ruler, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.
The investment will see the construction of three theme parks near Cergy-Pontoise, some 30 kilometres northwest of Paris, it said.
French President Emmanuel Macron on X hailed the "unprecedented announcement", saying the attractions would be a "new global destination".
The project will be led by Qiddiya investment firm, a subsidiary of Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund.
The parks are expected to create some 22,000 direct jobs, compared with around 20,000 generated by Disneyland Paris, according to the presidency.
The project "stemmed from a discussion between the President of the Republic and the Crown Prince in December 2024" in Riyadh, when they discovered their "shared passion" for manga, "and in particular Dragon Ball Z", an adviser to Macron told reporters.
Reports had emerged over the summer of plans for a park dedicated to the iconic Japanese franchise in the Val-d'Oise region, though no official confirmation was given.
Macron's office confirmed that one park is expected to be manga-themed.
The themes of the other two have yet to be disclosed.
The parks will be built and opened in stages, with construction expected to take several years, the Élysée said, without giving an opening date.
Asked about entrusting such a project to Riyadh despite criticism of its human rights record, his office said: "At no point, when we attract a project, do we seek to lecture others."
'Provocation'
France is keen to emphasise that the crown prince rarely leaves his home country other than for international summits and his trip to France was the first such for almost a year.
"The fact that he chose France for this visit is an important signal and testifies to the depth and dynamism of the Franco-Saudi relationship," said the French presidential official.
But three journalists' unions on Sunday protested against France hosting the Saudi strongman, who is known by his initials "MBS".
In a joint statement, the SNJ-CGT, CFDT-Journalistes and SGJ-FO unions noted that there was a live French investigation for torture and forced disappearance after a complaint lodged in 2021 over the killing of the journalist Jamal Khashoggi.
Read moreRebranded Saudi crown prince meets Macron as rights groups decry ‘hypocrisy’
Khashoggi, a Saudi with US residency who was a critic of the Saudi ruling family, was murdered in Saudi Arabia's consulate in Istanbul in 2018. His body, cut up, was never recovered.
US intelligence concluded that MBS was directly involved in Khashoggi's killing, and a UN investigation described the journalist's death as an "extrajudicial killing for which Saudi Arabia is responsible".
The unions said the visit, following a previous one hosted by Macron in July 2022, "looks like a provocation for defenders of media freedom and freedom of expression".
In December 2021, Macron became one of the first Western leaders to meet the prince in Saudi Arabia in the wake of the Khashoggi killing. The Saudi crown prince has made multiple visits to France since then.
Saudi Arabia is also set to host a string of key global events, notably the Expo 2030 and above all the football World Cup in 2034.
Saudi Arabia, a close US ally which has a history of tensions with Iran, is also closely watching developments in the Islamic republic in the wake of the US-Israeli war.

wittman estes revisits le corbusier’s ‘minimum cell’ with floating pacific northwest cabin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
18:10:48 UTC
03:10:48 KST

wittman estes revisits le corbusier’s idea of the minimum cell
On Washington’s Blakely Island, Wittman Estes has built a 400-square-foot guest house around an architectural question that goes back much further than the current tiny-house boom. The studio cites Thoreau’s Walden Cabin alongside Le Corbusier’s Cabanon, the compact retreat completed at Roquebrune-Cap-Martin in 1952. The latter offers the more specific design lineage.
Fondation Le Corbusier describes the 15-square-meter Cabanon as an ‘archetype of the minimum cell,’ a tiny timber interior developed according to the proportions of the Modulor and compressed around the essentials of a summer retreat.
Wittman Estes takes that interest in compression into the forests of the Salish Sea, where its Blakely Island Cabin occupies a 16-by-20-foot footprint between a large glacial erratic and a mature Douglas fir. Inside, a Murphy bed folds into the main room. The kitchen slips beneath a 115-square-foot loft with two bunks, while the bathroom occupies the northwest corner with a glass-to-glass window facing the trees. All together, the main level and loft bring the guest house on stilts to 400 square feet.
The Blakely Cabin replaces an earlier shack on the site, and the architects at Wittman Estes use its footprint while lifting the new structure above the steep terrain on slender supports. A suspended metal walkway threads through the woods from the uphill side, reaching the cabin at grade before the ground falls away beneath it. The glacial boulder sits just inches from the building, close enough to enter the view from the living room, while the elevated floor leaves much of the rocky terrain below exposed.
Le Corbusier gave the Cabanon two small windows, one facing the Mediterranean and another framing an old carob tree. Wittman Estes approaches the edge of its own minimum interior from another direction. Large sliding glass doors open the main room toward Thatcher Bay and onto a cantilevered terrace, so the 400-square-foot plan borrows much of its sense of space from everything beyond its walls. The Murphy bed faces east toward the morning light, and the same floor decking continues through the glass toward the exterior.
Wittman Estes sites the 400-square-foot cabin between a glacial erratic and mature Douglas fir
prefabrication connects two very different cabins
The Cabanon reference becomes more interesting again in the way the cabin was made. Le Corbusier had the wooden components of his retreat prefabricated by Corsican carpenter Charles Barberis in Ajaccio before they were assembled at Cap Martin.
For Blakely Island, access posed another version of the same logistical problem. Heavy construction equipment was difficult to bring onto the remote shoreline, so much of the new cabin was fabricated at the contractor’s yard in Everett before traveling across the water by barge.
Grid-organized steel frames support the wood volume and land on a minimal point foundation. Around them, Western red cedar milled from trees on Blakely Island forms the exterior cladding and is intended to weather with exposure. Birch plywood warms the walls inside, where fir beams remain visible overhead. At the center of the main room, a suspended black fireplace rotates 360 degrees so it can face the interior or turn toward the terrace when the doors are open.
slender supports lift the compact timber volume above the steep rocky terrain
from the cabanon to a floating forest room
Seasonal changes alter the cabin far more dramatically than its compact footprint might suggest. During warmer months, the glazed wall can slide away and turn the terrace into an extension of the room. Colder weather closes the volume around the fireplace while keeping long views through the glass toward the water and surrounding forest. The architecture stays deliberately small through both conditions, with furniture, storage, and sleeping space working within the same limited envelope.
The connection to Le Corbusier ultimately feels strongest as an investigation of sufficiency instead of an exercise in formal resemblance. The Cabanon compressed inhabitation through dimensions derived from the human body; Wittman Estes gives its contemporary version a little more room, then uses folding furniture and openings toward the landscape to stretch that space perceptually. Seventy-four years after Le Corbusier’s 1952 retreat, the ‘minimum cell’ remains a productive starting point. On Blakely Island, its walls simply open much wider.

a Murphy bed allows the central living space to shift between sleeping and gathering
